citations.quote: Fix four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, an inertial length-coordinate chart $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$, $x^0=ct$, and coordinates measured in metres, as specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Write $\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$. The mass-shell parameter $\mu\ge0$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same unit. For a massive species, $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c/\hbar$; $\mu=0$ is the separately admitted massless branch of the mathematical free-field construction. Thus $\hbar c\omega_\mu$ is physical energy and $\hbar\mathbf k$ is physical momentum. The natural-unit action is written $S/\hbar$. The scalar one-particle space is $\mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C)$, where $H_\mu^+=\{(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3,\ \omega_\mu(\mathbf k)>0\}$ and $d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))$; at $\mu=0$ the measure-zero apex $\mathbf k=0$ is omitted. These are the shell conventions of [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. For a smooth real classical scalar $\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$ with the canonical free-field length degree $-1$, adopt $$\frac{S_\phi}{\hbar}=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi_{\mathrm n}\partial_b\phi_{\mathrm n}+\mu^2\phi_{\mathrm n}^2\right)\,d^4x.$$ For a smooth commuting classical Dirac spinor $\psi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$ with canonical free-field length degree $-3/2$, put $\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}=\psi_{\mathrm n}^\dagger\beta$ and use the Clifford convention $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ from [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Adopt $$\frac{S_D}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}\,d^4x.$$ The smooth classical variables in these functionals commute; no Grassmann algebra or path-integral construction is being adopted. These formulas specify local action densities: for arbitrary smooth global fields the total integrals need not converge. Only compactly supported variations are used; the action difference under such a variation is an integral over a compact set and is finite for smooth fields. With these variations on the fixed background, the intended Euler–Lagrange equations are $(\Box-\mu^2)\phi_{\mathrm n}=0$ and $(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}=0$, conditional on the exact mathematical supplier recorded as [L1] below. As the physical interpretation of this selected free model, assign the real scalar species to the bosonic symmetric Fock representation and assign the Dirac field to the particle/antiparticle CAR representation on $\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. Choose the zero-particle Fock vectors as the scalar and Dirac vacuum states. This is an adopted species and statistics assignment. The CCR/CAR and operator properties of the specified representations are mathematical model consequences; they do not prove a general spin-statistics theorem or establish that nature realizes this model. The scalar construction is the Schwartz-smeared field $\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ on the finite-particle domain, with the future-shell phase $p\circ x=\omega_\mu x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$, exactly as in [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. The Dirac construction is the bounded spacetime-smeared CAR field of [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]], using the positive and negative projections of the specified free Dirac matrix. In that carrier, $\mathcal H_D=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3;\mathbb C^4)$, $h_D(\mathbf k)=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf k+\beta\mu$, and $P_\pm(\mathbf k)=(I_4\pm h_D(\mathbf k)/\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))/2$; the particle and antiparticle one-particle spaces are the closed ranges $\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. These carriers state their mathematical hypotheses and construction domains; their draft status is not an independent physics or proof approval. Tong's lecture notes and Srednicki's book draft provide independent presentations of the scalar and Dirac free-field formulations. Their formal mode notation supplies context for this adoption, not a proof of the operator-domain claims and not evidence that the adopted model describes nature.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let $H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form $\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ $$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$ This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is $\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$. Thus its Weyl unitary is $W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$, $$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$ For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is $$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$ Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and two-point function $$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$ which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields. The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is $$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$ understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance. For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ and for the bounded Weyl operators. For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector $(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions. No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice. For $\mu\ge0$, define the tempered distribution
$$\Delta_\mu(t,\mathbf x)= \int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3} \frac{\sin(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)t)}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)} e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x},$$
with the massless integrand defined off $\mathbf k=0$; its $1/|\mathbf k|$
behavior is locally integrable in three dimensions. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\Delta_\mu \subseteq\{(t,\mathbf x):t^2-|\mathbf x|^2\ge0\},$$
the closed causal cone for the $(-+++)$ metric. For real compactly supported
smooth $f,g$, put
$$\Delta_\mu(f,g)= \int_{\mathbb R^4}\!\int_{\mathbb R^4} f(x)g(y)\Delta_\mu(x-y)\,d^4x\,d^4y.$$
On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the smeared fields of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] satisfy
$$[\Phi_\mu(f),\Phi_\mu(g)]=-i\Delta_\mu(f,g)I.$$
Consequently spacelike-separated supports give commuting fields.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let $\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put $H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating [[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$, $s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set $$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$ For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate $s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain $$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$ Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a graph core. The joint projection-valued measure [[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is $$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$ For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$ by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then $$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$ is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is $iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint value $0$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open. For real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O)$ define
$$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2K_\mu f),$$
where the Segal normalization is exactly
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2$ on the finite-particle
domain, as in [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. This scale makes the generator
of $t\mapsto W_\mu(tf)$ equal to the real scalar field
$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. Define the unital norm-closed operator
algebra
$$\mathfrak A_\mu(O)= \overline{\operatorname{alg}}^{\|\cdot\|} \{I,W_\mu(f),W_\mu(f)^*:f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)\}.$$
Then $O_1\subseteq O_2$ implies
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)\subseteq\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. If every difference
$x-y$, with $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$, is spacelike, then every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)$ commutes with every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. These are algebraic properties of the constructed
representation; they are not empirical signaling or measurement claims.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

derivations.claim: The adopted scalar field is the defined complex-linear operator map on the common finite-particle domain.
The shell Fourier restriction annihilates the Klein–Gordon test operator, so both field coefficients vanish.
Vacuum covariance and positivity, Poincare covariance, and invariant vacuum follow from the inspected scalar carrier.
Causal support makes spacelike field commutators zero, and norm closure preserves Weyl-algebra commutation and isotony.
The sector-sum multiplier yields the exact self-adjoint Hamiltonian domain and the joint forward-cone spectrum.
The vacuum is the unique zero-energy vector; the massive threshold is hbar c mu and the massless positive spectrum has no gap.

citations.quote: Fix four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, an inertial length-coordinate chart $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$, $x^0=ct$, and coordinates measured in metres, as specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Write $\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$. The mass-shell parameter $\mu\ge0$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same unit. For a massive species, $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c/\hbar$; $\mu=0$ is the separately admitted massless branch of the mathematical free-field construction. Thus $\hbar c\omega_\mu$ is physical energy and $\hbar\mathbf k$ is physical momentum. The natural-unit action is written $S/\hbar$. The scalar one-particle space is $\mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C)$, where $H_\mu^+=\{(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3,\ \omega_\mu(\mathbf k)>0\}$ and $d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))$; at $\mu=0$ the measure-zero apex $\mathbf k=0$ is omitted. These are the shell conventions of [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. For a smooth real classical scalar $\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$ with the canonical free-field length degree $-1$, adopt $$\frac{S_\phi}{\hbar}=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi_{\mathrm n}\partial_b\phi_{\mathrm n}+\mu^2\phi_{\mathrm n}^2\right)\,d^4x.$$ For a smooth commuting classical Dirac spinor $\psi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$ with canonical free-field length degree $-3/2$, put $\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}=\psi_{\mathrm n}^\dagger\beta$ and use the Clifford convention $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ from [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Adopt $$\frac{S_D}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}\,d^4x.$$ The smooth classical variables in these functionals commute; no Grassmann algebra or path-integral construction is being adopted. These formulas specify local action densities: for arbitrary smooth global fields the total integrals need not converge. Only compactly supported variations are used; the action difference under such a variation is an integral over a compact set and is finite for smooth fields. With these variations on the fixed background, the intended Euler–Lagrange equations are $(\Box-\mu^2)\phi_{\mathrm n}=0$ and $(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}=0$, conditional on the exact mathematical supplier recorded as [L1] below. As the physical interpretation of this selected free model, assign the real scalar species to the bosonic symmetric Fock representation and assign the Dirac field to the particle/antiparticle CAR representation on $\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. Choose the zero-particle Fock vectors as the scalar and Dirac vacuum states. This is an adopted species and statistics assignment. The CCR/CAR and operator properties of the specified representations are mathematical model consequences; they do not prove a general spin-statistics theorem or establish that nature realizes this model. The scalar construction is the Schwartz-smeared field $\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ on the finite-particle domain, with the future-shell phase $p\circ x=\omega_\mu x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$, exactly as in [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. The Dirac construction is the bounded spacetime-smeared CAR field of [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]], using the positive and negative projections of the specified free Dirac matrix. In that carrier, $\mathcal H_D=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3;\mathbb C^4)$, $h_D(\mathbf k)=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf k+\beta\mu$, and $P_\pm(\mathbf k)=(I_4\pm h_D(\mathbf k)/\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))/2$; the particle and antiparticle one-particle spaces are the closed ranges $\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. These carriers state their mathematical hypotheses and construction domains; their draft status is not an independent physics or proof approval. Tong's lecture notes and Srednicki's book draft provide independent presentations of the scalar and Dirac free-field formulations. Their formal mode notation supplies context for this adoption, not a proof of the operator-domain claims and not evidence that the adopted model describes nature.

The Fock pairing is linear in its second variable. Creation $a^\dagger(h)$ is linear in $h$, while annihilation $a(h)$ is conjugate-linear in $h$. A smeared field is a domain-qualified operator-valued distribution; the item introduces no pointwise operator $\Phi_\mu(x)$. u_\mu^n<\inftyight\}.$$ The physical Hamiltonian of this selected model is the vacuum-subtracted self-adjoint operator $H_\mu^{\mathrm{phys}}=\hbar c\,d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu)$ on that domain, as defined by the multiplier construction of [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. It has units of joules and $H_\mu^{\mathrm{phys}}\Omega=0$. No infinite zero-point-energy sum is part of this definition. Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let $H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form $\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ $$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$ This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is $\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$. Thus its Weyl unitary is $W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$, $$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$ For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is $$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$ Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and two-point function $$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$ which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing rule. The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is $$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$ understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance. For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ and for the bounded Weyl operators. If $r=\|h\|$, $e=h/r$, $K=e^\perp$, $G=\mathcal F_s(K)$, choose a countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $G$ whose vectors are finite-particle, and use the one-mode splitting of [[lem-qft-fock-one-mode-splitting]] followed by the Hermite unitary $|n\rangle\mapsto g_n$ into $L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int\overline f g$ to write a vector as $(f_j)_{j\in J}\in\ell^2(J;L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C))$. There are unitaries $W(h)$ determined on these total exponential vectors by $$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$ They obey $$W(h)W(k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{2}\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle_2\right)W(h+k),\qquad \langle\Omega,W(h)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|h\|^2/4},$$ and $h\mapsto W(h)$ is strongly continuous. Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim is included.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$ is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable $f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$ Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this property.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]). 1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$ both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$. 2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. **The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When $\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression $|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]] leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$ and write $$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$ Let $$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$ This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then $(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and $$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$ is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in $\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]. Define $$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$ The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let $$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$ and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set ([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then: (a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$, $$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$ the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle; (b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$; (c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in C$. Openness of $C$ and continuity of $\lambda\mapsto\lambda x$ give an open interval $K_x\subset(0,\infty)$ around $1$ with $\lambda x\in C$ for $\lambda\in K_x$. Define $g:K_x\to\mathbb R$ by $g(\lambda)=f(\lambda x)$. By [F1], $g'(1)=Df(x)[x]$. This ambient derivative exists even if $1$ is an endpoint of the interval $J_x$ on which homogeneity is assumed.

Since $J_x$ is a nondegenerate interval containing $1$, it contains points $\lambda\ne1$ arbitrarily close to $1$, also lying in $K_x$. For these points, homogeneity and $g(1)=f(x)$ give $(g(\lambda)-g(1))/(\lambda-1)=f(x)$. The ambient derivative in step 1.1 exists, so its limit along this possibly one-sided set is $g'(1)=f(x)$. Therefore $f(x)=Df(x)[x]$, and writing the total derivative in Euclidean coordinates gives $Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\partial_j f(x)$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Suppose that for every $x\in C$ there is a nondegenerate interval $J_x\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $1$ such that $\lambda x\in C$ and $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda\in J_x$. Here nondegenerate means that $J_x$ contains a point different from $1$; $1$ may be an endpoint. Then

$$f(x)=Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\,\partial_j f(x)\qquad(x\in C).$$

The radial identity need only hold on one side of $1$: openness of $C$ and $C^1$ regularity supply an ambient derivative, and the interval makes $1$ a nonisolated point at which that derivative is determined by the radial identity. This uses the same function on the same domain; it asserts nothing about a family of functions on different tagged domains.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: The inverse identity gives $D_u f(g(x,z),z)=x$. By [F1], differentiating the composition in $\widehat f$ gives $d[f(g(x,z),z)]=x\cdot dg+D_z f(g(x,z),z)\cdot dz$.

Apply [F3] componentwise to the finite scalar products in $x\cdot g$ to obtain $d[x\cdot g]=g\cdot dx+x\cdot dg$. Subtracting this from step 1.1 cancels the $x\cdot dg$ terms and yields the stated differential.

The coefficient functions $g$ and $D_zf(g,z)$ are $C^1$, since $g$ is $C^1$, $f$ is $C^2$, and [F1] applies to their compositions. The first partial derivatives of $\widehat f$ are therefore $C^1$, so $\widehat f$ is $C^2$.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

Let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R^m$ be open with $k,m\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose the map $(u,z)\mapsto(x,z):=(D_u f(u,z),z)$ restricts to a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open neighborhoods, with inverse $(x,z)\mapsto(g(x,z),z)$. Define

$$\widehat f(x,z):=f(g(x,z),z)-x\cdot g(x,z).$$

Then $\widehat f$ is $C^2$ and

$$d\widehat f=-g\cdot dx+D_z f(g(x,z),z)\cdot dz.$$

This is a local statement. Existence of the inverse chart is a hypothesis; the lemma asserts no global inverse or boundary transform.

Apply [F3] to the $V$ transform with conjugate coordinate $-p=U_V$ and to the $s$ transform with conjugate coordinate $T=U_s$. With the signs fixed in [F2], this gives $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$ and $dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$.

citations.quote:
In addition to the general tagged bulk family of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and its entropy law in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], designate a common-constitutive-law bulk branch as follows. Fix a material constitution $c$ with an ordered species list and fixed intensive constitutive parameters. Let $C\subseteq D_c$ be a nonempty open single-phase chart in the fixed dimensionless SI numerical coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]], and assume it is a positive cone: $\lambda x\in C$ for all $x\in C$ and $\lambda>0$. Use the adopted $C^2$ entropy with $S_{c,U}>0$ on this chart.

For every $\lambda>0$, admit scaling of every $x\in C$, so $C\subseteq B_{c,\lambda}$, and retain the distinct scaled-system tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. The image $C^{(\lambda)}:=\delta_\lambda(C)$ is a chart in $D_{c^{(\lambda)}}$. Adopt a coordinate-preserving material-law transport $j_{c,\lambda}:C^{(\lambda)}\to C$ defined in numerical coordinates by $j_{c,\lambda}(y)=y$, and adopt entropy preservation under that transport:

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(y)=S_c(j_{c,\lambda}(y))\qquad(y\in C^{(\lambda)}).$$

The transport identifies the constitutive numerical law used for bodies in this branch; it does not equate their physical identities or material tags. It presumes a common ordered species list, units, internal-energy reference and entropy calibration. Fixed material parameters in this branch exclude a hidden size parameter whose independent variation changes the law. Combined with the existing tagged entropy law, this adopted transport gives the same-function relation

$$S_c(\lambda x)=S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x)\qquad(x\in C,\ \lambda>0).$$

This is additional idealized constitutive information for the designated bulk branch. It is not implied by coordinate additivity, SI units, the general tagged relation, or the existence of local equilibrium charts. No empirical proof, finite-size error bound, or assertion for surface-sensitive, interacting long-range or self-gravitating bodies is supplied. Euler and Gibbs–Duhem identities are conditional deductions on this branch, not part of the postulate's source review.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two named subsystems with disjoint physical regions as in [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]], combined as a compound system $A\sqcup B$ inside a declared outer boundary. The model's admitted separated pairs form a specified subset $\mathcal C_{AB}\subseteq D_A\times D_B$ using [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]] and [[def-cartesian-product]]. For every pair $(x_A,x_B)\in\mathcal C_{AB}$, the composition map $\kappa_{AB}:\mathcal C_{AB}\to D_{A\sqcup B}$ is a function ([[def-function-space]]) adopted so the dimensioned coordinates of its output satisfy
$$U_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=U_A(x_A)+U_B(x_B),\qquad V_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=V_A(x_A)+V_B(x_B),\qquad n_{A\sqcup B,j}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=n_{A,j}(x_A)+n_{B,j}(x_B).$$
Here each coordinate function is the dimensioned map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] for its material constitution, with SI units as in [[def-td-si-quantities]].

Here “extensive coordinates” means precisely the named coordinates declared additive by this postulate. Amount coordinates are aligned by species label; when a species is absent from one subsystem, its zero amount is in a separately declared composition boundary, not the positive-mole chart of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This is an idealized composition rule: cross-interface and long-range interaction energy is omitted from $U_{A\sqcup B}$, rather than asserted to vanish in nature. The postulate does not assert that every pair of subsystem states is physically admissible.

The framework's bulk family is a tagged family of material types. For each dimensionless scale $\lambda>0$ the model may designate a tag $c^{(\lambda)}$ and a subset $B_{c,\lambda}\subseteq D_c$ of states admitting a scaled copy, with inclusion as in [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in B_{c,\lambda}$, the scaling map is the function $\delta_\lambda:B_{c,\lambda}\to D_{c^{(\lambda)}}$ ([[def-function-space]]) given by $\delta_\lambda(x)=(\lambda\hat U,\lambda\hat V,\lambda\hat n_1,\ldots,\lambda\hat n_r)$. The tag matters: $c^{(\lambda)}$ is not silently identified with $c$. This postulate specifies the coordinate scaling model and energy additivity only; it does not postulate entropy additivity or exact scaling for every finite physical body.

This is an adopted physical composition rule, not a deduction from SI units or from the mathematics of Cartesian products.

For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

Let $c$ be a material constitution with $r$ named species, and let $O\subseteq D_c$ be an open dimensionless single-phase subset from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Its physical SI chart is $\Omega=\Phi_c(O)$ under the diagonal unit map $\Phi_c$ defined in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Let $(U_0,V_0,n_{0,1},\ldots,n_{0,r})\in\Omega$, with $U$ in joules, $V>0$ in cubic metres, and each $n_j>0$ in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). On $\Omega$, write $S_c(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representative $S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}$; its physical-coordinate partials include the unit factors as specified in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Assume this representative is $C^2$ and $S_{c,U}(U_0,V_0,n_0)>0$. Then there are open neighborhoods of $(S_c(U_0,V_0,n_0),V_0,n_0)$ and $(U_0,V_0,n_0)$ on which the equation

$$S_c(U,V,n)=s$$

has a unique solution $U=\mathcal U_c(s,V,n)$ of class $C^2$. On this local chart,

$$\mathcal U_{c,s}=T_c,\qquad \mathcal U_{c,V}=-p_c,\qquad \mathcal U_{c,n_j}=\mu_{c,j},$$

with the intensive functions defined by [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. This is a local representation only: it asserts neither global injectivity or domain coverage nor differentiability at a nonsmooth phase boundary.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Suppose that for every $x\in C$ there is a nondegenerate interval $J_x\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $1$ such that $\lambda x\in C$ and $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda\in J_x$. Here nondegenerate means that $J_x$ contains a point different from $1$; $1$ may be an endpoint. Then

$$f(x)=Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\,\partial_j f(x)\qquad(x\in C).$$

The radial identity need only hold on one side of $1$: openness of $C$ and $C^1$ regularity supply an ambient derivative, and the interval makes $1$ a nonisolated point at which that derivative is determined by the radial identity. This uses the same function on the same domain; it asserts nothing about a family of functions on different tagged domains.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: On the supplied branch [A2], fix $q=(s,V,n)\in W$ and $x=\Psi(q)$ in the original-coordinate uniqueness neighborhood of the local inverse [F3]. By openness, for $\lambda$ in some open interval about $1$, both $\lambda q\in W$ and $\lambda x$ remain in that uniqueness neighborhood and in the common-law entropy cone. Its fixed unit conversion commutes with multiplication by $\lambda$. Thus [A2] gives $S_c(\lambda\mathcal U_c(q),\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda S_c(x)=\lambda s$. By uniqueness of the inverse [F3], $\mathcal U_c(\lambda q)=\lambda\mathcal U_c(q)$ throughout this interval. Consequently [A2] supplies [A1] locally, without a global inverse claim.

For the general conclusion assume [A1], which step 1.1 supplies when [A2] applies. Since $W$ is open, at each $q\in W$ shrink the homogeneity interval so that $\lambda q\in W$ throughout it. The local-ray hypotheses of [L1] therefore apply to $\mathcal U_c$ restricted to $W$, giving $\mathcal U_c=s\mathcal U_{c,s}+V\mathcal U_{c,V}+\sum_j n_j\mathcal U_{c,n_j}$.
Substitute the conjugate derivatives from [F3] into step 2.1 to obtain $\mathcal U_c=Ts-pV+\sum_j\mu_jn_j$.
Differentiate the identity in step 3.1 on the C2 chart using [L2]. The right side has differential $T\,ds+s\,dT-p\,dV-V\,dp+\sum_j(\mu_j\,dn_j+n_j\,d\mu_j)$.
By [F4], the differential of the left side is $T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$. Equating these differentials and cancelling the common terms yields $s\,dT-V\,dp+\sum_j n_j\,d\mu_j=0$.

The general tagged premises [F1]–[F2] alone do not discharge [A1]. On the separately designated common-law branch, [A2] and the local inverse argument in step 1.1 do discharge it, so steps 3.1–5.1 give the full Euler and Gibbs–Duhem identities there. These are identities of local state functions with the stated rest-frame SI and reference conventions; no empirical validation or exact finite-size scaling is inferred.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $C$ be the open positive-temperature domain of a local C2 energy representation $\mathcal U_c(s,V,n)$ for a fixed material constitution $c$, with $V>0$, $n_j>0$, and conjugates $T=\mathcal U_{c,s}$, $p=-\mathcal U_{c,V}$, and $\mu_j=\mathcal U_{c,n_j}$. Let $W\subseteq C$ be open. In addition to the framework suppliers, assume the **same-tag homogeneity hypothesis**: for every $q=(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in W$ there is an $\varepsilon_q\in(0,1)$ such that

$$\mathcal U_c(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n_1,\ldots,\lambda n_r)=\lambda\mathcal U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$$

for every $\lambda>0$ with $|\lambda-1|<\varepsilon_q$ and $\lambda q\in C$. Then, throughout $W$,

$$\mathcal U_c=Ts-pV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j,$$

and on the same chart

$$s\,dT-V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j=0.$$

The same-tag hypothesis is supplied, in particular, when the inverse states $\Psi(q):=(\mathcal U_c(q),V,n)$ for $q\in W$ lie in the designated common-law cone of [[post-td-common-bulk-constitutive-law]], expressed in physical SI coordinate values using the fixed unit conversion. On this branch the adopted entropy transport implies the energy homogeneity locally by uniqueness of the local inverse; no global inverse or global energy-domain cone is assumed. citations.quote:
On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

derivations.claim: For $U(s,V,n)$ the coefficient of $ds$ is $T$, of $dV$ is $-p$, and of $dn_j$ is $\mu_j$ by [F1]. Apply [L1] to each unordered pair of its natural coordinates; the resulting equalities are exactly the four relations in the first bullet of the Statement.
For $H(s,p,n)$ the coefficients from [F1] are $T,V,\mu_j$. Equality of the mixed derivatives in [L1] for the pairs $(s,p)$, $(s,n_j)$, $(p,n_j)$, and $(n_i,n_j)$ gives the second bullet.
For $F(T,V,n)$ the coefficients are $-s,-p,\mu_j$. Applying [L1] to $(T,V)$, $(T,n_j)$, $(V,n_j)$, and $(n_i,n_j)$ yields the third bullet, including its minus signs.
For $G(T,p,n)$ the coefficients are $-s,V,\mu_j$. Applying [L1] to the same four types of coordinate pairs yields the fourth bullet.

For $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$ the coefficients are $-s,-p,-n_j$. Applying [L1] to $(T,V)$, $(T,\mu_j)$, $(V,\mu_j)$, and $(\mu_i,\mu_j)$ yields the fifth bullet. Each equality is confined to the same valid chart by [F2].

Let $U,H,F,G,\Omega$ and their natural-coordinate charts be as in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]], with the exact differentials supplied by [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]. Assume each potential is C2 on its named open chart. Every pair of conjugate coefficients in its exact differential has equal cross derivatives. Explicitly, with all unlisted natural coordinates held fixed, for each species $i,j$:

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.
- From $H(s,p,n)$: $T_p|_{s,n}=V_s|_{p,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,p}$.
- From $F(T,V,n)$: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$; $s_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=-\mu_{j,T}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,V}$.
- From $G(T,p,n)$: $-s_p|_{T,n}=V_T|_{p,n}$; $-s_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,T}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,p}$.
- From $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$: $s_V|_{T,\mu}=p_T|_{V,\mu}$; $s_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,T}|_{V,\mu}$; $p_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,V}|_{T,\mu}$; and $n_{i,\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,\mu_i}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne i}}$.

For every admitted $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$, fixed material constitution, zero change in center-of-mass kinetic energy, and zero change in separately tracked external-field potential energy in the fixed chart selected by the process model, the adopted model balance is
$$U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P],$$
where $U_c$ is the dimensioned energy-coordinate map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]].

Here the internal-energy coordinate is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], while $Q[P]$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ are the protocol transfers defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The sign convention is positive $Q$ into the system and positive $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ for work done on it. If $P$ is adiabatic, its defining condition is $Q[P]=0$, so the same adopted balance gives $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)$.

This equation is an adopted physical postulate of the stated framework. It is not deduced here from a mechanical model or from experimental observations. Records with matter exchange or nonzero changes in omitted kinetic or external-field energy require a separately specified balance and are outside this item.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound. Fix the finite constituent split $s_1,\ldots,s_m$ used for the endpoint bookkeeping, with $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, and constitutions $c_1,\ldots,c_m$. The split accounts for every constituent whose entropy can change; any included auxiliary not represented in it must have an explicitly model-declared zero entropy change between these endpoints. Its endpoint product is

$$\mathcal D:=D_{c_1}\times\cdots\times D_{c_m},\qquad \mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal D,$$

where $\mathcal F$ is the model-declared feasible endpoint set for the fixed totals, retained barriers, and permitted exchanges, as in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The process model supplies an endpoint association on the two formal endpoint labels $-$ and $+$:

$$\rho_P:\{-,+\}\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad \rho_P(-)=\mathbf x_P^-=(x_{1,P}^-,\ldots,x_{m,P}^-),\qquad \rho_P(+)=\mathbf x_P^+=(x_{1,P}^+,\ldots,x_{m,P}^+),$$

where $\mathbf x_P^-$ and $\mathbf x_P^+$ are respectively the declared constituent-state tuples representing the aggregate equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$ of $P$. Both tuples must belong to the same $\mathcal F$. Restrict to endpoint splits admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] as a collection of independent separated macroscopic systems, so that its additive entropy rule applies. On this admitted $\mathcal F$, define

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i)\qquad\left(\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal F\right).$$

This uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]].

The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))\ge0.$$

The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))=0$. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

Let $\mathcal F$ be the explicitly declared feasible endpoint set of an isolated compound whose constituents are independent separated macroscopic systems, as defined in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For this route, adopt the physical criterion that any endpoint tuple the model classifies as a stable equilibrium under these fixed totals, retained partitions, and permitted exchanges satisfies

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})=\max_{x\in\mathcal F}S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x),\qquad S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i),$$

Here $\max$ means that $x^{\mathrm{eq}}\in\mathcal F$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})\ge S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal F$, using maximum in the sense of [[def-max-min]]. The finite sum is as in [[def-finite-sum]], and the summands are those of the separated macroscopic constituents under [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Whenever the stable-equilibrium label is used, attainment is assumed: at least one maximizing endpoint lies in $\mathcal F$. If $\mathcal F$ is empty or the entropy supremum is not attained, this item supplies no equilibrium state.

“Global” refers to every endpoint in this exact $\mathcal F$, not just nearby states, states reachable by a restricted short-time dynamics, or states on a selected branch. A local maximum that is not global, or a long-lived preparation trapped by kinetic barriers, is not declared stable equilibrium by this postulate. No uniqueness or relaxation dynamics is assumed.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: In the fixed-volume case, the first-law balance [F1] has $W_{\mathrm{on}}=0$ by [A2], so $\Delta U=Q$. The bath relation [A1] gives $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta S-Q/T_0$. By [F2], $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0$, and therefore $\Delta F_{T_0}=Q-T_0\Delta S=-T_0\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\le0$.

In the fixed-pressure case, [A2] and [F1] give $\Delta U=Q-p_0\Delta V$, while [A1] gives $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta S-Q/T_0$. Hence $\Delta G_{T_0,p_0}=\Delta U+p_0\Delta V-T_0\Delta S=Q-T_0\Delta S=-T_0\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\le0$.

For fixed volume, [A1] and [A3] express total entropy on the feasible set as $S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mathrm{constant}-F_{T_0}/T_0$. Since $T_0>0$, maximizing total entropy is equivalent to minimizing $F_{T_0}$; on the natural-variable chart the function is the Helmholtz potential by [F4].

For fixed pressure, [A1]–[A3] express total entropy as $S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mathrm{constant}-G_{T_0,p_0}/T_0$. Again $T_0>0$, so every attained global entropy maximizer on that feasible set is a global minimizer of $G_{T_0,p_0}$; on the natural-variable chart it is the Gibbs potential by [F4]. Neither equivalence implies uniqueness or attainment beyond [F3].

Fix a closed macroscopic system with composition fixed and two admitted equilibrium endpoints. In the fixed-volume model, couple it only to an ideal thermal reservoir at constant $T_0>0$. In the fixed-pressure model, also couple it to an ideal pressure store at constant $p_0>0$. Define the constrained potentials

$$F_{T_0}(x):=U(x)-T_0S(x),\qquad G_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U(x)+p_0V(x)-T_0S(x).$$

Assume the ideal-reservoir bookkeeping specified in [A1]–[A3] of Facts & Assumptions and the adopted isolated-compound second law [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]. Then along every admitted spontaneous endpoint change at fixed volume, $F_{T_0}$ does not increase; at fixed pressure, $G_{T_0,p_0}$ does not increase. If an endpoint is an attained global entropy maximum on the same feasible set, the corresponding constrained potential attains a global minimum there. If the system endpoint is on its $T=T_0$ or $(T,p)=(T_0,p_0)$ natural-variable chart, these constrained functions agree with the Helmholtz or Gibbs potentials of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]].

The statement is conditional on the ideal bath/load model and is not a claim that every physical process has such a reservoir or reaches the minimum.

$$P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P).$$
For each finite closed time interval $I_P=[t_0,t_1]\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $t_0<t_1$ as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, its component fields have these types: $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$ are equilibrium endpoint coordinates from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; $Z_s$ is the model-declared configuration space of the system, its auxiliaries and devices; $Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq Z_s$ is the model-declared set of equilibrium configurations and $\xi_s:Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\to D_c$ assigns their state coordinates; $z_P:I_P\to Z_s$ is a function ([[def-function-space]]); $\mathcal K_s$ is the model-declared set of control/contact records and $\kappa_P\in\mathcal K_s$; and $\mathcal R_s$ is the model-declared set of signed transfer records and $r_P\in\mathcal R_s$. For an endpoint bookkeeping quantity $F$, write $\Delta F=F_P^+-F_P^-$. A closed record in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]] has no matter crossing the chosen outer boundary. The core closed-record class $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\subseteq\mathcal P_s$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]) contains only records for which the system has a supplied total mass $M>0$ and defined center-of-mass velocities at both endpoints in the fixed chart $g_s$, so the kinetic energies $K_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm\|_2^2$ are defined as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. It further requires $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$ and $\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$, where $U_{\mathrm{ext}}$ denotes any model-specified external-field potential energy tracked separately from the internal-energy coordinate in $g_s$. Other process classes require an expanded energy bookkeeping rule.

For each $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$, the protocol supplies maps $Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}:\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\to\mathbb R$ whose values are interpreted in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]] and whose energy bookkeeping uses $g_s$. $Q[P]>0$ means energy enters the system through the declared thermal-transfer channel; $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$ means mechanical work is done on the system. These are functionals of the process record, not state functions of $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$. Heat is the protocol-assigned thermal mode of energy transfer, not a quantity stored in the equilibrium state. A record is adiabatic exactly when $Q[P]=0$. A closed record may still exchange energy; it is not thereby isolated.

A preparation is a model-specified rule selecting the particular initial equilibrium state $x_P^-$. A statistical extension may instead specify a normalized probability measure on a declared measurable space, as in [[def-probability-measure]]; such a statistical preparation is outside this deterministic process class. A preparation does not assert later equilibration. An admitted record may pass through nonequilibrium configurations even though both endpoints lie in $D_c$.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and the work-transfer model [A2], $\Delta U=Q-p_0\Delta V-W_{\mathrm{out}}$. By [A1] and [A3], $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Delta S-Q/T_0$; [F2] gives $Q\le T_0\Delta S$. The signs of $Q$ and work transfers are those in [F3].

Rearranging the energy balance in step 1.1 gives $W_{\mathrm{out}}=Q-\Delta U-p_0\Delta V\le T_0\Delta S-\Delta U-p_0\Delta V=-\Delta G_{T_0,p_0}$. By [F4], all terms in this inequality have units of joules. This is the stated endpoint bound.

For a fixed-composition closed system coupled to an ideal thermal reservoir at $T_0>0$ and ideal pressure store at $p_0>0$, let $Q$ be heat into the system and let $W_{\mathrm{out}}$ be net energy delivered by the system to an ideal work store whose entropy is constant. Assume the isolated-composite bookkeeping of [A1]–[A3] in Facts & Assumptions. Then for any admitted process between equilibrium endpoints $x_i,x_f$,

$$W_{\mathrm{out}}\le G_{T_0,p_0}(x_i)-G_{T_0,p_0}(x_f),\qquad G_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U(x)+p_0V(x)-T_0S(x).$$

If the endpoint states lie on the $(T,p)=(T_0,p_0)$ natural-variable chart, this is the decrease in the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Equality requires zero total entropy production; the theorem does not assert that a protocol realizing equality exists.

Fix a constitution $c$ and an open dimensionless subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the single-phase region of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Its physical chart is $\Omega=\Phi_c(O)$, where $\Phi_c$ is the SI coordinate map defined in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. For fixed physical amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ with nonempty slice $\Omega_n:=\{(U,V):(U,V,n)\in\Omega\}$, this slice is open in $\mathbb R^2$. Use $T,p$ from [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] as functions of the physical coordinates on $\Omega_n$. For a response derivative, restrict to an open neighborhood in $\Omega_n$ where the required natural-coordinate map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto an open image, so its inverse expresses the physical $(U,V)$ as $C^1$ functions of those natural coordinates ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Specifically, $C_V$ uses $(U,V)\mapsto(T,V)$ at fixed $n$, while $C_p$, $\kappa_T$, and $\alpha_p$ use $(U,V)\mapsto(T,p)$ at fixed $n$. The existence of each such local chart is a hypothesis for its response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. Each derivative uses the indicated natural variables and holds all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

Let $U,H,F,G,\Omega$ and their natural-coordinate charts be as in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]], with the exact differentials supplied by [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]. Assume each potential is C2 on its named open chart. Every pair of conjugate coefficients in its exact differential has equal cross derivatives. Explicitly, with all unlisted natural coordinates held fixed, for each species $i,j$:

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.
- From $H(s,p,n)$: $T_p|_{s,n}=V_s|_{p,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,p}$.
- From $F(T,V,n)$: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$; $s_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=-\mu_{j,T}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,V}$.
- From $G(T,p,n)$: $-s_p|_{T,n}=V_T|_{p,n}$; $-s_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,T}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,p}$.
- From $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$: $s_V|_{T,\mu}=p_T|_{V,\mu}$; $s_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,T}|_{V,\mu}$; $p_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,V}|_{T,\mu}$; and $n_{i,\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,\mu_i}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne i}}$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: At fixed $V,n$, $U=F+Ts$ and $F_T=-s$ from [F2], so the product rule [F5] gives $C_V=U_T|_{V,n}=T s_T|_{V,n}$. At fixed $p,n$, $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp$ from [F2], hence $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}=T s_T|_{p,n}$.

On the valid isothermal response inverse, write $V=V(T,p,n)$, so $p(T,V(T,p,n),n)=p$, where the rightmost $p$ is the independent pressure coordinate. Differentiating in that pressure coordinate at fixed $T,n$ gives $1=p_V|_{T,n}V_p|_{T,n}$. By [F1], $V_p|_{T,n}=-V\kappa_T$, hence $p_V|_{T,n}=-1/(V\kappa_T)$. Differentiating the same identity in $T$ at fixed $p,n$ gives $0=p_T|_{V,n}+p_V|_{T,n}V_T|_{p,n}$. Again by [F1], $V_T|_{p,n}=V\alpha_p$, so $p_T|_{V,n}=\alpha_p/\kappa_T$. The stated inverse chart and $\kappa_T>0$ make these derivatives and reciprocals valid.
Along a constant-$p$, fixed-$n$ curve, [F4] gives $s_T|_{p,n}=s_T|_{V,n}+s_V|_{T,n}V_T|_{p,n}$. Subtract the two identities in step 1.1 and use [F3] to obtain $C_p-C_V=T p_T|_{V,n}V_T|_{p,n}$.

Substitute $p_T|_{V,n}=\alpha_p/\kappa_T$ and $V_T|_{p,n}=V\alpha_p$ into step 2.1 to obtain $C_p-C_V=TV\alpha_p^2/\kappa_T$. Since $\kappa_T>0$, no zero denominator is used. The units are $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ on both sides because $\mathrm{Pa\,m^3=J}$.
