$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

Fix a constitution $c$, a positive-temperature local energy chart with entropy coordinate $s$ and physical volume $V>0$, and fixed amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$. The energy representation and pressure on this chart are those of [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]] and the response-chart conventions are those of [[def-td-response-functions]]. Where $(s,V,n)\mapsto(s,p,n)$ has a C1 local inverse, define the **isentropic compressibility** of the whole system by

$$\kappa_S:=-\frac1V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{s,n}.$$

The entropy $s$ is held fixed, as are all amounts $n_j$. Since $V$ is in $\mathrm{m^3}$ and $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$ ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_S$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign, finiteness, or existence outside the specified inverse chart; in particular it does not assign a value at a singular or critical response point.

On a valid local energy-representation chart from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]], let $s,V,n_j,U,T,p,\mu_j$ and the potentials $H,F,G,\Omega$ be as defined in [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. On every open neighborhood where the corresponding natural-coordinate maps have their stated $C^1$ inverses, the potentials are C2 and their differentials are

$$dU=T\,ds-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,\qquad dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\,dn_j,$$

$$d\Omega=-s\,dT-p\,dV-\sum_{j=1}^r n_j\,d\mu_j.$$

All differentials are local state-function differentials. They do not assert that heat or work is an exact differential on process space.

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.
- From $H(s,p,n)$: $T_p|_{s,n}=V_s|_{p,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{s,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,p}$.
- From $F(T,V,n)$: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$; $s_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=-\mu_{j,T}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{T,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,V}$.
- From $G(T,p,n)$: $-s_p|_{T,n}=V_T|_{p,n}$; $-s_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,T}|_{p,n}$; $V_{n_j}|_{T,p,n}=\mu_{j,p}|_{T,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{T,p}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{T,p}$.
- From $\Omega(T,V,\mu)$: $s_V|_{T,\mu}=p_T|_{V,\mu}$; $s_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,T}|_{V,\mu}$; $p_{\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,V}|_{T,\mu}$; and $n_{i,\mu_j}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne j}}=n_{j,\mu_i}|_{T,V,\mu_{k\ne i}}$.

$$C_p-C_V=\frac{TV\alpha_p^2}{\kappa_T}.$$

Here $C_V,C_p$ are the whole-system heat capacities, $\alpha_p=V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}$, and $\kappa_T=-V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial p)_{T,n}$, all as in [[def-td-response-functions]]. Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], $C_V=U_T|_{V,n}$. On the fixed-volume path in the Helmholtz chart, [F3] gives $dU=T\,ds$; composing with the chart map and applying [F6] yields $C_V=T s_T|_{V,n}$. Likewise, by [F1], $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}$, and on the fixed-pressure path in the Gibbs chart [F3] gives $dH=T\,ds$; the chain rule yields $C_p=T s_T|_{p,n}$. Thus at fixed $n$, $ds=(C_V/T)\,dT+p_T|_{V,n}\,dV$. Along an isentrope $ds=0$, the valid chart gives $T_V|_{s,n}=-T p_T|_{V,n}/C_V$.
Differentiate $p(T,V,n)$ along the same isentrope using [F6]: $p_V|_{s,n}=p_V|_{T,n}+p_T|_{V,n}T_V|_{s,n}=p_V|_{T,n}-T(p_T|_{V,n})^2/C_V$.

On the valid isothermal response inverse, $p(T,V(T,p,n),n)=p$. Differentiating this identity in $p$ at fixed $T,n$ gives $1=p_V|_{T,n}V_p|_{T,n}$; by [F1] and $\kappa_T>0$, $p_V|_{T,n}=-1/(V\kappa_T)$. Differentiating it in $T$ at fixed $p,n$ gives $0=p_T|_{V,n}+p_V|_{T,n}V_T|_{p,n}$, so [F1] yields $p_T|_{V,n}=\alpha_p/\kappa_T$. Thus [F5] is equivalently $C_p-C_V=-T(p_T|_{V,n})^2/p_V|_{T,n}$. Substitution into step 2.1 yields $p_V|_{s,n}=p_V|_{T,n}(C_p/C_V)$. Since $p_V|_{T,n}<0$ and $C_V>0$, [F5] also gives $C_p=C_V-T(p_T|_{V,n})^2/p_V|_{T,n}\ge C_V>0$, hence $p_V|_{s,n}<0$.

On the valid isentropic inverse $V=V(s,p,n)$, the identity $p(s,V(s,p,n),n)=p$ gives $1=p_V|_{s,n}V_p|_{s,n}$ by [F6]. Hence the definitions [F1]–[F2] give $\kappa_T=-1/(V p_V|_{T,n})$ and $\kappa_S=-1/(V p_V|_{s,n})$. By step 3.1, $\kappa_T/\kappa_S=p_V|_{s,n}/p_V|_{T,n}=C_p/C_V$. All denominators are nonzero by the valid-chart and positivity hypotheses.

- From $U(s,V,n)$: $T_V|_{s,n}=-p_s|_{V,n}$; $T_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,s}|_{V,n}$; $-p_{n_j}|_{s,V,n}=\mu_{j,V}|_{s,n}$; and $\mu_{i,n_j}|_{s,V}=\mu_{j,n_i}|_{s,V}$.

Fix a constitution $c$ and an open dimensionless subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the single-phase region of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Its physical chart is $\Omega=\Phi_c(O)$, where $\Phi_c$ is the SI coordinate map defined in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. For fixed physical amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ with nonempty slice $\Omega_n:=\{(U,V):(U,V,n)\in\Omega\}$, this slice is open in $\mathbb R^2$. Use $T,p$ from [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] as functions of the physical coordinates on $\Omega_n$. For a response derivative, restrict to an open neighborhood in $\Omega_n$ where the required natural-coordinate map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto an open image, so its inverse expresses the physical $(U,V)$ as $C^1$ functions of those natural coordinates ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Specifically, $C_V$ uses $(U,V)\mapsto(T,V)$ at fixed $n$, while $C_p$, $\kappa_T$, and $\alpha_p$ use $(U,V)\mapsto(T,p)$ at fixed $n$. The existence of each such local chart is a hypothesis for its response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. Each derivative uses the indicated natural variables and holds all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

Fix a material constitution $c$ with finite species list $(1,\ldots,r)$ and a local energy representation $U_c=U_c(s,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from [[pthm-td-local-energy-representation]]. Here $s$ is entropy in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $V>0$ is volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, each $n_j>0$ is in $\mathrm{mol}$, $U_c$ is in joules, and the conjugates are $T=U_{c,s}$ in kelvins, $p=-U_{c,V}$ in pascals, and $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The derivatives hold every other listed natural coordinate fixed; the physical-coordinate and rest-frame conventions are those of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]].

For an open chart, a **local Legendre transformation** means the following partial transformation of $U_c$: select one or more of its extensive coordinates $q$, take their conjugate coordinates $x=D_qU_c$, and use only a neighborhood on which $(q,z)\mapsto(x,z)$, with $z$ the untransformed coordinates, has a $C^1$ inverse. Such a neighborhood is a valid local transform chart in the sense of [[def-td-response-functions]]. No inverse or potential as a function of the proposed natural coordinates is asserted outside that chart.

On their respective valid charts define the enthalpy, Helmholtz potential, Gibbs potential, and grand potential by

$$H_c:=U_c+pV,\qquad F_c:=U_c-Ts,\qquad G_c:=U_c-Ts+pV,\qquad \Omega_c:=U_c-Ts-\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_jn_j.$$

Their natural-coordinate charts are respectively $(s,p,n)$, $(T,V,n)$, $(T,p,n)$, and $(T,V,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r)$. In the volume transform the conjugate coordinate is $-p=U_{c,V}$, which accounts for the plus sign in $H_c$ and $G_c$; in the chemical transform the conjugates are $\mu_j=U_{c,n_j}$, which accounts for the minus signs in $\Omega_c$. All four potentials have units of joules. A displayed differential or global convex-duality characterization is not part of this definition; critical, coexistence, and other non-C2 boundaries are excluded.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

derivations.claim: At fixed $n$, write $ds=s_T|_{p,n}\,dT+s_p|_{T,n}\,dp$ in [F1]. The enthalpy $H$ and chart are those of [F4]. Since $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}$ and $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp$, the coefficient of $dT$ gives $C_p=T s_T|_{p,n}$. Therefore $dH=C_p\,dT+(T s_p|_{T,n}+V)\,dp$.
Substitute the Maxwell relation [F2] into step 1.1 to obtain $dH=C_p\,dT+(V-T V_T|_{p,n})\,dp$.
Along a curve of constant $H$ and fixed $n$, step 2.1 gives $0=C_p\,dT+(V-T V_T|_{p,n})\,dp$. The assumed $(H,p,n)$ chart and $C_p>0$ therefore give $\mu_{JT}=(T V_T|_{p,n}-V)/C_p$.
Substitute $V_T|_{p,n}=V\alpha_p$ from [F3] to obtain $\mu_{JT}=V(T\alpha_p-1)/C_p$. Its units are $\mathrm{K\,Pa^{-1}}$ by [F5].

On a C2 Gibbs chart $G(T,p,n)$ at fixed composition $n$, with $T>0$, $V>0$, finite $C_p>0$, and a valid local inverse between $(T,p,n)$ and $(H,p,n)$, define the **Joule-Thomson coefficient** by

$$\mu_{JT}:=\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial p}\right)_{H,n}.$$

Then

$$\mu_{JT}=\frac{T(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}-V}{C_p}=\frac{V(T\alpha_p-1)}{C_p},$$

where $\alpha_p=V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}$ and $C_p=(\partial H/\partial T)_{p,n}$ are the response functions of [[def-td-response-functions]]. This is a local derivative identity. It does not prove that a real throttle is isenthalpic or that a particular substance cools under expansion.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Fix a material constitution $c$, with $r$ named species and dimensionless equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in D_c$, define the diagonal SI coordinate map

$$\Phi_c(x):=(U_c(x),V_c(x),n_{c,1}(x),\ldots,n_{c,r}(x))=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\ldots,\hat n_r\,\mathrm{mol}).$$

In SI numerical coordinates this is a diagonal linear bijection with a diagonal linear inverse, so it maps ambient open sets to open sets and its inverse is defined on its image.

Choose an open subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the ambient dimensionless Euclidean coordinates that is designated as a single-phase chart, and set $\Omega:=\Phi_c(O)$, an open chart of physical SI coordinate values. Here $U$ is the internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. If $S_c:D_c\to\mathbb R$ is the entropy adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], define its physical-coordinate representative on $\Omega$ by

$$S_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R.$$

When its arguments are the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, write this representative as $S_c(U,V,n)$ for brevity. On $\Omega$, assume the finite representative is $C^2$ and has $S_{c,U}>0$, as adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in the physical $U$ coordinate while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; in particular the conversion factor from $\hat U$ is included.

Explicitly, with the partial derivatives on the right taken in the dimensionless coordinates on $O$ while holding every other hatted coordinate fixed, the physical partials are

$$S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial_{\hat U}S_c,\qquad S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{m^3})^{-1}\partial_{\hat V}S_c,\qquad S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{mol})^{-1}\partial_{\hat n_j}S_c,$$

using the coordinate-conversion convention of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]].

Define the physical-coordinate representatives of the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}},\qquad p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}},\qquad \mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}:=-T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}.$$

For a state-domain point $x\in O$, define the corresponding state functions by pullback, $T_c(x):=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, $p_c(x):=p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, and $\mu_{c,j}(x):=\mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$. When the argument is a physical tuple $(U,V,n)$, write $T_c(U,V,n)$, $p_c(U,V,n)$, and $\mu_{c,j}(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representatives. Thus both notations refer to the same state functions through $\Phi_c$.

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

Fix a constitution $c$ and an open dimensionless subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the single-phase region of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Its physical chart is $\Omega=\Phi_c(O)$, where $\Phi_c$ is the SI coordinate map defined in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. For fixed physical amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ with nonempty slice $\Omega_n:=\{(U,V):(U,V,n)\in\Omega\}$, this slice is open in $\mathbb R^2$. Use $T,p$ from [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] as functions of the physical coordinates on $\Omega_n$. For a response derivative, restrict to an open neighborhood in $\Omega_n$ where the required natural-coordinate map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto an open image, so its inverse expresses the physical $(U,V)$ as $C^1$ functions of those natural coordinates ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Specifically, $C_V$ uses $(U,V)\mapsto(T,V)$ at fixed $n$, while $C_p$, $\kappa_T$, and $\alpha_p$ use $(U,V)\mapsto(T,p)$ at fixed $n$. The existence of each such local chart is a hypothesis for its response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. Each derivative uses the indicated natural variables and holds all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $S_U=C/U$ and $S_V=a$. Hence [F3] gives $T=U/C>0$ and $p=aU/C=aT$. The Hessian of $S$ in $(U,V)$ is diagonal with entries $-C/U^2$ and $0$, so it is negative semidefinite on the open domain.

At fixed $T$, the equation $p=aT$ is independent of $V$. Therefore the map $(T,V)\mapsto(T,p)$ is not injective on any open neighborhood, so the inverse required by [F4] does not exist and $\kappa_T$ is not defined by that chart. This does not contradict a theorem whose hypotheses require a valid response inverse.

$$T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}},\qquad p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}},\qquad \mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}:=-T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}.$$

For a state-domain point $x\in O$, define the corresponding state functions by pullback, $T_c(x):=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, $p_c(x):=p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, and $\mu_{c,j}(x):=\mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$. When the argument is a physical tuple $(U,V,n)$, write $T_c(U,V,n)$, $p_c(U,V,n)$, and $\mu_{c,j}(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representatives. Thus both notations refer to the same state functions through $\Phi_c$.

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

For a simple-compressible system whose only admitted mechanical equilibrium coordinate is volume, adopt the following piston coupling. The boundary is a planar piston with constant area $A>0$ in $\mathrm{m^2}$ and outward displacement coordinate $\ell$ in metres; increasing $\ell$ increases the enclosed volume by $dV=A\,d\ell$. Define the positive mechanical pressure $p_{\mathrm{mech}}$ as the outward normal force exerted by the system on the piston divided by $A$, so $p_{\mathrm{mech}}$ is in pascals. When the system is in quasistatic frictionless mechanical equilibrium with this piston, adopt the identification

$$p_{\mathrm{mech}}=p_c,$$

where $p_c$ is the entropic pressure of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. With $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ positive for work done on the system, the same coupling assigns the incremental mechanical work

$$\delta W_{\mathrm{on}}=-p_{\mathrm{mech}}A\,d\ell=-p_c\,dV.$$

The sign agrees with [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]: compression has $dV<0$ and positive work on the system. This is an adopted, regime-limited physical assumption, not a deduction from the entropy derivative or from the first-law balance [[post-td-first-law-energy]]. It makes no claim for friction, nonquasistatic processes, changing piston area, shear, surface forces, fields, composition transfer, or other generalized coordinates.

For every admitted $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$, fixed material constitution, zero change in center-of-mass kinetic energy, and zero change in separately tracked external-field potential energy in the fixed chart selected by the process model, the adopted model balance is
$$U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P],$$
where $U_c$ is the dimensioned energy-coordinate map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]].

Here the internal-energy coordinate is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], while $Q[P]$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ are the protocol transfers defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The sign convention is positive $Q$ into the system and positive $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ for work done on it. If $P$ is adiabatic, its defining condition is $Q[P]=0$, so the same adopted balance gives $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)$.

This equation is an adopted physical postulate of the stated framework. It is not deduced here from a mechanical model or from experimental observations. Records with matter exchange or nonzero changes in omitted kinetic or external-field energy require a separately specified balance and are outside this item.

For a system $s$ of constitution $c$, the process model fixes one Galilean inertial chart $g_s$ for kinetic-energy bookkeeping and transfer records and holds that chart fixed throughout each process. A process record is a tuple
$$P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P).$$
For each finite closed time interval $I_P=[t_0,t_1]\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $t_0<t_1$ as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, its component fields have these types: $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$ are equilibrium endpoint coordinates from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; $Z_s$ is the model-declared configuration space of the system, its auxiliaries and devices; $Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq Z_s$ is the model-declared set of equilibrium configurations and $\xi_s:Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\to D_c$ assigns their state coordinates; $z_P:I_P\to Z_s$ is a function ([[def-function-space]]); $\mathcal K_s$ is the model-declared set of control/contact records and $\kappa_P\in\mathcal K_s$; and $\mathcal R_s$ is the model-declared set of signed transfer records and $r_P\in\mathcal R_s$. These fields form a finite Cartesian product ([[def-cartesian-product]]). The admitted records $\mathcal P_s$ are the model-specified subset of tuples with these types that additionally satisfy $z_P(t_0),z_P(t_1)\in Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\xi_s(z_P(t_0))=x_P^-$, and $\xi_s(z_P(t_1))=x_P^+$. No continuity or differentiability is imposed on $z_P$, and its values at interior times need not represent equilibrium states.

For an endpoint bookkeeping quantity $F$, write $\Delta F=F_P^+-F_P^-$. A closed record in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]] has no matter crossing the chosen outer boundary. The core closed-record class $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\subseteq\mathcal P_s$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]) contains only records for which the system has a supplied total mass $M>0$ and defined center-of-mass velocities at both endpoints in the fixed chart $g_s$, so the kinetic energies $K_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm\|_2^2$ are defined as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. It further requires $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$ and $\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$, where $U_{\mathrm{ext}}$ denotes any model-specified external-field potential energy tracked separately from the internal-energy coordinate in $g_s$. Other process classes require an expanded energy bookkeeping rule.

For each $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$, the protocol supplies maps $Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}:\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\to\mathbb R$ whose values are interpreted in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]] and whose energy bookkeeping uses $g_s$. $Q[P]>0$ means energy enters the system through the declared thermal-transfer channel; $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$ means mechanical work is done on the system. These are functionals of the process record, not state functions of $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$. Heat is the protocol-assigned thermal mode of energy transfer, not a quantity stored in the equilibrium state. A record is adiabatic exactly when $Q[P]=0$. A closed record may still exchange energy; it is not thereby isolated.

A preparation is a model-specified rule selecting the particular initial equilibrium state $x_P^-$. A statistical extension may instead specify a normalized probability measure on a declared measurable space, as in [[def-probability-measure]]; such a statistical preparation is outside this deterministic process class. A preparation does not assert later equilibration. An admitted record may pass through nonequilibrium configurations even though both endpoints lie in $D_c$.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ path in the sense of [[def-path-polygonal-length-and-rectifiability-in-rn]]. Its **reversal** is $\gamma^{-}(t):=\gamma(a+b-t)$. It is **closed** when $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$.

For paths $\alpha,\beta:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^n$ with $\alpha(1)=\beta(0)$, their **concatenation** is

$$ (\alpha*\beta)(t):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2t),&0\le t\le\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2t-1),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases} $$

When $a<b$ and $c<d$, if $h:[c,d]\to[a,b]$ is a continuous piecewise-$C^1$ bijection whose derivative has a fixed nonzero sign on every smooth piece, then $\gamma\circ h$ is an **oriented piecewise-$C^1$ reparametrization**. It is orientation-preserving when $h'>0$ and orientation-reversing when $h'<0$. Bijectivity excludes multiple coverings. Constant paths are allowed, although they are not regular; their speed-integral length is zero by [[cor-piecewise-c1-paths-have-additive-speed-integral-length]].

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to U$ be piecewise-$C^1$. Then

$$\int_\gamma\nabla\phi\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(\gamma(b))-\phi(\gamma(a)).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: By [F2] and [L4], the entropy derivatives are $S_U=C/U$ and $S_V=a(1-bV)$. Thus [F3] gives $T=U/C>0$ and $p=aT(1-bV)>0$ on the stated domain. The Hessian is diagonal with entries $-C/U^2$ and $-ab$, so the chart is C2 and concave.

On each isotherm the vector field in [L1] is continuous, so [L2] gives $\int_{V_1}^{V_2}p(T_1,V)\,dV=aT_1[(V_2-V_1)-\tfrac b2(V_2^2-V_1^2)]$; the reverse isotherm contributes the negative of the same bracket multiplied by $aT_2$, and the isochoric legs contribute zero.
Summing the four legs yields $\oint p\,dV=a(T_1-T_2)(V_2-V_1)[1-\tfrac b2(V_1+V_2)]>0$, since $T_1>T_2$ and $V_1,V_2<1/b$. Thus $W_{\mathrm{on}}=-\oint p\,dV<0$ by [F4].

The cycle returns to the same $U$, so [F5] gives $Q=-W_{\mathrm{on}}=\oint p\,dV>0$. If $p\,dV$ were an exact differential on a neighborhood containing this loop, [L3] would force its closed integral to be zero, contradicting step 3.1. Hence pressure work here is a process functional, not a state-function increment.

Fix a material constitution and amount $n$ and stipulate, on $U>0$ and $0<V<1/b$, the entropy chart

$$S(U,V)=C\ln(U/U_*)+aV-\frac{ab}{2}V^2+S_0,$$

where $C>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $U_*>0$ is in joules, $a>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$, $b>0$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, and $S_0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Consider a piecewise-C1 quasistatic cycle with isotherms $T_1>T_2>0$ and volumes $0<V_1<V_2<1/b$, joined by isochoric legs. The ideal frictionless piston load tracks the equilibrium pressure, controlled heat exchange is permitted along the path, and no other work coordinate acts. The calculation shows that the pressure-work integral is not an endpoint increment.

The displayed entropy is $S^{\rm SI}$ in physical SI coordinates. For this constructed local model, choose the positive-amount open neighborhood stated here (or any positive neighborhood of the fixed amount, extending this entropy independently of amount) and let $O_c$ be the numerical preimage of that product patch under $\Phi_c(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n\,\mathrm{mol})$. Declare $O_c$ as the model's local state-domain patch and set $S_c=S^{\rm SI}\circ\Phi_c$. The derivatives below are those of $S^{\rm SI}=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}$ on $\Phi_c(O_c)$, exactly as in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. This supplies the numerical-to-SI chart identification for the formal witness, with no assertion of a measured material or a global constitutive extension.

derivations.claim: On the component of configurations with exactly $n$ points, $N_B(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_B(x_j)$ is Borel for every Borel $B\subseteq C$. The count of $C$ identifies the component $n$, so every count map is Borel on the full disjoint union. Thus the count-generated sigma-algebra is contained in the sorted-list Borel sigma-algebra.

Let $(T,\mathcal T)$ be any measurable space. For $H\in\mathcal B(C)\otimes\mathcal T$, define $M_H(\eta,t)=\sum_{x\in\eta}\mathbf1_H(x,t)$. The class of such $H$ for which $M_H$ is measurable with respect to the count sigma-algebra times $\mathcal T$ contains every rectangle $A\times D$, since $M_{A\times D}(\eta,t)=N_A(\eta)\mathbf1_D(t)$. It is closed under relative complements because $M_{(C\times T)\setminus H}=N_C-M_H$, and under disjoint countable unions by pointwise convergence of finite partial sums. Rectangles form a generating pi-system, so [F2] proves measurability for every product-measurable $H$.

Fix a component with $n$ distinct points and an index $k\leq n$. Recover the coordinates of the $k$th lexicographic point recursively. Initially the selected prefix is empty and its rank is $r=k$. At coordinate $j$, with measurable prefix $p=(a_1,\ldots,a_{j-1})$, use step 2.1 on the Borel set $H_j=\{(x,p,t):x_\ell=p_\ell\ (\ell<j),\ x_j<t\}$, where $t\in[0,1]$. The interval containing the $r$th such coordinate is the first whose cumulative count reaches $r$; the nested interval closures have diameters tending to zero, so their left endpoints converge to that coordinate $a_j$. The count of matching points with $x_j<a_j$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,a_j)$, measurable by step 2.1 after composition with the measurable prefix and $a_j$. After coordinate $d$, distinctness leaves exactly one point, namely $x_k$. Thus all coordinate functions of every sorted point are count-measurable. The Borel sigma-algebra on the sorted-list component is generated by its coordinate maps, so it is contained in the count-generated sigma-algebra there.

The count $N_C$ partitions the full configuration space into its countable components. Applying step 4.1 on each component shows that every sorted-list Borel set is count-measurable; step 1.1 proves the reverse inclusion. The displayed sigma-algebra equality follows.

Each $I_{m,k}$ is Borel as the intersection of a closed ray and an open ray. Distinct interval interiors are disjoint and an adjacent endpoint belongs only to the interval beginning there. Induction on the number of adjacent intervals gives $\bigcup_{k<j}I_{m,k}=[0,j2^{-m})$; at $j=2^m$ this is $[0,1)$. Thus they partition the reference interval. Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to one by the exponential power series and addition formula. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

derivations.claim: Fix one unit cell $C_i$ and a finite Borel partition $B_0,\ldots,B_s$ of it. Put $v_j=|B_j|$, so $\sum_jv_j=1$. Conditional on the cell count $N=n$, the $n$ independent uniform points give category-count probability $n!\prod_jv_j^{n_j}/\prod_jn_j!$ for $\sum_jn_j=n$. Multiplying by the Poisson count probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ gives $e^{-\lambda}\prod_j(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!=\prod_je^{-\lambda v_j}(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!$, by [F3]. This factors into the Poisson probabilities of the disjoint cell pieces, including the complement $B_0$; hence their counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means $\lambda v_j$. Zero-volume pieces have count zero almost surely by the same formula.

Each bounded $A_j$ intersects only finitely many unit cells. Apply step 1.1 to the partition formed by the sets $A_j\cap C_i$ and their complement in each such cell. Independence within each cell and independence between cell configurations show that all component counts, indexed by both $j$ and $i$, are independent Poisson variables.

For fixed $j$, sum the component counts over its finitely many cells. The sum of independent Poisson variables of means $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_q$ has mass at $n$ equal to $e^{-\sum\mu_i}(\sum\mu_i)^n/n!$: expand $(\sum_i\mu_i)^n$ by [F2], then use the product of the component masses. Thus $N_{A_j}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda\sum_i|A_j\cap C_i|=\lambda|A_j|$. The groups of components for different $j$ are disjoint independent families, so their sums remain independent.

Put $\theta=\lambda|A|$. The count mass in step 3.1 gives, by nonnegative partial sums and [F5], $$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{an}e^{-\theta}\frac{\theta^n}{n!}=e^{-\theta}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\theta e^a)^n}{n!}=\exp\!\left(\theta(e^a-1)\right).$$ For $\theta=0$, the count is zero almost surely and both sides are one, so no ambiguous zero power is needed. This establishes the exponential-moment interface before entropy estimates use it.

Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and, for each $j$, consider a finite count-cylinder event in the restriction to $A_j$. Refine the finitely many counting sets in each event into their disjoint atoms inside $A_j$. Step 3.1 gives independent Poisson counts on all these atoms across every $j$; the event for each restricted configuration is a measurable function only of its own atom counts. Thus finite cylinder events factor across $j$. The restriction sigma-fields are generated by these cylinders, so repeated pi-lambda extension proves independence of the restrictions themselves.

For a finite family of bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_s$, partition their union into the finitely many disjoint Boolean atoms formed by the sets and their complements. Every $N_{A_j}$ is a sum of the counts on these atoms. Translation preserves each atom's volume, so step 3.1 gives the same joint distribution of this whole count vector under $Q_\lambda$ and its translate. Thus the laws agree on every finite count cylinder. These cylinders generate the configuration sigma-algebra by [F4], and pi-lambda uniqueness identifies the laws. The one-set count law gives $E_{Q_\lambda}N_A=\lambda|A|$ for bounded $A$. For arbitrary Borel $A$, increase bounded cubes to all space and apply [F5] to the counting measures and Lebesgue measure to obtain the same extended identity. For disjoint Borel $A_n$, the pointwise counting identity $N_{\cup_n A_n}=\sum_nN_{A_n}$ and [F5] show countable additivity of $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}$, while the empty set has expectation zero. Thus the defined intensity functional is a measure and equals $\lambda$ times Lebesgue measure.

boundaries.evidence: The statement covers every finite family; for an empty family the count vector is the unique empty vector and independence is vacuous.

For bounded A of zero Lebesgue volume the Poisson parameter is zero, N_A=0 almost surely and E exp(aN_A)=1; proof3.2 treats this case separately. The intensity measure is zero on every null Borel set.

Assume AC, fix $d\geq1$ and $\lambda>0$, and let $Q_\lambda$ be the configuration law of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Define the intensity measure on Borel sets by $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A):=E_{Q_\lambda}N_A$, where $N_A=\omega(A)$ and the nonnegative expectation may be infinite. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A)=\lambda|A|$ for every Borel $A$. For every bounded Borel $A$ and real $a$, its count also has the exact exponential moment
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$

derivations.claim: For $P\ll Q$ with density $h$, the negative part of $h\log h$ is integrable because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$; the density definition is therefore unambiguous. Also $u\log u\geq u-1$ for $u\geq0$, so $D(P\Vert Q)=\int h\log h\,dQ\geq\int(h-1)\,dQ=0$. If $P\not\ll Q$, the defined value is $+\infty\geq0$.

For bounded $\phi$, let $Q_\phi$ have density $e^\phi/Q(e^\phi)$ relative to $Q$. When $P\ll Q$ and $D(P\Vert Q)<\infty$, the density logarithm identity gives $D(P\Vert Q_\phi)=D(P\Vert Q)-P(\phi)+\log Q(e^\phi)\geq0$ by step 1.1. Thus every variational test is at most $D(P\Vert Q)$; the same upper bound is immediate if $D=+\infty$. If $P\not\ll Q$, choose a measurable $Q$-null set $N$ with $P(N)>0$ and use $\phi=t\mathbf1_N$: then $Q(e^\phi)=1$ and $P(\phi)=tP(N)\to\infty$.

In the remaining case $P\ll Q$, let $h=dP/dQ$ and set $\phi_m=\max(-m,\min(m,\log h))$, taking $\phi_m=-m$ on $\{h=0\}$. Then $e^{\phi_m}\to h$ and $e^{\phi_m}\leq1+h$, so [F4] gives $Q(e^{\phi_m})\to1$. The negative part of $h\phi_m$ is bounded by $1/e$, and its positive part increases to $(h\log h)^+$; hence [F4] gives $P(\phi_m)=\int h\phi_m\,dQ\to D(P\Vert Q)$, including when the positive entropy part is infinite. Combining this with step 2.1 proves the variational identity.

If $T$ is measurable, every bounded test $\psi$ on the target pulls back to the bounded test $\psi\circ T$ on the source, and $Q(e^{\psi\circ T})=(Q\circ T^{-1})(e^\psi)$ while $P(\psi\circ T)=(P\circ T^{-1})(\psi)$. Taking suprema in step 3.1 proves the restriction inequality.

Finiteness of $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)$ gives a joint density and its conditional kernel by [F2]. Pushing forward by $(s,y)\mapsto(r(s),y)$ and using step 4.1 gives finite $D(P_{R,Y}\Vert P_R\otimes Q_Y)$, so [F2] supplies the corresponding conditional kernel for $R$ as well. Thus all conditional densities and references in this clause are defined. For a conditioning observation $R$, applying the variational identity pointwise to the conditional density $k_R(r,y)$ shows $$G(R)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(E_P\phi(R,Y)-E_P\!\left[\log\int e^{\phi(R,y)}Q_Y(dy)\right]\right),$$ where the tests range over bounded measurable functions of $(R,Y)$. The upper bound follows from step 2.1 for each conditional law; the reverse bound follows by using the jointly measurable bounded truncations of $\log k_R$ from step 3.1 and then [F3]–[F4]. When $R$ is a measurable function of $S$, every test depending on $(R,Y)$ is an admissible test depending on $(S,Y)$ with the same objective value, since the $Q_Y$ normalizer still depends only on $R$. Thus $G(R)\leq G(S)$; nonnegativity is step 1.1 applied conditionally.

Suppose $P_{XY}$ has density $h(x,y)$ relative to $Q_X\otimes Q_Y$. Put $h_X(x)=\int h(x,y)Q_Y(dy)$. By [F3], $h_X$ is a density for $P_X$. Where $0<h_X(x)<\infty$, [F2] supplies the conditional density $k(x,y)=h(x,y)/h_X(x)$ relative to $Q_Y$; elsewhere use its supplied filler. On the full $P_X$-measure set of finite positive $h_X$, $h=h_Xk$ and $\log h=\log h_X+\log k$ $P_{XY}$-almost everywhere. Integrating this identity, with nonnegative conditional entropies and finite total entropy, gives the displayed chain rule. If a restriction entropy is infinite, step 4.1 makes the joint entropy infinite as well, so no subtraction of two infinite terms is used.

Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 prove nonnegativity and the variational identity, step 4.1 proves restriction monotonicity, step 5.2 proves the product chain rule, and step 5.1 proves monotonicity under additional conditioning.

Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for random variables $R,S,Y$ taking values in standard-Borel spaces $\mathcal R,\mathcal S,\mathcal Y$, with $R=r(S)$ for a measurable $r:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$, and a probability reference $Q_Y$ on $\mathcal Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)<\infty$.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to one by the exponential power series and addition formula. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$

derivations.claim: If $G_1,G_2$ are disjoint bounded Borel sets, [F1] decomposes $D(P_{G_1\cup G_2}\Vert Q_{G_1}\otimes Q_{G_2})$ into $D(P_{G_1}\Vert Q_{G_1})$ plus the mean conditional relative entropy of $G_2$ given $G_1$. That conditional increment is at least $D(P_{G_2}\Vert Q_{G_2})$ by the conditioning monotonicity in [F1], comparing observation by $G_1$ with no observation. Thus relative entropy is superadditive over disjoint regions; if the left side is infinite the inequality is immediate, and otherwise all terms in the chain rule are finite.

Fix an integer $m\geq1$ and let $q_N=\lfloor N/m\rfloor$. Tile $[0,q_Nm)^d$ by $q_N^d$ disjoint translates of $\Lambda_m$, leaving the Borel remainder $\Lambda_N\setminus[0,q_Nm)^d$. Iterating step 1.1 and using nonnegativity on the remainder gives $$D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})\geq q_N^dD(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m}),$$ because stationarity gives the same entropy for each translated $m$-cube. If $D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})=+\infty$, this forces $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})=+\infty$ for every $N\geq m$.

Put $s=\sup_{m\geq1}m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$. If $s=+\infty$, step 2.1 makes the liminf of $N^{-d}D_N$ exceed every finite bound, so the integer-cube limit is $+\infty=s$. If $s<+\infty$, step 2.1 gives $$\liminf_{N\to\infty}N^{-d}D_N\geq m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$$ for every $m$, since $q_N^d/N^d\to m^{-d}$. Taking the supremum gives liminf at least $s$, while the definition of $s$ gives $N^{-d}D_N\leq s$ for every integer $N$. Hence the integer-cube limit exists and equals $s$.

For real $L\to\infty$, let $N=\lfloor L\rfloor$. The inclusions $\Lambda_N\subseteq\Lambda_L\subseteq\Lambda_{N+1}$ and [F3] give $D_N\leq D_L\leq D_{N+1}$. Since $N/L\to1$ and $(N+1)/L\to1$, step 3.1 squeezes $L^{-d}D_L$ to the same extended limit $s$; if some integer-cube entropy is infinite, monotonicity gives the same conclusion directly.

If $I(P)<\infty$ and $A$ is bounded, choose an integer cube $\Lambda_N+x$ containing $A$. Stationarity [F2] and restriction monotonicity [F3] give $$D(P_A\Vert Q_A)\leq D(P_{\Lambda_N+x}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N+x})=D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})\leq N^d I(P)<\infty.$$ Thus every bounded restriction has finite relative entropy.

Assume AC and let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be stationary for the translations of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For a bounded Borel set $G$, write $P_G$ and $Q_G$ for the restrictions of $P$ and the unit-intensity Poisson reference $Q$ to configurations in $G$. For $L>0$, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and
$$D_L:=D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
Then the specific relative entropy density
$$I(P):=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{D_L}{L^d}$$
exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and satisfies
$$I(P)=\sup_{m\in\mathbb N,\ m\geq1}\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})}{m^d}.$$
If $I(P)<\infty$, every bounded Borel restriction has finite relative entropy. This is an information functional relative to the specified unit-intensity Poisson law; changing the reference changes its value.

derivations.claim: Let $A\subset F_+$ be finite. By [F1], $D(P_{A\cup C}\Vert Q_{A\cup C})$ is finite, so the joint density $h_{A,C}$ relative to $Q_A\otimes Q_C$ exists. The marginal density $h_A$ is its $Q_C$ integral. On $0<h_A<\infty$, [F2] gives the conditional density $k_A=h_{A,C}/h_A$ relative to $Q_C$; the exceptional fibers have $P_A$-measure zero. The chain rule in [F2] gives $g(A)=E_P D(P_{C|A}\Vert Q_C)=D(P_{A\cup C}\Vert Q_{A\cup C})-D(P_A\Vert Q_A)$, so $g(A)$ is finite and nonnegative.
If $A\subseteq B\subset F_+$ are finite, apply the conditional-increment monotonicity in [F2] to observation of the cell configuration on $A$ and then on $B$. It yields $g(A)\leq g(B)$.

To identify the supremum, let $\Lambda_N=[0,N)^d$, the union of $N^d$ unit cells, and order those cells lexicographically. Repeated use of the conditional chain rule decomposes $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})$ as the sum of $g(B_i)$ over its cells $i$, where $B_i$ is the finite set of earlier cells in $\Lambda_N$. Each $B_i$ is a finite subset of $F_+$ after translating cell $i$ to $C$, so $g(B_i)\leq\sup_Ag(A)$ by stationarity and step 2.1. Hence $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})/N^d\leq\sup_Ag(A)$. Conversely, fix finite $A\subset F_+$. For every cell $i$ in the inner cube whose distance from the boundary exceeds the largest coordinate magnitude in $A$, the translated set $i+A$ lies in $B_i$. By step 2.1 and stationarity, $g(B_i)\geq g(A)$. The proportion of these interior cells tends to one, and all other increments are nonnegative by step 1.1. Taking $N\to\infty$ and applying [F1] gives $\gamma\geq g(A)$. Taking the supremum over $A$ proves $\sup_Ag(A)=\gamma$.

Choose an increasing sequence of finite pasts $A_m$ exhausting $F_+$ and set $R=P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$. Lift each $k_{A_m}$ to the common space $(\Omega_{F_+}\times E_C,R)$. Consistency of the conditional densities shows $E_R[k_{A_{m+1}}\mid\mathcal G_m]=k_{A_m}$, where $\mathcal G_m$ is generated by $A_m$ and $C$; also $E_Rk_{A_m}=1$. By step 3.1, $E_R[k_{A_m}\log k_{A_m}]=g(A_m)\leq\gamma$. For $K>1$, splitting at $k_{A_m}=1$ and using $-u\log u\leq1/e$ gives $$\int_{\{k_{A_m}>K\}}k_{A_m}\,dR\leq\frac{\gamma+1/e}{\log K}.$$ Thus these martingale densities are uniformly integrable. By [F3] they converge almost surely and in $L^1(R)$ to $k_\infty\geq0$ with $E_Rk_\infty=1$.

For any finite-past cylinder event and any event in $C$, integrate $k_\infty$ over their product. $L^1(R)$ convergence makes this equal the limit of the same integral against $k_{A_m}$, which is the corresponding joint probability under $P$. These rectangles form a generating pi-system, so [F6] identifies $k_\infty R$ with $P_{F_+\cup C}$. Therefore $k_A=E_R[k_\infty\mid\mathcal G_A]$ for every finite $A\subset F_+$. Fatou applied to $u\log u+1/e\geq0$ gives $D(P_{F_+\cup C}\Vert P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C)\leq\liminf_m g(A_m)=\gamma$. Conversely, its variational supremum contains all finite-past tests, so step 3.1 gives the reverse inequality. Hence $E_P\log k_\infty=\gamma$.

The $L^1(R)$ convergence of $k_{A_m}$ implies convergence in $R$-probability. Since the full joint law has density $k_\infty$ relative to $R$, absolute continuity transfers this to convergence in $P$-probability. Also $k_\infty>0$ $P$-almost surely, so continuity of $\log$ on $(0,\infty)$ gives $\log k_{A_m}\to\log k_\infty$ in $P$-probability. For $t\geq1$, $$E_P\!\left[(-\log k_A)^+\mathbf1_{\{(-\log k_A)^+>t\}}\right]=\int_{\{0<k_A<e^{-t}\}}k_A(-\log k_A)\,dR\leq te^{-t}.$$ Thus the negative parts are uniformly integrable; [F4] gives their $L^1(P)$ convergence.

Since $E_P\log k_{A_m}=g(A_m)\to\gamma=E_P\log k_\infty$ and the negative parts converge in $L^1$, the expectations of the positive parts converge as well. These positive parts converge in probability. For nonnegative variables $Y_m\to Y$ in probability with $E Y_m\to E Y<\infty$, bounded truncations satisfy $E(Y_m\wedge K)\to E(Y\wedge K)$: for any $\eta>0$ the difference is at most $\eta+K\,P(|Y_m-Y|>\eta)$. Consequently $E(Y_m-K)^+\to E(Y-K)^+$; choosing $K$ large and then bounding $Y_m\mathbf1_{Y_m>2K}\leq2(Y_m-K)^+$ proves uniform integrability, including the finite initial segment. Applying [F4] gives $L^1$ convergence of the positive parts. Together with the negative parts this proves $\log k_{A_m}\to\log k_\infty$ in $L^1(P)$.

For any finite $B\supseteq A_m$, the tower property gives $k_B=E_R[k_\infty\mid\mathcal G_B]$ and $k_{A_m}=E_R[k_\infty\mid\mathcal G_m]$. Conditional expectation is an $L^1$ contraction, so $$\sup_{B\supseteq A_m}\|k_B-k_\infty\|_{L^1(R)}\leq2\|k_{A_m}-k_\infty\|_{L^1(R)}\longrightarrow0.$$ Absolute continuity of $P=k_\infty R$ transfers this uniform probability convergence to $P$. The negative-part tail bound in step 6.1 is uniform over all finite $B$, while $g(A_m)\leq g(B)\leq\gamma$ by steps 2.1–1.3. The truncation argument in step 7.1 therefore applies to every sequence $B_m\supseteq A_m$ with $m\to\infty$; if the asserted directed $L^1$ convergence were not uniform, choosing a contradicting sequence $B_m$ would violate that argument. This proves the directed form.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume AC. Let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], have finite specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma<\infty$ relative to the unit-intensity reference $Q$ of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Let $C=[0,1)^d$ be the reference cell and order the other unit cells lexicographically; $F_+$ is the set of cells preceding $C$. For each finite $A\subset F_+$ let $k_A$ be the conditional density of the configuration in $C$ given the configuration in $A$, relative to $Q_C$, as supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$g(A):=E_P[\log k_A]=D(P_{A\cup C}\Vert Q_{A\cup C})-D(P_A\Vert Q_A)$$
is finite, nonnegative, and increasing with finite $A$, with $\sup\{g(A):A\subset F_+\text{ finite}\}=\gamma$. For any increasing finite exhaustion $A_m\uparrow F_+$, the densities $k_{A_m}$ converge in $L^1(P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C)$ to a density $k_\infty$ of $P_{F_+\cup C}$ relative to $P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$, and
$$\log k_{A_m}\longrightarrow\log k_\infty\quad\text{in }L^1(P).$$
The logarithmic convergence is directed: for every $\varepsilon>0$ some finite $A_m$ satisfies $\sup_{B\supseteq A_m,\ B\subset F_+\text{ finite}}E_P|\log k_B-\log k_\infty|<\varepsilon$.

Assume AC, fix $d\geq1$ and $\lambda>0$, and let $Q_\lambda$ be the configuration law of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Define the intensity measure on Borel sets by $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A):=E_{Q_\lambda}N_A$, where $N_A=\omega(A)$ and the nonnegative expectation may be infinite. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A)=\lambda|A|$ for every Borel $A$. For every bounded Borel $A$ and real $a$, its count also has the exact exponential moment
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to one by the exponential power series and addition formula. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. derivations.claim: Let $W=a+[0,m)^d$ be any integer cube, with $a\in\mathbb Z^d$ and integer $m\geq1$. Translation invariance and [F1] give $D(P_W\Vert Q_W)\leq c|W|$. If $A$ is any bounded Borel set, choose one such cube $W$ containing it; by restriction monotonicity [F2], every $P\in\mathcal H_c$ satisfies $D(P_A\Vert Q_A)\leq C_A:=c|W|$.

For any probability density $h$ relative to a probability $Q$ with $D(hQ\Vert Q)\leq C$, and any $K>1$, $$\int_{\{h>K\}}h\,dQ\leq\frac{C+1/e}{\log K}.$$ Indeed, $-u\log u\leq1/e$ on $[0,1]$, while $h\log h\geq h\log K$ on $\{h>K\}$. Split the entropy integral at $h=1$ and combine these bounds. Thus, for each fixed cube $W$, the densities $dP_W/dQ_W$ with $P\in\mathcal H_c$ have $L^1(Q_W)$ norm one and are uniformly integrable.

Fix $W$. By [F3], the weak closure $K_W$ of these densities in real $L^1(Q_W)$ is weakly compact. It is Hausdorff by [F6]. Every $h\in K_W$ remains nonnegative and has integral one: testing against each indicator and against $1$ gives weakly closed conditions by [F6]. Also $D(hQ_W\Vert Q_W)\leq c|W|$, because [F2] expresses $D$ as the supremum of weakly continuous affine functions of $h$, with continuity given by [F6]. Hence all entropy sublevels used below are closed in their local weak topologies.

Index all integer cubes $W=a+[0,m)^d$ with $a\in\mathbb Z^d$ and integer $m\geq1$ by their countable set of pairs $(a,m)$, and form the product $K_*:=\prod_WK_W$. It is compact by [A2] and Hausdorff because each weak $L^1$ topology is Hausdorff by [F6]. Impose the following closed conditions on its tuples: whenever $W\subseteq V$, the $W$-marginal of $h_VQ_V$ equals $h_WQ_W$; and, for every real translation $x$ and bounded local measurable test $f$, the two marginals containing the supports of $f$ and $f\circ T_x$ satisfy $E_Pf=E_P(f\circ T_x)$. Each equality is closed because it tests weak convergence against bounded measurable functions on a containing cube, which are continuous by [F6]. The intersection $K_{\rm stat}$ of these closed conditions is compact.

A tuple in $K_{\rm stat}$ defines consistent finite-dimensional laws on the countable standard-Borel cell spaces: for a finite set of cells, choose any integer cube containing it and take that marginal. If two cubes contain the same finite set, a larger integer cube contains both; the imposed nested consistency makes their induced laws agree. By [F4] there is a unique law $P$ on $\Omega$ with those marginals. The imposed equalities make $P$ stationary, and each origin-anchored cube $[0,m)^d$ retains $D(P_{[0,m)^d}\Vert Q_{[0,m)^d})\leq c m^d$. Therefore [F1] gives $I(P)\leq c$. The extension map identifies $K_{\rm stat}$ with the set of laws having these local marginals and entropy constraints.

The same variational inequality controls particle-count tails uniformly. Fix bounded $A$, choose $W\supseteq A$ as in step 1.1, and let $K\geq0$, $a>0$, and $M\in\mathbb N$. The bounded local test $\phi_M=a\min(N_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}},M)$ in [F2] gives $$aE_P\min(N_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}},M)\leq C_A+\log E_Q\exp(\phi_M).$$ As $M\to\infty$, monotone convergence yields $$aE_P[N_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}}]\leq C_A+\log E_Qe^{aN_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}}}.$$ By [F5] and dominated convergence the logarithmic term tends to zero as $K\to\infty$. First choose $a$ large and then $K$ large; this proves uniform integrability of the counts $N_A$ over every law in the closure family, and in particular finite intensity for its limit laws.

The product compactness in step 3.1 first gives compactness for all bounded local tests. For any tame $f$ supported in $A$ with $|f|\leq b(1+N_A)$, set $f_K=f\mathbf1_{\{N_A\leq K\}}$. Then $f_K$ is bounded and local, and its expectation is weakly continuous by [F6], while $$\sup_{P\in\mathcal H_c}|E_P(f-f_K)|\leq b\sup_{P\in\mathcal H_c}E_P[(1+N_A)\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}}]\longrightarrow0$$ by step 5.1. Thus on the entropy level the tame expectation maps are uniform limits of bounded-local continuous maps. Every $P\in\mathcal H_c$ supplies its cube densities and gives a tuple in $K_{\rm stat}$, so the extension map from $K_{\rm stat}$ is onto; the local expectations just shown make it continuous. Its image $\mathcal H_c$ is compact in $\tau_L$.

Each $K_W$ is weakly compact in real $L^1(Q_W)$ and hence weakly sequentially compact by [F3]. Given a sequence in $K_{\rm stat}$, successively take subsequences converging in the first, second, and later cube coordinates and diagonalize; AC supplies the countable choices. The limit tuple preserves all closed consistency, stationarity, and entropy constraints from step 3.1, so it gives a law in $\mathcal H_c$ by step 4.1. Count-tail uniformity from step 5.1 upgrades coordinate convergence on bounded local tests to convergence for every tame test by the same truncation estimate in step 6.1. Hence $\mathcal H_c$ is sequentially compact in $\tau_L$.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB. Let
$$\mathcal H_c:=\{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega): I(P)\leq c\},\qquad c\in[0,\infty),$$
where $I$ and the local-tame topology $\tau_L$ are defined by [[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]] and [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]. Then $\mathcal H_c$ is compact and sequentially compact in $\tau_L$. This is a pure measure-theoretic compactness theorem for simple locally finite configurations relative to the independent unit-intensity Poisson reference; it makes no thermodynamic-limit or physical claim.

Define the intensity measure on Borel sets by $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A):=E_{Q_\lambda}N_A$, where $N_A=\omega(A)$ and the nonnegative expectation may be infinite. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A)=\lambda|A|$ for every Borel $A$. For every bounded Borel $A$ and real $a$, its count also has the exact exponential moment
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$
