derivations.claim: Let $S_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^d$ be the cell indices in $\Lambda_N$. For $i\in S_N$, set $A_{i,N}=\{j-i:j\in S_N,\ j<_{\rm lex}i\}$; this is a finite subset of the past of the reference cell. Repeated conditional-density factorization from [F3] gives, $P$-almost surely, $$\log h_N(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_N}\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega).$$ Every finite factor is defined $P$-almost surely because the corresponding local relative entropy is finite by [F1].

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the directed convergence in [F2], choose a finite past $A_*$ such that every finite $B\supseteq A_*$ satisfies $E_P|\log k_B-Z|<\varepsilon$. Put $R=\max\{|a_j|:a\in A_*,1\leq j\leq d\}$, with $R=0$ if $A_*=\varnothing$. Let $S_N^\circ$ consist of cells at least $R$ cells from each face of $S_N$. If $i\in S_N^\circ$, then $A_*\subseteq A_{i,N}$, so by stationarity $E_P|\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega)-Z(T_{-i}\omega)|<\varepsilon$. The boundary has $N^d-(N-2R)^d=o(N^d)$ cells (for $N>2R$). For every finite past $B$, $E_P\log k_B=g(B)\leq\gamma$ and $E_P(-\log k_B)^+\leq1/e$, hence $E_P|\log k_B|\leq\gamma+2/e$. For $Z=\log k_\infty$, $E_P(-\log k_\infty)^+=\int_{0<k_\infty<1}k_\infty(-\log k_\infty)\,dR_0\leq1/e$ on its reference probability $R_0=P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$, so [F2] gives $E_P|Z|\leq\gamma+2/e$ as well. Summing the interior errors and bounding each boundary error by $2(\gamma+2/e)$ yields $$\left\|N^{-d}\log h_N-N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z(T_{-i}\cdot)\right\|_{L^1(P)}\longrightarrow0,$$ since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary.

For $j=1,\ldots,d$, the shift $U_jf=f\circ T_{-e_j}$ is a linear isometry on complex $L^2(P)$ by stationarity. Apply [F4] to $N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_j^n$, obtaining strong convergence to the orthogonal projection $P_j$ onto the $U_j$-invariant subspace. The coordinate shifts commute, so every average for coordinate $j$ commutes with every average for coordinate $k$; taking strong limits shows that the $P_j$ commute with each other and with the other coordinate averages. Since all these operators have norm at most one, a finite telescoping estimate gives strong convergence of the product of the $d$ averages to $P_1\cdots P_d$. This product is the orthogonal projection onto the intersection of the coordinate-invariant subspaces, because the $P_j$ are commuting orthogonal projections. The product averages are exactly the rectangular cube averages $N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z_M(T_{-i}\cdot)$, so these converge in $L^2$ for bounded $Z_M$ to a function invariant under every integer shift.

Since $Z\in L^1(P)$, dominated convergence gives $\|Z-Z_M\|_1\to0$. Cube averages are $L^1$ contractions, so the averages of $Z$ are Cauchy in $L^1$: for large $M$ their distance from the convergent averages of $Z_M$ is at most $\|Z-Z_M\|_1$. Let their $L^1$ limit be $s$. Every cube average has mean $E_PZ=\gamma$, hence $E_Ps=\gamma$. For each coordinate shift $e_j$, the averaging index cube and its translate have symmetric difference of exactly $2N^{d-1}$ indices, so $\|U_j A_NZ-A_NZ\|_1\leq2\|Z\|_1/N$. Passing to the $L^1$ limit gives $U_js=s$. These generators imply invariance under every integer translation.

Fix $r\in\mathbb R^d$, put $G=\Lambda_N$, $G'=G+r$, and $B=G\cap G'$. For $N>2\|r\|_\infty$, $B$ contains a cube $J$ of side $N-2\|r\|_\infty$. By [F1] and restriction monotonicity, $D(P_G\Vert Q_G)\leq\gamma N^d$ and $D(P_B\Vert Q_B)\geq D(P_J\Vert Q_J)$; the latter divided by $N^d$ tends to $\gamma$. Therefore $N^{-d}(D(P_G\Vert Q_G)-D(P_B\Vert Q_B))\to0$. The conditional chain rule [F3] identifies $\log h_G-\log h_B$ with a conditional log density. Its mean is this entropy difference, and [F3] bounds its negative-part expectation by $1/e$; thus its $L^1(P)$ norm is at most the entropy difference plus $2/e$. The same bound applies to $G'$. Translation covariance gives $\log h_{G'}=(\log h_G)\circ T_{-r}$; thus the normalized information in $G$ and $G'$ have the same $L^1$ limit. Since $N^{-d}\log h_G\to s$, it follows that $s\circ T_{-r}=s$ $P$-almost surely for this $r$.

Step 5.1 applies to every fixed $r\in\mathbb R^d$. For each rational $q$, the event $\{s\leq q\}$ is therefore invariant modulo null sets under every translation. Full-translation ergodicity makes each such event have probability $0$ or $1$. If $s$ were not almost surely constant, some rational sublevel set would have probability strictly between $0$ and $1$; hence $s$ is constant. Its mean from step 4.1 is $\gamma$, so $s=\gamma$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the asserted $L^1(P)$ limit.

Assume AC. Let $d\geq1$, let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be ergodic under the full translation group $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose its specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma$ relative to the unit-intensity Poisson law $Q$ is finite. Ergodic means that every measurable event invariant modulo $P$-null sets under each translation has probability $0$ or $1$. For an integer $N\geq1$, let $\Lambda_N=[0,N)^d$, and let $h_N=dP_{\Lambda_N}/dQ_{\Lambda_N}$, which exists because $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})<\infty$. Then
$$\frac{1}{N^d}\log h_N\longrightarrow\gamma\qquad\text{in }L^1(P).$$
Without the full-translation ergodicity hypothesis the proof yields an invariant $L^1(P)$ limit of mean $\gamma$; it need not be constant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to one by the exponential power series and addition formula. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

derivations.claim: In one unit cell, the conditional distribution of point positions given the count is identical for $Q_z$ and $Q_1$. The ratio of their count probabilities at $n$ is $$\frac{e^{-z}z^n/n!}{e^{-1}/n!}=e^{1-z}z^n.$$ Thus this is the Radon–Nikodym density on that cell.

The cube $\Lambda_m=[0,m)^d$ is the disjoint union of $m^d$ unit cells. Independence in [F1] makes the finite-cube density the product of the cell densities: $$h_m(\omega)=e^{(1-z)m^d}z^{N_{\Lambda_m}(\omega)}.$$

The count $N_{\Lambda_m}$ is Poisson with mean $zm^d$ by [F1]. Directly from its mass function and the exponential series, $$E_PN_{\Lambda_m}=e^{-zm^d}\sum_{n\geq1}n\frac{(zm^d)^n}{n!}=zm^d e^{-zm^d}\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{(zm^d)^k}{k!}=zm^d.$$ Therefore [F2] gives $$\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})}{m^d}=\frac{E_P\log h_m}{m^d}=1-z+z\log z$$ for every positive integer $m$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to one by the exponential power series and addition formula. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. Axiom of Countable Choice
Adopt as one selected regulated physical model

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Gamma=(V,E,s,t,\mathcal P)$ be a finite oriented graph with nonempty finite vertex set $V$, nonempty finite link set $E$, endpoint maps $s,t:E\to V$, and a finite list $\mathcal P$ of oriented simple cycles. Parallel links and self-loops are allowed. An oriented simple cycle $p\in\mathcal P$ is a finite closed path using each link at most once; write $\sigma_{p,e}\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for its signed use of link $e$, so its signed incidence at every vertex is zero. Fix enumerations $E=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_N)$ and $V=(v_1,\ldots,v_M)$, where $N=|E|$ and $M=|V|$. Write $\mathbb T_1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb T_{2\pi}=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$, and set $\mathbb T=\mathbb T_{2\pi}$ with normalized Haar measure $d\theta/(2\pi)$ and product measure $m_E$ on $\mathbb T^E$.

The coordinatewise map
$$\Phi_E:\mathbb T_{2\pi}^E\to\mathbb T_1^E,\qquad ([\theta_e])_{e\in E}\mapsto([\theta_e/(2\pi)])_{e\in E},$$
is a well-defined measure-preserving group isomorphism for the normalized product Haar measures. The fixed enumeration of $E$ identifies $\mathbb T_1^E$ with $\mathbb T_1^N$; pulling back the Fourier characters $x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\sum_{e\in E}n_ex_e)$ along $\Phi_E$ gives $e_{\mathbf n}(\theta)=\exp(i\sum_{e\in E}n_e\theta_e)$. Thus the Fourier basis theorem [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], whose torus is $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and whose characters are $\exp(2\pi i kx)$, gives an orthonormal basis $\{e_{\mathbf n}:\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^E\}$ of $L^2(\mathbb T^E)$. The second-variable-linear $L^2$ pairing used below is the conjugate of the first-variable-linear pairing in that theorem, so orthonormality and completeness are unchanged.

Fix an integer $s\ge1$ and let $\mathcal K=\bigoplus_{x\in V}\mathbb C^s$ with orthonormal modes $e_{x\alpha}$, $1\le\alpha\le s$. This is finite-dimensional and hence separable. Fix the lexicographic order on $J=V\times\{1,\ldots,s\}$ induced by the chosen order on $V$ and the usual order on $\{1,\ldots,s\}$. Use the antisymmetric Fock space and second-variable-linear inner product convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The current draft supplier [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] states that, assuming Countable Choice, $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$ is a Hilbert space and its creation and annihilation operators are bounded and satisfy the CAR; that supplier is still a draft carrier, not an accepted result in this run. For $\mathbf m=(m_{x\alpha})\in\{0,1\}^J$, put $S(\mathbf m)=\{(x,\alpha):m_{x\alpha}=1\}$ and write $\xi_{\mathbf m}=\xi_{S(\mathbf m)}$ for the ordered wedge basis vector of [[lem-qft-finite-mode-occupation-basis]]. This is a complete orthonormal basis of $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$; changing the chosen order changes individual wedge vectors only by signs. Write $c_{x\alpha}=c(e_{x\alpha})$, $c^\dagger_{x\alpha}=c^\dagger(e_{x\alpha})$, and $n_x=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s c^\dagger_{x\alpha}c_{x\alpha}$. On $\xi_{\mathbf m}$, $n_x$ acts by $N_x(\mathbf m)=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}$; it is bounded self-adjoint with spectrum contained in $\{0,\ldots,s\}$.

Use the second-variable-linear $L^2$ pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb T^E}\overline{f(\theta)}g(\theta)\,dm_E(\theta)$. The kinematical Hilbert space is
$$\mathcal H_{\rm kin}=L^2(\mathbb T^E)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K),$$
where $\widehat\otimes$ has the same completion norm as [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] and the second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating its first-variable-linear tensor pairing, as in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Concretely, the tensor supplier is applied to the conjugate first-variable-linear pairings $(f,g)_1=\langle g,f\rangle_2$ and $(\Phi,\Psi)_1=\langle\Psi,\Phi\rangle_2$, and the resulting tensor pairing is conjugated; this preserves the norm and the product-basis assertion. Consequently
$$\{e_{\mathbf n}\otimes\xi_{\mathbf m}:\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^E,\ \mathbf m\in\{0,1\}^J\}$$
is a complete orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ by the product-basis assertion of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. This is the joint basis used for all diagonal multipliers below. Write
$\psi=\sum_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}e_{\mathbf n}\otimes\xi_{\mathbf m}$.
All matter operators previously defined on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$ act on
$\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ as identity on the rotor factor tensor that operator.
On the full kinematical basis define
$$E_e(e_{\mathbf n}\otimes\xi_{\mathbf m})=n_e(e_{\mathbf n}\otimes\xi_{\mathbf m}),\qquad D(E_e)=\left\{\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}:\sum_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}n_e^2|\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Thus $E_e$ is the maximal real diagonal multiplier, self-adjoint with integer
spectrum, and on its domain its coefficients are $n_e\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}$.
Define the bounded unitary $U_e$ as multiplication by $e^{i\theta_e}$ on the
rotor factor and identity on the matter factor. Equivalently,
$$U_e(e_{\mathbf n}\otimes\xi_{\mathbf m})=e_{\mathbf n+\delta_e}\otimes\xi_{\mathbf m},\qquad (U_e\psi)_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}=\psi_{\mathbf n-\delta_e,\mathbf m}.$$
Each $U_f$ preserves $D(E_e)$, since
$(n_e+\delta_{ef})^2\le2n_e^2+2$ and the coefficient sequence is square
summable; its inverse preserves that domain by the same estimate. Computing
on coefficients gives $[E_e,U_f]=\delta_{ef}U_f$ on $D(E_e)$.


Fix background integers $b_x\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$. In the joint basis define the real integer multiplier
$$\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)=\sum_{e:s(e)=x}n_e-\sum_{e:t(e)=x}n_e-\left(\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}-b_x\right),$$
and let $G_x$ be its maximal diagonal operator, with domain $D(G_x)=\{\psi:\sum_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)|^2|\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty\}$. On the common link-electric domain this is the finite sum $\sum_{s(e)=x}E_e-\sum_{t(e)=x}E_e-(n_x-b_xI)$. These are the Gauss operators; the operator constraint defines $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}:=\bigcap_{x\in V}\ker G_x$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb T^V$ define the diagonal multiplier $U(\alpha)=\exp(i\sum_x\alpha_xG_x)$; the next lemma proves that these operators form a strongly continuous representation and that their normalized Haar average is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$.

For each $x$, choose a Hermitian matrix $M_x\in M_s(\mathbb C)$, and for each link $e$ choose a matrix $T_e\in M_s(\mathbb C)$. Choose real coefficients $\lambda_E>0$ and $\lambda_p\in\mathbb R$ for $p\in\mathcal P$. Write
$$W_p=\prod_{e\in E}U_e^{\sigma_{p,e}},\qquad V_B=-\frac12\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\lambda_p(W_p+W_p^\dagger),$$
and
$$V_F=\sum_{x\in V}\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^s c^\dagger_{x\alpha}(M_x)_{\alpha\beta}c_{x\beta}+\sum_{e\in E}\left(A_e+A_e^\dagger\right),\qquad A_e=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^s c^\dagger_{s(e),\alpha}(T_e)_{\alpha\beta}U_e c_{t(e),\beta}.$$
The operator $H_0=\lambda_E\sum_{e\in E}E_e^2$ is the diagonal multiplier with domain
$$D(H_0)=\left\{\psi:\sum_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}\left(\lambda_E\sum_{e\in E}n_e^2\right)^2|\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty\right\},$$
where $\mathbf m=(m_{x\alpha})$ ranges over occupation configurations with each $m_{x\alpha}\in\{0,1\}$, and $N_x(\mathbf m)=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}$ is the eigenvalue of $n_x$ on that basis vector. The coefficients $\lambda_E,\lambda_p$ and entries of $M_x,T_e$ are ordinary real or complex scalars here; no physical units are assigned. Set $H=H_0+V_B+V_F$ on $D(H_0)$. This is a mathematical finite-graph regulator definition. It asserts no physical adoption, continuum limit, Lorentz invariance, or identification with a particular continuum QED model.

For sign comparison only, if a smooth path $\gamma_e:[0,1]\to X$ in a smooth manifold $X$, a real $C^1$ connection one-form $a$, and a real $C^1$ function $\lambda$ are supplied, take $U_e^{\rm cont}=\exp(-ig\int_0^1a_{\gamma_e(r)}(\dot\gamma_e(r))\,dr)$ for real $g$. $$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$

For $\mathbf n\in S^2$, set
$b(\mathbf n)=\lambda(I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T)\mathbf e$. Then
$\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$. Since $\mathbf e$ is unit,
$|b(\mathbf n)|^2=\lambda^2(1-(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e)^2)$. The function
is continuous on $S^2$ and hence measurable.

By the orthogonal invariance in [F4], take $\mathbf e$ as the third coordinate axis and put $u=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e$. The chart $X(u,\phi)=(\sqrt{1-u^2}\cos\phi,\sqrt{1-u^2}\sin\phi,u)$ for $-1<u<1$, $0<\phi<2\pi$ has orthogonal tangent vectors with squared lengths $(1-u^2)^{-1}$ and $1-u^2$, so [F5] gives area density $1$. The omitted seam is a coordinate line in sphere graph charts and the poles are singletons; [F7] makes their chart integrals zero. Thus spherical integration gives
$$C_b=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2d\Omega =2\pi\lambda^2\int_{-1}^1(1-u^2)\,du =\frac{8\pi\lambda^2}{3}>0.$$
Using $d^3\mathbf k=r^2dr\,d\Omega$ and
$|f_\epsilon(r\mathbf n)|^2=r^{-3}|b(\mathbf n)|^2$ gives
$$\|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\int_\epsilon^\kappa\frac{dr}{r} =C_b\log(\kappa/\epsilon),\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}\hbar c|\mathbf k||f_\epsilon(\mathbf k)|^2d^3\mathbf k =\hbar c C_b\int_\epsilon^\kappa dr =\hbar c C_b(\kappa-\epsilon).$$
Both integrals are finite because $0<\epsilon<\kappa$. The profile has units
$\mathrm m^{3/2}$ because $|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}$ has those units and $b$ is
dimensionless; the energy integral has units joules because $\hbar c$ has
units joule-metres. Thus $b$ satisfies the nonzero transverse-profile
hypothesis of [L2] with the conventions [F1].

The definition of $b$ gives
$f_\epsilon(\mathbf k)=\mathbf1_{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa}
|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b(\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|)$. Applying [L2] with
$C_b=8\pi\lambda^2/3$ and the Hamiltonian of [L1] gives the normalized
coherent vector, its energy domain membership, both expectation
formulas, weak convergence to zero, and failure of strong Fock-space
convergence. For the number domain, put $r=\|f_\epsilon\|^2$. By [F3],
its squared sector norms are $e^{-r}r^n/n!$, so reindexing the absolutely
convergent exponential series gives
$\sum_{n\ge1}n^2e^{-r}r^n/n!=r^2+r<\infty$. The maximal number
multiplier from [F6] therefore contains this vector in its domain. This
restriction to the transverse space preserves the domain because each
sector multiplier $nI$ preserves every transverse symmetric sector. The item-level suppliers are present in the active manifests,
but [L1] has no Step-1 record and [L2] is escalated, so this application
remains conditional rather than accepted.

Let $\epsilon_j=\kappa 2^{-j}$ for $j\ge1$. By step 3.1 the difference
$f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}$ is supported on
$\epsilon_{j+1}<|\mathbf k|<\epsilon_j$, so spherical integration gives
$$\|f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}\|^2 =C_b\int_{\epsilon_{j+1}}^{\epsilon_j}\frac{dr}{r} =C_b\log 2>0.$$
From the Fock direct-sum pairing in [F3], the tensor product pairing on

$$\langle C(f),C(g)\rangle =e^{-(\|f\|^2+\|g\|^2)/2} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\langle f,g\rangle^n}{n!} =e^{-(\|f\|^2+\|g\|^2)/2+\langle f,g\rangle},$$
where the series is absolutely convergent by
$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|\|g\|$. Hence
 $|\langle C(f),C(g)\rangle|=e^{-\|f-g\|^2/2}$. By [L2],
$\|C(f_{\epsilon_j})\|=1$ for each $j$. For any choices of phases

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

citations.quote:
Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$
The function $L:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: The integrand is nonnegative, so [F3] factors the position and momentum integrals: $$Z_N=\frac1{N!h^{dN}}\int_{\Lambda_N^N}\int_{\mathbb R^{dN}} e^{-\beta\sum_i|p_i|^2/(2m)}\,dp\,dq =\frac{V_N^N}{N!h^{dN}}\left(\int_\mathbb R e^{-\beta p^2/(2m)}\,dp\right)^{dN}.$$ By [F4]–[F5] the one-coordinate integral is $\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$, proving the stated exact formula with $\lambda_\beta=h\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. The dimensions are consistent: $\lambda_\beta$ is a length, so $V_N^N/\lambda_\beta^{dN}$ and $Z_N$ are dimensionless. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5]

Let $G$ have the density in [A2]. By [F4]–[F5], it is normalized. Apply [F7] on $[-R,R]$ first with $u(x)=x$, $v'(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$, and then with $u(x)=x^3$, $v'(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$. In each case $v(x)=-e^{-x^2/2}$. Letting $R\to\infty$, the endpoint terms vanish by [F8], giving $\mathbb E G^2=1$ and $\mathbb E G^4=3$. Thus $\mathbb E(G^2-1)=0$ and $\mathbb E(G^2-1)^2=2$. Product measure and [F3] make distinct coordinates independent, so expanding the square and factoring cross integrals gives $$\mathbb E(A_N-1)^2=M^{-2}\sum_{a=1}^M2=2/M.$$ For any $\eta>0$, $\eta^2\mathbf1_{\{|A_N-1|>\eta\}}\le(A_N-1)^2$, so integration proves $P(|A_N-1|>\eta)\le2/(M\eta^2)\to0$. Hence $A_N\to1$ in probability. [A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

Monotonicity of $\log$ from [F6] gives $\int_1^N\log x\,dx\le\log N!\le\int_1^{N+1}\log x\,dx$, hence $\log N!=N\log N-N+O(\log(N+1))$. Substituting the exact $Z_N$ yields $$N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log(V_N/N)+1-d\log\lambda_\beta+o(1)\to-\log\rho+1-d\log\lambda_\beta.$$ Multiplication by $-\beta^{-1}$ proves the per-particle limit; multiplying by $N/V_N\to\rho$ proves the per-volume limit. [A1, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

Since $A_N>0$ almost surely, the shell-prepared variables are defined. Algebra gives $$\sum_{a=1}^{dN}\frac{(P_a^{\rm sh})^2}{2m} =\frac1{2\beta A_N}\sum_aG_a^2=\frac{M}{2\beta}=\frac{dN}{2\beta}.$$ This exact energy constraint holds on every outcome where $A_N>0$, an event of probability one since the joint Gaussian density assigns zero mass to the origin. [A2, step 1.2]

For fixed $r$, the scalar multiplier $A_N^{-1/2}$ tends to $1$ in probability by continuity at $1$ and step 1.2. Therefore $(P_1^{\rm sh},\ldots,P_r^{\rm sh})-(P_1^{\rm can},\ldots,P_r^{\rm can})$ tends to zero in probability: restrict first to the event $\sum_{a=1}^rG_a^2\le R^2$, where its norm is at most $\sqrt{m/\beta}R|A_N^{-1/2}-1|$, and then bound the complement by $P(\sum_{a=1}^rG_a^2>R^2)\le r/R^2$ using the second moment. For bounded continuous $\psi$, choose $R$ so this tail is small, use uniform continuity of $\psi$ on the compact ball of radius $2\sqrt{m/\beta}R$, and then use convergence in probability of the difference. On the complement the expectation difference is at most $2\|\psi\|_\infty$. Sending first $N\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$ proves the claimed expectation limit. [A2, F1, F3, step 1.2]

If positions are included, choose them independently and uniformly in the same cube under both preparations. After coordinatewise rescaling by the side length, every fixed position block already has the same uniform law in both models and is independent of the momentum vector. The same bounded-continuous test argument as in 2.3, first on compact sets and then on their small tails, proves the joint fixed-block limit. This does not change the energy computation because the Hamiltonian has no position dependence. [A1, A2, F1, step 2.3] ∎

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Fix dimension $d\ge1$, particle mass $m>0$, action reference $h>0$, inverse energy $\beta>0$, and positive cube volumes $V_N$ with $N/V_N\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$. For $N$ indistinguishable classical noninteracting particles in a cube of volume $V_N$, use the phase-space reference $dq\,dp/(N!h^{dN})$ and Hamiltonian $H_N(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N|p_i|^2/(2m)$. Define $\lambda_\beta=h\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. Then the dimensionless partition integral and free-energy limits are
$$Z_N=\frac{V_N^N}{N!\lambda_\beta^{dN}},\quad\frac{-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N}{N}\longrightarrow\beta^{-1}[\log(\rho\lambda_\beta^d)-1],\quad\frac{-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N}{V_N}\longrightarrow\beta^{-1}\rho[\log(\rho\lambda_\beta^d)-1].$$
There is also the following finite-momentum-block limit. Let $M=dN$, let $G_1,\ldots,G_M$ be independent standard normal variables, set $A_N=M^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^MG_a^2$, and define canonical momenta $P_a^{\rm can}=\sqrt{m/\beta}\,G_a$ and shell-prepared momenta $P_a^{\rm sh}=\sqrt{m/\beta}\,G_a/\sqrt{A_N}$. The shell-prepared vector has exactly energy $dN/(2\beta)$, and for every fixed $r$ and bounded continuous $\psi:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E\psi(P_1^{\rm sh},\ldots,P_r^{\rm sh})\longrightarrow\mathbb E\psi(P_1^{\rm can},\ldots,P_r^{\rm can}).$$
This is weak convergence for each fixed block in this free-particle model. The shell preparation is the stated normalized-Gaussian construction, and no finite-width shell or interacting-gas equivalence is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$, its **Hamiltonian vector field** is the vector field
$X_H$ determined by the library sign convention

$$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH.$$

A vector field $X$ is **Hamiltonian** if $\iota_X\omega=dH$ for some smooth
function $H$; such an $H$ is a **Hamiltonian function for $X$**. A function and
its vector field are distinct data, and completeness of $X_H$ is not assumed.

If $(M^{2n},\omega)$ is symplectic, then
$\mu_\omega=\omega^n/n!$ is a nowhere-zero volume form. Its positive ray gives
the canonical **symplectic orientation** of $M$.

On a $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold, every Hamiltonian local flow
preserves the Liouville volume form $\Omega=\omega^n/n!$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable self-map $T:X\to X$ is **measure preserving** if $\mu(T^{-1}E)=\mu(E)$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$. The quadruple $(X,\mathcal A,\mu,T)$ is a **measure-preserving system**; it is a probability system if $\mu(X)=1$. Here $T^{-1}E=\{x:T(x)\in E\}$ denotes an inverse image, whether or not $T$ is invertible. Neither completeness nor finiteness is implicit. The measure-space and measurable-map conventions are [[def-measure-space]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

If $T$ preserves $\mu$ and $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable, then $\int f\circ T\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu$, allowing infinity. If $f$ is integrable real or complex valued, $f\circ T$ is integrable and the same equality holds. Conversely, for a measurable self-map, equality for every measurable indicator implies measure preservation.
In a measure-preserving system $(X,\mathcal A,\mu,T)$ with $\mu(X)<\infty$, for every $E\in\mathcal A$ almost every $x\in E$ has $T^nx\in E$ for infinitely many positive integers $n$.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

Let $\mu$ be sigma-finite, let $T$ preserve $\mu$, and let $f$ be a
finite-valued real- or complex-valued measurable representative in
$\mathcal L^1(\mu)$.  Then $A_nf$ converges $\mu$-almost everywhere to a
finite-valued integrable function $f^*$ satisfying

$$f^*\circ T=f^*\quad\mu\text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \lVert f^*\rVert_1\leq\lVert f\rVert_1.$$

The a.e. class of $f^*$ depends only on the a.e. class of $f$.  No ergodicity,
finite total measure, completeness, or invertibility is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.  Let $T$ preserve an ergodic measure $\mu$ with
$0<\mu(X)<\infty$.  For every real- or complex-valued $f\in L^1(\mu)$,

$$A_nf\longrightarrow \frac1{\mu(X)}\int_Xf\,d\mu$$

both $\mu$-almost everywhere and in $L^1(\mu)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\omega$ is closed and $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. The Hamiltonian-flow theorem [F2], under its local existence domain, gives $\phi_t^*\omega=\omega$ and hence $\phi_t^*(\omega^n/n!)=\omega^n/n!$. The volume measure defined by this positive form is therefore preserved on each invariant domain; restriction to $R$ gives the measure-preserving system of [F3]. Also $dH(X_H)=\omega(X_H,X_H)=0$ because a two-form is alternating, so each defined orbit stays on its energy level. This argument grants no flow outside its domain. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

Apply [F3] to $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$. It preserves $\int p_t\,dm=\int p_0\,dm=1$. The scalar function $u\mapsto u\log u$, defined to be $0$ at $u=0$ by [A3], is Borel; its absolute integrability is preserved because the same measure-preserving substitution gives $$\int_R|p_t\log p_t|\,dm=\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty.$$ Applying integral invariance to its positive and negative parts proves $\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm=\int_Rp_0\log p_0\,dm$, hence the stated fine-grained entropy conservation. [A2, A3, F3, F6, step 1.1]

The map $T$ on $R$ is measure preserving by 1.1 and [A2]. Its total measure is finite, so [F4] gives infinite returns for almost every point in each measurable $E\subseteq R$. The conclusion is explicitly almost everywhere and applies to the sampled map at the specified $\tau$. [A2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

Under the additional probability and ergodicity assumptions in [A2], the hypotheses of [F5] hold for each $f\in L^1(R,m)$. Birkhoff therefore gives almost-everywhere and $L^1$ convergence to the invariant conditional expectation, and its ergodic corollary identifies that limit with $\int_R f\,dm$. If ergodicity is removed, only the invariant conditional expectation conclusion remains. Neither [F2] nor recurrence [F4] supplies ergodicity. [A2, F5, step 1.1] ∎

Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $a:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The **convex hull** $\operatorname{conv}K$ is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$. A **phase generator** is a point $y\in K$ with declared energy $a(y)$. A **mixture** is a Borel probability measure $P$ on $K$. Its barycenter and mean energy are the coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals
$$\bar y(P):=\int_K y\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R^d,\qquad \bar a(P):=\int_K a(y)\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R.$$
These integrals are finite because each coordinate and $a$ are bounded on compact $K$. For prescribed mean $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, the **mixture energy** is
$$a_{\rm mix}(x):=\inf\{\bar a(P):P\text{ is a Borel probability on }K,\ \bar y(P)=x\}.$$
The admissible set is nonempty since every finite convex combination of points of $K$ is the barycenter of a finite atomic probability. The definition does not assert that the infimum is attained; the theorem on this page gives a compact continuous sufficient condition.

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: Define $\Phi(y)=(y,a(y))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and $G=\Phi(K)$. The map $\Phi$ is continuous. The set $G$ is bounded because $\Phi[K]$ is bounded on compact $K$; it is closed because from any convergent sequence $\Phi(y_n)$, [F3] gives a subsequence $y_{n_j}\to y\in K$, and continuity gives $\Phi(y_{n_j})\to\Phi(y)$. Thus [F3] makes $G$ compact.

Any finite convex combination of more than $d+2$ points of $G\subset\mathbb R^{d+1}$ has an affine dependence: there are coefficients $c_i$, not all zero, with $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i g_i=0$. Both signs occur. If its positive weights are $\theta_i$, replacing them by $\theta_i-tc_i$, where $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$, preserves their sum and combination, keeps them nonnegative, and makes at least one zero. Repeating gives at most $d+2$ points. Pad shorter combinations by zero weights and repeat any fixed point of nonempty $G$. It follows that $\operatorname{conv}G$ is the continuous image of the compact finite-dimensional parameter set $G^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$, where $\Delta_{d+2}=\{\theta_i\ge0:\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$. This set is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F3]; the same sequential argument as in 1.1 shows its image is compact.

Fix $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Its fiber $F_x=\{r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G\}$ is nonempty, since each finite convex combination of generators gives such a point, and compact, since it is a closed section of compact $\operatorname{conv}G$. Therefore [F4] gives a minimum $r_x$. A convex-combination representation of $(x,r_x)$ by points $(y_i,a(y_i))$ defines a finite atomic Borel probability $P_x$ with barycenter $x$ and energy $r_x$.

Conversely, for any Borel probability $P$ on $K$, the vector-valued map $\Phi$ is bounded and coordinatewise integrable by [F2]. Its integral is in $\operatorname{conv}G$: for each $\epsilon>0$, uniform continuity of $\Phi$ gives a finite Borel partition of $K$ whose pieces have image diameter at most $\epsilon$. Choose a point in each nonempty piece and weight it by that piece's $P$-mass. The resulting finite convex combination differs coordinatewise from $\int\Phi\,dP$ by at most $\epsilon$; as $\operatorname{conv}G$ is closed by step 2.1, the integral belongs to it. If $\bar y(P)=x$, then $(x,\bar a(P))\in\operatorname{conv}G$, so $\bar a(P)\ge r_x$. Together with step 3.1 this proves that the all-measure infimum equals $r_x$ and is attained by $P_x$.

To prove lower semicontinuity, let $x_n\to x$ in $\operatorname{conv}K$ and pass to a subsequence along which $a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$ tends to its liminf. The values lie between $\min_K a$ and $\max_K a$, attained by [F4], so a further subsequence of $(x_n,a_{\rm mix}(x_n))$ converges. Each pair lies in the compact set $\operatorname{conv}G$ by step 4.1; its limit is therefore $(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G$. The minimum in the fiber at $x$ satisfies $a_{\rm mix}(x)\le r=\liminf_n a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$.

Combine minimizers $P_x$ and $P_z$ with weights $s$ and $1-s$, $0\le s\le1$. The combined finite measure has barycenter $sx+(1-s)z$ and energy $s a_{\rm mix}(x)+(1-s)a_{\rm mix}(z)$. By step 4.1, the minimum at the combined barycenter is no greater than this value. Hence $a_{\rm mix}$ is convex.

The support reduction in 2.1 first gives at most $d+2$ atoms. If an optimal representation has more than $d+1$ positive weights, the points $y_i\in\mathbb R^d$ have an affine dependence $\sum_i c_i y_i=0$, $\sum_i c_i=0$. For sufficiently small positive $t$, both weight lists $\theta_i\pm t c_i$ remain nonnegative and preserve the barycenter. If $\sum_i c_i a(y_i)\ne0$, one of these lists strictly lowers energy, contradicting optimality; hence this sum is zero. Increase $t$ in one sign to the first value at which a positive coefficient becomes zero. The new weights preserve barycenter and energy and still attain the minimum; iteration leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights.

Finally, let $g$ be any convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ with $g(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$. For the finite optimal measure from 4.1, finite Jensen (obtained by iterating the two-point convexity inequality) gives $g(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i g(y_i)\le\sum_i\theta_i a(y_i)=a_{\rm mix}(x)$. Since $a_{\rm mix}(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$ by the point mass at $y$, it is itself such a convex minorant and dominates every other one.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: The nonempty generator hypothesis is used to construct G and a fiber minimizer .
Statement: Zero energy values are allowed; bounded minima and the point-mass comparison cover them .
Statement: The single-generator case has a singleton fiber and a one-atom optimizer .
Statement: Affine dependence removes redundant or repeated support points without changing the optimum .
Statement: Every boundary point x of conv K has a nonempty compact fiber; does not require interiority.
Statement: The minimum is obtained from a compact nonempty fiber and represented by finitely many generators .

citations.quote:
Fix a finite alphabet $A=\{1,\ldots,q\}$, $q\ge1$, and real single-site energies $e_1,\ldots,e_q$ in a fixed energy unit. At inverse parameter $\beta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$Z_1(\beta):=\sum_{j=1}^q e^{-\beta e_j},\qquad p_j(\beta):=e^{-\beta e_j}/Z_1(\beta),\qquad E(\beta):=\sum_{j=1}^q p_j(\beta)e_j.$$
For $N\ge1$, a configuration $i=(i_1,\ldots,i_N)\in A^N$ has additive energy $H_N(i):=\sum_{r=1}^Ne_{i_r}$. Given a width $\delta_N\ge0$, the **shell** is
$$\Gamma_N(\beta,\delta_N):=\{i\in A^N:|H_N(i)-NE(\beta)|\le\delta_N\}.$$
When this finite set is nonempty, its microcanonical law means the uniform probability on $\Gamma_N$, and its dimensionless entropy is $\log|\Gamma_N|$. A type is a vector $t=(n_1/N,\ldots,n_q/N)$, where the nonnegative integer counts sum to $N$; its multiplicity is $N!/\prod_j n_j!$.

The convention fixes both the shell center and the law within the shell. It makes no physical claim that an apparatus has resolution $\delta_N$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: For a type $t_j=n_j/N$, the number of configurations of that type is $M(n)=N!/\prod_j n_j!$. The increasing function $\log x$ gives $$\int_1^m\log x\,dx\le\log(m!)\le\int_1^{m+1}\log x\,dx\quad(m\ge1).$$ Evaluating the antiderivative $x\log x-x$ and using $\log(1+1/m)\le1/m$ shows $\log(m!)=m\log m-m+O(\log(m+1)+1)$ with an absolute constant; the case $m=0$ uses $0!=1$ and $0\log0=0$. Subtracting the $q$ denominator estimates from the numerator estimate gives a constant $C_q$ such that $$NH(t)-C_q\log(N+1)-C_q\le\log M(n)\le NH(t)+C_q\log(N+1)+C_q,$$ where $H(t)=-\sum_jt_j\log t_j$. The sharper upper bound $M(n)\le e^{NH(t)}$ follows by expanding $1=(\sum_jt_j)^N$ and retaining the nonnegative terms with counts $n$.

For any probability vector $t$, define $D(t\Vert p)=\sum_{j:t_j>0}t_j\log(t_j/p_j)$. Since $\log u\le u-1$ for $u>0$ (integrate $1/x$ on either side of $1$ using [F4]), $$D(t\Vert p)\ge\sum_{j:t_j>0}(t_j-p_j)=1-\sum_{j:t_j>0}p_j\ge0.$$ Equality forces every $p_j$ to be included and each ratio $t_j/p_j$ to equal $1$, so $t=p$. Also $\log p_j=-\beta e_j-\log Z_1$, hence $D(t\Vert p)=-H(t)+\beta\sum_jt_je_j+\log Z_1$. In particular, among types of exact mean energy $E$, entropy is at most $H(p)$, with equality only at $p$.

Round down $Np_j$ for $j<q$ and put the remainder in $n_q$. Then $|n_j/N-p_j|\le1/N$ for $j<q$ and $|n_q/N-p_q|\le(q-1)/N$. Thus $$\left|\sum_jn_je_j-NE\right|\le\sum_{j<q}|e_j|+(q-1)|e_q|\le q\sum_j|e_j|\le\delta_N.$$ This type belongs to $\Gamma_N$, proving nonemptiness. Its frequencies tend to $p$, and continuity of $-x\log x$ at zero gives $H(t)\to H(p)$. By the lower bound in 1.1, the shell contains at least $\exp(NH(p)-o(N))$ configurations.

Fix $\epsilon>0$. There are $\eta>0$ and $\tau>0$ such that $|t-p|\ge\epsilon$ and $|\sum_jt_je_j-E|\le\tau$ imply $H(t)\le H(p)-\eta$. Otherwise, choosing tolerance $1/n$ and entropy at least $H(p)-1/n$, compactness [F5] gives a subsequential limit $t_*$ with mean $E$, distance at least $\epsilon$, and entropy $H(p)$. Continuity of $H$ and the equality characterization in step 1.2 force $t_*=p$, a contradiction. For large $N$, $\delta_N/N\le\tau$; therefore every shell type outside the $\epsilon$-ball has entropy at most $H(p)-\eta$. There are at most $(N+1)^q$ types, and 1.1 bounds the number of configurations of each by $\exp[NH(t)]$. Dividing this upper bound by the shell lower bound in step 2.1 shows that the shell probability of types outside that ball tends to zero exponentially. Thus the random type converges in probability to $p$.

Conditional on a type $t$, a uniform configuration is a uniformly ordered list of its $N$ labeled positions. Couple the first $k$ draws without replacement with $k$ independent uniform position draws: if the independent positions are distinct, keep them; if not, replace them by an independently chosen uniform ordered distinct $k$-tuple. The resulting tuple is uniform among distinct positions and agrees with the original draws except on the collision event. A union bound over the $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs gives collision probability at most $k(k-1)/(2N)$. Hence the type-conditional label marginal differs in total variation from $t^{\otimes k}$ by at most this quantity. Since $t\to p$ in probability and each of the finitely many probabilities $\prod_{r=1}^k t_{i_r}$ is continuous and bounded on the simplex, averaging over shell types proves convergence of the marginal to $p^{\otimes k}$ in total variation.

The rounded shell type and lower bound in step 2.1 give $\liminf_NN^{-1}\log|\Gamma_N|\ge H(p)$. For any shell type $t$, step 1.2 gives the exact identity
$$H(t)=H(p)+\beta\left(\sum_jt_je_j-E\right)-D(t\Vert p)\le H(p)+|\beta|\delta_N/N.$$
There are at most $(N+1)^q$ types, and step 1.1 bounds each multiplicity by $e^{NH(t)}$. Therefore
$$|\Gamma_N|\le(N+1)^q\exp\!\left(NH(p)+|\beta|\delta_N\right).$$
Since $q\log(N+1)/N\to0$ and $\delta_N/N\to0$, the limsup is at most $H(p)$. Together with the lower bound this proves the entropy-density limit, including $\beta=0$, without invoking a nonexistent compactness step.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a finite alphabet $A=\{1,\ldots,q\}$, $q\ge1$, and real single-site energies $e_1,\ldots,e_q$ in a fixed energy unit. At inverse parameter $\beta\in\mathbb R$, define
$$Z_1(\beta):=\sum_{j=1}^q e^{-\beta e_j},\qquad p_j(\beta):=e^{-\beta e_j}/Z_1(\beta),\qquad E(\beta):=\sum_{j=1}^q p_j(\beta)e_j.$$
For $N\ge1$, a configuration $i=(i_1,\ldots,i_N)\in A^N$ has additive energy $H_N(i):=\sum_{r=1}^Ne_{i_r}$. Given a width $\delta_N\ge0$, the **shell** is
$$\Gamma_N(\beta,\delta_N):=\{i\in A^N:|H_N(i)-NE(\beta)|\le\delta_N\}.$$
When this finite set is nonempty, its microcanonical law means the uniform probability on $\Gamma_N$, and its dimensionless entropy is $\log|\Gamma_N|$. A type is a vector $t=(n_1/N,\ldots,n_q/N)$, where the nonnegative integer counts sum to $N$; its multiplicity is $N!/\prod_j n_j!$.

The convention fixes both the shell center and the law within the shell. It makes no physical claim that an apparatus has resolution $\delta_N$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
