citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. Fix constants $\gamma>0$ and $\sigma>0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real random variable $X_0$ with finite second moment. A **continuous adapted solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation** on $[0,T]$ is a continuous adapted process $X$ satisfying, almost surely for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The canonical centered Gaussian coordinate process
with covariance $E[X_sX_t]=\min(s,t)$ has a continuous modification $B$, and
$B$ is a standard Brownian motion. In particular, standard Brownian motion
exists.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]] and a standard
Brownian motion $B$ [[def-brownian-motion]] on it. **Standing hypothesis
(H).** $B$ is adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$ and for all $0\le s<t$ the increment
$B_t-B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$. The raw
natural filtration and the usual augmented natural filtration
[[def-natural-and-usual-augmented-brownian-filtrations]] both satisfy (H) for a
standard Brownian motion, by
[[thm-brownian-future-path-markov-property]]; for a general filtration, (H) is
part of the data and is not automatic. Every statement in this development
names (H) when it is used.

Throughout, fix a finite horizon $T>0$. An **elementary predictable Brownian
integrand** on $[0,T]$ is a process of the form
$$H_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k(\omega)\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad s\in[0,T],$$
where $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$ is a finite partition of $[0,T]$, each
$\xi_k$ is a bounded real $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable random variable, and
the values at the partition points are irrelevant because the intervals are
left-open and right-closed. The **mesh** of the representation is
$\max_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)$, and the **supremum norm** of the representation is
$\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty$. The integrand itself is the process $H$; a second
list of the same name with different coefficients is the same elementary
integrand only if the two processes coincide in the almost-everywhere sense
made precise below.

The following properties are part of the definition and are used at once.

1. **Predictability.** $H$ is predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Indeed, for a
   Borel set $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R$,
   $$\{H\in\Gamma\}=Z_\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigl((t_k,t_{k+1}]\times\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\bigr), \qquad Z_\Gamma:=\begin{cases}\{0\}\times\Omega,&0\in\Gamma,\\\varnothing,&0\notin\Gamma,\end{cases}$$
   a finite union of generators of the predictable sigma-algebra because
   $\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\in\mathcal F_{t_k}$ and
   $\{0\}\times\Omega$ is a time-zero generator. Consequently $H$ is progressively
   measurable and measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F$, and $H$ belongs to
   $L^2([0,T]\times\Omega,\mathrm dt\otimes P)$: with
   $c:=\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty<\infty$ one has
   $E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds\le c^2T<\infty$.

2. **Endpoint and null-set conventions.** Replacing the intervals by
   $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ makes the value at $s=0$ zero for every elementary
   integrand. More generally, if two elementary integrands agree for all
   $s\in[0,T]$ except at finitely many deterministic times, then they agree
   $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere, since a finite set of times is
   Lebesgue-null and Tonelli computes
   $\mathrm dt\otimes P(\{u\}\times\Omega)=0$. All integrands and all
   integrals below are therefore elements of the quotient spaces of
   $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ and $L^2(P)$; a claim about a process is a claim
   about its almost-everywhere class unless a representative is explicitly
   named, and path statements name the continuous representative.

3. **Deterministic coefficients.** If every $\xi_k$ is a deterministic real
   number, $H$ is a deterministic step function on $[0,T]$, so the elementary
   integrands include all step functions with deterministic coefficients. These
   are the integrands for which the integral is a Gaussian variable below.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the Brownian construction and the
conditional-expectation interface used in items 6, 7 and 13 assume it; the
definition itself, including the predictability computation of clause 1, uses
no choice. The countable-choice obligations inherited from that interface are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   [[thm-ito-isometry-for-elementary-integrands]] and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]].

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

derivations.claim: On $[0,T]$, $g(s)=e^{\gamma s}$ is deterministic, continuous, and square-integrable. Thus $W_t=\int_0^t g(s)\,dB_s$ is defined by [F3], and [F4] supplies a continuous version. For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_n=t$, the deterministic step sums $\sum_k g(t_k)(B_{t_{k+1}}-B_{t_k})$ converge in $L^2$ to $W_t$ by the Itô isometry and uniform approximation of $g$. Discrete summation by parts rewrites them as $g(t)B_t-g(0)B_0-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}B_{t_{k+1}}(g(t_{k+1})-g(t_k))$ up to an endpoint term tending to zero. Brownian path continuity makes the last sums converge pathwise to $\int_0^t g'(s)B_sds$. The $L^2$ limit and this almost-sure limit agree in probability, so $$W_t=e^{\gamma t}B_t-\gamma\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}B_s\,ds$$ almost surely for each fixed $t$. Both sides have continuous versions; equality on rational $t$ holds on one probability-one event and therefore extends to all $t\in[0,T]$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, F5]

Split the stochastic integral at $s$ and use its linearity: $$X_t=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s+\sigma\int_s^t e^{-\gamma(t-u)}\,dB_u.$$ Step-function approximants to the last deterministic-integrand integral depend only on increments after $s$, so [A1] makes them independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Their $L^2$ limit remains independent of $\mathcal F_s$: for bounded $\mathcal F_s$-measurable $Y$ and bounded continuous $\varphi$, convergence in probability plus boundedness gives convergence of $\mathbb E[Y\varphi(\cdot)]$, preserving the factorization. By [F4] the limit is centered Gaussian; [F3] computes its variance as $\sigma^2\int_s^t e^{-2\gamma(t-u)}du=V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. This proves the conditional transition law and the Markov property. [A1, A2, F3, F4]

Set $X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}W_t$. By [F4] it is continuous and adapted. Step 1.1 rewrites it as $$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma B_t-\sigma\gamma\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}B_s\,ds.$$ Integrating this continuous expression in $t$, ordinary Fubini [F5] gives $$\int_0^tX_sds=X_0(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma+\sigma\int_0^tB_sds-\sigma\int_0^tB_u(1-e^{-\gamma(t-u)})\,du.$$ Substitution into $X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_sds+\sigma B_t$ cancels the two $\int B_sds$ terms and leaves exactly the displayed expression for $X_t$. Thus [F1] holds. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1]

Taking expectations in the explicit solution, the stochastic integral has mean zero by [F4], giving $\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0$. The integral is independent of $X_0$ and centered, so its variance adds to $e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)$; [F3] evaluates the added variance as $V(1-e^{-2\gamma t})$. The independent Gaussian term tends in law to $N(0,V)$ because its variance tends to $V$ and $e^{-\gamma t}X_0\to0$ in $L^2$; for any bounded continuous test, restrict to a compact interval, use uniform continuity and the second-moment tail bound, then take the interval radius to infinity. [A1, A2, F3, F4, step 1.2]

Write $r=e^{-\gamma t}$ and $\pi(x)=(2\pi V)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2V)}$. The transition density is $$K_t(x,y)=[2\pi V(1-r^2)]^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-rx)^2}{2V(1-r^2)}\right).$$ Multiplying by $\pi(x)$ gives a symmetric prefactor and exponent proportional to $-[x^2+y^2-2rxy]/[2V(1-r^2)]$, unchanged when $x$ and $y$ are exchanged. Hence $\pi(x)K_t(x,y)=\pi(y)K_t(y,x)$, the detailed-balance identity. [A1, A2, F6, F7, step 1.2]

For $t>0$ let $\mu=e^{-\gamma t}x$, $v=V(1-e^{-2\gamma t})$, and $p(t,x,y)$ be the normal density with mean $\mu$ and variance $v$. Direct differentiation gives $$\partial_t p=p\left(\frac{\mu'(y-\mu)}v+\frac{v'}2\left[\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{v^2}-\frac1v\right]\right),\quad \mu'=-\gamma\mu,\quad v'=\sigma^2-2\gamma v.$$ Also direct $y$-differentiation gives $\gamma\partial_y(yp)+(\sigma^2/2)\partial_{yy}p$ equal to the same expression after writing $y=\mu+(y-\mu)$. Thus $\partial_t p=\gamma\partial_y(yp)+(\sigma^2/2)\partial_{yy}p$. The Gaussian formula has total integral one and converges to point mass at $x$ as $t\downarrow0$; this is the stated positive-time Fokker–Planck solution. [A2, F5, F7, step 1.2]

If $X$ and $\widetilde X$ are two continuous solutions with the same data, their difference $z$ satisfies $z(t)=-\gamma\int_0^tz(s)ds$. Let $D(t)=\int_0^t|z(s)|ds$. Then $D(0)=0$, $D\ge0$, and $D'(t)=|z(t)|\le\gamma D(t)$ by the equation. The derivative of $e^{-\gamma t}D(t)$ is nonpositive, so this nonnegative function is at most its initial value zero. Hence $D=0$ and continuity gives $z=0$ at every time. [A2, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

If $X_0$ is centered normal with variance $V$, step 1.2 gives centered Gaussian finite-dimensional laws, since each stochastic integral over a disjoint increment interval is an independent Gaussian and $X_0$ is independent of future increments. Its one-time variance is $V$. For $s\le t$, the split formula in 2.1 and independence of the later increment yield $\mathbb E[X_sX_t]=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbb E[X_s^2]=Ve^{-\gamma(t-s)}$. Thus covariance depends only on $|t-s|$. A centered Gaussian finite-dimensional law is determined by its covariance matrix; shifting every time by the same amount preserves that matrix and proves stationarity. [A1, A2, F4, step 1.2, step 2.2]

The stationary covariance is integrable. By evenness, $$S(\omega)=\frac V\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{-(\gamma-i\omega)t}dt =\frac V\pi\operatorname{Re}\frac1{\gamma-i\omega} =\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)}.$$ The integral converges absolutely because $\gamma>0$. [A2, F6, step 3.2]

For the stationary time average, Fubini applies since $C$ is bounded on the finite square. Changing variables in the two triangular halves gives $$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(T^{-1}\int_0^TX_tdt\right) =\frac{2V}{T^2}\int_0^T(T-s)e^{-\gamma s}ds \le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$ The bound tends to zero, so these averages converge to zero in $L^2$ and in probability. It asserts no almost-sure theorem for arbitrary observables. [A1, A2, F5, step 3.2] ∎

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. Fix constants $\gamma>0$ and $\sigma>0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real random variable $X_0$ with finite second moment. A **continuous adapted solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation** on $[0,T]$ is a continuous adapted process $X$ satisfying, almost surely for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]] and a standard
Brownian motion $B$ [[def-brownian-motion]] on it. **Standing hypothesis
(H).** $B$ is adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$ and for all $0\le s<t$ the increment
$B_t-B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$. The raw
natural filtration and the usual augmented natural filtration
[[def-natural-and-usual-augmented-brownian-filtrations]] both satisfy (H) for a
standard Brownian motion, by
[[thm-brownian-future-path-markov-property]]; for a general filtration, (H) is
part of the data and is not automatic. Every statement in this development
names (H) when it is used.

Throughout, fix a finite horizon $T>0$. An **elementary predictable Brownian
integrand** on $[0,T]$ is a process of the form
$$H_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k(\omega)\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad s\in[0,T],$$
where $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$ is a finite partition of $[0,T]$, each
$\xi_k$ is a bounded real $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable random variable, and
the values at the partition points are irrelevant because the intervals are
left-open and right-closed. The **mesh** of the representation is
$\max_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)$, and the **supremum norm** of the representation is
$\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty$. The integrand itself is the process $H$; a second
list of the same name with different coefficients is the same elementary
integrand only if the two processes coincide in the almost-everywhere sense
made precise below.

The following properties are part of the definition and are used at once.

1. **Predictability.** $H$ is predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Indeed, for a
   Borel set $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R$,
   $$\{H\in\Gamma\}=Z_\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigl((t_k,t_{k+1}]\times\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\bigr), \qquad Z_\Gamma:=\begin{cases}\{0\}\times\Omega,&0\in\Gamma,\\\varnothing,&0\notin\Gamma,\end{cases}$$
   a finite union of generators of the predictable sigma-algebra because
   $\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\in\mathcal F_{t_k}$ and
   $\{0\}\times\Omega$ is a time-zero generator. Consequently $H$ is progressively
   measurable and measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F$, and $H$ belongs to
   $L^2([0,T]\times\Omega,\mathrm dt\otimes P)$: with
   $c:=\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty<\infty$ one has
   $E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds\le c^2T<\infty$.

2. **Endpoint and null-set conventions.** Replacing the intervals by
   $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ makes the value at $s=0$ zero for every elementary
   integrand. More generally, if two elementary integrands agree for all
   $s\in[0,T]$ except at finitely many deterministic times, then they agree
   $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere, since a finite set of times is
   Lebesgue-null and Tonelli computes
   $\mathrm dt\otimes P(\{u\}\times\Omega)=0$. All integrands and all
   integrals below are therefore elements of the quotient spaces of
   $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ and $L^2(P)$; a claim about a process is a claim
   about its almost-everywhere class unless a representative is explicitly
   named, and path statements name the continuous representative.

3. **Deterministic coefficients.** If every $\xi_k$ is a deterministic real
   number, $H$ is a deterministic step function on $[0,T]$, so the elementary
   integrands include all step functions with deterministic coefficients. These
   are the integrands for which the integral is a Gaussian variable below.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the Brownian construction and the
conditional-expectation interface used in items 6, 7 and 13 assume it; the
definition itself, including the predictability computation of clause 1, uses
no choice. The countable-choice obligations inherited from that interface are declared
as dependencies of this item.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   [[thm-ito-isometry-for-elementary-integrands]] and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]].

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

with covariance $E[X_sX_t]=\min(s,t)$ has a continuous modification $B$, and

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

citations.quote:
Fix $d\ge2$. The **elastic collision set** is
$$Q_{\rm el}:=\{(v,w,v',w')\in\mathbb R^{4d}:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\},$$
with its relative Borel sigma-algebra. A collision measure is a nonnegative countably additive measure $\nu$ on this measurable space. It is symmetric if it is invariant under the exchanges $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(w,v)$, $(v',w')\leftrightarrow(w',v')$, and $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(v',w')$. These invariances are hypotheses on $\nu$, not consequences of energy and momentum conservation.

For a positive function $f:\mathbb R^d\to(0,\infty)$, write $Q(f)$ for a collision operator when the following **weak collision identity** holds for each test function $\varphi$ used:
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(v)Q(f)(v)\,dv=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(f(v')f(w')-f(v)f(w))(\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w'))\,d\nu,$$
with absolute convergence. This identity is the adopted mathematical collision model. Molecular chaos or a microscopic derivation of it is not part of the definition.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: For a fixed time, write $\ell=\log(f/f_{\rm ref})$. By [F3]–[F4], dominated differentiation gives $$\frac{dH}{dt}=\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+\ell)\,\partial_t f\,dv\,dr.$$ Substitute the transport equation. The spatial contribution is $$-\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+\ell)\,v\cdot\nabla_r f\,dv\,dr =-\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}v\cdot\nabla_r(f\ell)\,dv\,dr.$$ For each fixed $v$, the integral of each coordinate derivative over the periodic rectangle is zero by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus and opposite-face identification; absolute integrability in [A2] permits Fubini [F2]. Thus the transport contribution vanishes. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

The weak identity with test $1$ has zero bracket on every elastic collision, so $\int Q(f)\,dv=0$ at each $r,t$. Consequently the collision contribution from $(1+\ell)Q(f)$ equals that from $\ell Q(f)$. Apply the weak identity with $\varphi=\ell$ at fixed $(r,t)$. The sum $\ell(v)+\ell(w)-\ell(v')-\ell(w')$ is $\log A-\log B$, since the constant reference terms cancel. Hence $$\int \ell(v)Q(f)(v)\,dv=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(B-A)(\log A-\log B)\,d\nu.$$ Integrate in $r$; the absolute convergence in [A2] justifies the rearrangement by [F2]. This is the asserted derivative identity. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1]

For positive $A,B$, strict increase of $\log$ [F5] makes $(A-B)(\log A-\log B)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $A=B$. The derivative in 1.2 is therefore nonpositive. If its nonnegative production integral is zero, the integrand vanishes almost everywhere: for each $n$, the set on which it is at least $1/n$ must have measure zero, since otherwise its integral is positive. Thus $A=B$ for $\nu$-almost every collision at almost every $r$. The converse follows by substitution in the derivative identity. [A2, F2, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

Under [A3], fix an $r$ for which collision balance holds $\nu$-almost everywhere. The function $(v,w,v',w')\mapsto A-B$ is continuous. If it were nonzero at an allowed collision, it would remain nonzero on a relative open neighborhood; full support of $\nu$ gives that neighborhood positive measure, contradicting balance. Hence balance holds for every elastic collision. The set of such $r$ has full Lebesgue measure and is dense in $\Omega$; continuity in $r$ extends the identity to any limit point when needed. [A1, A3, F1, step 3.1, algebra]

Fix such an $r$ and put $g(v)=\log(f(r,v,t)/f_{\rm ref})$. For any $a,u\in\mathbb R^d$ and any orthogonal rotation $R$, the pairs $(a+u,a-u)$ and $(a+Ru,a-Ru)$ have the same total momentum $2a$ and total squared speed $2|a|^2+2|u|^2$. Step 4.1 therefore gives $$g(a+u)+g(a-u)=g(a+Ru)+g(a-Ru).$$ For unit vectors $\theta,\eta$, put $u=s\theta$ and $R\theta=\eta$. The second-order Taylor expansion at $a$ gives $$g(a+s\theta)+g(a-s\theta)=2g(a)+s^2\theta^\top D^2g(a)\theta+o(s^2).$$ Equating the expansion for $\eta$, dividing by $s^2$ and sending $s\to0$ shows that the quadratic form of the symmetric Hessian is constant on the unit sphere. Testing coordinate vectors makes all diagonal entries equal; testing $(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2$ makes each off-diagonal entry zero. Thus $D^2g(a)=\lambda(a)I$. [A1, A3, step 4.1, algebra]

Since $\partial_{ij}g=0$ for $i\ne j$, the fundamental theorem of calculus along coordinate segments shows $\partial_i g(v)$ depends only on $v_i$. Write it as $G_i(v_i)$. The diagonal Hessian equalities give $G_i'(v_i)=G_j'(v_j)$ for every pair of independent real coordinates $v_i,v_j$. Because $d\ge2$, varying these coordinates independently forces all these derivatives to be one constant $\lambda$. Integrating each first derivative gives $g(v)=\alpha+b\cdot v+\lambda|v|^2/2$. [A1, step 5.1, algebra]

If $\lambda>0$, $e^{g(v)}$ grows quadratically in every sufficiently large direction and is not integrable. If $\lambda=0$, $e^{\alpha+b\cdot v}$ is constant when $b=0$ and grows on a half-line when $b\ne0$, so it is not integrable over $\mathbb R^d$. Thus integrability forces $\lambda<0$. Completing the square writes $f(r,v,t)=C(r,t)\exp[-c(r,t)|v-u(r,t)|^2]$ for $C,c>0$, the Maxwellian velocity form. Conversely, when $g=\alpha+b\cdot v+\lambda|v|^2/2$, the sum $g(v)+g(w)$ is unchanged by every collision because total momentum and total squared speed are conserved; hence $A=B$ and the production is zero. This equality branch concerns the collision term only; a spatially varying Maxwellian may still evolve under transport. [A1, A3, F1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

Fix $d\ge2$. The **elastic collision set** is
$$Q_{\rm el}:=\{(v,w,v',w')\in\mathbb R^{4d}:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\},$$
with its relative Borel sigma-algebra. A collision measure is a nonnegative countably additive measure $\nu$ on this measurable space. It is symmetric if it is invariant under the exchanges $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(w,v)$, $(v',w')\leftrightarrow(w',v')$, and $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(v',w')$. These invariances are hypotheses on $\nu$, not consequences of energy and momentum conservation.

For a positive function $f:\mathbb R^d\to(0,\infty)$, write $Q(f)$ for a collision operator when the following **weak collision identity** holds for each test function $\varphi$ used:
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(v)Q(f)(v)\,dv=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(f(v')f(w')-f(v)f(w))(\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w'))\,d\nu,$$
with absolute convergence. This identity is the adopted mathematical collision model. Molecular chaos or a microscopic derivation of it is not part of the definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $O\subset\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, be open, let $H\in C^2(O,\mathbb R)$, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. An energy $E\in J$ is **regular** if $\nabla H(x)\ne0$ for every $x\in\Sigma_E:=H^{-1}(\{E\})$. By the implicit-function theorem, a neighborhood of each point of a nonempty regular level is a graph $x_i=h(z)$.

In a graph chart, use the local area density $\sqrt{1+|\nabla h(z)|^2}\,dz$, where $dz$ is $(m-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. A **graph partition** on $\Sigma_E$ is a locally finite graph-chart cover with nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_a$ supported in their respective charts and summing to one on the level. Whenever such a partition is supplied, define the candidate weighted shell integral by
$$\mu_E(g):=\sum_a\int g(z,h_a(z))\chi_a(z,h_a(z))|\partial_iH(z,h_a(z))|^{-1}\,dz$$
for nonnegative Borel $g$. Its independence from the chosen chart partition, and its equality with $\int_{\Sigma_E}g|\nabla H|^{-1}dA_E$, are proved in the theorem on this page. If $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$, the **microcanonical shell probability** is $\widehat\mu_E:=\mu_E/\mu_E(1)$.

This is an explicit chart-based definition, not a formal delta distribution $\delta(H-E)$. Critical levels are excluded.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. For a region $R$ on which a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$ and all its iterates are defined, $T$ is a measure-preserving transformation. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ be
nonempty and let $x, y \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y),$$

with $d(\cdot,A)$ the distance to a nonempty set ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
Thus the real-valued function $u \mapsto d(u,A)$ changes by at most $d(u,v)$
between $u$ and $v$: it is **$1$-Lipschitz**.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$,
with closure, derived set and limit points as in
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]. Then:

1. If $A \ne \emptyset$, then $\overline{A} = \{\, x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \,\}$,
   where $d(x,A)$ is the distance from a point to a nonempty set
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
2. $\overline{A} = A \cup A'$.
3. $\overline{A}$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed
   $F \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq F$. So $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed
   superset of $A$, and $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

Claims 2 and 3 hold for every $A$, the empty set included: $\overline{\emptyset}$
is empty because no ball meets $\emptyset$, and $\emptyset$ is closed because $X$
is open ([[def-metric-topology]]). Claim 1 carries the hypothesis $A \ne \emptyset$
because $d(x,A)$ is defined only for nonempty $A$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=\nu(X)$, then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

derivations.claim: Let $C$ be a compact energy band containing the support of $f$. At each $x\in H^{-1}(C)$, some coordinate derivative $\partial_iH(x)$ is nonzero. By [F2] a neighborhood is parameterized by the remaining coordinates $z$ and energy $E$, with $x_i=h(z,E)$. Compactness gives a finite cover by such charts. Refine the cover by finitely many balls whose closures lie in chart domains and whose smaller concentric balls cover $H^{-1}(C)$. Choose standard smooth bump functions $\psi_a$ supported in the larger balls and positive on the smaller balls, and let $\Psi=\sum_a\psi_a$. Its minimum on $H^{-1}(C)$ is positive. Choose a smooth scalar cutoff $\eta$ that is zero below one quarter of this minimum and one above one half of it. Then $\chi_a=\eta(\Psi)\psi_a/\Psi$, extended by zero where $\Psi=0$, is smooth, supported in its chart, and the sum is one near $H^{-1}(C)$. [A1, A2, F2, F4, construct]

In each chart, the map $(z,E)\mapsto(z,h_a(z,E))$ is injective after shrinking the chart, and its absolute Jacobian is $|\partial_Eh_a|=|\partial_iH|^{-1}$. By [F3] and Tonelli [F4], $$\int_O f(x)\chi_a(x)\,dx =\int_J\int f(z,h_a(z,E))\chi_a(z,h_a(z,E))|\partial_iH|^{-1}\,dz\,dE.$$ Implicit differentiation gives $\partial_{z_j}h_a=-\partial_jH/\partial_iH$, so the graph area density is $$\sqrt{1+|\nabla_zh_a|^2}\,dz=\frac{|\nabla H|}{|\partial_iH|}\,dz.$$ The inner integral is therefore the corresponding chart contribution to the candidate $\mu_E(f)$ in [F1]. Sum the finitely many charts and use $\sum_a\chi_a=1$ on the support to obtain the asserted coarea identity. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

On overlaps, if one graph parameterization is obtained from another by a $C^1$ coordinate change $\psi$, its Gram matrix is transformed by $G\mapsto(D\psi)^	op G(D\psi)$. Taking determinants shows the area density changes by $|\det D\psi|$, exactly the ordinary chart Jacobian. Implicit differentiation gives $\sqrt{1+|
abla h|^2}/|
abla H|=|\partial_iH|^{-1}$, so the chart contributions define the same measure independent of the partition and equal $\int_{\Sigma_E}g|
abla H|^{-1}dA_E$. Each shell is a closed subset of compact $H^{-1}(\{E\})$, hence compact. A finite collection of graph charts with $
abla H$ bounded away from zero on that compact level gives finite area and hence $\mu_E(1)<\infty$. If the shell is nonempty, one graph chart contains an open patch; its coordinate domain has positive $(2n-1)$-dimensional measure and the continuous density $|
abla H|^{-1}dA_E/dz$ is positive there, so $\mu_E(1)>0$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Fix a compact band and a compactly supported continuous test $g$ on it. For a continuous compactly supported scalar function $q$ on $J$, the coarea identity from 1.2 and the Hamiltonian volume/energy invariance [F5] give $$\int_Jq(E)\mu_E(g\circ\phi_t)\,dE =\int_Oq(H(x))g(\phi_tx)\,dx =\int_Oq(H(x))g(x)\,dx =\int_Jq(E)\mu_E(g)\,dE.$$ The second equality is the change of variables by the volume-preserving diffeomorphism $\phi_t$; $H\circ\phi_t=H$ keeps the energy weight fixed. For each test $g$, both functions of $E$ in the outer integrals are continuous locally: use the finite chart representation in 1.2, compact chart support, the positive lower bound for $|\nabla H|$, and dominated convergence [F6]. Their difference integrates to zero against every compactly supported continuous $q$. If the continuous difference were nonzero at one energy, it would keep one strict sign on a neighborhood; a nonnegative continuous bump $q$ supported there would make the integral nonzero. Thus $\mu_E(g\circ\phi_t)=\mu_E(g)$ for every $E$ in the band. [A1, A2, F1, F5, F6, step 2.1]

Fix a closed subset $F$ of a nonempty shell. If $F=\varnothing$, both measures assign it zero. Otherwise let $\chi$ be a continuous compactly supported cutoff equal to one on the compact shell; the same finite-ball bump construction used in 1.1 supplies it. In the ambient band set $g_n(x)=\chi(x)\max\{0,1-n\,\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\}$. By [F7], $g_n$ is continuous, $0\le g_n\le1$, and its restriction to $\Sigma_E$ converges pointwise to $\mathbf1_F$. Because $\phi_t$ maps the shell onto itself, $g_n\circ\phi_t$ converges there to $\mathbf1_{\phi_t^{-1}F}$. Apply 2.1 to each $g_n$ and use dominated convergence [F6] for the finite shell measure from 1.3; this gives $\mu_E(\phi_t^{-1}F)=\mu_E(F)$ for every closed $F\subseteq\Sigma_E$. Closed sets form a pi-system generating the shell Borel sigma-algebra, and both $\mu_E$ and its pushforward have the same finite total mass because $\phi_t$ maps the shell onto itself. [F5, F6, F7, step 2.2, step 3.1]

By [F8], agreement on closed sets and equality of total masses imply that $\mu_E$ equals its pushforward on every Borel subset of $\Sigma_E$. Divide by $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$ from 1.3. Hence the normalized regular-shell probability is invariant for each such $E$, not merely almost every energy. [F8, step 2.2, step 4.1] ∎

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $O\subset\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, be open, let $H\in C^2(O,\mathbb R)$, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. An energy $E\in J$ is **regular** if $\nabla H(x)\ne0$ for every $x\in\Sigma_E:=H^{-1}(\{E\})$. By the implicit-function theorem, a neighborhood of each point of a nonempty regular level is a graph $x_i=h(z)$.

In a graph chart, use the local area density $\sqrt{1+|\nabla h(z)|^2}\,dz$, where $dz$ is $(m-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. A **graph partition** on $\Sigma_E$ is a locally finite graph-chart cover with nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_a$ supported in their respective charts and summing to one on the level. Whenever such a partition is supplied, define the candidate weighted shell integral by
$$\mu_E(g):=\sum_a\int g(z,h_a(z))\chi_a(z,h_a(z))|\partial_iH(z,h_a(z))|^{-1}\,dz$$
for nonnegative Borel $g$. Its independence from the chosen chart partition, and its equality with $\int_{\Sigma_E}g|\nabla H|^{-1}dA_E$, are proved in the theorem on this page. If $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$, the **microcanonical shell probability** is $\widehat\mu_E:=\mu_E/\mu_E(1)$.

This is an explicit chart-based definition, not a formal delta distribution $\delta(H-E)$. Critical levels are excluded.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ be
nonempty and let $x, y \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y),$$

with $d(\cdot,A)$ the distance to a nonempty set ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
Thus the real-valued function $u \mapsto d(u,A)$ changes by at most $d(u,v)$
between $u$ and $v$: it is **$1$-Lipschitz**.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$,
with closure, derived set and limit points as in
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]. Then:

1. If $A \ne \emptyset$, then $\overline{A} = \{\, x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \,\}$,
   where $d(x,A)$ is the distance from a point to a nonempty set
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
2. $\overline{A} = A \cup A'$.
3. $\overline{A}$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed
   $F \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq F$. So $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed
   superset of $A$, and $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

Claims 2 and 3 hold for every $A$, the empty set included: $\overline{\emptyset}$
is empty because no ball meets $\emptyset$, and $\emptyset$ is closed because $X$
is open ([[def-metric-topology]]). Claim 1 carries the hypothesis $A \ne \emptyset$
because $d(x,A)$ is defined only for nonempty $A$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. For a region $R$ on which a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$ and all its iterates are defined, $T$ is a measure-preserving transformation. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.
