citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, let
$T\in\mathcal S_1(H)$ be trace class, and let $(P_n)_{n\ge1}$ be any supplied sequence of
finite-rank orthogonal projections on $H$ such that $P_n\to I$ strongly. Then
$$\|P_nTP_n-T\|_1\longrightarrow0.$$
The projections need not be increasing. For example, the initial projections
onto the first $n$ vectors of a supplied countable orthonormal basis satisfy
the hypothesis.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let
$S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$
If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert
basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and
$BA$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Each multiplier $e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}$ has modulus one by [F6]. Thus $U_t$ preserves the norm of finite linear combinations of the complete orthonormal basis; it extends by density to an isometry on the Hilbert space. The similarly defined $U_{-t}$ is its inverse, so $U_t$ is unitary and depends continuously on $t$ on each finite-dimensional energy span. The arguments $E_jt/\hbar$ are dimensionless.

By [F2], $\rho_t=U_t\rho U_t^*$ is trace class. It is positive because $\langle\rho_t x,x\rangle=\langle\rho U_t^*x,U_t^*x\rangle\ge0$, and cyclicity [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_t=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$.

Enumerate the distinct energy eigenspaces and let $P_N$ project onto the first $N$ of them, with $P_N=I$ after the list is exhausted if it is finite. Their union spans the eigenbasis, so $P_N\to I$ strongly. The Hilbert space is separable by the countable complete basis in [A1]. Therefore [F3] gives $\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1\to0$. Unitary invariance of trace norm follows from [F2] in both directions: $\|U_tRU_t^*\|_1\le\|R\|_1$ and $R=U_t^*(U_tRU_t^*)U_t$ gives the reverse inequality. Consequently $$\|U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*-\rho_t\|_1=\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1$$ uniformly in $t$.

For fixed $N$, the matrix of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ on its finite-dimensional range has continuous entries, hence is continuous in trace norm. Step 2.2 makes $\rho_t$ a uniform trace-norm limit on compact time intervals of these continuous maps; therefore $t\mapsto\rho_t$ is trace-norm continuous. On $[0,T]$ it is uniformly continuous. Riemann sums for a uniformly continuous Banach-valued function are Cauchy: two sums are compared on a common refinement and their difference is bounded by $T$ times the modulus of continuity at the larger mesh. Completeness in [F2] supplies the trace-class integral and its usual norm bound.

In the eigenbasis, the $(i,j)$ matrix entry of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ is $\langle\rho u_j,u_i\rangle e^{i(E_j-E_i)t/\hbar}$. Its time-average factor is $1$ if $E_i=E_j$; if $E_i\ne E_j$, direct integration using [F6] gives absolute value at most $2\hbar/(T|E_j-E_i|)$, which tends to zero. Since the compression is finite dimensional, entrywise convergence implies trace-norm convergence. Hence the finite compressed average tends to $\sum_{E\text{ among the first }N}P_E\rho P_E$.

Each block $P_E\rho P_E$ is positive trace class. The sum of their traces is $$\sum_E\sum_{u_j\in\operatorname{ran}P_E}\langle\rho u_j,u_j\rangle =\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$$ by [F4] and the complete basis in [A1]. Therefore their finite partial sums are Cauchy in trace norm: for a positive finite block tail its trace norm equals its trace, and the scalar trace tail tends to zero. Their limit $\rho_{\rm diag}$ exists in trace norm, is positive, and has trace one.

Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $N$ so the compression error in step 2.2 and the diagonal tail in step 5.1 are each below $\epsilon/3$. The norm bound for the Riemann integral in step 3.1 makes the average of the compression error at most $\epsilon/3$, uniformly in $T$. For this fixed $N$, step 4.1 makes the finite compressed average differ from its finite diagonal limit by less than $\epsilon/3$ for all sufficiently large $T$. The triangle inequality then gives $\|\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag}\|_1<\epsilon$.

For bounded observable $B$, the trace-class ideal and trace estimates in [F2] and [F4] give $|\operatorname{Tr}((\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag})B)|\le\|\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag}\|_1\|B\|$. Step 6.1 sends the right-hand side to zero. The conclusion is only convergence of time-averaged states in the stated trace norm.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],

$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $a:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The **convex hull** $\operatorname{conv}K$ is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$. A **phase generator** is a point $y\in K$ with declared energy $a(y)$. A **mixture** is a Borel probability measure $P$ on $K$. Its barycenter and mean energy are the coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals
$$\bar y(P):=\int_K y\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R^d,\qquad \bar a(P):=\int_K a(y)\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R.$$
These integrals are finite because each coordinate and $a$ are bounded on compact $K$. For prescribed mean $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, the **mixture energy** is
$$a_{\rm mix}(x):=\inf\{\bar a(P):P\text{ is a Borel probability on }K,\ \bar y(P)=x\}.$$
The admissible set is nonempty since every finite convex combination of points of $K$ is the barycenter of a finite atomic probability. The definition does not assert that the infimum is attained; the theorem on this page gives a compact continuous sufficient condition.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.

derivations.claim: For each integer $n\ge2$, the set $E_n=[1/n,1)$ is Borel, and $\bigcup_{n\ge2}E_n=(0,1)$. Since $P((0,1))=1$, countable subadditivity implies $P(E_n)>0$ for at least one $n$; otherwise the union would have probability zero. On $E_n$, $x\ge1/n$, while elsewhere $x\ge0$, so $$\int_{(0,1)}x\,dP\ge \frac1nP(E_n)>0.$$ Therefore every admissible probability has strictly positive objective. [A1, F1, algebra]

The point mass $\delta_{1/n}$ at $1/n$ is a Borel probability on $(0,1)$ and has objective $1/n$. These values tend to zero, while 1.1 shows all objectives are positive. Hence the infimum is zero and is not attained. The generator set is noncompact, so this conclusion does not contradict the compact result [F2]; it shows why an attainment theorem must retain its compactness/coercivity hypotheses. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: Since $e_{N,k}\ge1$, $e^{Ne_{N,k}^2}\ge e^N$. For $x\ge e^N$, $x-1\le\lfloor x\rfloor\le x$, so $$e_{N,k}^2+\frac1N\log(1-e^{-N})\le \frac1N\log g_{N,k}\le e_{N,k}^2.$$ The error tends to zero uniformly in $k$. The grid mesh is $1/N$; for a continuous function on $[1,2]$, uniform continuity makes its grid maxima converge to its interval maximum. [A1, F1, F2]

Let $Z_N(b)=\sum_{k=0}^Ng_{N,k}e^{-Nb e_{N,k}}$ and $m_N=\max_k[N^{-1}\log g_{N,k}-b e_{N,k}]$. The largest summand is $e^{Nm_N}$ and there are $N+1$ summands, so $$m_N\le N^{-1}\log Z_N(b)\le m_N+N^{-1}\log(N+1).$$ By 1.1, $m_N\to\max_{e\in[1,2]}(e^2-be)$. If $e=\theta\cdot1+(1-\theta)\cdot2$ with $0<\theta<1$, direct expansion gives $$e^2-be=\theta(1-b)+(1-\theta)(4-2b)-\theta(1-\theta),$$ strictly below the weighted endpoint values. Thus the maximum is at an endpoint and equals $\max(1-b,4-2b)$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

For compact $K\subset(1,2)$, strict convexity gives $$\eta:=\min_{e\in K}\left[\max(1-b,4-2b)-(e^2-be)\right]>0$$ by [F3]. Uniform approximation in 1.1 makes every grid exponent in $K$ at most the maximum minus $\eta/2$ for all sufficiently large $N$. On the other hand, an endpoint group has exponent tending to the maximum. Therefore the canonical probability of $K$ is at most $(N+1)e^{-N\eta/2+o(N)}$, which tends to zero. [A1, A2, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

Choose integers $k_N$ with $e_{N,k_N}\to e\in(1,2)$. The microcanonical exact-group law has energy density exactly $e_{N,k_N}$ at every state. By 1.1 its entropy density $N^{-1}\log g_{N,k_N}$ tends to $e^2$. Thus, for example at the crossing $b=3$, canonical mass escapes every compact neighborhood of any interior target while the microcanonical group remains there. Finally $s(3/2)=9/4<5/2=(s(1)+s(2))/2$, so $s(e)=e^2$ is not concave. The example is a constructed model, not an observation about a material. [A1, A2, step 1.1, step 3.1] ∎

citations.quote:
A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$, its **Hamiltonian vector field** is the vector field
$X_H$ determined by the library sign convention

$$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH.$$

A vector field $X$ is **Hamiltonian** if $\iota_X\omega=dH$ for some smooth
function $H$; such an $H$ is a **Hamiltonian function for $X$**. A function and
its vector field are distinct data, and completeness of $X_H$ is not assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. For a region $R$ on which a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$ and all its iterates are defined, $T$ is a measure-preserving transformation. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

derivations.claim: Write $X_H=a\partial_q+b\partial_p$. Then $\iota_{X_H}(dq\wedge dp)=a\,dp-b\,dq$, while $dH=-\sin q\,dq$. Equating coefficients gives $a=0$ and $b=\sin q$. The explicit solution is $$\phi_t(q,p)=(q,p+t\sin q\pmod{2\pi}),$$ which is defined for every real $t$ and is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\phi_{-t}$. [A1, F1, algebra]

Since $H\circ\phi_t=H$, the set $A$ is invariant under every $\phi_t$. The torus has total area $(2\pi)^2=4\pi^2$. The allowed $q$ values in $A$ have total length $\pi$, while $p$ ranges over length $2\pi$, so $m(A)=2\pi^2$, strictly between zero and total area. The map preserves area by [F2], and the invariant set violates the criterion [F3]; hence it is not ergodic for any nonzero sampling time. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

citations.quote: For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: The unitary evolution sends $\psi$ to $(e^{-iE_1t/\hbar}u_1+e^{-iE_2t/\hbar}u_2)/\sqrt2$, which remains a unit vector by [F2]. Its rank-one density has eigenvalues $1,0$, so its entropy is $-k_B(1\log1+0\log0)=0$ for every $t$.

The two energy eigenspaces are one-dimensional. The matrix entry between them is an exponential with nonzero frequency; by [F1] its average has magnitude at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ and tends to zero. The diagonal entries remain $1/2$, so the direct finite-dimensional average yields $\rho_{\rm diag}=\tfrac12P_1+\tfrac12P_2$. Its eigenvalues are $(1/2,1/2)$, so $$S(\rho_{\rm diag})=-k_B\left(\tfrac12\log\tfrac12+\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)=k_B\log2.$$ Since every $S(\rho_t)=0$, the time average of instantaneous entropy is exactly zero.

In the basis $(u_1,u_2)$, $\bar\rho_T$ has diagonal entries $1/2$ and off-diagonal entry $$c_T=\frac1{2T}\int_0^T e^{-i(E_1-E_2)t/\hbar}\,dt,$$ whose magnitude is at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ by direct integration. Its eigenvalues are $1/2\pm|c_T|$, so both tend to $1/2$. Continuity of $x\mapsto-x\log x$ at $1/2$ gives $S(\bar\rho_T)\to k_B\log2$. Thus entropy of the averaged state has a nonzero limit even though the averaged instantaneous entropy remains zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the exact first-clause interface of [[thm-tdmath-general-trace-gibbs-model]]: a nonzero complex Hilbert space has a finite or countable complete orthonormal energy eigenbasis $(u_j)$ for a self-adjoint semibounded $A$, with each energy eigenspace finite-dimensional. The supplier is a current draft whose statement and complete argument have been inspected; this theorem is conditional on that interface and does not claim its independent acceptance. Let $\hbar>0$, define $U_tu_j=e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}u_j$, and extend linearly and continuously. For any positive trace-class density operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, set $\rho_t=U_t\rho U_t^*$. If $P_E$ denotes the projection onto the full eigenspace of energy $E$, then the trace-norm Riemann average
$$\bar\rho_T:=\frac1T\int_0^T\rho_t\,dt$$
converges as $T\to\infty$ to
$$\rho_{\rm diag}:=\sum_E P_E\rho P_E$$
in trace norm. The full degenerate energy blocks are retained. Thus expectations of every bounded observable converge to their diagonal-ensemble values. This asserts Cesàro convergence, not convergence of $\rho_t$ at individual late times, and is restricted to the stated discrete trace-class spectrum.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]];
it supplies the stated Hilbert-space construction and is not a physical
measurement assumption. Fix one finite nonempty label set $J$ with
$N:=|J|\ge1$, an enumeration of
$J$ by $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and dimensionless real coordinates
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may represent sites of a
fixed finite spatial lattice or a fixed finite set of modes; any graph,
geometry, and couplings are additional fixed regulator data. The coordinate
space, Hilbert space, and polynomial differential expression are those of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]:
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with inner product linear in its first
variable, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, and

$$h_0u=-\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\partial_j^2u+V(q)u,\qquad u\in D_0,$$

where $a_j>0$ and $V$ is a real polynomial. Require fixed constants $c>0$ and
$C_0\ge0$ such that

$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$

For this physical model, take $q_j$, $a_j$, $c$, $C_0$, and the coefficients
of $V$ to be dimensionless. Adopt a positive energy scale $E_*$ in joules as
primitive finite-regulator data, and use $\hbar$ in joule-seconds under
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. When the mathematical supplier
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]] constructs its specified
self-adjoint form realization $h$ of $h_0$, the model Hamiltonian is
$H_{\rm phys}:=E_*h$ on that supplied domain. This postulate adopts the
finite-regulator polynomial data; it does not assert that the initial
differential expression is self-adjoint or choose an operator domain by
itself.

The finite label set and polynomial are held fixed. A finite spatial regulator
is not thereby Lorentz invariant, and this model asserts no continuum or
infinite-volume limit, no convergence of a perturbation series, and no
reported observation. Its parameters are selected model inputs, not measured
values.

Adopt the following physical reading only for an explicitly selected model
whose mathematical data have actually been constructed. Let $\mathscr H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $\rho_t$ be the model's density operator at
a time $t$ at which a measurement is made, and let
$\{M_{a,r}:r=1,\ldots,q_a\}_{a=1}^m$ be a supplied normalized finite bounded
Kraus instrument on $\mathscr H$ in the exact sense of
[[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ when using the normalization result of
[[lem-qft-finite-instrument-normalization]]. Its hypotheses include that
$\rho_t$ is a density operator and that the instrument really satisfies
$\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_{\mathscr H}$; the supplier's result is a draft
with a complete conditional proof, not an independent approval or an
apparatus-realization theorem.

Put

$$E_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad
\mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_rM_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*.$$

As the **Born interpretation postulate** for this selected model, read

$$p_a(t):=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho_t))
=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_tE_a)$$

as the model probability for outcome $a$. The mathematical supplier proves
$p_a(t)\in[0,1]$ and $\sum_{a=1}^mp_a(t)=1$ under the hypotheses just
listed. When $p_a(t)>0$, adopt
$\mathcal J_a(\rho_t)/p_a(t)$ as the model's conditional state after outcome
$a$; at zero probability no normalized update is assigned. These are
model-level probability assignments, not observations.

If the selected construction supplies a self-adjoint observable in the sense
of [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]] and its
spectral projection-valued measure as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]], a declared finite Borel partition may be
used only after its projections have been constructed and verified as a
finite projective instrument. In that case the projections are the single
Kraus operators for their outcomes. A supplied bounded effect is read as an
outcome effect only as part of a supplied normalized instrument; this item
does not construct square roots, a spectral measure, or an instrument from an
arbitrary formal observable.

If a model has actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $\widehat H$
and its unitary evolution, adopt the Schrödinger convention
$U(t)=\exp(-it\widehat H/\hbar)$ and
$\rho_t=U(t)\rho_0U(t)^*$ when that construction establishes that $\rho_t$
is a density operator. In the Heisenberg representation use
$O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. This postulate neither constructs the Hamiltonian,
unitary group, state, field representation, nor their domains.

The model declaration identifies the selected species, field normalization,
regulator, preparation and measurement data using
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. It does not assert that every classical action
has a quantization, that every formal state is positive, or that any cutoff
can be removed. In particular it supplies no interacting continuum
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, asymptotic
completeness, LSZ limit, or nonperturbative convergence. A formal coefficient
is not an exact probability without an additional controlled approximation
map and a constructed model. Agreement with reported data would test the
selected approximation and empirical inputs; it would not prove this
postulate or the model. No reported data are asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.

Assume Countable Choice and let $h$ be the self-adjoint operator of
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]], with complete orthonormal
eigenfamily $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$ and real eigenvalues
$\lambda_n=E_n-C_0-1$. For $t\in\mathbb R$ define
$$U(t)f:=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-it\lambda_n}\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n \qquad(f\in H_N).$$
Then the series converges in $H_N$ for every $f$; $U(t)$ is unitary,
$U(0)=I$, $U(s+t)=U(s)U(t)$, and $t\mapsto U(t)f$ is norm-continuous for
every $f$. Its norm derivative at any $t$ exists exactly for $f\in D(h)$, and
then
$$\frac{d}{dt}U(t)f=-i\,hU(t)f.$$
This is a mathematical one-parameter group with a dimensionless real
parameter; it makes no physical unit or empirical claim.

derivations.claim:
Under Countable Choice [A1], the hypotheses of [F1] hold, so $h$ is
self-adjoint on $D(h)$. Multiplication by the positive
real scalar $E_*$ preserves self-adjointness and the domain, so
$H_{\rm phys}=E_*h$ is self-adjoint on $D(h)$ with eigenvalues
$E_*\lambda_n$. The units in [A2] make $E_*\tau/\hbar$ dimensionless.

Put $s=E_*\tau/\hbar$. Since this is a real linear change of parameter,
Countable Choice [A1] discharges the hypothesis of [F2], which gives
unitarity, strong continuity, the identity at zero, and the group
law for $U_{\rm phys}(\tau)=U(s)$. Unitarity also gives
$\|U_{\rm phys}(\tau)\psi\|=\|\psi\|$.

If $\psi\in D(h)$, the chain rule and [F2] give
$\frac{d}{d\tau}U(E_*\tau/\hbar)\psi
=-i(E_*/\hbar)hU(E_*\tau/\hbar)\psi
=-iH_{\rm phys}U_{\rm phys}(\tau)\psi/\hbar$.
Conversely, because $E_*/\hbar>0$, the change $s=E_*\tau/\hbar$ is
invertible, so norm differentiability in $\tau$ is equivalent to
differentiability in $s$; [F2] makes its domain exactly $D(h)$.

[A3] supplies the physical reading of this already constructed
self-adjoint Hamiltonian and group as the selected model's Schrödinger
evolution. It adds no existence claim beyond [F1] and [F2], and no empirical
premise is used.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the finite-regulator
spectral and trace construction. For the fixed model of
[[post-qft-regulated-polynomial-model]] and a declared
temperature input $T>0$, use
[[def-qft-regulated-thermal-parameter]] to set
$\beta_{\rm phys}=(k_BT)^{-1}$ and
$\widehat\beta=E_*\beta_{\rm phys}>0$. Let $h$ be the model's specified
self-adjoint form realization and $H_{\rm phys}=E_*h$. When the finite-mode
coercivity hypotheses hold, [[thm-qft-regulated-gibbs-trace]] proves that
$e^{-\widehat\beta h}$ is positive trace class with finite positive trace.
Adopt the normalized operator

$$\rho_T:=\frac{e^{-\beta_{\rm phys}H_{\rm phys}}}{Z_T},\qquad Z_T:=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta_{\rm phys}H_{\rm phys}})$$

as this finite-regulator model's canonical equilibrium state. This is a
physical state assignment, not a deduction that the dynamics reach
equilibrium. It asserts no infinite-volume trace, no zero-temperature state,
and no empirical observation.

Adopt the following physical reading only for an explicitly selected model
whose mathematical data have actually been constructed. Let $\mathscr H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $\rho_t$ be the model's density operator at
a time $t$ at which a measurement is made, and let
$\{M_{a,r}:r=1,\ldots,q_a\}_{a=1}^m$ be a supplied normalized finite bounded
Kraus instrument on $\mathscr H$ in the exact sense of
[[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ when using the normalization result of
[[lem-qft-finite-instrument-normalization]]. Its hypotheses include that
$\rho_t$ is a density operator and that the instrument really satisfies
$\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_{\mathscr H}$; the supplier's result is a draft
with a complete conditional proof, not an independent approval or an
apparatus-realization theorem.

Put

$$E_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad
\mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_rM_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*.$$

As the **Born interpretation postulate** for this selected model, read

$$p_a(t):=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho_t))
=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_tE_a)$$

as the model probability for outcome $a$. The mathematical supplier proves
$p_a(t)\in[0,1]$ and $\sum_{a=1}^mp_a(t)=1$ under the hypotheses just
listed. When $p_a(t)>0$, adopt
$\mathcal J_a(\rho_t)/p_a(t)$ as the model's conditional state after outcome
$a$; at zero probability no normalized update is assigned. These are
model-level probability assignments, not observations.

If the selected construction supplies a self-adjoint observable in the sense
of [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]] and its
spectral projection-valued measure as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]], a declared finite Borel partition may be
used only after its projections have been constructed and verified as a
finite projective instrument. In that case the projections are the single
Kraus operators for their outcomes. A supplied bounded effect is read as an
outcome effect only as part of a supplied normalized instrument; this item
does not construct square roots, a spectral measure, or an instrument from an
arbitrary formal observable.

If a model has actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $\widehat H$
and its unitary evolution, adopt the Schrödinger convention
$U(t)=\exp(-it\widehat H/\hbar)$ and
$\rho_t=U(t)\rho_0U(t)^*$ when that construction establishes that $\rho_t$
is a density operator. In the Heisenberg representation use
$O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. This postulate neither constructs the Hamiltonian,
unitary group, state, field representation, nor their domains.

The model declaration identifies the selected species, field normalization,
regulator, preparation and measurement data using
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. It does not assert that every classical action
has a quantization, that every formal state is positive, or that any cutoff
can be removed. In particular it supplies no interacting continuum
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, scattering operator, asymptotic
completeness, LSZ limit, or nonperturbative convergence. A formal coefficient
is not an exact probability without an additional controlled approximation
map and a constructed model. Agreement with reported data would test the
selected approximation and empirical inputs; it would not prove this
postulate or the model. No reported data are asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice and use the finite-mode data, form domain $Q$, and
self-adjoint $h$ from [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let
$\lambda_0\le\lambda_1\le\cdots$ be its eigenvalues repeated with
multiplicity, and let $\psi_k$ be a corresponding orthonormal eigenbasis. For
$\beta>0$ define the finite-rank truncations
$$\rho_{\beta,M}f:=\sum_{k=0}^M e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$
The proof establishes their operator-norm limit $\rho_\beta$, with action
$$\rho_\beta f:=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$
Put $\alpha_j:=\sqrt{a_jc}$ and let the oscillator eigenvalues
$\epsilon_k$ be the nondecreasing ordering, with multiplicity, of
$$\epsilon_{\mathbf n}=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\alpha_j, \qquad\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N.$$
Then $\rho_\beta$ is positive trace class and its trace
$$Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}$$
satisfies the finite bound
$$0<Z_\beta\le e^{\beta C_0} \prod_{j=1}^N\frac{e^{-\beta\alpha_j}}{1-e^{-2\beta\alpha_j}}<\infty.$$
For every bounded linear operator $B:H_N\to H_N$, the normalized trace
expectation is well defined and
$$Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B) =Z_\beta^{-1}\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k} \langle B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle,$$
with absolute convergence. This is a finite-$N$ mathematical trace result;
it assumes no statistical data and makes no continuum-limit claim.

For the fixed model of [[post-qft-regulated-polynomial-model]], use the SI
energy-unit convention of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. A declared temperature
input is a scalar $T>0$ with unit kelvin (K). Take $k_B>0$, with
unit $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, as the fixed Boltzmann conversion constant in this
branch. Define the physical inverse-energy parameter

$$\beta_{\rm phys}:=\frac{1}{k_BT}\quad[\mathrm{J^{-1}}],$$

and its dimensionless form

$$\widehat\beta:=E_*\beta_{\rm phys}.$$

The product $k_BT$ has unit joule, and $\widehat\beta$ is dimensionless
because $E_*$ has unit joule. Since $k_B>0$ and $T>0$, both inverse parameters
are defined and positive. The values of $T$ and the model's choice of $k_B$
are inputs; this definition does not infer them from a state or an
experiment. It defines a parameter convention only and asserts no dynamical
thermalization.

derivations.claim:
By [F2], $\widehat\beta=E_*\beta_{\rm phys}>0$ is dimensionless.
The eigenvalues of $H_{\rm phys}=E_*h$ are $E_*\lambda_k$, so its Gibbs
weights are
$e^{-\beta_{\rm phys}E_*\lambda_k}
=e^{-\widehat\beta\lambda_k}$. Therefore
$Z_T=\sum_ke^{-\widehat\beta\lambda_k}$.

Under Countable Choice [A1], apply [F1] at $\widehat\beta>0$. It gives
$Z_T>0$, the stated finite
upper bound, and trace-class positivity of $e^{-\widehat\beta h}$.
Dividing by $Z_T$ yields $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_T)=1$ and preserves
positivity and trace class.

Under the same Countable Choice assumption [A1], for bounded $B$, [F1]
gives the absolutely convergent sum for
$\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\widehat\beta h}B)$. Since
$\rho_T=Z_T^{-1}e^{-\widehat\beta h}$, linearity of the trace and
$Z_T>0$ give the displayed normalized formula. If $B=E_a$ is an effect in
the instrument of [A3], that postulate supplies its physical model
probability interpretation; the finite trace calculation supplies its
value.

statement.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]];
it supplies the stated Hilbert-space construction and is not a physical
measurement assumption. Fix one finite nonempty label set $J$ with
$N:=|J|\ge1$, an enumeration of
$J$ by $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and dimensionless real coordinates
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may represent sites of a
fixed finite spatial lattice or a fixed finite set of modes; any graph,
geometry, and couplings are additional fixed regulator data. The coordinate
space, Hilbert space, and polynomial differential expression are those of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]:
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with inner product linear in its first
variable, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, and

$$h_0u=-\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\partial_j^2u+V(q)u,\qquad u\in D_0,$$

where $a_j>0$ and $V$ is a real polynomial. Require fixed constants $c>0$ and
$C_0\ge0$ such that

$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$

For this physical model, take $q_j$, $a_j$, $c$, $C_0$, and the coefficients
of $V$ to be dimensionless. Adopt a positive energy scale $E_*$ in joules as
primitive finite-regulator data, and use $\hbar$ in joule-seconds under
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. When the mathematical supplier
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]] constructs its specified
self-adjoint form realization $h$ of $h_0$, the model Hamiltonian is
$H_{\rm phys}:=E_*h$ on that supplied domain. This postulate adopts the
finite-regulator polynomial data; it does not assert that the initial
differential expression is self-adjoint or choose an operator domain by
itself.

The finite label set and polynomial are held fixed. A finite spatial regulator
is not thereby Lorentz invariant, and this model asserts no continuum or
infinite-volume limit, no convergence of a perturbation series, and no
reported observation. Its parameters are selected model inputs, not measured
values.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume Countable Choice and use $Q$, $q_h$, and the operator $h$ from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\lambda_1$ be the least
eigenvalue of $h$. Then
$$\inf\{q_h(u):u\in Q,\ \|u\|_2=1\}=\lambda_1.$$
The infimum is attained by every normalized vector in the lowest eigenspace;
no simplicity or nondegeneracy is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.

derivations.claim:
Since $V_\lambda(q)=r^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4\ge (r^2/2)q^2$, the
coercivity hypotheses of [F1] and [F4] hold with $c=r^2/2$ and $C_0=0$.
Countable Choice [A1] therefore gives the form domains of [F1] and the
self-adjoint compact-resolvent form realizations with attained least
eigenvalues from [F4], for both $q_\lambda$ and $q_0$.

On $C_c^\infty$, the shifted form norms obey
$\|u\|_{Q_0}^2\le\|u\|_{Q_\lambda}^2$ because their difference is
$\lambda\int q^4|u|^2dq\ge0$. Hence the identity extends continuously
$Q_\lambda\to Q_0$, and the two continuous injections into $L^2$ identify
the same representative. On the core,
$q_\lambda(u)=q_0(u)+\lambda\int q^4|u|^2dq\ge q_0(u)$; approximating any
$u\in Q_\lambda$ by core elements and using continuity of both forms passes
this inequality to $u$. For a normalized $u$, [F3] gives
$q_0(u)\ge\epsilon_g(0)$, so taking the infimum on $Q_\lambda$ yields
$\epsilon_g(\lambda)\ge\epsilon_g(0)$.

Let $g_b(q)=(b/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-bq^2/2}$ with $b=r/\sqrt{2a}$, the
normalized ground function in [F2] for $c=r^2/2$. Choose the smooth cutoff
$\chi_R(q)=\chi(q/R)$ from [F2], with $\chi=1$ on $[-1,1]$,
$\chi=0$ outside $[-2,2]$, and $|\chi_R'|\le C/R$. Then
$u_R=\chi_Rg_b\in C_c^\infty$. For $S>R$, $u_R-u_S$ is supported where
$|q|\ge R$, and
$\|(u_R-u_S)'\|_2\le\|1_{|q|\ge R}g_b'\|_2
+C(R^{-1}+S^{-1})\|1_{|q|\ge R}g_b\|_2\to0$.
The weighted part of its $Q_\lambda$ norm is bounded in square by
$\int_{|q|\ge R}(r^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4+2)|g_b(q)|^2dq\to0$.
These tails vanish because each polynomial times $e^{-bq^2}$ is integrable:
for large $|q|$, its product with $|q|^2$ is bounded. Thus $(u_R)$ is
$Q_\lambda$-Cauchy. Its $L^2$ limit is $g_b$, so injectivity in [F1] gives
$g_b\in Q_\lambda$.

From $g_b'=-bqg_b$ and $\|g_b\|_2=1$, integrate the derivatives of
$q e^{-bq^2}$ and $q^3e^{-bq^2}$ over $\mathbb R$. Their boundary terms
vanish by Gaussian decay, giving
$\int q^2|g_b|^2dq=1/(2b)$ and
$\int q^4|g_b|^2dq=3/(4b^2)$. Hence
$q_\lambda(g_b)=ab/2+r^2/(4b)+3\lambda/(4b^2)$. At
$b=r/\sqrt{2a}$, the first two terms equal
$\epsilon_g(0)=r\sqrt{a/2}$ by [F2], and the last term is
$3a\lambda/(2r^2)$.

Since $g_b\in Q_\lambda$ is normalized, [F3] gives
$\epsilon_g(\lambda)\le q_\lambda(g_b)$. Combining this with step 2.1 and
step 3.1 yields
$0\le\epsilon_g(\lambda)-\epsilon_g(0)\le3a\lambda/(2r^2)$.

Multiplication by $E_*>0$ preserves both inequalities and gives the
stated joule-valued bound. By [A3], this is a selected-model energy

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Use one fixed finite-regulator data set from
[[post-qft-regulated-polynomial-model]], and let $h$ be the self-adjoint form
realization supplied by
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]], with domain $D(h)$ and
eigenpairs $(\psi_n,\lambda_n)$. Let $E_*>0$ joules and set
$H_{\rm phys}:=E_*h$ on $D(h)$. For physical time $\tau$ in seconds define

$$U_{\rm phys}(\tau):=U(E_*\tau/\hbar),$$

where $U(s)$ is the dimensionless-parameter group of
[[thm-qft-regulated-global-unitary-evolution]]. Then $U_{\rm phys}$ is a
strongly continuous unitary group, $U_{\rm phys}(0)=I$,
$U_{\rm phys}(\tau_1+\tau_2)=U_{\rm phys}(\tau_1)U_{\rm phys}(\tau_2)$,
and $\|U_{\rm phys}(\tau)\psi\|=\|\psi\|$ for every $\psi\in H_N$.
Its norm derivative exists exactly for $\psi\in D(h)$, and then

$$\frac{d}{d\tau}U_{\rm phys}(\tau)\psi=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H_{\rm phys}U_{\rm phys}(\tau)\psi.$$

The result is a conditional deduction for the selected finite-regulator
model. It is not an empirical observation or a continuum-limit theorem.

Assume Countable Choice and use one fixed one-mode regulator with
dimensionless $a>0$, $r>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$. Here $r$ is a polynomial
coefficient, not an SI rest mass. Take
$V_\lambda(q)=\frac{r^2}{2}q^2+\lambda q^4$ on
$H_1=L^2(\mathbb R,dq;\mathbb C)$, with the form realization from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\epsilon_g(\lambda)$
be its least eigenvalue. The physical ground-energy prediction for the
adopted scale $E_*>0$ joules is
$E_g^{\rm phys}(\lambda):=E_*\epsilon_g(\lambda)$. Then

$$0\le E_g^{\rm phys}(\lambda)-E_g^{\rm phys}(0)\le \frac{3E_*a\lambda}{2r^2}.$$

For $\lambda>0$ this is an interacting one-mode model on the full
$L^2(\mathbb R)$ space. The inequality is an exact fixed-regulator model
deduction; it supplies neither an observed energy nor a perturbation-series
or continuum-limit claim.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). A **finite-mode regulator** in this item is a fixed
finite nonempty label set $J$ with $N:=|J|\ge1$, a fixed enumeration of $J$ by
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and the real coordinate vector
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may name sites of a finite
lattice or finitely many modes; their geometry enters only through the chosen
polynomial below. No limit in $N$ is part of this definition.

Choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$, constants $c>0$ and $C_0\ge0$,
and a real polynomial $V\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$ such that
$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$
Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost
everywhere equality and inner product
$$\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}u(q)\overline{v(q)}\,dq,$$
linear in the first variable. Under Countable Choice this is a complex Hilbert
space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let
$D_0:=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, the smooth compactly supported
complex-valued functions. The associated **polynomial differential expression**
is the map
$$h_0:D_0\to H_N,\qquad h_0u:=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Vu.$$
It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are
smooth and compactly supported. Set $W:=V+C_0+1$, so
$W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$. This definition specifies finite mathematical data and a
differential expression; it does not choose a self-adjoint operator domain or
assert a continuum or infinite-volume limit.

domain. The quartic coefficient is positive, and the Hilbert space is
infinite-dimensional by step 1.1; thus this is an interacting operator model,
not a finite matrix replacement. No observation or continuum extrapolation

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.
