An element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$ is this finite symmetric
coefficient family, evaluated on fields by $F_f$. Pointwise sums, scalar
multiples, and products again have finite symmetric compactly supported
coefficient families: for products, expand the two finite sums and
symmetrize each tensor product $f_m\otimes g_n$. Thus these elements form
an algebra; the product-integral identity follows from Riemann Fubini on a
rectangle containing the compact supports
([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

For $k=0$, set $F_f^{(0)}(\phi)=F_f(\phi)$. For $1\le k\le N$,
the $k$-th functional derivative kernel assigned to this coefficient
family is
$$ F_f^{(k)}(\phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sum_{n=k}^{N}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\int_{X^{n-k}}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_{k+1}\cdots dx_n. $$
For $k>N$ it is zero. Each displayed kernel is smooth, symmetric and compactly supported in its $k$ remaining variables: compactness follows by projection of the finite union of coefficient-kernel supports, and derivatives pass through the finite-compact integrals by [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]].
In the term $n=k$, the empty integral and empty product mean simply
$f_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$.

The scope is exactly smooth compact coefficient kernels. A local functional
whose higher derivative kernels are distributions on a thin diagonal is not
included merely because its field expression is polynomial.

Let $d,n\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and give
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ its LF test-function topology.
The finite linear span of elementary product tests
$$ (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\longmapsto\prod_{j=1}^{n}g_j(x_j),\qquad g_j\in\mathcal D(X), $$
is dense. More precisely, for each $\Phi\in\mathcal D(X^n)$, there is a
sequence of such finite sums whose supports lie in one fixed compact product
and whose derivatives of every multi-index converge uniformly to those of
$\Phi$. Symmetrized finite sums are dense in
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$. Consequently the symmetric-kernel
representation in [[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]] is
unique: if a finite symmetric-kernel polynomial vanishes on every real smooth
field, every coefficient kernel vanishes.

Let $X=\mathbb R^4$ and let $\Delta_X=\{(x,y)\in X\times X:x=y\}$.
For $\Psi\in\mathcal D(X\times X)$, define
$$ \langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle =\int_X\Psi(x,x)\,d^4x. $$
Then $\delta_{\Delta_X}\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ is a continuous
complex-linear distribution with support exactly $\Delta_X$, and it is
symmetric under exchanging $x$ and $y$. No nonzero smooth function on
$X\times X$ is supported on $\Delta_X$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

Fix $\mu\ge0$ and the $(-+++)$, shell, Fourier, and coordinate conventions
of [[lem-qft-free-time-ordered-kernel]]. That current supplier states that
its relative-coordinate tempered distribution $H_\mu$ is symmetric, agrees
with the ordered Wightman kernels on strictly ordered time supports and on
spacelike-separated supports, and has no prefactor $i$ in its definition.
Its current carrier is a draft with a supplied conditional proof; the formula
below uses that exact interface.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is the space
of smooth compactly supported complex tests with the LF topology, and
$\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ is its continuous complex-linear dual, paired
bilinearly with no conjugation
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-test-function-topology]],
[[def-distribution]]). Schwartz space consists of smooth functions with all
polynomially weighted derivatives bounded; $\mathcal S'$ is its continuous
complex-linear dual with bilinear pairing
([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]],
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]], [[def-tempered-distribution]]).

For any relative-coordinate distribution $K\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^4)$,
define its translation-invariant two-point bidistribution
$\widetilde K\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4)$ by
$$ \langle\widetilde K,\Psi\rangle =\left\langle K,\ z\longmapsto\int_{\mathbb R^4}\Psi(y+z,y)\,dy\right\rangle, \qquad \Psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4). $$
The inner function is a test function: its support lies in the difference
of the two compact coordinate projections of $\operatorname{supp}\Psi$;
each derivative in $z$ is the Riemann integral of the corresponding
first-variable derivative of $\Psi$ over a compact rectangle containing
the fixed compact second-variable projection
([[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]).
On each fixed compact support space, every output derivative seminorm is
bounded by the volume of a compact rectangle containing the second-variable
projection times the corresponding source derivative seminorm. The support
of the output lies in the compact difference of the two projections. Thus
this map is continuous on each fixed-support test space, and hence on the LF
test topology [[def-test-function-topology]].
Thus the displayed formula defines a distribution without multiplying
singular distributions. Write $\mathsf H_\mu=\widetilde H_\mu$.

For $F\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)$, define its support as the
finite union of the coordinate projections of the supports of its nonconstant
symmetric coefficient kernels. This is a compact set and is presentation
independent by [[lem-qft-tensor-test-function-density]]. For compact
$A,B\subset\mathbb R^4$, write $A\succcurlyeq_{\mathrm{out}} B$ when
$$ x-y\notin C_-:=\{(t,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4:t\le-|\mathbf x|\} \quad\text{for every }x\in A,\ y\in B. $$
This means the first support has no point in the closed causal past of the
second, using the supplier's fixed inertial chart.

For $n\ge2$ and $1\le i<j\le n$, let $D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}$ contract one
functional derivative in slots $i,j$ against $\mathsf H_\mu$, pairing
independent variables. Define
$$ T_n^H(F_1,\ldots,F_n)(\phi) =\left.m_n\exp\!\left(\eta\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}\right) \prod_{i=1}^nF_i(\phi_i)\right|_{\phi_1=\cdots=\phi_n=\phi}, \qquad T_0^H=1,\quad T_1^H(F)=F. $$
Here $m_n$ multiplies the remaining factors and then substitutes the same
field $\phi$ in every slot; on coefficient kernels it symmetrizes their
finite tensor products. The parameter $\eta$ is formal and fixed by
complex conjugation. Each contraction removes two polynomial degrees, so the
exponential is a finite sum on polynomial inputs. The dependencies
[[thm-tensor-product-distributions-and-iterated-pairings]] and
[[lem-distribution-pairing-with-smooth-parameter-families]] make every
contraction well defined and leave smooth compact kernels in the uncontracted
variables; no diagonal product occurs. Symmetry of $\mathsf H_\mu$ makes
$T_n^H$ symmetric in its inputs.

For a regular compactly supported interaction $V$ and formal coupling $z$,
define
$$ S_z^H(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(iz/\eta)^n}{n!}\,T_n^H(V,\ldots,V) \quad\text{with coefficients in }\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)[\eta,\eta^{-1}]. $$
This is a coefficientwise formal series; the definition asserts no
convergence in $z$, no time-ordered product for singular local functionals,
and no continuum interacting field.

derivations.claim: For real test directions $h,k$, the coefficient of $st$ in $L_g(1+s h+t k)$ is $12\int g(x)h(x)k(x)\,d^4x$, by expanding $(1+s h+t k)^4$. By [F3], this is exactly the pairing of $K_g$ with the product test $h\otimes k$. Thus $K_g$ represents the second derivative on product tests.

For every nonempty fixed compact $K\subseteq X\times X$, choose a compact rectangle $R$ containing its first-coordinate projection. Then $$ |\langle K_g,\Psi\rangle| \le 12\|g\|_\infty\operatorname{vol}(R)\|\Psi\|_\infty \qquad(\operatorname{supp}\Psi\subseteq K), $$ so $K_g$ is continuous on each fixed-support test space and hence on the LF test topology by [F7]. It vanishes on every test supported off the diagonal, so its support is contained there by [F6]. Choose $\rho\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$ with $\rho(0)=1$ using [F5], and set $\Psi(x,y)=g(x)\rho(x-y)$. This is a test function: its support has $x\in\operatorname{supp}g$ and $x-y\in\operatorname{supp}\rho$, so both coordinate projections are compact. Then $$ \langle K_g,\Psi\rangle=12\int_{\mathbb R^4}g(x)^2\,d^4x>0, $$ because a nonzero continuous real function is bounded away from zero on a small ball. Thus $K_g\ne0$.

Suppose $L_g$ had a regular presentation. By [F1], its second derivative at $1$ would have a smooth compactly supported kernel. Its pairings with product tests agree with those of $K_g$ by step 1.1; complex linearity extends agreement to complex product tests, and density [F2] extends it to all tests. Hence the smooth kernel would equal $K_g$ as a distribution. Its support would be contained in the diagonal by step 2.1.

The diagonal has empty interior. A continuous function supported there must vanish: any nonzero value would persist on an open neighborhood not contained in the diagonal. This contradicts $K_g\ne0$ from step 2.1. Therefore $L_g$ has no regular presentation.

By step 4.1, $L_g\notin\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Fact [F8] defines $\star_W$ only on pairs of regular polynomial functionals, and [F9] defines each $T_n^H$ on regular polynomial inputs. Neither operation therefore applies to $L_g$. Any extension across the diagonal is a separate construction and is not proved here.

$$\partial_R\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\leq R\},$$

case_scope.source_excerpt:
For a bounded set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $R>0$, define its two-sided boundary layer
$$\partial_R\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\leq R\},$$
where distance is Euclidean distance and $|\cdot|$ denotes $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. A van Hove sequence is a sequence of bounded Lebesgue measurable sets $(\Omega_k)_{k\geq1}$ with $0<|\Omega_k|<\infty$, $|\Omega_k|\to\infty$, and
$$\frac{|\partial_R\Omega_k|}{|\Omega_k|}\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{for every fixed }R>0.$$
The condition controls both inner and outer boundary neighborhoods. It does not impose connectedness, a bounded aspect ratio, smooth boundaries, or a periodic identification.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume AC. Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. The far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is

$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. The far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a stationary probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. When the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
The cited results below establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume it for every stationary law.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Use the cube $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and the translation $T_x$ defined in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$, let $\omega^{(L)}=\{q+Lk:q\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ be its periodic continuation. Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$. For a probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$, define its **empirical-field barycenter** $\bar C_L$ by
$$\bar C_L(f):=\int C_L(d\omega)\,R_{L,\omega}(f)=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}E_{C_L}[f(T_x\omega^{(L)})]\,dx$$
for local tame $f$ from [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]. This is a spatial average over the finite box, not the raw finite-volume law viewed at a fixed origin.

citations.quote:
It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$.

derivations.claim: Since $\psi$ is nonincreasing, $0\leq g^d\psi(g)\leq \frac{d}{1-2^{-d}}\int_{g/2}^{g}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$ for $g>2R_0$: on $[g/2,g]$, $\psi(r)\geq\psi(g)$, and integration of $r^{d-1}$ gives the displayed coefficient. Both the interval integral and the tail integral in $\eta(g)$ tend to zero as $g\to\infty$, so $\eta(g)\to0$.

For $m\geq2$ and $r\in[(m-1)g,mg]$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(mg)$ and $r^{d-1}\geq((m-1)g)^{d-1}$. Hence $$ \int_{(m-1)g}^{mg}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq g^d(m-1)^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Since $m^{d-1}\leq2^{d-1}(m-1)^{d-1}$, summing over disjoint intervals yields $\sum_{m\geq2}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq2^{d-1}g^{-d}\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$. The $m=1$ term equals $g^{-d}g^d\psi(g)$, so adding it proves the stated bound because $2^{d-1}\geq1$.

For integer $m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(m-1)$ on $[m-2,m-1]$, so $\int_{m-2}^{m-1}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq(m-2)^{d-1}\psi(m-1)$. Since $m^{d-1}\leq c_d(m-2)^{d-1}$ for these $m$, summing over disjoint unit intervals proves $\sum_{m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil} m^{d-1}\psi(m-1)<\infty$.

For each integer $k\geq1$, let $G_k$ be the least integer greater than $2R_0$ such that $\eta(g)\leq k^{-2d}$ for every $g\geq G_k$; it exists by step 1.1 and the well-ordering of the positive integers. Choose a strictly increasing sequence $L_k$ with $L_k\geq kG_k$ and $L_k\geq k^2$. For $\ell\geq L_1$, let $k(\ell)=\max\{k:L_k\leq\ell\}$ and $g(\ell)=\ell/k(\ell)$. Then $k(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)\geq G_{k(\ell)}$ and $g(\ell)\geq k(\ell)$, while $g(\ell)/\ell=1/k(\ell)$. Therefore $$ \left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\leq k(\ell)^d k(\ell)^{-2d}=k(\ell)^{-d}\to0. $$ This gives all three gap limits.

Fix distinct points $x,y$ in a finite configuration and a period $L>0$. For $|k|_\infty$ larger than $2|x-y|_\infty/L+2R_0/L$, the triangle inequality gives $|x-y+Lk|_\infty\geq L|k|_\infty/2>2R_0$. Grouping lattice indices by $m=|k|_\infty$ and applying the sum bound of step 1.2 with gap $g=L/2$ shows $\sum_k|\phi(x-y+Lk)|<\infty$ whenever $L/2>2R_0$. There are finitely many remaining images; any $+\infty$ term makes the periodic energy $+\infty$ by definition, while otherwise their finite sum is well-defined. This proves the periodic-image convention used in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] for all sufficiently large $L$.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $d\geq1$ and let $\phi$ be a regular potential with a nonnegative nonincreasing envelope $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, where $R_0<\infty$ and $\int_{R_0}^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr<\infty$. Thus $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ for $|x|_\infty\geq R_0$. For $g>2R_0$ set
$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent. The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable. This lemma is a deterministic tail estimate; it uses no superstability or thermodynamic-limit conclusion.

boundaries.evidence: Statement the chosen tail gap is positive and tends to infinity, and g>2R_0 is used only in its tail regime. No estimate divides by a zero gap; an empty block contributes zero without division by its count.

derivations.claim:
Choose an integer $k\geq1$ with $1/k\leq r_0$. Partition each unit cell $C_i$ into $k^d$ half-open subcubes of side $1/k$, and denote their occupancies by $n_{i,j}$, $1\leq j\leq k^d$. Distinct points in one subcube have $|x-y|_\infty<1/k\leq r_0$, so their repulsive pair energy is at least $\delta$. Therefore
$$H_{\phi_r}(\omega)\geq\frac{\delta}{2}\sum_{i,j}n_{i,j}(n_{i,j}-1).$$
Writing $\bar n=N_{C_i}(\omega)/k^d$, nonnegativity of $\sum_j(n_{i,j}-\bar n)^2$ expands to $\sum_j n_{i,j}^2\geq N_{C_i}(\omega)^2/k^d$, and $\sum_{i,j}n_{i,j}=N(\omega)$. Thus $H_{\phi_r}(\omega)\geq\frac{\delta}{2k^d}\sum_iN_{C_i}^2-\frac\delta2N$.

The stable part obeys $H_{\phi_s}(\omega)\geq-B_sN$. Add this inequality to step 1.1 and take $A=\delta/(2k^d)$ and $B=B_s+\delta/2$. This proves the cell-quadratic bound. If any term is $+\infty$, the inequality holds in the extended order; otherwise all sums are finite.

derivations.claim:
By [F1], $R_{L,\omega}$ is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue probability on $\Lambda_L$, so it is a probability measure. For a bounded measurable local $f$ and $y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}f(T_{x+y}\omega^{(L)})\,dx.$$
The integrand is $L\mathbb Z^d$-periodic in $x$. The translated cube $\Lambda_L+y$ is another fundamental region for this lattice; partitioning it and $\Lambda_L$ into their finitely many translated intersections and using translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives equal integrals. Hence $R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=R_{L,\omega}(f)$ for every $y$, so $R_{L,\omega}$ is stationary.

For bounded Borel $A$, Tonelli's theorem and the periodic continuation give
$$R_{L,\omega}(N_A)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\sum_{q\in\omega}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}\mathbf1_A(q+Lk+x)\,dx.$$
For each fixed $q\in\omega$, the sets $\Lambda_L+Lk$ partition $\mathbb R^d$ up to null boundaries. Translating variables in each integral therefore makes the inner sum of integrals equal to $|A|$. Summing over the $N$ representatives gives $R_{L,\omega}(N_A)=N|A|/L^d$. Taking $A=[0,1)^d$ proves $\rho(R_{L,\omega})=N/L^d$ and finite intensity.

The barycenter $\bar C_L$ is a probability mixture of the stationary laws $R_{L,\omega}$, so it is stationary. By step 2.1 and Tonelli,
$$\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}[R_{L,\omega}(N_{[0,1)^d})]=E_{C_L}N/L^d<\infty.$$
Thus it belongs to the finite-intensity stationary domain of $\tau_L$.

A fixed pair counted at scale $k$ has separation $s<1/k$, hence $k<1/s$; summing its nonnegative weights over all scales where it is counted is at most $\sum_{k=k_0}^{\lfloor1/s\rfloor}\Delta\chi_k\leq\chi(s)$. Thus the positive core energy in the cell dominates the sum of these weighted pair counts. With $K_N=\lfloor(N/2)^{1/d}\rfloor$, each $k\leq K_N$ satisfies $N^2/k^d-N\geq N^2/(2k^d)$, so the core energy is at least $$ \frac{N^2}{4}\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N}\frac{\Delta\chi_k}{k^d}. $$ Summation by parts writes the coefficient as an initial constant plus $\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N-1}\chi_k(k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d})$; and $k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d}\geq d/(2^{d+1}k^{d+1})$. The series $\sum_k\chi(1/k)k^{-d-1}$ diverges: on dyadic intervals $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]$, monotonicity bounds the integral above by $C_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$, while the corresponding block $2^{j+1}\leq k<2^{j+2}$ contributes at least $c_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$ to that series. The divergent core integral therefore forces the displayed coefficient to tend to infinity.

In case (i), sum the cell core bound from step 1.2 and subtract the negative-pair bound from step 1.1. The resulting coefficient of $N_i^2$ tends to infinity with $N_i$. Above a finite threshold it dominates $2CN_i^2$; below that threshold its possible negative remainder is bounded by a constant times $N_i$. Taking $h(N)$ to be half the positive cell lower bound above the threshold and zero below it gives a nondecreasing extended-valued function with $h(N)/N^2\to\infty$ and $H_\phi\geq\sum_i h(N_i)-bN$.

In case (ii), choose $k$ with $1/k<r_h$ and partition every unit cell into $k^d$ subcubes. A finite-energy configuration has at most one point in each subcube, so $N_i\leq k^d$ for every $i$. Define $h(N)=0$ for $N\leq k^d$ and $h(N)=+\infty$ for $N>k^d$. If any cell exceeds this occupancy, the configuration has a forbidden pair and $H_\phi=+\infty$; otherwise stability gives $H_\phi\geq-BN=\sum_i h(N_i)-BN$. This proves the hard-core alternative.

Assume the potential of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] is stable and regular. In addition, assume either (i) $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ is finite-valued and nonincreasing, $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$, and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; or (ii) there is a hard-core radius $r_h>0$ such that $\phi(x)=+\infty$ whenever $|x|_\infty<r_h$. Then there are a nonnegative nondecreasing $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,+\infty]$ with $h(0)=0$ and $h(N)/N^2\to+\infty$, and a constant $b<\infty$, such that
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}h(N_{C_i}(\omega))-bN(\omega).$$
The hard-core alternative permits $h(N)=+\infty$ above the finite packing capacity of a unit cell. This is stronger than ordinary superstability and is not inferred from stability or regularity alone.

derivations.claim: Stability and [F3] give $Z(L,N;\beta)\leq e^{\beta BN}L^{dN}/N!$. If $N/L^d\to\rho>0$, the factorial integral bounds [F4] imply $$ \limsup L^{-d}\log Z(L,N;\beta)\leq \rho(1+\beta B-\log\rho), $$ so $b(\rho)$ and $F(\rho)$ are bounded above on every compact positive-density interval. The vacuum term gives $b(0)=0$: $Z(L,0)=1$ is a lower bound, and the same stability estimate with $N/L^d\to0$ gives a nonpositive upper limit.

The effective domain of $F$ has nonempty interior. Fix a core cube of side $s>0$ and a gap $g>2R_0$; place one particle in each selected core of a lattice of spacing $s+g$ inside a large box. The absolute interaction from any one occupied core to all others is bounded by $C\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2], with the gap satisfying the stated hypothesis of the diagonal-gap estimate. Restricting each particle to a subcube of volume $v_0>0$ therefore gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\geq v_0^N e^{-C_0N}$ for every density strictly below $(s+g)^{-d}$, after omitting unused lattice cells. Thus $F$ is finite on a nonempty interval of positive densities; by its definition as a finite-mixture envelope it is concave.

Fix a finite list of core preparations $(s_i,n_i)$ with $0<Z(s_i,n_i;\beta)<\infty$. For each $i$, choose a gap $g_i=g(s_i)$ from [F2] along a sequence $s_i\to\infty$ so that $g_i/s_i\to0$ and the positive interaction between distinct cores in the same lattice packing, divided by core volume, tends to zero. Set tile side $a_i=s_i+g_i$ and effective density $r_i=n_i/a_i^d$. If $M_i$ such tiles carry exactly $n_i$ particles in their central $s_i$-cubes, the same shell count as in the proof of [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]] gives cross-energy penalty per occupied volume at most $C (n_i/s_i^d)^2(s_i/g_i)^d\eta(g_i)$, which tends to zero by [F2]. Exact factorization over disjoint core cubes follows because assigning the labeled coordinates to their cores contributes $N!/\prod_i(n_i!)^{M_i}$, cancelling the global $N!$.

For any finite convex combination in the definition of $F(\rho)$, choose core preparations with densities tending to its $\rho_i$ and rates tending to $b(\rho_i)$. If their effective densities do not strictly bracket the target $\rho$, add arbitrarily small weights at one attainable density below and one above $\rho$; such densities exist because $\rho$ is interior. Their mixture coefficients can then be perturbed by quantities tending to zero so the effective mean is exactly $\rho$. Place the fixed core types in finitely many macroscopic slabs with these volume fractions, inserting fixed empty layers wider than $R_0$ between slabs. For fixed core sizes and gaps, the distinct-slab cross energy divided by total volume tends to zero: for interaction distances at most $R$, only $O(RL^{d-1})$ particles lie in the interface strips, while the remaining contribution is bounded by a constant times $L^d\sum_{|j|_\infty>R}\Psi_j$; take $L\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$.

First reserve an outer layer of fixed width $W$. For each large $L$, put $\rho_L=N_L/L^d$ and choose the slab fractions in the remaining volume to match the count $N_L$ at density $\rho_L L^d/(L^d-O(WL^{d-1}))$. This target tends to $\rho$, so the strict bracketing in step 3.1 applies uniformly for large $L$ and absorbs the reserved layer without assuming its one-particle capacity replaces a bulk density. Rounding the finitely many slab and core counts then leaves at most $C_1L^{d-1}$ particles unplaced, with $C_1$ depending on the fixed preparations but not on $W$; the error comes only from the finitely many slab faces and incomplete boundary tiles. Choose $W$ large enough to contain at least $C_1L^{d-1}$ small cells separated from each other and every core by more than $R_0$. Put each missing particle in one such cell. Its interaction with the fixed preparations is bounded by the same summable tail, so the correction changes log weight by only $O(L^{d-1})$. This constructs exactly $N_L$ particles for every sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, and gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z(L,N_L;\beta)\geq\sum_i\theta_i\frac{\log Z(s_i,n_i;\beta)-\mathrm{cross}_i}{a_i^d}, $$ where $\mathrm{cross}_i/a_i^d\to0$ by step 2.1. Taking preparations approaching the selected convex combination and then the supremum gives $\liminf\geq F(\rho)$.

By the definition of $b$, every sequence with density tending $\rho$ has limsup rate at most $b(\rho)\leq F(\rho)$. Together with step 4.1 this proves the asserted limit. A finite concave function on an open interval is continuous: fix $a<\rho<b$ in the interval; the chord slopes from $a$ and $b$ bound the difference quotients on a smaller interval around $\rho$, yielding a finite local Lipschitz bound. This establishes finiteness and continuity of $F$ on its effective interior while leaving excluded endpoints undecided.

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], fix $\beta>0$, and define $Z(L,N;\beta)$ as in that definition. For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$. On the interior of $\{\rho:F(\rho)>-\infty\}$, $F$ is finite and continuous. For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], fix $\beta>0$, and define $Z(L,N;\beta)$ as in that definition. For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$. On the interior of $\{\rho:F(\rho)>-\infty\}$, $F$ is finite and continuous. For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.

derivations.claim: Put $q=ae^{\beta B}$. For every $N$-point configuration, $0\leq e^{-\beta H_\phi}\leq e^{\beta BN}$ by [A1]. Applying [F3] to the finite-volume integral gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Summing by [F4] yields $\Xi_L\leq e^{qL^d}$; the empty configuration contributes exactly $1$, so $\Xi_L\geq1$.

Choose $K>eq+1$ and an integer cutoff $n_\ell$ with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$. For $N>n_\ell$, $1\leq e^{N-K\ell^d}$, so $$ \sum_{N>n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)\leq e^{-K\ell^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eq\ell^d)^N}{N!}=e^{(eq-K)\ell^d}\leq e^{-\ell^d}. $$ Because $\Xi_\ell\geq1$, the truncated sum $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)$ satisfies $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$.

Fix a core side $\ell$ and a gap $g>2R_0$. Place $M=\lfloor L/(\ell+g)\rfloor^d$ disjoint core cubes of side $\ell$ in $[0,L)^d$ on the lattice of spacing $\ell+g$. Restrict every core to at most $n_\ell$ particles. If two core indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, every pair between them has separation at least $mg$ in maximum norm. The number of offsets in shell $m$ is $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\leq c_dm^{d-1}$. By [F1], the sum of positive cross-core pair energies is therefore at most $$ D_{L,\ell,g}\leq c_dM n_\ell^2\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Negative cross-core energies only increase the Boltzmann weight. Splitting the grand sum by the particle counts in these disjoint cores, Tonelli [F5] and the multinomial coefficient show that the global $N!$ cancels the assignments of labeled coordinates to cores. Thus $$ \Xi_L\geq e^{-\beta D_{L,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^M. $$

Divide the last inequality by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell,g$ fixed. Since $M/L^d\to(\ell+g)^{-d}$, [F2] gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L\geq\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g}\right)^d\left[\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-C_dK_1^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)\right], $$ where $K_1=K+1$ bounds $n_\ell/\ell^d$ for $\ell\geq1$ and $C_d$ absorbs the fixed shell-count constant and $\beta$.

The numbers $p_\ell=\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell$ lie in $[0,q]$ by step 1.1, so choose $\ell_j\to\infty$ with $p_{\ell_j}\to\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. Set $g=g(\ell_j)$ from [F2]. Then $g/\ell_j\to0$, the volume fraction tends to $1$, the cutoff logarithm divided by $\ell_j^d$ tends to zero, and the cross-core error tends to zero. Step 4.1 therefore yields $\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\geq\limsup_{L\to\infty}p_L$. The reverse inequality is automatic for every real sequence, so the limit exists; step 1.1 makes it finite.

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$. Then
$$1\leq\Xi_L(a,\beta)\leq\exp(ae^{\beta B}L^d),\qquad p(a,\beta):=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(a,\beta)$$
exists and is finite. This theorem assumes only stability and the decreasing integrable two-sided tail in regularity; it does not assert canonical fixed-density convergence, periodic-boundary equality, or arbitrary-region limits.

derivations.claim: Fix an interior attainable density $\rho>0$ and a sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. The grand sum contains the nonnegative term $e^{\alpha N_L}Z(L,N_L;\beta)$, so $\liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta)\geq F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho$ by [F1]. Taking the supremum over interior densities gives the lower bound. The vacuum term $Z(L,0)=1$ gives the value $0$ at density zero. Endpoint values are limits from the interior by their definition, so they do not enlarge the supremum.

Put $q=e^{\alpha+\beta B}$. For each $N\geq0$, stability and the box-volume formula give $e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Choose $K>eq+1$. For $N>KL^d$, $1\leq e^{N-KL^d}$, so the factorial bound gives $\sum_{N>KL^d}e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta) \leq e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eqL^d)^N}{N!} \leq e^{-L^d}.$ The remaining at most $KL^d+2$ terms are bounded by their maximum times this number; its logarithm divided by $L^d$ tends to zero.

Choose maximizing retained particle numbers and a subsequence with $N_L/L^d\to\rho\in[0,K]$; nested-interval bisection on the compact interval $[0,K]$ supplies the subsequence. The canonical upper rate is at most $b(\rho)\leq F_\beta(\rho)$, since the one-term mixture in the definition of $F_\beta$ includes $b(\rho)$. At $\rho=0$, stability gives upper rate at most $0=F_\beta(0)$. If $u$ is a finite upper endpoint and $b(u)>-\infty$, mix a preparation approaching $b(u)$ with an interior preparation of density $r<u$, in slab fractions $1-\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$. The exact packing inequality in [F1] gives $F_\beta((1-\epsilon)u+\epsilon r)\geq(1-\epsilon)b(u)+\epsilon b(r).$ As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, the left side tends to the assigned interior endpoint limit; hence $b(u)\leq F_\beta(u)$. If $b(u)=-\infty$ this bound is automatic. Outside the closed effective domain, $b(\rho)=-\infty$, again because a finite $b(\rho)$ would make $F_\beta(\rho)\geq b(\rho)$. Thus the maximum retained term has limiting rate at most $\sup_{\rho\geq0}(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho)$. The tail estimate in step 1.2 and the lower bound in step 1.1 prove the first equality.

The extension $F_\beta$ is proper, upper-semicontinuous and concave. It is finite and concave on its open effective interior by [F1], hence continuous there. At zero, stability and the concavity of $g(\rho)=\rho(1+\beta B-\log\rho)$ give $F_\beta(\rho)\leq g(\rho)\to0$. The sparse separated-cell lower bound in [F1] gives $F_\beta(\rho)\geq c\rho$ for a fixed finite $c$, so $F_\beta(\rho)\to0=F_\beta(0)$. At any finite upper endpoint use the assigned interior upper-semicontinuous limit; outside the closed effective domain set $F_\beta=-\infty$. Hence $G=-F_\beta$, with $G=+\infty$ on negative densities, is a proper closed convex extended-real function on $\mathbb R$. Its conjugate is $G^*(\alpha)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{\alpha\rho+F_\beta(\rho)\}=P(\alpha,\beta)$ by steps 1.1–2.2. Applying [F3] gives $G(\rho)=\sup_\alpha\{\alpha\rho-P(\alpha,\beta)\}$, which is the second equality. The endpoint convention is needed for closedness; it asserts no finite-volume endpoint realization.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Extend it by $F_\beta(0)=0$, by its interior upper-semicontinuous limit at any finite upper endpoint of its effective domain, and by $-\infty$ outside the closed effective domain; retain the value $-\infty$ if the endpoint limit is $-\infty$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$.

For a bounded set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $R>0$, define its two-sided boundary layer
$$\partial_R\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\leq R\},$$
where distance is Euclidean distance and $|\cdot|$ denotes $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.
For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable.

derivations.claim:
Use the half-open unit-cell partition $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$ from [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]] and first take a finite union $\mathcal R$ of these cells. Let $\Pi_{\mathcal R}$ be the unnormalized positional sector measure whose $N$-point part is $z^N/N!$ times product Lebesgue measure, and let $\mu_{\mathcal R}$ have density $e^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{free}}}/\Xi_{\mathcal R}$ relative to $\Pi_{\mathcal R}$. By [L1] and Tonelli [F5],
$$E N_i^2=E N_i+E[N_i(N_i-1)] \leq \xi |C_i\cap\mathcal R|+\xi^2|C_i\cap\mathcal R|^2 \leq M:=\xi+\xi^2.$$
This gives a uniform second-moment bound for every unit cell in every such region.

For each $\Omega_k$, let $\mathcal R_k$ be the union of unit cells meeting $\Omega_k$. Then $\Xi_{\Omega_k}\leq\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}$ by domain monotonicity, and $|\mathcal R_k|/|\Omega_k|\to1$ by the van Hove boundary condition. Put $J_0=\lceil R_0+2\rceil$, where $R_0$ is the regular-tail cutoff in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and choose $M_0\geq\max\{2B,\psi(J_0-1)\}$. For $j\in\mathbb Z^d$, define $\kappa_j=M_0$ when $|j|_\infty<J_0$ and $\kappa_j=\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ otherwise. If two particles occupy cells with offset $j$, their negative pair energy is bounded by $\kappa_j$: for near offsets, stability on a two-point configuration gives $\phi(x)\geq-2B$, and for far offsets the regularity envelope applies. Also $\sum_j\kappa_j<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Partition the cells of $\mathcal R_k$ into boxes $B$ of $\ell$ unit cells per side and, for each occupied cell $i$, set $e_i=\sum_{j:\,B(j)\neq B(i)}\kappa_{i-j}$. The negative cross-box energy obeys $W^-\leq\sum_i e_iN_i^2$, by $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$ and summation over ordered cross-box cell pairs. Step 1.1 gives $E W^-\leq M\sum_i e_i$, so Markov's inequality shows $W^-\leq2M\sum_i e_i$ with probability at least $1/2$ (with probability one if the sum vanishes). On this event $H_{\mathrm{total}}\geq H_{\mathrm{in}}-2M\sum_i e_i$, where $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the sum of within-box energies. Therefore
$$\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}/2\leq e^{2\beta M\sum_i e_i}\prod_B\Xi_{\mathcal R_k\cap B}.$$
Indeed, $\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}\mu_{\mathcal R_k}(E)=\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{total}}}d\Pi_{\mathcal R_k}$; bound this by $e^{2\beta M\sum_i e_i}\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{in}}}d\Pi_{\mathcal R_k}$, then factor the latter integral by boxes. Each unrestricted partial-box partition is at most the full $\ell$-cube partition. For one full box, put $E_\ell=\sum_{i\in B,j\notin B}\kappa_{i-j}$. For fixed $R$, cells within distance $R$ of the boundary contribute at most $O_R(\ell^{d-1})\sum_j\kappa_j$, while every other cell contributes at most $\ell^d\sum_{|j|_\infty>R}\kappa_j$. Thus $E_\ell/\ell^d\to0$, by first letting $\ell\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$. Consequently
$$\limsup_k|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k} \leq\ell^{-d}\bigl[\log\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}+2\beta M E_\ell\bigr].$$
Let $\ell\to\infty$ and use [F4].

For the lower bound, put $q=ze^{\beta B}$ and choose $K>eq+1$. For integer core side $\ell\geq1$, let $n_\ell$ be an integer with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$ and set $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}z^NZ(\Lambda_\ell,N;\beta)$. The stability tail estimate in the proof of [F4] gives $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}(z,\beta)$. Fix $g>2R_0$ and retain every complete $(\ell+g)$-tile whose core lies in $\Omega_k$. By [F2], the retained count $M_k$ divided by $|\Omega_k|$ tends $(\ell+g)^{-d}$. Each core has at most $(K+1)\ell^d$ particles. If two tile indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, their core points are separated by at least $mg$; hence the positive cross energy per core is at most
$$C_d(K+1)^2\ell^{2d}\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq C'_d(K+1)^2\ell^{2d}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Summing over cores, using the exact ordered-label assignment count to cancel the global $N!$, and discarding negative cross energy gives
$$\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)\geq e^{-\beta D_{k,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^{M_k},\qquad \frac{D_{k,\ell,g}}{|\Omega_k|}\leq C'_d(K+1)^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)+o_k(1).$$
First let $k\to\infty$. Then choose $g=g(\ell)$ from [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]] and let integer $\ell\to\infty$; $g/\ell\to0$, the packing fraction tends one, $(\ell/g)^d\eta(g)\to0$, and $\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})\to0$. The resulting liminf is at least the cube pressure [F4].

Assume a superstable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the van Hove definition [[def-tdmath-van-hove-sequence]]. For a bounded Lebesgue-measurable $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$, define $\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)=\{(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\Lambda^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ and $H_N(q)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. With $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, set
$$Z_\Lambda(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)}e^{-\beta H_N(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_\Lambda(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_\Lambda(N;\beta).$$
This is the labelled positional Lebesgue integral with indistinguishable-particle normalization and includes no exterior interaction. For $\Lambda=[0,L)^d$ it agrees with $Z(L,N;\beta)$ and $\Xi(L;z,\beta)$ from [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For every van Hove sequence $(\Omega_k)$ and fixed $z,\beta>0$, the free-wall grand pressure satisfies
$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac1{|\Omega_k|}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)=p(z,\beta),$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The extra superstability hypothesis supplies the uniform cell-occupation bound used below; no arbitrary-shape theorem under stability alone is claimed.

derivations.claim: Put $S_n=\{i\in\mathbb Z^d:|i|_\infty\leq n\}$, $v_n=|S_n|=V_n$, $N_i(\omega)=|\omega\cap C_i|$, $T_n(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_n}N_i(\omega)^2$, and $T_n^h(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_n}h(N_i(\omega))$. Choose $m_0\geq\lceil R_0+1\rceil$ and $M_0\geq\max\{2B,\psi(m_0-1)\}$. Set $\gamma_m=M_0$ for integers $m<m_0$ and $\gamma_m=\psi(m-1)$ for $m\geq m_0$. Then $\gamma$ is nonincreasing, dominates the negative part at every cell offset, dominates $|\phi|$ at offsets $m\geq m_0$, and $\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}\gamma_{|j|_\infty}<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Let $\Delta_m=\gamma_m-\gamma_{m+1}\geq0$ and $v_m=(2m+1)^d$. Since $\gamma_r=\sum_{m\geq r}\Delta_m$, Tonelli gives $\sum_m\Delta_m v_m=\sum_j\gamma_{|j|_\infty}<\infty$. Thus $\delta_k:=\frac12\sum_{m\geq k}\Delta_m v_m\to0$.

For an interior configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$ and any $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, the long-offset cell sum satisfies
$$\sum_{i\in S_n,\ j\in\mathbb Z^d:\,|i-j|_\infty\geq k}\gamma_{|i-j|_\infty}N_i(\omega)N_j(\zeta)\leq\delta_k\bigl(T_n(\omega)+2^dtV_n\bigr).$$
Indeed, expand $\gamma_r=\sum_{m\geq r}\Delta_m$ and enlarge the offset set in the $m$th term to $j\in S_m+i$. With
$$S_{n,m}(\zeta)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}N_j(\zeta)^2\,\#\{i\in S_n:j\in S_m+i\},$$
the inequality $ab\leq(a^2+b^2)/2$ bounds that term by $\frac12\Delta_m(v_mT_n+S_{n,m})$. The multiplicity is at most $\min(v_n,v_m)$ and vanishes unless $j\in S_{n+m}$, so $S_{n,m}\leq\min(v_n,v_m)t v_{n+m}\leq2^dtv_nv_m$. Summing proves the estimate.

Set $g(r)=r\sqrt{h(r)}$ for $r\in\mathbb N_0$ and $g^*(s)=\sup_{r\in\mathbb N_0}\{rs-g(r)\}$. Then $g(r)/r^2\to\infty$ and $g(r)/h(r)\to0$, so $g^*(s)/s^2\to0$: for each $a>0$, eventually $g(r)\geq r^2/(4a)$, and completing the square gives $g^*(s)\leq as^2+C_a$. Also $rs\leq g(r)+g^*(s)$. For a fixed $k\geq m_0$, every near cross pair has its inside cell in $S_n\setminus S_{n-k}$ and its exterior cell in $S_{n+k}\setminus S_n$; its negative energy is at most $M_0$. Counting the finitely many offsets of size below $k$, for every $a>0$ we obtain
$$W^-_{\rm near}\leq C_k\left(aT_n^h+C_a|S_n\setminus S_{n-k}|+atv_{n+k}+C_a|S_{n+k}\setminus S_n|\right).$$
Here $g(r)\leq ah(r)+C_a$ and $g^*(s)\leq as^2+C_a$ were used, with $\sum_{j\in S_{n+k}\setminus S_n}N_j(\zeta)^2\leq tv_{n+k}$. First choose $k$ large in step 2.1 so that its far negative-energy bound is at most $\epsilon(T_n^h+V_n)/2$. For this fixed $k$, both boundary-cell counts are $O_k(n^{d-1})$ and $v_{n+k}/v_n\to1$, so choosing $a$ small and then $n$ large makes the near bound at most $\epsilon(T_n^h+V_n)/2$. The far estimate uses $T_n\leq T_n^h+q^2V_n$ for a fixed $q$ with $h(r)\geq r^2$ when $r\geq q$. Consequently, for each $0<\epsilon<1$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)\geq-\epsilon T_n^h(\omega)-\epsilon V_n$$
uniformly over $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$.

By [F3], $T_n^h\leq H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+bN$. For each $0<\epsilon<1$ and all sufficiently large $n$, step 3.1 therefore gives
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)\leq e^{\beta\epsilon V_n}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+\beta\epsilon T_n^h}\,dq^N$$
and
$$\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+\beta\epsilon T_n^h}\,dq^N\leq\Xi(2n+1;ze^{\beta\epsilon b},\beta(1-\epsilon)).$$
The inequality is uniform over $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$.

For the lower bound, restrict interior particles to $\Lambda_{n-k}$, leaving the corridor empty. Choose $k\geq m_0$, so every interior-exterior cell offset is in the far tail. The two-sided estimate of step 2.1 gives
$$|W(\omega,\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n)|\leq\delta_k\bigl(T_{n-k}(\omega)+2^dtV_{n-k}\bigr).$$
With $T_{n-k}\leq T_{n-k}^h+q^2V_{n-k}$, choose $k$ large enough that the right side is at most $\epsilon(T_{n-k}^h+V_n)$. Since $T_{n-k}^h\leq H_{n-k,\mathrm{free}}+bN$, integration over the restricted positions yields
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)\geq e^{-\beta\epsilon V_n}\Xi(2(n-k)+1;ze^{-\beta\epsilon b},\beta(1+\epsilon))$$
uniformly over $\zeta$. For fixed $\epsilon$, the selected $k$ is fixed as $n\to\infty$, and the removed corridor volume fraction vanishes.

Divide the bounds in steps 4.1–3.2 by $V_n$ and let $n\to\infty$; [F4] supplies the perturbed free-cube pressure limits. These limits are finite convex functions of $(\beta,\log z)$ by Hölder's inequality [F5], since finite-volume log partition functions are convex and pointwise limits preserve convexity. A finite convex function is continuous on the open parameter domain $\beta>0$, $z>0$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ in both uniform bounds. Their upper and lower limits coincide with $p(z,\beta)$ uniformly over $\Omega(t)$. For $t=0$, every exterior configuration in $\Omega(0)$ is empty, so the equality with the free-wall pressure is immediate.

Assume a stable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the genuine finite-valued positive-core condition of [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]]: for some $r_0>0$, a nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_0]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_0$ and $\int_0^{r_0}\chi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr=+\infty$. Let $\Lambda_n=[-n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)^d$, $V_n=(2n+1)^d$, $C_i=i+[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)^d$, and $\mathcal C_{\rm lf}$ be the set of locally finite simple configurations $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$. For $t\geq0$ define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta\in\mathcal C_{\rm lf}:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\text{ for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For $\omega=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)$, write $H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. For $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, let $\zeta_n^{\rm out}=\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n$ and define the finite-volume boundary Hamiltonian
$$H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)=H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{y\in\zeta_n^{\rm out}}\phi(q_i-y).$$
The exterior series has finite negative part by the proof below; its extended value may be $+\infty$, with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$. Define
$$Z_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_{n,\zeta}(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta).$$
For fixed $z,\beta>0$ and $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure with this exterior pair energy satisfies
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\zeta\in\Omega(t)}\left|\frac1{V_n}\log\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)-p(z,\beta)\right|=0,$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube pressure from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The exterior configuration is restricted to the stated fixed square-count class; no volume-filling external field is included. The conclusion is conditional on the genuine positive core and does not infer it from superstability alone.

citations.quote: Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB.

The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$.

For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.
Then $\mathcal H_c$ is compact and sequentially compact in $\tau_L$.

Let $d\geq1$, let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be ergodic under the full translation group $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose its specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma$ relative to the unit-intensity Poisson law $Q$ is finite.
A real measurable function $f$ on $\Omega$ is local if there is a bounded Borel set $A$ such that $f$ is measurable with respect to the restriction $\omega\mapsto\omega|_A$.
Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$.

Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for random variables $R,S,Y$ taking values in standard-Borel spaces $\mathcal R,\mathcal S,\mathcal Y$, with $R=r(S)$ for a measurable $r:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$, and a probability reference $Q_Y$ on $\mathcal Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever $D(P_{S,Y}\Vert P_S\otimes Q_Y)<\infty$.

If $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures on the same measurable space, define
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int h\log h\,dQ,&P\ll Q\text{ and }h=dP/dQ,\\+\infty,&P\not\ll Q.\end{cases}$$
Use $0\log0=0$.

derivations.claim: Georgii's Theorem 1 [L1] gives existence of $\Phi(P)$ and lower semicontinuity for every stationary finite-intensity law. Its Euclidean radial tail hypothesis follows from ours: $|x|_\infty\leq|x|_2\leq\sqrt d\,|x|_\infty$, so replacing $\psi(r)$ by $\psi(r/\sqrt d)$ preserves monotonicity and finite weighted integral by a change of variables. The stable-plus-positive-core definition matches the source's superstable condition after choosing a smaller Euclidean core ball. Thus $\Phi$ has exactly the domain and convention in the Statement.

The cell estimate [F2] and $\beta>0$ imply $J=I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$ is lower semicontinuous and coercive on bounded-$J$ sets: the Poisson entropy variational inequality with bounded truncations of $aN_{C_0}$ gives $I(P)\geq a\rho(P)-(e^a-1)$; the pointwise square inequality gives $E_PN_{C_0}^2\geq\rho(P)^2$. Hence bounded $J$ bounds $\rho$, $I$, and $\Phi$ from above. A finite candidate exists: take independent Bernoulli occupancy of widely separated small cubes, at most one absolutely continuously distributed point per cube, and a uniform random lattice phase. Each tile has finite relative entropy to Poisson, and the summable regular tail bounds its absolute intertile energy per volume. Thus $J$ is proper. By [F3] and the choice assumptions [A1], its bounded sublevels are compact in $\tau_L$.

For the finite-volume Gibbs tilt $G_{L,z,\beta,bc}$, direct integration gives $$ L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc} =-L^{-d}D(G_{L,z,\beta,bc}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}) -\beta L^{-d}E_GH_{L,bc} +L^{-d}\log z\,E_GN. $$ Georgii's Theorem 2 [L2], applied with the present superstable regular interaction and $F=0$, supplies the matching upper and lower empirical-field bounds and the free/periodic pressure limit. Its upper proof uses this entropy identity, block stationarization, and the superstable cell cutoff; its lower proof conditions finite blocks on bounded finite-energy events, inserts empty corridors, and applies the spatial likelihood limit. The inspected source hypotheses match [F1]–[F8]: the Poisson reference is independent unit intensity, $\tau_L$ is the local-tame topology [F5], entropy compactness is [F3], and the energy-density interface is [L1]. The theorem therefore yields $$ p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_P\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\} $$ for both boundary conditions, with compact variational sublevels.

The minimum is attained: a minimizing sequence lies in a finite sublevel by the sparse finite candidate in step 1.2; compactness [F3] gives a convergent subsequence and lower semicontinuity from step 1.1 gives a minimizer. The set of minimizers is the closed minimum level within that compact sublevel, hence nonempty and compact. This agrees with the compact-sublevel conclusion in [L2].

The unit-intensity Poisson law on $\Lambda_L$ has density $e^{-L^d}/N!$ relative to Lebesgue measure on the $N$-point sector. Therefore the physical partition $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}=e^{L^d}Z_{L,z,\beta,\mathrm{free}}$; its log rate is $p_Q+1$. This is only a positional normalization conversion.

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB. Let $\phi$ be superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and fix $z,\beta>0$. For stationary finite-intensity configuration laws, let $I(P)$ be relative entropy density with respect to the independent unit-intensity Poisson law, $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$, and $\Phi(P)$ the limiting positional energy density. The existence and lower semicontinuity of $\Phi$ under these hypotheses are part of the proof below. For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$. This theorem concerns positional configurations only. If $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}$ is instead normalized against Lebesgue measure with $1/N!$, then $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}=e^{L^d}Z_{L,z,\beta,\mathrm{free}}$, so its logarithmic rate is $p_Q+1$.

L1.title: H.-O. Georgii, Large deviations and the equivalence of ensembles for Gibbsian particle systems with superstable interaction
L1.source_section: Theorem 1, Section 3, printed p.174 / PDF p.4.
L1.source_statement: Suppose φ is superstable and lower regular. Then, for each P, the limit of the expected energy density exists and is lower semicontinuous.

L2.title: H.-O. Georgii, Large deviations and the equivalence of ensembles for Gibbsian particle systems with superstable interaction
L2.source_section: Theorem 2, Section 3, equations (2.20)–(2.22), printed pp.175–176 / PDF pp.5–6.
L2.source_statement: For a superstable regular potential and z, β>0, the free and periodic partition rates agree with the stationary variational minimum, whose rate levels are compact.

citations.quote:
With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$.

A van Hove sequence is a sequence of bounded Lebesgue measurable sets $(\Omega_k)_{k\geq1}$ with $0<|\Omega_k|<\infty$, $|\Omega_k|\to\infty$, and
$$\frac{|\partial_R\Omega_k|}{|\Omega_k|}\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{for every fixed }R>0.$$
The condition controls both inner and outer boundary neighborhoods.

For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$.

Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$.

Assume a superstable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the van Hove definition [[def-tdmath-van-hove-sequence]]. For a bounded Lebesgue-measurable $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$, define $\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)=\{(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\Lambda^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ and $H_N(q)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. With $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, set
$$Z_\Lambda(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)}e^{-\beta H_N(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_\Lambda(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_\Lambda(N;\beta).$$
This is the labelled positional Lebesgue integral with indistinguishable-particle normalization and includes no exterior interaction. For $\Lambda=[0,L)^d$ it agrees with $Z(L,N;\beta)$ and $\Xi(L;z,\beta)$ from [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For every van Hove sequence $(\Omega_k)$ and fixed $z,\beta>0$, the free-wall grand pressure satisfies
$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac1{|\Omega_k|}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)=p(z,\beta),$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The extra superstability hypothesis supplies the uniform cell-occupation bound used below; no arbitrary-shape theorem under stability alone is claimed.
Let $d\geq1$ and let $\phi$ be a regular potential with a nonnegative nonincreasing envelope $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, where $R_0<\infty$ and $\int_{R_0}^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr<\infty$.

derivations.claim: For any $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $e^{\alpha N_k}Z(\Omega_k,N_k)\leq\Xi_{\Omega_k}(e^\alpha,\beta)$. Divide by volume, use [F5], and take the infimum over $\alpha$. The duality [F4] gives $\limsup |\Omega_k|^{-1}\log Z(\Omega_k,N_k)\leq F_\beta(\rho)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ so $\rho-\delta,\rho+\delta$ lie in the attainable interior. For large core side $\ell$, choose integers $n_-,n_+$ with $n_\pm/\ell^d\to\rho\pm\delta$. Put a central $\ell$-cube inside each $(\ell+g)$-cell, with $g=g(\ell)$ from [F6]. The effective densities $n_\pm/(\ell+g)^d$ still bracket $\rho$ when $\ell$ is large.

At fixed $\ell,g$, pack every complete $(\ell+g)$-cell contained in $\Omega_k$. Its count $M_k$ satisfies $M_k/|\Omega_k|\to(\ell+g)^{-d}$ by [F2]. Assign $n_+$ particles to $j_k$ cores and $n_-$ to the remaining cores, except one correction core with remainder $r_k$ chosen to make the total exactly $N_k$. Bracketing ensures $0\leq j_k<M_k$ for large $k$; Euclidean division gives $0\leq r_k<n_+-n_- \leq n_+$. Every correction integral $Z(\ell,r)$, $0\leq r\leq n_+$, is positive: delete particles from a positive-measure finite-energy set realizing $Z(\ell,n_+)>0$. There are finitely many such $r$, so the correction contributes $O_\ell(1)$ to the log weight.

Exact assignment of labels cancels the global $N_k!$, leaving the product of core canonical integrals. The core lattice shell estimate bounds cross-energy per volume by $C K^2(\ell/g)^d\eta(g)$, where $K\ell^d\geq n_+$. Let $k\to\infty$ first, then $\ell\to\infty$. The packing fraction tends one, the cross error tends zero, and the two rates tend $F_\beta(\rho-\delta)$ and $F_\beta(\rho+\delta)$. The bracketing proportions tend one half, so the lower rate is at least their average. Finally $\delta\downarrow0$; finite concavity makes $F_\beta$ continuous at the interior density. Combined with step 1.1 this proves the limit.

Assume superstability and regularity, let $(\Omega_k)$ be van Hove, and let $N_k/|\Omega_k|\to\rho$ for an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. Use the general-region free-wall convention of [[thm-tdmath-superstable-van-hove-pressure]], namely
$$Z(\Lambda,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\{q\in\Lambda^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}}\exp\!\left(-\beta\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)\right)dq_1\cdots dq_N\quad(N\geq1),$$
with $Z(\Lambda,0;\beta)=1$ and $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, for bounded Lebesgue-measurable $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$. For the free-wall exact-$N_k$ positional partition with this $1/N_k!$ normalization,
$$|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log Z(\Omega_k,N_k;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$
the free-cube canonical rate of [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Superstability is used for the arbitrary-shape pressure upper bound; no stability-only upper theorem is asserted.

citations.quote:
With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$.

For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]].

For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$.

Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$.

For $L>0$ and a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ with $N(\omega)=N$, the measure $R_{L,\omega}$ of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] is a stationary probability law of finite intensity and
$$\rho(R_{L,\omega})=\frac{N}{L^d}.$$
For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$, its empirical-field barycenter $\bar C_L$ is also a stationary probability law of finite intensity and $\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}N/L^d$.

derivations.claim: The canonical law is the grand law conditioned on $N=N_L$, since the grand weight on the $N_L$ sector differs from the canonical density only by the constant activity factor $z^{N_L}$. Its conditioning probability is $$G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)=\frac{z^{N_L}e^{-L^d}Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)}{Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)}.$$ Divide the logarithm by $L^d$. The numerator terms tend to $\rho\log z+F_\beta(\rho)-1$ by the assumed canonical rate and [F1]; the denominator tends to $p_Q(z,\beta)$. By [F2]–[F3], $p_Q(z,\beta)=F_\beta(\rho)+\rho\log z-1$, so $$L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the exact-number conditioning event has subexponential, positive grand probability for all sufficiently large $L$.

Let $U$ be an open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ and set $F=U^c$. The good rate in [L1] has zero set exactly $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. Its infimum on the closed set $F$ is strictly positive: otherwise a sequence in $F$ with rates tending to zero would lie in a compact rate sublevel, have a limit in $F$, and by lower semicontinuity that limit would be a zero of the rate outside $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. The large-deviation upper bound therefore gives some $c>0$ with $$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}\leq-c.$$

Conditioning on $N=N_L$ yields $$C^b_{L,N_L}\{R_{L,\omega}\notin U\}\leq \frac{G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}}{G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)}.$$ The numerator decays exponentially by step 1.2 and the denominator has zero exponential rate by step 1.1, so the ratio tends to zero. This proves concentration on every neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. If the minimizer is unique, these neighborhood bounds are exactly convergence in probability in $\tau_L$.

Let $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $\beta,z>0$, and $b\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}$. On the simple labelled sector $\mathcal S_{L,N}=\{q\in\Lambda_L^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ use $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}(q)=\sum_{i<j}\phi(q_i-q_j)$ and the periodic energy $H_{L,\mathrm{per}}$ from [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For $N\geq1$ define
$$Z_b(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_{L,N}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_b(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, and put $\Xi_b(L,z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_b(L,N;\beta)$. The unit-intensity Poisson reference $Q_{\Lambda_L}$ has sector density $e^{-L^d}/N!$ relative to labelled Lebesgue measure, so its normalized grand partition is
$$Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}]=e^{-L^d}\Xi_b(L,z,\beta).$$
The exact-$N$ canonical law $C^b_{L,N}$ has density $e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/(N!Z_b(L,N;\beta))$ on $\mathcal S_{L,N}$, and the grand-canonical law $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ has density $z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)$ relative to $Q_{\Lambda_L}$. Let $\rho>0$ be an interior attainable density, choose $\alpha=\log z$ supporting the free canonical rate $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, and take $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. Assume
$$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$
Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]], and let
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
Then for every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ there is $c_U>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log C^b_{L,N_L}\{\,\omega:R_{L,\omega}\notin U\,\}\leq-c_U.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$ under $C^b_{L,N_L}$. This is a statement about spatially averaged local observables through the empirical field, not about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin.

The exact-$N$ canonical law $C^b_{L,N}$ has density $e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/(N!Z_b(L,N;\beta))$ on $\mathcal S_{L,N}$, and the grand-canonical law $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ has density $z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)$ relative to $Q_{\Lambda_L}$. Let $\rho>0$ be an interior attainable density, choose $\alpha=\log z$ supporting the free canonical rate $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, and take $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. Assume
$$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$
Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]], and let
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
Then for every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ there is $c_U>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log C^b_{L,N_L}\{\,\omega:R_{L,\omega}\notin U\,\}\leq-c_U.$$

derivations.claim: Since $\rho$ is interior and $F_\beta$ is finite and concave there by [F1], it has a finite supporting slope $\alpha$ at $\rho$. Put $z=e^\alpha>0$.

The free exact-$N$ rate hypothesis of [F5] is exactly [F1], and [F2] supplies its supporting activity. The normalized/physical pressure conversion in [F3] is the equality required by [F5]; the empirical field is the stationary one in [F4]. Applying [F5] with free boundary gives concentration on $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ in every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood.

If the minimizer set is the singleton $\{P_*\}$, every open neighborhood of $P_*$ is a neighborhood of the full set. Step 2.1 therefore gives $C_{L,N_L}(R_{L,\omega}\notin U)\to0$ for every open $U\ni P_*$, which is convergence in probability in $\tau_L$.
