Let $\Omega_{\rm per}=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with opposite faces identified, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval in seconds, and let $f(x,v,t)\ge0$ be a one-particle number density for $x\in\Omega_{\rm per}$, $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and $t\in I$. With $x$ in metres and $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $f$ has units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$ relative to $d^3x\,d^3v$; its moments used below are assumed finite. For this postulate, require $f$ to be jointly measurable and periodic in $x$, with $(x,t)\mapsto f(x,v,t)$ continuously differentiable for each fixed $v$ and its derivatives jointly measurable. Require $f$, $\partial_t f$, and $v\cdot\nabla_x f$ to be locally integrable with respect to product Lebesgue measure. Periodic boundary conditions are imposed in $x$.

Adopt the incoming molecular-chaos closure: at a collision location and time, the incoming two-particle velocity density used in the collision term is $f(x,v,t)f(x,w,t)$. This is a one-sided factorization assumption; no factorization of the outgoing pair and no derivation from reversible many-particle mechanics is asserted.

For the elastic data $Q_{\rm el},\nu$ of [[def-td-regular-elastic-collision-model]], adopt a collision operator $Q_\nu(f)$, with units of $f$ per second, as a jointly measurable locally integrable representative whose velocity-wise weak action satisfies, for almost every $(x,t)$ and every measurable test function $\varphi$ for which both sides converge absolutely,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)Q_\nu(f)(x,v,t)\,d^3v=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}\big(f(x,v',t)f(x,w',t)-f(x,v,t)f(x,w,t)\big)\big(\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w')\big)\,d\nu.$$
The adopted kinetic equation is
$$\partial_t f+v\cdot\nabla_x f=Q_\nu(f),$$
as an equality of locally integrable functions almost everywhere on the product domain. These are admissibility conditions for solutions of the adopted model, not an existence assertion. The equation and weak collision identity are model postulates. This item does not assert a hard-sphere Boltzmann–Grad limit, propagation of chaos, or universal equilibration.

Fix a particle mass $m_p>0$ in kilograms and velocity space $V=\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The elastic collision set is
$$Q_{\rm el}=\{(v,w,v',w')\in V^4:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\}.$$
Thus each allowed event conserves momentum $m_p(v+w)$ and kinetic energy $m_p(|v|^2+|w|^2)/2$. Equip $Q_{\rm el}$ with the Borel sets generated by its relative topology.

Collision-rate data consist of a nonnegative, countably additive, $\sigma$-finite Borel measure $\nu$ on these Borel sets. It is invariant under exchanging $v$ with $w$, exchanging $v'$ with $w'$, and exchanging the incoming pair $(v,w)$ with the outgoing pair $(v',w')$: for each of these maps $S$ and Borel set $E$, $\nu(S^{-1}E)=\nu(E)$. This is the three-dimensional physical restriction of the collision set and exchange conventions in [[def-tdmath-elastic-collision-kernel]], with $\sigma$-finiteness stated explicitly for the product integrals used by the entropy theorem. Its physical units and rate normalization are chosen so the associated weak collision operator has units of density per second. The measure is a declared model input; no differential cross section or microscopic limit is inferred from this Definition.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

Let $\Omega=\mathbb T^d$ be a spatial rectangle with opposite faces identified, $d\ge2$, and let $I$ be an open time interval. Suppose $f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\times I\to(0,\infty)$ is $C^1$ in space and time and $C^2$ in velocity. Fix a positive reference density $f_{\rm ref}$ with the same units as $f$. Assume $f$, $f|v|^2$, and $f|\log(f/f_{\rm ref})|$ are integrable, and assume an integrable envelope on every compact time interval justifying differentiation of the entropy integral and every displayed collision integral. Let $Q$ and the symmetric collision measure $\nu$ satisfy the weak identity in [[def-tdmath-elastic-collision-kernel]] for tests $1$ and $\log(f/f_{\rm ref})$, with absolute convergence, and suppose
$$\partial_t f+v\cdot\nabla_r f=Q(f).$$
Then for $H[f](t)=\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\log(f/f_{\rm ref})\,dv\,dr$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}H[f](t)=-\frac14\int_\Omega\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(A-B)(\log A-\log B)\,d\nu\,dr\le0,\qquad A=f(r,v,t)f(r,w,t),\quad B=f(r,v',t)f(r,w',t).$$
The integrand is nonnegative because $\log$ is strictly increasing. Equality in the entropy-production integral holds exactly when $A=B$ for $\nu$-almost every collision at almost every $r$. Under the additional assumptions that $\nu$ is locally finite, has full support on $Q_{\rm el}$, and $f$ is positive and $C^2$ in $v$, this balance implies for almost every $r$ that
$$\log(f(r,v,t)/f_{\rm ref})=\alpha(r,t)+b(r,t)\cdot v+\frac{\lambda(r,t)}2|v|^2.$$
If $f(r,\cdot,t)$ is integrable over $\mathbb R^d$, then $\lambda(r,t)<0$, so its velocity profile is Maxwellian. Conversely, every profile of this form has zero collision entropy production. The weak collision identity is an explicit model hypothesis; this is not a derivation from reversible many-particle mechanics or a PDE existence theorem.

derivations.claim:
Set $H(t)=\int_{\Omega_{\rm per}}\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\log(f/f_{\rm ref})\,d^3v\,d^3x$. The hypotheses match [L1]: the spatial dimension is $d=3$, the opposite-face identification is periodic, the density is positive with the required regularity and moments, [A3] supplies the dominated differentiation and absolute convergence conditions, and [A1] supplies the kinetic equation and weak identity. The collision measure is symmetric by [F1]; its $\sigma$-finiteness in [A3] permits the product-space integrals. Thus [L1] gives
$$H'(t)=-\frac14\int_{\Omega_{\rm per}}\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(A-B)\log\!\left(\frac AB\right)\,d\nu\,d^3x\le0,$$
and its equality condition applies at each time where the derivative and production integral are defined.

By definition $S_{\rm kin}=-k_BH$, and $k_B>0$ by [F2]. Multiplying the identity in step 1.1 by $-k_B$ reverses its sign and yields the displayed entropy-production formula with nonnegative right-hand side. Since the multiplier is strictly positive, $S'_{\rm kin}(t)=0$ holds exactly when the production integral vanishes; the equality characterization in [L1] gives $A=B$ for $\nu$-almost every collision at almost every spatial point. This remains a conditional model deduction and uses no outgoing-pair molecular-chaos assumption.

citations.quote:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be lengths in metres, and set $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with closure $\overline\Omega$. A rectangular local-equilibrium field record consists of an open temperature interval $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$, a temperature field $T:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathcal T$ whose time derivative through order one and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times I$, a function $u\in C^1(\mathcal T,\mathbb R)$ of internal-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and its volumetric heat capacity $c(T):=u'(T)>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The coordinates $x_i$ are lengths in metres, and $T$ is measured in kelvins, using [[def-td-si-quantities]].

The record may also include a heat-flux field $j_Q:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and a conductivity field $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and uniformly continuous. Define
$u(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)u_0(y)\,dy$ for $t>0$ and
$u(x,0):=u_0(x)$. Then $u$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$, satisfies $\partial_tu=\Delta_xu$ there, is
bounded with $\|u(\cdot,t)\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty$, and converges locally
uniformly at the initial time:
$\sup_{x\in K}|u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$ for every compact
$K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$
and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling:
$\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there,
$\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$
there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with
$|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for
all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and
$(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.

$f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ (bounded measurable data are included). The absolutely
convergent representative
$u(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy$ is $C^\infty$ for $t>0$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ and $k\ge0$
$D_x^\alpha\partial_t^ku=(D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma_t)*f$. Moreover
$|D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha,k}t^{-(n+|\alpha|+2k)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$.
Domination is uniform on compact subsets $x\in K$, $\tau\le t\le T$ with
$0<\tau<T<\infty$; $u_t=\Delta u$.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be bounded and
continuous. Then for every compact set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$ \sup_{x \in K} |(f*K_\varepsilon)(x)-f(x)| \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be lengths in metres, and set $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with closure $\overline\Omega$. A rectangular local-equilibrium field record consists of an open temperature interval $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$, a temperature field $T:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathcal T$ whose time derivative through order one and spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times I$, a function $u\in C^1(\mathcal T,\mathbb R)$ of internal-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and its volumetric heat capacity $c(T):=u'(T)>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The coordinates $x_i$ are lengths in metres, and $T$ is measured in kelvins, using [[def-td-si-quantities]].

The record may also include a heat-flux field $j_Q:\overline\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with components in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and a conductivity field $K:\overline\Omega\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The flux and tensor are field data here; no relation between them is imposed by this Definition. In Euclidean coordinates, $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$ and $\operatorname{div}j_Q=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}(j_Q)_i$. On a flat face, $n$ denotes its outward unit normal.

This is a specified regular field class on a fixed rigid body. It does not assert that every physical medium has local-equilibrium fields, nor does it adopt a heat equation, a boundary condition, Fourier's law, or an entropy-production law.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n\ge1$ and $t>0$. The **heat kernel on $\mathbb R^n$** is the function

$$\Gamma(x,t):=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{|x|^2}{4t}\Bigr),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n,$$

where $|x|^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ is the Euclidean square of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\exp$ is the real exponential function of
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]. For fixed $t>0$ the map
$x\mapsto\Gamma(x,t)$ is a composite of the quadratic form with the exponential
and a scalar multiple, so it is $C^\infty$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] by
[[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and
[[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]], and it is
strictly positive by [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]. The
spatial Laplacian entering the heat equation is that of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

The **causal extension** of the heat kernel is $\Gamma(x,t)$ for $t>0$ and
$\Gamma(x,t):=0$ for $t\le0$; the displayed formula is not evaluated at $t=0$
as a function value. The normalisation is fixed by the unit-mass identity
proved for the kernel on this page, and the causal extension is used only as a
locally integrable function or, after embedding, as a distribution.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

derivations.claim: The assumptions on $g$ make it bounded and uniformly continuous, so [F1] applies. Write $U(x,\theta)=\Gamma_\theta*g(x)$ and set $T(x,t)=U(x,at)$. The chain rule gives $\partial_tT=aU_\theta(x,at)=a\Delta U(x,at)=a\Delta T$ for $t>0$; [F1] also gives the formula, smoothness, and local uniform initial convergence. Since $k=ac$, this is $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$. With $u'(T)=c$, $u_t=cT_t$, and $j_Q=-k\nabla T$ from [A3, A4], the same equality gives $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}j_Q=c\partial_tT-k\Delta T=0$.

Positivity and unit mass in [F2] imply $T_{\min}\int\Gamma\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}\int\Gamma$, hence $T_{\min}\le T\le T_{\max}$. Translation by $2L_i$ in the convolution variable preserves $g$ and Lebesgue measure by [F6], so $T$ is $2L_i$-periodic in $x_i$. Reflection $y_i\mapsto-y_i$ preserves Lebesgue measure by [F7] because its matrix has determinant of absolute value one; evenness of the kernel [F9] and of $g$ then makes $T$ even in each coordinate. For $t>0$, evenness gives $\partial_{x_i}T=0$ on the face $x_i=0$; periodicity gives $\partial_{x_i}T=\partial_{x_i}T$ at opposite faces $x_i=-L_i,L_i$, while evenness makes these two values negatives, so both vanish. The same boundary derivative holds at $t=0$ for $g$, and [A4] gives $j_Q\cdot n=0$ on every face.

By [F11], the stated $C^2$ hypothesis gives continuous derivatives through spatial order two. For $|\alpha|\le2$ and $t>0$, differentiating under the integral and then integrating by parts in each coordinate gives $D^\alpha T(x,t)=\int\Gamma(x-y,at)D^\alpha g(y)\,dy$. The products of kernel derivatives with bounded derivatives of $g$ are absolutely integrable by the Gaussian bound [F2], so [F10] licenses the iterated integrals; on each finite coordinate interval Newton–Leibniz [F8] gives the integration-by-parts identity, and the boundary terms vanish as the interval expands because of the Gaussian tails. Each $D^\alpha g$ is bounded and continuous, so [F4] makes this expression converge uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ to $D^\alpha g$ as $t\downarrow0$. Thus the spatial derivatives through order two extend continuously to the initial time.

For $t>0$, the heat equation and the same integration-by-parts argument give $\partial_tT(x,t)=a\int\Gamma(x-y,at)\Delta g(y)\,dy$. By [F4] this converges uniformly on $\overline\Omega$ to $a\Delta g(x)$. For $0<\varepsilon<t$, [F8] gives $T(x,t)-T(x,\varepsilon)=\int_\varepsilon^t\partial_sT(x,s)\,ds$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ is valid uniformly in $x$ by step 1.1 and the uniform limit just established; consequently $T(x,t)-g(x)=\int_0^t\partial_sT(x,s)\,ds$, and dividing by $t$ proves the right derivative $\partial_tT(x,0)=a\Delta g(x)$.

For uniqueness, let $T_1,T_2$ be two solutions in the stated regularity class and set $w=T_1-T_2$. Then $w_t=a\Delta w$, $\partial_nw=0$, and $w(\cdot,0)=0$. At each fixed time, $w$ and its spatial derivatives through order two are continuous on the compact rectangle, so the integrands $w\,\partial_i^2w$ and $|\partial_iw|^2$ are bounded and hence $L^1$ for the finite Lebesgue product measure. Apply [F10] successively in the three coordinate factors to identify the rectangle integrals with the iterated one-dimensional integrals. The product rule and [F8] then give $\int_0^{L_i}w\,\partial_i^2w=[w\partial_iw]_0^{L_i}-\int_0^{L_i}|\partial_iw|^2$. The boundary terms vanish by the homogeneous Neumann condition, so $E'(t)=2a\int_\Omega w\Delta w=-2a\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\le0$. Thus $E(0)=0$ and $E(t)\ge0$ imply $E(t)=0$; continuity of $w$ gives $w=0$ everywhere. The formula therefore gives the unique solution in the stated class.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

For a field record on $\Omega\times I$ from [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt the local balance
$$\partial_t u(T(x,t))+\operatorname{div}j_Q(x,t)=0$$
and the insulated-boundary condition $j_Q(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ on every face of $\partial\Omega$. Both terms in the local equation have units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$. The boundary condition says that no heat energy crosses the body's outer faces in this model.

This local continuum balance is an additional adopted postulate, with the sign and energy convention of [[post-td-first-law-energy]]. It is not deduced from that global process-record balance. Matter transfer, volume work, internal sources, moving boundaries, and external-field energy require separately specified balance models and are outside this item.

For the field record of [[def-td-rectangular-local-equilibrium-fields]], adopt
$$j_Q(x,t)=-K(x,T(x,t))\nabla T(x,t).$$
Here $K$ has entries in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $j_Q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, so the equation is dimensionally consistent. Write $K_s=(K+K^{\mathsf T})/2$ for the symmetric part and assume $z^{\mathsf T}K_s(x,T)z\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^3$. The antisymmetric part may contribute to the flux but not to the quadratic entropy production.

This is an adopted constitutive model in the stated continuum regime. It is neither a consequence of equilibrium entropy alone nor a universal law for all media. In particular, it does not assert a finite propagation speed or an empirical value for $K$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be bounded and
continuous. Then for every compact set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$ \sup_{x \in K} |(f*K_\varepsilon)(x)-f(x)| \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $n\ge1$ and $t>0$. The **heat kernel on $\mathbb R^n$** is the function

$$\Gamma(x,t):=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{|x|^2}{4t}\Bigr),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n,$$

where $|x|^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ is the Euclidean square of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\exp$ is the real exponential function of
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]. For fixed $t>0$ the map
$x\mapsto\Gamma(x,t)$ is a composite of the quadratic form with the exponential
and a scalar multiple, so it is $C^\infty$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] by
[[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and
[[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]], and it is
strictly positive by [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]. The
spatial Laplacian entering the heat equation is that of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

The **causal extension** of the heat kernel is $\Gamma(x,t)$ for $t>0$ and
$\Gamma(x,t):=0$ for $t\le0$; the displayed formula is not evaluated at $t=0$
as a function value. The normalisation is fixed by the unit-mass identity
proved for the kernel on this page, and the causal extension is used only as a
locally integrable function or, after embedding, as a distribution.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$
and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling:
$\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there,
$\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$
there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with
$|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for
all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and
$(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ (bounded measurable data are included). The absolutely
convergent representative
$u(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)f(y)\,dy$ is $C^\infty$ for $t>0$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ and $k\ge0$
$D_x^\alpha\partial_t^ku=(D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma_t)*f$. Moreover
$|D_x^\alpha\partial_t^k\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha,k}t^{-(n+|\alpha|+2k)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$.
Domination is uniform on compact subsets $x\in K$, $\tau\le t\le T$ with
$0<\tau<T<\infty$; $u_t=\Delta u$.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and uniformly continuous. Define
$u(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)u_0(y)\,dy$ for $t>0$ and
$u(x,0):=u_0(x)$. Then $u$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$, satisfies $\partial_tu=\Delta_xu$ there, is
bounded with $\|u(\cdot,t)\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty$, and converges locally
uniformly at the initial time:
$\sup_{x\in K}|u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$ for every compact
$K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. Here $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$, $\Delta T:=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2T$, and on a face with outward unit normal $n$, $\partial_nT:=n\cdot\nabla T$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

Let $d\ge1$, let $L_1,\ldots,L_d>0$, and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(0,L_i)$. If $w\in C^1(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ satisfies $\int_\Omega w(x)\,dx=0$, write $
abla w=(\partial_1w,\ldots,\partial_dw)$ and $|
abla w|^2=\sum_{i=1}^d|\partial_iw|^2$. Then
$$\int_\Omega |w(x)|^2\,dx\le  rac d2\sum_{i=1}^d L_i^2\int_\Omega |\partial_iw(x)|^2\,dx\le C_\Omega\int_\Omega |
abla w(x)|^2\,dx,$$
where $C_\Omega= rac d2\max_iL_i^2$. All integrals are the multidimensional Riemann integrals of continuous functions on the indicated closed rectangles, with the usual extension to their interiors.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

derivations.claim: On each finite time interval the time derivative is continuous on the compact box, so its difference quotients converge uniformly under the spatial integral. By [F1] and [F4], coordinatewise application of [F3] gives $\overline T'(t)=aV^{-1}\int_\Omega\Delta T\,dx=0$: the integral of each second coordinate derivative is the difference of the corresponding first derivative on its two faces, and both normal derivatives vanish. Hence $\overline T(t)=\overline T(0)$.

Set $w(x,t)=T(x,t)-\overline T(0)$. Then [F4] and step 1.1 give $\int_\Omega w=0$, while $w_t=a\Delta w$ and $\partial_nw=0$. Differentiating $E(t)=\int_\Omega w^2$ and using [F4], the product rule, and [F3] in each coordinate gives $E'(t)=2a\int_\Omega w\Delta w=-2a\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2$; each endpoint term is $w\partial_nw=0$.
Apply [F2] to $w(\cdot,t)$ in step 2.1. It gives $E(t)\le C_\Omega\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2$, so $E'(t)\le-(2a/C_\Omega)E(t)$.

The product rule gives $(e^{2at/C_\Omega}E(t))'=e^{2at/C_\Omega}(E'(t)+(2a/C_\Omega)E(t))\le0$ by step 3.1. Integrating this derivative with [F3] from $0$ to $t$ yields $e^{2at/C_\Omega}E(t)\le E(0)$, which is the asserted estimate.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. Here $\nabla T=(\partial_{x_1}T,\partial_{x_2}T,\partial_{x_3}T)$, $\Delta T:=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2T$, and on a face with outward unit normal $n$, $\partial_nT:=n\cdot\nabla T$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses and solution $T$ of [[pthm-td-constant-conductivity-neumann-existence]], let $V=|\Omega|=L_1L_2L_3$, define the spatial mean $\overline T(t)=V^{-1}\int_\Omega T(x,t)\,dx$, and put $E(t)=\int_\Omega|T(x,t)-\overline T(t)|^2\,dx$. With $a=k/c$ and $C_\Omega=\frac32\max_iL_i^2$, the mean is constant and
$$E(t)\le e^{-2at/C_\Omega}E(0)\qquad(t\ge0).$$
Thus this model solution converges exponentially to its initial spatial mean in $L^2(\Omega)$; no pointwise-uniform convergence rate is asserted.

derivations.claim: Write $q(r)=r^2(1-r)^2$. Then $q'(r)=2r(1-r)(1-2r)$, so $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$, and $q''(0)=q''(1)=2$. Also $0\le q\le1/16$ on $[0,1]$. The constant and first two derivatives therefore match across the even-reflection and periodic seams; the extension is $C^2$, with bounded uniformly continuous derivatives. Since $h=q-1/30$, its values lie in $[-1/30,7/240]$, so $g\ge T_b-\epsilon/30>0$.

Expand $q(r)=r^2-2r^3+r^4$, so $\int_0^1q(r)\,dr=1/3-1/2+1/5=1/30$. Also $q(r)^2=r^4-4r^5+6r^6-4r^7+r^8$, whence
$$\int_0^1q(r)^2\,dr=\frac15-\frac46+\frac67-\frac48+\frac19=\frac1{630}.$$
Therefore $\int_0^1h(r)\,dr=0$ and
$$\int_0^1h(r)^2\,dr=\int_0^1(q-1/30)^2\,dr=\frac1{630}-\frac1{900}=\frac1{2100}.$$
Integrating over the other two coordinates now gives $\overline g=T_b$ and $E(0)=\epsilon^2L_2L_3L_1/2100=\epsilon^2|\Omega|/2100$.

The profile satisfies every initial-data hypothesis of [F1]; its vanishing normal derivative follows from $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$. Apply [F1] for existence and [F2] with the computed $E(0)$ to obtain the stated conserved mean and decay bound. This is a deduction within the adopted continuum model.

boundaries.evidence: Example three positive side lengths and T_b>epsilon/30>0 give the stated nonempty insulated rectangle. A constant zero perturbation is a separate allowed limiting datum, not the nonzero polynomial witness prescribed here.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice as in [[pthm-td-constant-conductivity-neumann-existence]]. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$, let $c,k>0$, and let $T_b>\epsilon/30>0$, where $T_b$ and $\epsilon$ are in kelvins. For $r\in[0,1]$ set $h(r)=r^2(1-r)^2-1/30$ and prescribe
$$g(x)=T_b+\epsilon h(x_1/L_1)\qquad(x\in\overline\Omega).$$
Use its even $2L_i$-periodic extension in each coordinate as the initial datum on $\mathbb R^3$. The unique insulated heat solution has constant spatial mean $T_b$ and satisfies
$$\int_\Omega|T(x,t)-T_b|^2\,dx\le \frac{\epsilon^2|\Omega|}{2100}e^{-2(k/c)t/C_\Omega},\qquad C_\Omega=\frac32\max_iL_i^2.$$
This gives an exactly computed initial variance and the conditional relaxation estimate of the model.

derivations.claim: Inside the ball write $h(x)=1-|x-x_c|^2/r^2$, so $\phi=h^3$. On the sphere $h=0$, the first derivatives $3h^2\partial_i h$ and second derivatives $6h(\partial_i h)(\partial_j h)+3h^2\partial_i\partial_jh$ tend to zero; outside the ball they are zero. Hence $\phi$ is $C^2$ and nonnegative, and it is identically zero in a neighborhood of every face because $r<\frac12\min_iL_i$. The reflected periodic extension is therefore $C^2$, bounded, uniformly continuous with bounded derivatives, and positive on the original open ball.

The initial field $g=T_b+\epsilon\phi_{\rm per}$ is positive and satisfies the even-periodic compatibility hypotheses of [F1]. For $t>0$ and any $x\in\Omega$, the Gaussian $\Gamma(x-y,(k/c)t)$ is strictly positive on the ball. Choose a smaller closed ball on which the continuous $\phi_{\rm per}$ has a positive minimum; the Gaussian also has a positive minimum there. Its integral over that ball is positive, so the convolution in [F1] gives $T(x,t)-T_b>0$.

At $t=0$, $\phi_{\rm per}$ restricted to $\Omega$ vanishes outside $\overline B(x_c,r)$, a proper compact subset of the rectangle, while step 2.1 shows the positive-time perturbation is nonzero at every interior point. This is instantaneous support growth in the specified diffusion model only.

boundaries.evidence: Example the radius r is positive and less than half every side length, so its interior initial-support ball is nonempty. The heat kernel is positive for t>0, and its convolution concerns that actual supported perturbation.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice as in [[pthm-td-constant-conductivity-neumann-existence]]. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$, choose $x_c=(L_1/2,L_2/2,L_3/2)$ and $0<r<\frac12\min_iL_i$, and define on $\overline\Omega$
$$\phi(x)=\begin{cases}(1-|x-x_c|^2/r^2)^3,&|x-x_c|<r,\\0,&|x-x_c|\ge r.\end{cases}$$
For $L>0$, define the even periodic fold $\rho_L:\mathbb R\to[0,L]$ by $\rho_L(s)=s-2nL$ for $2nL\le s\le(2n+1)L$ and $\rho_L(s)=(2n+2)L-s$ for $(2n+1)L\le s\le(2n+2)L$, $n\in\mathbb Z$. Put $\phi_{\rm per}(x)=\phi(\rho_{L_1}(x_1),\rho_{L_2}(x_2),\rho_{L_3}(x_3))$ and take $g=T_b+\epsilon\phi_{\rm per}$ with $T_b,\epsilon>0$. In the constant-$c,k$ insulated Fourier model, the heat-kernel solution satisfies
$$T(x,t)-T_b=\epsilon\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,(k/c)t)\phi_{\rm per}(y)\,dy>0$$
for every interior $x\in\Omega$ and every $t>0$, although the initial perturbation is supported in the compact ball $\overline B(x_c,r)\subset\Omega$. Thus the adopted diffusion model has no finite propagation speed for this temperature perturbation.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$ with $L_i>0$ metres, let $c>0$ be a constant volumetric heat capacity in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$ with $u'(T)=c$ throughout the range of $g$, let $k>0$ be a constant scalar conductivity in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ with $K\equiv kI_3$ in [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], and put $a=k/c$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

For $t>0$ define
$$T(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(x-y,at)g(y)\,dy,\qquad \Gamma(z,\theta)=(4\pi\theta)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/(4\theta)},$$
and set $T(x,0)=g(x)$ on $\overline\Omega$. This field is the unique $C^1$-in-time, $C^2$-in-space solution on each finite time interval of $c\partial_tT=k\Delta T$ on $\Omega$, with $\partial_nT=0$ on every face and the given initial value. It satisfies $T_{\min}\le T(x,t)\le T_{\max}$ for all $t\ge0$, has $C^2$ spatial derivatives continuous to $t=0$, and its right time derivative there is $a\Delta g$. Under [[post-td-local-energy-balance]] and [[post-td-fourier-conductivity]], it is a global-in-time solution of that restricted physical continuum model.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). A **finite-mode regulator** in this item is a fixed
finite nonempty label set $J$ with $N:=|J|\ge1$, a fixed enumeration of $J$ by
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and the real coordinate vector
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may name sites of a finite
lattice or finitely many modes; their geometry enters only through the chosen
polynomial below. No limit in $N$ is part of this definition.

Choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$, constants $c>0$ and $C_0\ge0$,
and a real polynomial $V\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$ such that
$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$
Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost
everywhere equality and inner product
$$\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}u(q)\overline{v(q)}\,dq,$$
linear in the first variable. Under Countable Choice this is a complex Hilbert
space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let
$D_0:=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, the smooth compactly supported
complex-valued functions. The associated **polynomial differential expression**
is the map
$$h_0:D_0\to H_N,\qquad h_0u:=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Vu.$$
It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are
smooth and compactly supported. Set $W:=V+C_0+1$, so
$W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$. This definition specifies finite mathematical data and a
differential expression; it does not choose a self-adjoint operator domain or
assert a continuum or infinite-volume limit.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. Then $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is dense in
$L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

derivations.claim: Since $W+1\ge2$ and every $a_j>0$, $a$ is a Hermitian positive-definite sesquilinear form on $D_0$: in particular $a(u,u)=\sum_j a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2\ge2\|u\|_2^2$, and $a(u,u)=0$ forces $u=0$ in $H_N$. Thus its Cauchy-sequence completion with the stated equivalence relation is a well-defined inner-product space.

To see that the completion is complete, let $(X_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence of its classes. By [A1], choose $u_n\in D_0$ with $\|[u_n]-X_n\|_Q<2^{-n}$ for each $n$. The triangle inequality makes $(u_n)$ $Q$-Cauchy; its class $X$ is defined by the Cauchy-sequence construction, and $\|X_n-X\|_Q\le2^{-n}+\|[u_n]-X\|_Q\to0$. Hence $Q$ is complete and therefore Hilbert.

For a $Q$-Cauchy representative sequence $(u_n)$, the inequalities $\|u_n-u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, $\sqrt{a_j}\|\partial_j u_n-\partial_j u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, and $\|\sqrt{W+1}(u_n-u_m)\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$ show that $u_n$, each $\partial_j u_n$, and $\sqrt{W+1}u_n$ converge in $L^2$ by [F2]; write their limits as $u$, $g_j$, and $h$. The first limit defines a continuous map $Q\to H_N$, since $\|u\|_2\le\|[u_n]\|_Q$, and equivalent Cauchy sequences have the same $L^2$ limit.

For every $\varphi\in D_0$, integration by parts gives $\int u_n\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int (\partial_j u_n)\overline\varphi$. Passing to the limit in both integrals by $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\int u\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$, so $g_j$ is the stated weak derivative.

On each compact ball $B_R$, the continuous polynomial $W+1$ is bounded. Therefore $\sqrt{W+1}u_n\to\sqrt{W+1}u$ in $L^2(B_R)$, while the same sequence converges there to $h$; uniqueness of limits gives $h=\sqrt{W+1}u$ almost everywhere on every integer-radius ball and hence almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^N$. Taking limits of the component norms in $a(u_n,u_n)$ now gives the displayed formula for $\|u\|_Q^2$.

If $u=0$ in $L^2$, then step 3.1 says $\langle g_j,\varphi\rangle=0$ for every $\varphi\in D_0$; this pairing is continuous by [F3] and $D_0$ is dense by [F4], so it vanishes on all of $H_N$, and taking $\varphi=g_j$ gives $g_j=0$. Step 3.2 then gives $h=0$; the norm formula yields $\|[u_n]\|_Q=0$, so the embedding is injective. Finally its image contains $D_0$, which is dense in $H_N$ by [F4]; thus the continuous injection has dense image and all claims follow.

$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Let $C$ be a cube of side $\delta>0$ and $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, with $u_C:=|C|^{-1}\int_Cu$. Expanding the square and using Fubini on the finite cube gives
$$\int_C|u-u_C|^2=\frac1{2|C|}\int_C\int_C|u(x)-u(y)|^2\,dx\,dy.$$
Telescope $u(x)-u(y)$ through the $N$ coordinate changes and use $|\sum_{j=1}^Nz_j|^2\le N\sum_j|z_j|^2$. For the $j$th change, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|D_j(x,y)|^2\le\delta\int_{\min(x_j,y_j)}^{\max(x_j,y_j)}|\partial_ju|^2$. For fixed values of the other coordinates and fixed $s\in[0,\delta]$, the measure of pairs $(x_j,y_j)$ whose segment contains $s$ is $2s(\delta-s)\le\delta^2/2$; integrating the displayed bound over the cube variables and dividing by $2|C|$ therefore yields the safe estimate
$$\|u-u_C\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le N\delta^2\sum_{j=1}^N\|\partial_j u\|_{L^2(C)}^2.$$
It applies to complex $u$ because the squared-modulus Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is used.

For $R>0$ and $u\in Q$, the coercive weight gives
$$\int_{|q|>R}|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\int_{|q|>R}c|q|^2|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\|u\|_Q^2.$$
Thus the $L^2$ tails of the $Q$ unit ball are uniformly small for large $R$.

The estimate of step 1.1 passes to every $u\in Q$: approximate $u$ in the $Q$ norm by elements of $C_c^\infty$ (the defining completion), restrict to $C$, and use [F1] to pass the $L^2$ and derivative limits.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so the squared tail in step 1.2 is below $\varepsilon^2/16$. For the $Q$ unit ball, [F1] gives $\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2\le\sum_j a_j^{-1}$. Choose an integer $M$ large enough that $\delta:=2R/M$ satisfies $N\delta^2\sum_j a_j^{-1}<\varepsilon^2/16$, and partition $[-R,R]^N$ into the resulting finitely many cubes of side $\delta$. Summing the squared estimates of step 2.1 over these disjoint cubes bounds the total mean-approximation error by $N\delta^2\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2<\varepsilon^2/16$. The squared error outside $[-R,R]^N$ is the tail from step 1.2; thus replacing $u$ on each cube by its mean and setting it to zero outside the large cube has total squared $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon^2/8$, hence norm error below $\varepsilon/2$.

For the finite partition in step 3.1, the piecewise-constant mean function $m_u$ satisfies $\|m_u\|_2^2=\sum_C|C||u_C|^2\le\sum_C\|u\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le\|u\|_2^2\le1$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F3]. Thus each mean coordinate has modulus at most $|C|^{-1/2}$, so the vectors of means lie in a bounded box in a finite-dimensional complex coordinate space. Subdivide its real-and-imaginary coordinates into finitely many boxes of sufficiently small side length so that the associated piecewise-constant functions approximate every mean vector to $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 3.1 gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball. Scaling shows that the image of every bounded $Q$ set is totally bounded.

Let $K$ be the $H_N$ closure of the image of the $Q$ unit ball. It is complete because it is closed in the complete space $H_N$ [F1]. Suppose an open cover of $K$ has no finite subcover. For each $n\ge1$, step 4.1 supplies a finite $2^{-n-2}$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball with centers in $H_N$; the corresponding closed balls of radius $2^{-n-1}$ cover its closure $K$. Starting with $C_0=K$, choose the least ball index for which $C_n:=C_{n-1}\cap\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$ has no finite subcover. Such an index exists, since otherwise finitely many finite subcovers would cover $C_{n-1}$. Each $C_n$ is nonempty, closed, nested, and has diameter at most $2^{-n}$. For $m>n$, any point of nonempty $C_m$ lies in both selected balls, so $\|p_m-p_n\|_2\le2^{-m-1}+2^{-n-1}$; hence $(p_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $p\in H_N$. Since $C_n$ is nonempty and is contained in both $K$ and $\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$, the distance from $p_n$ to $K$ is at most $2^{-n-1}$. Therefore $\operatorname{dist}(p,K)\le\|p-p_n\|_2+2^{-n-1}\to0$; closedness of $K$ gives $p\in K$. For fixed $n$ and every $m>n$, nonempty $C_m\subseteq C_n$ has a point $y\in C_m$ with $\|p_m-y\|_2\le2^{-m-1}$. Thus there are points of $C_n$ arbitrarily close to $p$, and closedness gives $p\in C_n$. An open set of the cover containing $p$ contains $K\cap B(p,r)$ for some $r>0$; for large $n$, $\operatorname{diam}(C_n)<r$, so that one open set covers $C_n$, a contradiction. Thus $K$ is compact. All recursive ball choices are least admissible indices in finite lists.
Step 5.1 proves that the closed-unit-ball image under $J$ has compact closure; applying the equivalent criterion in [F2] to the linear inclusion proves that $J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
