citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Fix an integer $n\geq1$.  A **tempered distribution** on $\mathbb R^n$ is a
continuous complex-linear functional

$$u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb C,$$

where Schwartz space and its locally convex topology are those of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]].  The space of all such functionals
is denoted $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

We write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$.  This pairing is bilinear:
the test variable is not conjugated.  Thus $u(a\varphi+b\psi)=
a\langle u,\varphi\rangle+b\langle u,\psi\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
The zero functional is tempered.  Continuity is topological continuity, and,
because the Schwartz topology is generated by a countable cofinal family of
seminorms, it is equivalently continuity on every convergent sequence.  No
choice principle is used in this definition.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

derivations.claim:
Assume Countable Choice as required by [F4]. For a spacetime test
$\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$ set
$q_\varphi(t,\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\varphi(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x$.
Integration by parts in the spatial variables gives
$$(1+|\mathbf k|^2)^2q_\varphi(t,\mathbf k)=\int e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}(1-\Delta_{\mathbf x})^2\varphi(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x.$$
Let $P(\varphi)$ be the maximum, over spatial multi-indices $|\beta|\le4$,
of $\sup_{t,\mathbf x}(1+|t|)^4(1+|\mathbf x|^2)^2|\partial_{\mathbf x}^\beta\varphi(t,\mathbf x)|$.
By [F9] this is bounded by a finite sum of the defining Schwartz seminorms.
Since $\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\mathbf x|^2)^{-2}\,d^3\mathbf x<\infty$,
$$|q_\varphi(t,\mathbf k)|\le C P(\varphi)(1+|t|)^{-4}(1+|\mathbf k|^2)^{-2}.$$
For every $\mu\ge0$, $|\sin(\omega_\mu t)/\omega_\mu|\le|t|$ off the
massless apex. Consequently the joint pairing
$$\langle\Delta_\mu,\varphi\rangle=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\sin(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)t)}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}q_\varphi(t,\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k\,dt$$
is absolutely convergent and has modulus at most $C'P(\varphi)$, because
$\int |t|(1+|t|)^{-4}\,dt$ and $\int(1+|\mathbf k|^2)^{-2}\,d^3\mathbf k$
are finite. It is complex-linear and continuous on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$,
so it defines the claimed spacetime tempered distribution [F5]. The estimate
also supplies the required polynomial growth in time and proves that this
pairing is the integral of its fixed-time spatial pairings. The apex value
can be assigned arbitrarily without changing any integral; the separate
$1/|\mathbf k|$ shell factor is locally integrable in three dimensions.
For the fixed-time family, derivatives of $\sin(\omega_\mu t)/\omega_\mu$
have at most polynomial growth in $\mathbf k$, uniformly on bounded time
intervals. Taking enough spatial Schwartz weights therefore permits all time
derivatives under its spatial pairing. It follows both for this family and,
by integration by parts in $t$, for the joint distribution that
$(\partial_t^2-\Delta_{\mathbf x}+\mu^2)\Delta_\mu=0$,
$\Delta_\mu(0,\cdot)=0$, and
$\partial_t\Delta_\mu(0,\cdot)=\delta_0$; the last identity is Fourier
inversion [F4].

Choose a nonnegative smooth spatial mollifier $\rho_\epsilon$ of integral
one supported in $|\mathbf x|<\epsilon$, using [F7], and let
$u_\epsilon(t,\cdot)=\Delta_\mu(t,\cdot)*\rho_\epsilon$. Its Fourier
multiplier is $\widehat\rho_\epsilon(\mathbf k)\sin(\omega_\mu t)/\omega_\mu$;
this is Schwartz in $\mathbf k$ for every fixed $t$, including $\mu=0$
because $\sin(|\mathbf k|t)/|\mathbf k|$ has a power series in
$|\mathbf k|^2$. Thus $u_\epsilon$ and its derivatives are Schwartz and have
finite energy by [F8]. By 1.1 it is a smooth solution of the
Klein–Gordon equation with data
$u_\epsilon(0)=0$, $\partial_tu_\epsilon(0)=\rho_\epsilon$. Its initial
energy is finite. Choose $R>\epsilon$ and for $t\ge0$ set
$$E_R(t)=\frac12\int_{|\mathbf x|>R+t} \bigl(|\partial_tu_\epsilon|^2+|\nabla u_\epsilon|^2+ \mu^2|u_\epsilon|^2\bigr)\,d^3\mathbf x.$$
The equation and integration by parts on the exterior region give
$$E_R'(t)=-\frac12\int_{|\mathbf x|=R+t} \left(|\partial_tu_\epsilon+\partial_ru_\epsilon|^2+ |\nabla_Tu_\epsilon|^2+\mu^2|u_\epsilon|^2\right)dS\le0.$$
For a complex solution apply this identity to real and imaginary parts.
Cutoff at a large radius and use finite energy to pass to the exterior
integral. Since $E_R(0)=0$ and $E_R(t)\ge0$, it vanishes for all $t\ge0$.
For $\mu>0$ this forces $u_\epsilon=0$ outside $R+t$; for $\mu=0$ it forces
its spatial gradient and time derivative to vanish there, so it is constant
on the connected exterior and the inverse Fourier transform tends to zero at
spatial infinity, hence the constant is zero. Reversing time gives support
inside $|\mathbf x|\le R+|t|$ for both signs of $t$.

Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ and choose $R=2\epsilon$. For every compact
smooth test $\varphi(t,\mathbf x)$, its spatial convolution with the
reflected mollifier converges with all derivatives uniformly on one compact
set to $\varphi$; this follows by writing the difference as the average of
$\varphi(t,\mathbf x-\mathbf y)-\varphi(t,\mathbf x)$ for
$|\mathbf y|<\epsilon$ and applying the mean-value bound to each derivative.
Continuity of the tempered distribution [F5] therefore gives
$\Delta_\mu*_{\,\mathbf x}\rho_\epsilon\to\Delta_\mu$ distributionally.
If a compact test support lies in the spacelike open set
$|\mathbf x|>|t|$, its positive distance from the closed cone on that compact
set gives a margin $\delta>0$; choosing $3\epsilon<\delta$ makes its pairing
with $u_\epsilon$ vanish by 2.1. Passing to the distributional limit proves
the support inclusion.

For real $f,g$, expand the commutator using [F1]. The two like-type
commutators vanish; [F3] leaves
$$\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2 -\langle K_\mu\overline g,K_\mu f\rangle_2.$$
Define the compact smooth difference test
$h(z)=\int f(z+y)g(y)\,d^4y$. Thus the double smearing in the Statement
means $\langle\Delta_\mu,h\rangle$, which is well-defined by 1.1.
Substitute the shell integrals [F2], use the second-variable-linear pairing,
and combine the two exponentials. The Fourier transform of $h$ is the
product of the corresponding transforms of $f$ and $g$, by ordinary Fubini
for compact tests. The resulting shell integrals are absolutely convergent:
the transforms decay faster than any power and the massless $1/|\mathbf k|$
factor is locally integrable. This justifies the comparison with the joint
pairing in 1.1, without interchanging an unsmeared oscillatory integral. The result is
$-i\int f(x)g(y)\Delta_\mu(x-y)\,d^4x\,d^4y$; the sign follows from
$e^{-ip\circ(x-y)}-e^{ip\circ(x-y)}=-2i\sin(p\circ(x-y))$ and the
definition of $\Delta_\mu$. If every pair $(x,y)$ in the two supports is
spacelike separated, then $x-y$ lies outside the support in 3.1, so the
distributional pairing vanishes.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb

$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$

\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes

then

Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.

$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Choose $\delta>0$. By [F4], choose a nonnegative nonzero
$\chi\in C_c^\infty((-\delta,\delta))$. Choose two nonnegative nonzero
$u,v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ supported in closed balls of radii
$r_1,r_2$ whose center separation $D$ satisfies
$D-r_1-r_2>2\delta$. Such bumps follow by translating and rescaling [F4].
Set $f(t,\mathbf x)=\chi(t)u(\mathbf x)$ and
$g(t,\mathbf x)=\chi(t)v(\mathbf x)$. For every point in the two supports,
$|t-s|<2\delta$ and $|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|\ge D-r_1-r_2>2\delta$;
therefore all support differences are spacelike.
For example, $\delta=1$, $r_1=r_2=1$ and $D=5$ give a spatial gap of $3>2$,
so these strict inequalities are attainable.

Insert a radial regulator $e^{-\epsilon|\mathbf k|}$, $\epsilon>0$, in
the massless two-point kernel. Angular integration using [F3] gives for
$r=|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|>0$ and $\tau=t-s$
$$W_\epsilon(\tau,r)= \frac{1}{4\pi^2r}\int_0^\infty e^{-(\epsilon+i\tau)q}\sin(qr)\,dq =\frac{1}{4\pi^2\bigl(r^2+(\epsilon+i\tau)^2\bigr)}.$$
The integral identity follows by integrating the two exponentials in the
sine and using $\operatorname{Re}(\epsilon+i\tau)>0$. On the compact
support product in 1.1, $r\ge d:=D-r_1-r_2>2\delta>|\tau|$. Thus the
denominator is bounded away from zero uniformly as $\epsilon\downarrow0$,
and $W_\epsilon$ converges uniformly there to
$[4\pi^2(r^2-\tau^2)]^{-1}$, which is strictly positive.

$\langle K_0 f,K_0 g\rangle_2$ by dominated convergence [F5]: the absolute
value of the unregulated product is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz [F7],
because $K_0f,K_0g\in H_0$. To identify the regulated shell integral with
the spacetime pairing of $W_\epsilon$, Fubini [F6] applies because its
absolute integral is at most
$\|f\|_1\|g\|_1\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-\epsilon|\mathbf k|}
d^3\mathbf k/[(2\pi)^3 2|\mathbf k|]<\infty$.
The formula in 2.1 and uniform convergence on the compact support product give
$$\langle K_0 f,K_0 g\rangle_2 =\int f(t,\mathbf x)g(s,\mathbf y) \frac{d^4x\,d^4y}{4\pi^2(|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|^2-(s-t)^2)}>0,$$
because both test functions are nonnegative and nonzero and the denominator

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), $m_o>0$ in kilograms, $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\hbar>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Take the complete oscillator family $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ and self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H_{\rm osc}$ of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], with oscillator length $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_o\omega)}$ and $H_{\rm osc}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$. Let $\mathcal C=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n:n\ge0\}$ be the finite Hermite span. Multiplication by position $Xf(x)=xf(x)$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself by the Hermite recurrence. Define $U(t)$ on $\mathcal C$ by $U(t)\psi_n=e^{-i\omega(n+1/2)t}\psi_n$ and extend continuously to a unitary on the oscillator Hilbert space. For $\psi_0$ the normalized ground state, define
$$C_F(t)=\frac{m_o}{\hbar}\bigl(T X(t)X(0)\psi_0,\psi_0\bigr)_1,\qquad X(t)=U(t)^\dagger XU(t),$$
where time ordering means $T X(t)X(0)=X(t)X(0)$ for $t\ge0$ and $X(0)X(t)$ for $t<0$. Define $G_R(t)=1_{[0,\infty)}(t)\sin(\omega t)/\omega$.

Then, for every real $t$,
$$C_F(t)=\frac{e^{-i\omega|t|}}{2\omega},\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)C_F=-i\delta_0,\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)G_R=\delta_0.$$
The derivatives are distributional on $\mathbb R$, and $\delta_0(\varphi)=\varphi(0)$. Both kernels have units of seconds, so the differential identities have units of inverse seconds. In particular, $C_F(t)\ne0$ for $t<0$ while $G_R(t)=0$ there.

For a Schwartz test function $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and $\epsilon>0$, define $\operatorname{PV}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx:=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\int_{|x|>r}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ and $\delta_a(\varphi):=\varphi(a)$. The Plemelj boundary identity is
$$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x+i\epsilon}\,dx =\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}x\,dx-i\pi\varphi(0),$$
with the opposite sign of $i\epsilon$ reversing the delta sign. In this boundary formula $x$ and $\epsilon$ use one common coordinate unit. For $\nu\in\mathbb R$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the frequency regulator $\epsilon>0$ is in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $\epsilon t$ is dimensionless; the ordinary positive-sign Fourier transform of $e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)$ is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i\epsilon}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i\epsilon}\right).$$
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$ its distributional limit is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left[ \operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu-\omega}-\operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu+\omega} -i\pi\delta_{\omega}-i\pi\delta_{-\omega}\right],$$
which is conventionally denoted $i/(\nu^2-\omega^2+i0)$. Here that notation means the displayed pair of opposite boundary values at the two simple poles. This one-mode result makes no spatial-causality or interacting-field claim.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Since $\mu_0$ has units kg m C$^{-2}$ and $\hbar c$ has units kg m$^3$ s$^{-2}$, $S_0$ has units kg m$^2$(C s)$^{-1}$. Dividing $A_a$, whose units are kg m(C s)$^{-1}$, by $S_0$ gives $[a_a]=$m$^{-1}$. Also $[\mu]=[mc/\hbar]=$m$^{-1}$ and $[\mu_0c/\hbar]=$C$^{-2}$, so $[g]=1$. $$D'_a\psi'=(\partial_a-ig(a_a+\partial_a\alpha))(e^{ig\alpha}\psi) =e^{ig\alpha}\bigl(\partial_a\psi+ig(\partial_a\alpha)\psi-ig a_a\psi-ig(\partial_a\alpha)\psi\bigr) =e^{ig\alpha}D_a\psi.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

For every positive even integer $n$, no continuous map $v:S^n\to\mathbb R^{n+1}$ can satisfy both $\langle v(x),x\rangle=0$ and $v(x)\ne0$ for all $x$. Thus an even-dimensional sphere has no continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field.

derivations.claim: If such a frame existed, then $e_1(n)\in n^\perp$ for every $n$ by [F1], and $|e_1(n)|=1$ by orthonormality. Therefore $e_1$ is a continuous nowhere-zero tangent vector field on $S^2$.
Since $2$ is a positive even integer, [F2] forbids the vector field produced in step 1.1. This contradiction proves the nonexistence of the global frame.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

derivations.claim: The map $Q:\mathcal K\to L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ defined by $Q\epsilon=-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon$ is bounded because $|Q\epsilon|^2\le2(|\epsilon^0|^2+|\boldsymbol\epsilon|^2)$ pointwise. Thus $\mathcal K_0=\ker Q$ is closed. For $\epsilon\in\mathcal K_0$, $n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=\epsilon^0$, so $n\cdot T\epsilon=0$ and $T\epsilon\in\mathcal H_T$ by [F1]. Also $\|T\epsilon\|_2\le\|\boldsymbol\epsilon\|_2+\|\epsilon^0\|_2$, proving boundedness.

Write $\boldsymbol\epsilon=T\epsilon+n\epsilon^0$ and $\boldsymbol\delta=T\delta+n\delta^0$. The cross terms in $\boldsymbol\epsilon^\dagger\boldsymbol\delta$ vanish because each $T$ vector is orthogonal to $n$, while the remaining $n$ term is $\overline{\epsilon^0}\delta^0$ and cancels the time component $-\overline{\epsilon^0}\delta^0$ of $\eta$. Hence $[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2$. Given any $u\in\mathcal H_T$, $\epsilon=(0,u)$ belongs to $\mathcal K_0$ and $T\epsilon=u$, so $T$ is onto.

The equation $T\epsilon=0$ is equivalent to $\boldsymbol\epsilon=n\epsilon^0$, so $\epsilon=b(1,n)$ with $b=\epsilon^0\in L^2$; each such vector is in $\mathcal K_0$. Step 2.1 shows these vectors pair to zero with every member of $\mathcal K_0$. Conversely, if $\epsilon$ pairs to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$, choose $\delta=(0,T\epsilon)$, which lies in $\mathcal K_0$ by [F1]; then $0=[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\|T\epsilon\|_2^2$, so $T\epsilon=0$. Thus the radical is exactly $\mathcal N$.

The induced map $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N\to\mathcal H_T$, $[\epsilon]\mapsto T\epsilon$, is well-defined, injective by the kernel calculation, onto by step 2.1, and preserves the inner product by that same step. It is therefore an isometry onto the complete Hilbert space $\mathcal H_T$, proving positivity and completeness of the quotient.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

derivations.claim: The integral in $g_j$ is the spacetime Fourier transform of a compactly supported smooth function, hence decreases faster than every inverse power of $|(\omega,\mathbf k)|$ by repeated integration by parts. Near $\mathbf k=0$, it is bounded by $\int|j|$, while the squared prefactor is $1/(2\omega)=1/(2|\mathbf k|)$. The radial integral of this bound is a constant times $\int_0^1r^2/r\,dr<\infty$. At infinity the rapid Fourier decay and $\|P_T\|\le1$ make the squared norm integrable. Also $P_Tg_j=g_j$ almost everywhere. Therefore $g_j\in\mathcal H_T$.

By [F3], a vector in $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has only finitely many nonzero sectors. On each such sector [F2] bounds creation and annihilation by the corresponding square-root particle number times $\|g_j\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Thus both maps and their sum are defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The same estimates bound every matrix element between fixed finite-particle vectors by a constant times $\|g_j\|$. On each fixed compact support, repeated integration by parts in step 1.1 bounds $\|g_j\|$ by finitely many smooth-test seminorms, so these matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology. This proves the asserted distributional smearing without defining a point field.

Apply the CCR [F2] to the positive- and negative-frequency terms of the mode expansion and use $E=-\partial_0A$. At equal time the two cross terms combine to
$$-i\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3} \left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{k_i k_j}{|\mathbf k|^2}\right)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)}.$$
This is the distributional Fourier multiplier $-iP_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)$; its action is defined by pairing the bounded multiplier against Schwartz tests. Thus the equal-time commutator holds after smearing, as claimed.

$$A_T(j)=a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j).$$
Its matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology; it is an operator-valued distribution and does not assign a pointwise operator to $A_i(x)$. With $E_i=-\partial_0A_i$, the equal-time canonical commutator is the distribution
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)] =-i\,P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y).$$
