supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, and use [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], and the antisymmetric Fock and CAR conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. For $F\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4)$, define
$$\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}F(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad u_F(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)\,dt.$$
Then $u_F\in\mathcal H_D$, continuously in the Schwartz topology, and
$$\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})$$
defines a bounded operator on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-})$, antilinear in $F$. It satisfies
$$\{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)\}=0,\qquad \{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)^\dagger\}=\langle u_F,u_G\rangle_{\mathcal H_D}I.$$
The positive and negative contraction kernels, defined as tempered distributions by their Fourier integrals, are
$$C_+(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{-i(\omega\tau-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_+(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3},\qquad C_-(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{+i(\omega\tau+\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_-(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}.$$
Their tested pairings give respectively $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$; their sum is the anticommutator kernel $R$ below.
Its tested free equation is $u_{(i\partial_0-h_D(-i\nabla))F}=0$. For spatial Schwartz spinors $u,v$, the equal-time field $\Psi_t(u)=c(P_+W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u})$ satisfies $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)^\dagger\}=\int u(\mathbf x)^\dagger v(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x\,I$ and $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)\}=0$.

The spacetime anticommutator kernel is
$$R(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}W_D(-\tau,\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}=\partial_\tau\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x)I_4-i h_D(-i\nabla)\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x),$$
where $\Delta_\mu$ is the scalar causal commutator distribution of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. Thus the kernel is supported in the closed causal cone. Spinor tests with compact spacelike-separated supports have vanishing anticommutators with one another and with each other's adjoints. Consequently, even polynomials in the bounded smeared fields commute across spacelike-separated regions. These are mathematical properties of the specified free-field construction.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
The adopted physical systems are exactly the two selected Fock
representations in [F2], and [F1] fixes the spacetime and unit convention.
The test spaces and meanings of $\mathfrak A_s(O)$ and $\mathfrak A_D(O)$ are
those defined in [F4]; thus all fields used here are smeared and all Dirac
local observables are even products.

Apply [F6] to the listed real scalar smearings and sector-sum generators.
It supplies their exact maximal domains and, for every normalized
$\Psi\in D(A)$, finite $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and finite variance.
The same statement gives the product-domain condition, so no claim about
$D(A^2)$ or an everywhere-defined product follows.

The region hypotheses in the Statement are exactly the spacelike-support
hypotheses of [F8] and [F10]. The first gives commutativity of the scalar
Weyl algebras; the second gives commutativity of the bounded even Dirac local
algebras. If either region is empty, its test space is $\{0\}$ and
its unital generated algebra is $\mathbb C I$, which commutes with the other
algebra as well.

For every Schwartz $g$, changing variables gives
$\int\rho_{\epsilon,x_0}(x)g(x)\,d^4x=
\int\rho(y)g(x_0+\epsilon y)\,d^4y\to g(x_0)$ by dominated convergence [F11].
For every spatial Schwartz spinor $h$, the corresponding pairing is
$$\int u_{\epsilon,x_0}(\mathbf x)^\dagger h(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x=
\int\sigma(y)z^\dagger h(\mathbf x_0+\epsilon y)\,d^3y
\longrightarrow z^\dagger h(\mathbf x_0),$$
again by dominated convergence with the integrable bound
$\|h\|_\infty\sigma(y)$ [F11]. The equal-time Dirac operator in this family
is the $\Psi_t(u)$ of [F9].
The actual current proof of [F7] gives diverging scalar vacuum-vector norms
and equal-time Dirac operator norms for these Gaussian families. A norm-convergent vector or bounded-operator family
must have bounded norms, so neither family has such a limit.

The selected definition [F5] supplies no other point field or diagonal
product. The norm obstruction in step 1.4 is specific to the displayed
representations and topologies.

When the state and finite instrument required by [F3] are supplied, the
Born postulate assigns the stated model probabilities. No such state,
instrument, apparatus, or observation is introduced by this theorem, so it
establishes no empirical outcome.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put
$\omega(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here
$\omega$ is the temporal wave number, not the SI angular frequency; the
corresponding SI angular frequency is $c\omega$. Energy and momentum are
$E=\hbar c\omega$ in joules and $\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

The natural action is $S/\hbar$. Its canonical density in four dimensions has
unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$; the corresponding physical energy density is
$\hbar c$ times that density and has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
write $\phi_{\rm n}$ for a scalar field with length degree $-1$ and
$\psi_{\rm n}$ for a Dirac field with length degree $-3/2$. These are the
dimensions fixed by the selected free kinetic terms, not exact scaling
dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous dimensions, when present, are
separate quantities. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad
f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$\mathcal L_\phi=-\frac12\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b\phi+\mu^2\phi^2\right),\qquad \mathcal L_D=\bar\psi\left(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu\right)\psi,\qquad \bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta.$$

$$\delta S_\phi(\phi;h)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h(\Box-\mu^2)\phi\,d^4x,\qquad \delta S_D(\psi;\chi)=2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R^4}\chi^\dagger\beta\left(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu\right)\psi\,d^4x.$$
Each field is stationary under all such variations if and only if its corresponding Euler–Lagrange equation holds pointwise:
$$(\Box-\mu^2)\phi=0,\qquad (i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0.$$
The adjoint Dirac equation follows from the second equation because the fixed matrices satisfy $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$. These are mathematical variation identities for commuting classical fields; they assert no quantization, Grassmann calculus, or physical measurement.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, and use [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], and the antisymmetric Fock and CAR conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. For $F\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4)$, define
$$\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}F(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad u_F(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)\,dt.$$
Then $u_F\in\mathcal H_D$, continuously in the Schwartz topology, and
$$\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})$$
defines a bounded operator on $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-})$, antilinear in $F$. It satisfies
$$\{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)\}=0,\qquad \{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)^\dagger\}=\langle u_F,u_G\rangle_{\mathcal H_D}I.$$
The positive and negative contraction kernels, defined as tempered distributions by their Fourier integrals, are
$$C_+(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{-i(\omega\tau-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_+(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3},\qquad C_-(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int e^{+i(\omega\tau+\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}P_-(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}.$$
Their tested pairings give respectively $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$; their sum is the anticommutator kernel $R$ below.
Its tested free equation is $u_{(i\partial_0-h_D(-i\nabla))F}=0$. For spatial Schwartz spinors $u,v$, the equal-time field $\Psi_t(u)=c(P_+W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat u})$ satisfies $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)^\dagger\}=\int u(\mathbf x)^\dagger v(\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x\,I$ and $\{\Psi_t(u),\Psi_t(v)\}=0$.

The spacetime anticommutator kernel is
$$R(\tau,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}W_D(-\tau,\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}=\partial_\tau\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x)I_4-i h_D(-i\nabla)\Delta_\mu(\tau,\mathbf x),$$
where $\Delta_\mu$ is the scalar causal commutator distribution of [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. Thus the kernel is supported in the closed causal cone. Spinor tests with compact spacelike-separated supports have vanishing anticommutators with one another and with each other's adjoints. Consequently, even polynomials in the bounded smeared fields commute across spacelike-separated regions. These are mathematical properties of the specified free-field construction.

=i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu,$$

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice, $\mu\ge0$, and the selected free-field model of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]]. Use the four-dimensional affine Minkowski chart,
signature $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinate $x^0=ct$,
and inverse-length parameter $\mu$ of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. For an open
region $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, use the scalar and Dirac test functions and
bounded local observable algebras defined in
[[def-qft-free-field-observables]]: scalar tests are real members of
$C_c^\infty(O)$, Dirac tests are members of
$C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb C^4)$, and the Dirac observable algebra is generated by
even products of bounded smeared CAR fields and their adjoints.

For a real Schwartz scalar test $f$, the closure of $\Phi_\mu(f)$ is
self-adjoint on its exact Segal-field multiplier domain. The scalar number,
Hamiltonian and momentum operators and the Dirac Hamiltonian and momentum
operators have the exact maximal sector-sum domains stated in
[[lem-qft-free-domain-observables]]. In particular,
$$D(N_s)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
If $A$ is one of these self-adjoint operators and $\Psi$ is normalized with
$\Psi\in D(A)$, then its model mean $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and variance
$$\operatorname{Var}_\Psi(A)=\|(A-\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle)\Psi\|^2$$
are finite; this needs $\Psi\in D(A)$, not $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. The product
$AB\Psi$ is defined only when $\Psi\in D(B)$ and $B\Psi\in D(A)$.

If $O_1,O_2$ are open regions and
$\eta_{ab}(x-y)^a(x-y)^b>0$ for every $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$, then the
scalar Weyl algebras of the two regions commute, and the even local Dirac
algebras of the two regions commute. These are algebraic properties of the
specified free representations.

The chosen construction supplies only test-smeared fields and does not define
$\Phi_\mu(x)$, $\Psi(x)$, or coincident diagonal products. Fix a point
$x_0\in\mathbb R^4$ and a nonnegative normalized Schwartz Gaussian
$\rho\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$, and put
$\rho_{\epsilon,x_0}(x)=\epsilon^{-4}\rho((x-x_0)/\epsilon)$. These tests
approximate $\delta_{x_0}$ on Schwartz functions, but
$\|\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\epsilon,x_0})\Omega\|\to\infty$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.
For an equal-time Dirac field, fix a unit spinor $z$ and a nonnegative
normalized Schwartz Gaussian $\sigma$ on $\mathbb R^3$, and put
$u_{\epsilon,x_0}(\mathbf x)=\epsilon^{-3}
\sigma((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/\epsilon)z$. These tests approximate a
spatial point mass, while $\|\Psi_t(u_{\epsilon,x_0})\|\to\infty$. Neither
family has a finite limit in its respective Fock or operator-norm topology.
This restriction does not rule out other distributional or renormalized
constructions. The Born interpretation of
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]] applies only after a density
state and normalized finite bounded instrument have actually been supplied;
this item reports no apparatus or outcome.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
For any Schwartz test $g$, the change of variables
$y=(x-x_0)/\epsilon$ gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^4}\rho_{\epsilon,x_0}(x)g(x)\,d^4x
=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\rho(y)g(x_0+\epsilon y)\,d^4y.$$
The integrand converges pointwise to $\rho(y)g(x_0)$ and is dominated by
$\|g\|_\infty\rho(y)$, which is integrable. Dominated convergence [F2]
therefore gives the limit $g(x_0)$, so these are point-mass approximants.

Take the explicit sequence $\epsilon_n=1/n$. By [F1],
$\|\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\epsilon_n,x_0})\Omega\|\to\infty$. A norm-convergent
sequence in a Hilbert space has bounded norms, so this sequence cannot
converge to a finite vacuum vector. Hence the claimed norm-limit point field
does not exist in this representation. This refutes only the stated norm
limit and does not exclude distributional or renormalized constructions.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $Q\sim N_N(0,C)$ be the centered finite-dimensional Gaussian vector of [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]], and write $C_{jj}=\mathbb E[Q_j^2]\ge0$ for the variance of its $j$th coordinate. For each coordinate $j$ and integer $n\ge0$, its **finite covariance Wick normal power** is the polynomial $:Q_j^n:_C$ defined by the formal generating identity

$$\exp\!\left(tQ_j-\frac12t^2C_{jj}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}:Q_j^n:_C\,\frac{t^n}{n!}.$$

Equivalently,

$$:Q_j^n:_C=n!\sum_{s=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{(-C_{jj}/2)^sQ_j^{n-2s}}{s!(n-2s)!},\qquad :Q_j^4:_C=Q_j^4-6C_{jj}Q_j^2+3C_{jj}^2.$$

This is a finite-dimensional polynomial definition; it does not define a product of unsmeared continuum fields.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $Q\sim N_N(0,C)$ be the centered finite-dimensional Gaussian vector of [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]], and write $C_{jj}=\mathbb E[Q_j^2]\ge0$ for the variance of its $j$th coordinate. For each coordinate $j$ and integer $n\ge0$, its **finite covariance Wick normal power** is the polynomial $:Q_j^n:_C$ defined by the formal generating identity

$$\exp\!\left(tQ_j-\frac12t^2C_{jj}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}:Q_j^n:_C\,\frac{t^n}{n!}.$$

Equivalently,

$$:Q_j^n:_C=n!\sum_{s=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{(-C_{jj}/2)^sQ_j^{n-2s}}{s!(n-2s)!},\qquad :Q_j^4:_C=Q_j^4-6C_{jj}Q_j^2+3C_{jj}^2.$$

This is a finite-dimensional polynomial definition; it does not define a product of unsmeared continuum fields.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ covariance matrix, and let $Q\sim\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$ be the law of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. For $k\ge0$ and vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\mathbb R^N$, every product $\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$ is integrable. For $k=0$ its expectation is $1$. If $k$ is odd, its expectation is $0$; if $k=2m$, then

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every polynomial in $Q$ has a finite absolute moment, computed by finitely many covariance pairings.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. For the physical internal-energy interpretation, use one declared fixed Galilean chart for every stage, with the bulk center-of-mass and separately tracked external-energy sectors suppressed from this finite protocol. The companion mechanical model supplies the center-of-mass data required by the microstate supplier; when the common chart is called a center-of-mass rest chart throughout the protocol, its center-of-mass velocity is constant over the modeled interval, and one constant boost selects that chart. This fixed-chart idealization does not infer a rest chart from the finite set or transition kernels, and does not describe an accelerating bulk body. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. The initial law is a probability vector $\mu_0:\Omega\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\mu_0(i)=1$. Its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$; summing over all paths gives $1$ by the normalization of $\mu_0$ and the row sums of the kernels.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

e i}[p_jq_{ji}-p_iq_{ij}]$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

For a discrete transition kernel $K$ on a finite state set, $\pi$-detailed balance means $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every pair. If $\pi$ is strictly positive, this identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

The companion mechanical model supplies the center-of-mass data required by the microstate supplier; when the common chart is called a center-of-mass rest chart throughout the protocol, its center-of-mass velocity is constant over the modeled interval, and one constant boost selects that chart. This fixed-chart idealization does not infer a rest chart from the finite set or transition kernels, and does not describe an accelerating bulk body. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Put $c=1+\max_i\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$ and $P=I+Q/c$, where $Q=(q_{ij})$. Then $P$ has nonnegative entries and row sums one. The series $p(t)=e^{-ct}\sum_{n=0}^\infty (ct)^n p(0)P^n/n!$ and its differentiated series converge uniformly on bounded time intervals; its coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one, so it is a probability vector, starts at $p(0)$, and differentiates to $\dot p=pQ$. Its $n=0$ term gives $p_i(t)\ge e^{-ct}p_i(0)>0$. For uniqueness, the difference $z$ of two solutions satisfies $z'=zQ$; with $C=\max_i\sum_j|q_{ij}|$ and $U(t)=\int_0^t\|z(s)\|_1ds$, one has $U'(t)=\|z(t)\|_1\le C U(t)$. Thus $(e^{-Ct}U(t))'\le0$ and $U(0)=0\le U(t)$ force $U=0$, hence $z=0$.

With $r_i=p_i/\pi_i$, detailed balance gives $\dot p_i=\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(r_j-r_i)$. By [F4], differentiating the finite entropy sum gives $D'=\sum_i\dot p_i(\log r_i+1)=\sum_i\dot p_i\log r_i$, since $\sum_i\dot p_i=0$. Pairing the $i,j$ terms gives $D'=-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(r_i-r_j)(\log r_i-\log r_j)\le0$: if $r_i\ge r_j$, then $\log r_i-\log r_j=-\log(r_j/r_i)\ge0$ by [F3], and the reversed order gives the same product sign. The mean value theorem [F5] on each compact time interval makes $D$ nonincreasing.

Set $u_i=r_i-1$, so $\sum_i\pi_i u_i=0$, and $V(t)=\sum_i\pi_i u_i^2$. Since $\dot u_i=\pi_i^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)$, differentiating and pairing the two orientations of each edge gives $V'=2\sum_i u_i\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)=-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$.

Let $a_*=\min_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}>0$. Fix a root state and choose one simple path from it to each state; this is only a finite family of choices, obtainable successively, and each path has length at most $N-1$. Telescoping and [F6] give $(u_i-u_r)^2\le(N-1)\sum_{\{j,k\}\in E}(u_j-u_k)^2$. The zero-mean identity gives $u_r=-\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)$; expanding $\sum_i\pi_i[(u_i-u_r)-\sum_j\pi_j(u_j-u_r)]^2\ge0$ yields $u_r^2\le\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)^2$. Since $(x+y)^2\le2x^2+2y^2$ and $\sum_i\pi_i=1$, it follows that $V\le4(N-1)\sum_E(u_i-u_j)^2\le4(N-1)a_*^{-1}\sum_Ea_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$.

Thus $V'\le-2\lambda V$ with $\lambda=a_*/[4(N-1)]>0$. By [F5], the derivative of $e^{2\lambda t}V(t)$ is nonpositive and that function is nonincreasing, so $V(t)\le e^{-2\lambda t}V(0)$. Since $\pi_i u_i(t)^2\le V(t)$ and $p_i-\pi_i=\pi_i u_i$, each $p_i(t)\to\pi_i$.

Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. For the physical internal-energy interpretation, use one declared fixed Galilean chart for every stage, with the bulk center-of-mass and separately tracked external-energy sectors suppressed from this finite protocol. The companion mechanical model supplies the center-of-mass data required by the microstate supplier; when the common chart is called a center-of-mass rest chart throughout the protocol, its center-of-mass velocity is constant over the modeled interval, and one constant boost selects that chart. This fixed-chart idealization does not infer a rest chart from the finite set or transition kernels, and does not describe an accelerating bulk body. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. The initial law is a probability vector $\mu_0:\Omega\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\mu_0(i)=1$. Its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$; summing over all paths gives $1$ by the normalization of $\mu_0$ and the row sums of the kernels.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i
e j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; write $\Delta(S)=\{p\in[0,1]^S:\sum_i p_i=1\}$. A time-dependent law is a coordinatewise continuously differentiable map $p:[0,\infty)	o\Delta(S)$, with a right derivative at $t=0$, that satisfies the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i(t)=\sum_{j
e i}[p_j(t)q_{ji}-p_i(t)q_{ij}]$ for every $t\ge0$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

For a discrete transition kernel $K$ on a finite state set, $\pi$-detailed balance means $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every pair. If $\pi$ is strictly positive, this identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

For a protocol of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], fix a bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and set $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$, using the exact constant and SI conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state clause of the adopted [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] then gives the stage-zero law $\pi_0(i)=e^{-\beta E_0(i)}/Z_0$; adopt that the initial microstate is drawn from this law, so $\mu_0=\pi_0$. Here $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $E_0(i)$ is finite, so $0<Z_0<\infty$ as required by that clause. This is a model premise about the preparation distribution. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. The countable-state and measure-integral branches of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] are not used.

For the protocol in [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], adopt, at each stage $k=1,\ldots,m$, the stationarity condition $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=\pi_k(j)$ for every $j\in\Omega$. This says that if the bath transition begins with law $\pi_k$ at fixed energy $E_k$, it ends with the same law. It is a physical modeling assumption for this protocol family, not a consequence of the transition-kernel definition and not an assertion that the kernel mixes every initial law to $\pi_k$.
For every path $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)$ of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], the endpoint energy change is $E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)=W(\omega)+Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)$, with the stated sign convention.

derivations.claim: Define the reverse path law by starting with $\pi_m(i_m)$ and, in reverse order, using $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})$ at fixed energy $E_k$ before undoing that quench. By detailed balance, if $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)>0$ then $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})>0$, because $\pi_k$ is strictly positive. Thus positive forward paths pair with positive reverse paths.

On a paired path, divide the endpoint Gibbs weights and use detailed balance for each transition: $P_F(\omega)/P_R(\omega^R)=[\pi_0(i_0)/\pi_m(i_m)]\prod_{k=1}^m[\pi_k(i_k)/\pi_k(i_{k-1})]$. Substituting $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$ and collecting terms gives $\log(P_F/P_R)=\beta[E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)-Q_{\mathrm{in}}]+\log(Z_m/Z_0)=\beta(W-\Delta F)$ by [F3].

The reversed quench at stage $k$ occurs at state $i_{k-1}$, so its work term is $E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})-E_k(i_{k-1})=-[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$; summing proves $W_R(\omega^R)=-W(\omega)$. Summing the path ratio over the finite set of paths with $W=w$ proves the stated distribution identity.

citations.quote: Choose a Galilean inertial chart $\mathcal F$ as defined in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]] for the specified fixed closed trap-and-bath body, assumed to have positive total mass and the center-of-mass map required there, and supply its componentwise differentiable center-of-mass trajectory on the whole modeled time interval. Assume that its center-of-mass velocity is one constant vector on that interval, so the single constant boost of that supplier selects $\mathcal F$ with zero center-of-mass velocity throughout. Take $\mathcal F$ to be this common rest chart. The trap-and-bath background is held fixed in this idealization; center-of-mass recoil or accelerating-frame dynamics are not part of the scalar process. In this chart let $\mathbf r_c\in\mathbb R^3$ be the fixed trap-center position and let $\mathbf e\in\mathbb R^3$ be a fixed unit vector along the modeled trap axis. For a particle position $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$, define the signed displacement $x=\langle\mathbf r-\mathbf r_c,\mathbf e\rangle$ in metres; the process $X_t$ in [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]] is this coordinate of the particle position at time $t$. Thus $U(x)=kx^2/2$ is the harmonic potential relative to the trap center, not an absolute spatial coordinate. Using the SI conventions and exact $k_{\mathrm B}$ of [[def-td-si-quantities]], take stiffness $k>0$ in joules per square metre, constant mobility $\mu>0$ in square metres per joule-second, and bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin. Adopt the one-dimensional overdamped model $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, interpreted through the integral equation of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], with $\gamma=\mu k$ in seconds$^{-1}$ and $\sigma^2=2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b$ in square metres per second. Here $B$ is standard Brownian motion with its stated filtration and increment hypotheses, and the bath noise is independent of the initial preparation. This Einstein noise relation and the linear Markov model are physical assumptions. They do not follow from equilibrium thermodynamics alone and do not report a measured spectrum or calibration.

Assume the filtered probability space, Brownian increment hypothesis, and initial data of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], including $\mathbb E X_0^2<\infty$ and future increments independent of $\mathcal F_0$. For $\gamma,\sigma>0$, on every finite time interval the process
$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}\,dB_s$$
has a continuous adapted version, solves the stated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck integral equation, and is the unique continuous solution driven by the same $(X_0,B)$. Put $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)$. For $0\le s<t$, its transition law conditional on $\mathcal F_s$ is normal with mean $e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s$ and variance $V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. Consequently
$$\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+V(1-e^{-2\gamma t}).$$
From any such initial law, $X_t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,V)$. If $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ and is independent of future Brownian increments, the process is stationary Gaussian with covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\gamma|\tau|}$, and its transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with the $N(0,V)$ density. Its transition density solves the Fokker–Planck equation for positive time. Under the convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, the stationary spectrum and time-average bound are
$$S(\omega)=\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T X_t\,dt\right)\le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$
All these statements concern the specified linear stochastic model. An Einstein relation between $\sigma$ and a physical bath temperature would be an additional physical postulate.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. Fix constants $\gamma>0$ and $\sigma>0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real random variable $X_0$ with finite second moment. A **continuous adapted solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation** on $[0,T]$ is a continuous adapted process $X$ satisfying, almost surely for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].

derivations.claim: The physical postulate gives $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)=(2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b)/(2\mu k)=k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k$. This has units of square metres because $k_{\mathrm B}T_b$ is joules and $k$ is joules per square metre.

The inspected mathematical supplier's stationary clause applies with this $V$ and $\gamma=\mu k$, so $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\mu k|\tau|}$ and $S(\omega)=V\mu k/[\pi((\mu k)^2+\omega^2)]=\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b/[\pi((\mu k)^2+\omega^2)]$.

The same supplier's time-average bound becomes $2V/(\gamma T)=2k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\mu k^2T)$. All three formulas are conditional deductions of the adopted model; no apparatus, observed value, or measured uncertainty is asserted.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a finite memory-state set and $R$ a finite retained-register set. A joint preparation is a probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. Use the finite Shannon entropy in nats and the conditional entropy $H(M|R)$ exactly as defined by [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]. For a fixed target memory state $m_0$, a reset is the endpoint map $p'(m,r)=\mathbf 1_{\{m=m_0\}}a_r$: it places the memory at $m_0$ while leaving the register marginal unchanged. The definition alone assigns no physical entropy, work cost, heat transfer, or implementation.

Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. For the physical internal-energy interpretation, use one declared fixed Galilean chart for every stage, with the bulk center-of-mass and separately tracked external-energy sectors suppressed from this finite protocol. The companion mechanical model supplies the center-of-mass data required by the microstate supplier; when the common chart is called a center-of-mass rest chart throughout the protocol, its center-of-mass velocity is constant over the modeled interval, and one constant boost selects that chart. This fixed-chart idealization does not infer a rest chart from the finite set or transition kernels, and does not describe an accelerating bulk body. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. The initial law is a probability vector $\mu_0:\Omega\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\mu_0(i)=1$. Its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$; summing over all paths gives $1$ by the normalization of $\mu_0$ and the row sums of the kernels.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i
e j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; write $\Delta(S)=\{p\in[0,1]^S:\sum_i p_i=1\}$. A time-dependent law is a coordinatewise continuously differentiable map $p:[0,\infty)	o\Delta(S)$, with a right derivative at $t=0$, that satisfies the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i(t)=\sum_{j
e i}[p_j(t)q_{ji}-p_i(t)q_{ij}]$ for every $t\ge0$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

For a discrete transition kernel $K$ on a finite state set, $\pi$-detailed balance means $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every pair. If $\pi$ is strictly positive, this identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

Let $S$ have $N\ge2$ states, positive detailed-balance law $\pi$, and connected undirected rate graph as in [[def-td-detailed-balance-rate-model]]. For every strictly positive initial probability vector $p(0)$, the master equation has a unique strictly positive probability solution $p(t)$ for all $t\ge0$. The relative entropy $D(p(t)\Vert\pi)=\sum_i p_i(t)\log(p_i(t)/\pi_i)$ is nonincreasing, and $p_i(t)\to\pi_i$ for every state. No monotonicity of Shannon entropy $-\sum_i p_i\log p_i$ is asserted.

Use the finite Shannon entropy in nats and the conditional entropy $H(M|R)$ exactly as defined by [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]. For a fixed target memory state $m_0$, a reset is the endpoint map $p'(m,r)=\mathbf 1_{\{m=m_0\}}a_r$: it places the memory at $m_0$ while leaving the register marginal unchanged. citations.quote: Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

Then $W\ge k_{\mathrm B}T_bH(M|R)$, with both sides in joules. Equality is not asserted without a separately specified reversible implementation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ of [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]], $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a system $s$ as in [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]]. A material constitution $c$ specifies a finite ordered list of named species $(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)$, with $r\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and $r\ge1$, and the model parameters that identify the material. An equilibrium-preparation label in the set $E_c$ selects a single macrostate that the model designates as an equilibrium state for constitution $c$. The equilibrium designation is primitive model input here; it is not a dynamical equilibration theorem or a global-stability claim. For each admitted preparation, its mechanical model supplies a positive total mass and a defined center-of-mass velocity as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], so the allowed boost can select a center-of-mass rest chart in which its internal energy is recorded. A preparation for which these mechanical data are unavailable lies outside this framework. A statistical preparation that instead supplies a normalized probability measure on a declared measurable space is as in [[def-probability-measure]] and belongs to a separate statistical branch; it is an element of $E_c$ only if that model also assigns it a single equilibrium macrostate.

Each $e\in E_c$ is assigned a unique coordinate tuple $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, where $U$ is the adopted internal-energy coordinate in joules as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], $V>0$ is volume in cubic metres, and each $n_j>0$ is an amount in moles; the SI unit assignments are those of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. These are real-valued mole amounts in the bulk continuous chart, not integer particle counts. Define the dimensionless numerical coordinates $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$, $\hat V=V/(1\,\mathrm{m^3})$, and $\hat n_j=n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. The representation map $\pi_c:E_c\to\mathbb R^{r+2}$ is a function as in [[def-function-space]], sends $e$ to $(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)$, and the equilibrium state domain is its image $D_c:=\pi_c(E_c)\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+2}$ using inclusion as in [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in D_c$, write $U_c(x):=\hat U\,\mathrm J$, $V_c(x):=\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3}$, and $n_{c,j}(x):=\hat n_j\,\mathrm{mol}$ for its dimensioned coordinates. Preparation labels with the same coordinate tuple represent the same thermodynamic state in this framework. Statistical preparations that specify a probability law belong to a separate branch and are not used in this state-domain definition.

For fixed $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ in a chart used by the model, write $\Gamma_{c,n}=\{(\hat U,\hat V):(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)\in D_c\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, with inclusion notation as in [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]. This designated slice is a specified nonempty open convex subset. With the dimensionless Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] (a norm by [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]), openness means that every $z\in\Gamma_{c,n}$ has some $\epsilon>0$ for which $\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\|w-z\|_2<\epsilon\}\subseteq\Gamma_{c,n}$. Convexity means that $(1-t)z_0+tz_1\in\Gamma_{c,n}$ whenever $z_0,z_1\in\Gamma_{c,n}$ and $t\in[0,1]$, as in [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]. Both properties are assumptions about the particular slice, not conclusions about every $D_c$; no coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable merely because it lies in an ambient Euclidean space. A zero amount for an absent species belongs only to a separately specified boundary domain and is not in this positive-mole chart.

In a simple-compressible chart, volume $V$ is the only mechanical coordinate in the equilibrium representation; composition changes, fields, polarization, surface terms, and other mechanical coordinates require a separately declared state domain and exchange rules. No pressure or reversible-work formula follows from this definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For this nonrelativistic framework, a Newtonian event-coordinate domain is the Cartesian product $I\times\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cartesian-product]]), where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open time interval as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, and $\mathbb R^3$ has the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] (the norm properties follow from [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]); lengths are measured in metres as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. A Galilean inertial chart labels events in such a domain by coordinates $(t,\mathbf x)$. If a second chart uses the translated time domain $I'=I+\tau$, the allowed coordinate changes are
$$t'=t+\tau,\qquad \mathbf x'=R\mathbf x+\mathbf a-\mathbf b t,$$
where $\tau$ is a constant time shift measured in seconds, $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation measured in metres, $\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant boost velocity measured in metres per second, and $R\in M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ is a dimensionless constant matrix ([[def-matrix-space]]) satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ using matrix transpose and product ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), with $I_3$ the identity matrix. In the coordinate formula, $(R\mathbf x)_i:=\sum_{k<3}R_{ik}x_k$ for $i<3$. Thus time is absolute in this model and no Lorentzian structure is used. Here “frame” means this coordinate chart, not an observer congruence or a basis/tetrad field.

For a finite point-mass representation with $N\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $N\ge1$, masses $m_i>0$ in kg at positions $\mathbf x_i\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres for $i<N$, assume $M:=\sum_{i<N}m_i>0$ ([[def-finite-sum]]) and define the center-of-mass coordinates by $X_{\mathrm{cm},j}:=M^{-1}\sum_{i<N}m_i x_{i,j}$ for $j<3$; these three real coordinates form $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}$. The masses are invariant under the allowed chart changes. Other mechanical models must supply their total mass and center-of-mass map; this thermodynamic item does not construct those quantities for a continuum or field model. Every admitted mechanical model must also supply center-of-mass maps and velocities that transform under the displayed Galilean chart changes by $\mathbf X'_{\mathrm{cm}}(t')=R\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}(t)+\mathbf a-\mathbf b t$ and $\mathbf v'_{\mathrm{cm}}=R\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}-\mathbf b$, where $t'=t+\tau$; these are kinematic compatibility conditions, not dynamical theorems about arbitrary mechanical models. When the model supplies a center-of-mass position $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-function-space]]), its velocity at a time $t$ is the componentwise limit $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}(t)=\lim_{h\to0}(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}(t+h)-\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}(t))/h$ through $H_t:=\{h\in\mathbb R:t+h\in I,\ h\ne0\}$ ([[def-function-limit]]), when that limit exists. A center-of-mass rest frame is a Galilean inertial chart in which this velocity is zero; the adopted covariance condition allows the pure boost $\mathbf b=\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ to select one whenever the velocity is defined. For a fixed closed body with total mass $M>0$ in kg, its separately tracked translational kinetic energy in a selected inertial chart is $K_{\mathrm{cm}}=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}\|_2^2$ in joules; under a pure boost it is $K'_{\mathrm{cm}}=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}-\mathbf b\|_2^2$.

In this framework $U$ denotes the scalar internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame. Bulk translational kinetic energy and any separately tracked external-field potential energy are excluded from $U$. The model treats $U$ as invariant between rest charts that differ only by spatial translation or orthogonal orientation, and fixes its numerical zero, including any retained or subtracted constituent rest-energy offsets, consistently across the composition changes it admits. This is a nonrelativistic modeling convention, not a derived energy-transformation law.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in that coordinate direction while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

$$T_c:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}},\qquad p_c:=T_cS_{c,V},\qquad \mu_{c,j}:=-T_cS_{c,n_j}.$$

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
A thermodynamic system $s$ is a model-selected body or collection of bodies together with a specified outer boundary $\partial s$. The boundary separates the system from its environment for the purpose of classifying transfers; it need not be a material wall. A compound system has named subsystems inside one outer boundary. Transfers between its subsystems are internal to the compound; only transfers across $\partial s$ are external.

The model specifies which transfers across $\partial s$ are permitted. A system is closed when no matter crosses its outer boundary; energy may cross. A system is open when only the named matter species and other named transfer channels may cross its boundary. A system or compound is isolated when no matter or energy crosses its outer boundary. These terms classify the declared model boundary, not the accuracy with which a real apparatus approximates it.

This boundary classification alone asserts neither an energy-balance law nor equilibration.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For a system $s$ of constitution $c$, the process model fixes one Galilean inertial chart $g_s$ for kinetic-energy bookkeeping and transfer records and holds that chart fixed throughout each process. A process record is a tuple
$$P=(I_P,x_P^-,x_P^+,z_P,\kappa_P,r_P).$$
For each finite closed time interval $I_P=[t_0,t_1]\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $t_0<t_1$ as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, its component fields have these types: $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$ are equilibrium endpoint coordinates from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; $Z_s$ is the model-declared configuration space of the system, its auxiliaries and devices; $Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq Z_s$ is the model-declared set of equilibrium configurations and $\xi_s:Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}\to D_c$ assigns their state coordinates; $z_P:I_P\to Z_s$ is a function ([[def-function-space]]); $\mathcal K_s$ is the model-declared set of control/contact records and $\kappa_P\in\mathcal K_s$; and $\mathcal R_s$ is the model-declared set of signed transfer records and $r_P\in\mathcal R_s$. These fields form a finite Cartesian product ([[def-cartesian-product]]). The admitted records $\mathcal P_s$ are the model-specified subset of tuples with these types that additionally satisfy $z_P(t_0),z_P(t_1)\in Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}$, $\xi_s(z_P(t_0))=x_P^-$, and $\xi_s(z_P(t_1))=x_P^+$. No continuity or differentiability is imposed on $z_P$, and its values at interior times need not represent equilibrium states.

For an endpoint bookkeeping quantity $F$, write $\Delta F=F_P^+-F_P^-$. A closed record in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]] has no matter crossing the chosen outer boundary. The core closed-record class $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\subseteq\mathcal P_s$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]) contains only records for which the system has a supplied total mass $M>0$ and defined center-of-mass velocities at both endpoints in the fixed chart $g_s$, so the kinetic energies $K_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}^\pm\|_2^2$ are defined as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. It further requires $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$ and $\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$, where $U_{\mathrm{ext}}$ denotes any model-specified external-field potential energy tracked separately from the internal-energy coordinate in $g_s$. Other process classes require an expanded energy bookkeeping rule.

For each $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$, the protocol supplies maps $Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}:\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\to\mathbb R$ whose values are interpreted in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]] and whose energy bookkeeping uses $g_s$. $Q[P]>0$ means energy enters the system through the declared thermal-transfer channel; $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$ means mechanical work is done on the system. These are functionals of the process record, not state functions of $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$. Heat is the protocol-assigned thermal mode of energy transfer, not a quantity stored in the equilibrium state. A record is adiabatic exactly when $Q[P]=0$. A closed record may still exchange energy; it is not thereby isolated.

A preparation is a model-specified rule selecting the particular initial equilibrium state $x_P^-$. A statistical extension may instead specify a normalized probability measure on a declared measurable space, as in [[def-probability-measure]]; such a statistical preparation is outside this deterministic process class. A preparation does not assert later equilibration. An admitted record may pass through nonequilibrium configurations even though both endpoints lie in $D_c$.
