Assume Countable Choice and use $\mathcal H_T$ from [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]]. On $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^4)$ define
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\epsilon(\mathbf k)^\dagger\eta\,\delta(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,\qquad \eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1).$$
For $\mathbf k\ne0$, let $n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and set
$$\mathcal K_0=\{\epsilon\in\mathcal K:-\epsilon^0+n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon=0\text{ a.e.}\},\qquad T\epsilon=\boldsymbol\epsilon-n\epsilon^0.$$
Then $\mathcal K_0$ is closed, $T:\mathcal K_0\to\mathcal H_T$ is bounded and onto, and
$$[\epsilon,\delta]_\eta=\langle T\epsilon,T\delta\rangle_2\quad(\epsilon,\delta\in\mathcal K_0).$$
Its radical (the vectors pairing to zero with all of $\mathcal K_0$) is
$$\mathcal N=\ker T=\{b(\mathbf k)(1,n(\mathbf k)):b\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)\}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal K_0/\mathcal N$ with the induced form is a positive Hilbert space isometric to $\mathcal H_T$. The form on the four-component auxiliary space is indefinite; only the subsidiary quotient is the positive physical one-particle space.

derivations.claim:
The scale $\kappa$ in [F2] is a positive wave number. Apply [F1] with
radii $\kappa/8$ and $\kappa/4$, then translate the
result to the center of $\Omega$. Translation preserves smoothness and
support, so $b$ is smooth, bounded, and compactly supported in $\Omega$;
it equals one on an inner ball of positive volume. Thus
$0<\|b\|_2<\infty$ and $g=b/\|b\|_2$ is the stated normalized wavepacket.
Since the timelike coordinate has metric coefficient $-1$, direct
substitution gives
$[\epsilon_{\rm aux},\epsilon_{\rm aux}]
=\int -|g(\mathbf k)|^2\,d^3\mathbf k=-1$. On the support of $g$, the
subsidiary expression is
$-\epsilon_{\rm aux}^0+\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon_{\rm aux}=-g$,
which is nonzero on the inner ball where $b=1$, a set of positive measure.
Hence
$\epsilon_{\rm aux}\notin\mathcal K_0$ and it has no class in the physical
quotient.

Countable Choice [A2] is carried by the selected Fock model. For every
$\mathbf k\in\Omega$, $k_3\ge3\kappa/4$ and $|k_1|\le\kappa/4$, so
$|n_1|=|k_1|/|\mathbf k|\le1/3$. Hence
$\|P_T(\mathbf k)e_1\|^2=1-|n_1|^2\ge8/9$ on $\Omega$. The vector
$u(\mathbf k)=P_T(\mathbf k)e_1g(\mathbf k)$ is transverse and satisfies
$$\|u\|_{\mathcal H_T}^2=\int_\Omega\|P_Te_1\|^2|g|^2d^3\mathbf k \ge\frac89\|g\|_2^2=\frac89>0.$$
Thus normalizing it gives $\|u\|_{\mathcal H_T}=1$. For every
$\epsilon\in\mathcal K_0$, [L1] gives
$[\epsilon,\epsilon]=\|T\epsilon\|_{\mathcal H_T}^2\ge0$, and quotienting
by $\mathcal N$ removes precisely the zero-norm radical. The physical
wavepacket therefore has positive Hilbert norm, whereas the auxiliary
negative norm belongs to no physical state.

It supplies no observed event, measurement outcome, or probability
assignment to an auxiliary vector; the Born interpretation applies only to
normalized states and supplied measurements in the physical model.

Adopt a smooth local classical Maxwell–Dirac model on an open region of the
flat spacetime specified by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Let $A_{{\rm SI},a}$
be a supplied real $C^\infty$ electromagnetic covector potential and let
$\psi:\!U\to\mathbb C^4$ be a $C^\infty$ commuting spinor field. The charge
$q_{\rm SI}$ and rest mass $m_{\rm SI}>0$ are model inputs; for the electron
take $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$. Use the component, metric, Clifford, charge,
field-normalization, and unit conventions of
[[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]], [[def-qft-qed-physical-gauge-quantities]],
[[def-qft-framework-units]], and the electromagnetic suppliers of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. In particular,
$D_a=\partial_a-iq_{\rm SI}A_{{\rm SI},a}/\hbar
=\partial_a-iq_{\rm n}a_a$ and $\mu=m_{\rm SI}c/\hbar$.

Adopt the local action density in natural normalization

$$\mathcal L_{\rm nat} =-\frac14 f_{ab}f^{ab} +\frac{i}{2}\bigl(\bar\psi\gamma^aD_a\psi -(D_a\bar\psi)\gamma^a\psi\bigr)-\mu\bar\psi\psi,$$

where $f_{ab}=\partial_a a_b-\partial_ba_a$ on the region where the
potential is supplied, $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$, and
$D_a\bar\psi=\partial_a\bar\psi+iq_{\rm n}a_a\bar\psi$. The physical action
is $S_{\rm cl}=\hbar\int_U\mathcal L_{\rm nat}\,d^4x$ with $x^0=ct$. For
compactly supported local variations this is the adopted classical
Maxwell–Dirac formulation; its Euler–Lagrange consequences are not postulated
as a proof in this item.

For a smooth gauge function $\chi$ in webers, the adopted local
transformation is
$A_{{\rm SI},a}\mapsto A_{{\rm SI},a}+\partial_a\chi$ and
$\psi\mapsto e^{iq_{\rm SI}\chi/\hbar}\psi$. It leaves $F=dA$ invariant and
makes $D_a\psi$ transform by the same phase. This is the covector form of the
SI potential rule in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. Gauge functions in the
local variation argument are compactly supported; no assertion is made about
large gauge transformations, nontrivial bundles, boundary charges, or
asymptotic sectors.

The model adopts the separately specified free Dirac representation of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]] and the positive free photon representation of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]] as the free-field correspondence used to
describe the selected species. This extra correspondence does not quantize
the interacting classical action. In particular, this postulate supplies no
interacting continuum four-dimensional QED Hilbert space, no globally
well-posed coupled PDE, no pointwise operator-valued composite current, no
scattering or LSZ construction, and no regulator-removal or
nonperturbative-existence result.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] for the torus Fourier
construction. Let $L>0$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time
interval, and let the spatial domain be the flat torus
$\mathbb T_L^3=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$, where $L$ is a positive length
in metres. Coordinates use $x^0=ct$ with $t$ in seconds under
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Use the smooth classical branch of
[[post-qft-qed-local-coupling]] with smooth periodic electromagnetic
potentials and spinor. Here $\psi$ has the canonical length dimension
$\mathrm m^{-3/2}$ of [[def-qft-framework-units]], so the scalar-potential
source $\rho_q:=q_{\rm SI}\psi^\dagger\psi$ has unit $\mathrm{C,m^{-3}}$.
On stationary solutions it agrees
with the current density in [[pthm-qft-qed-classical-coupling]]. Use the
gamma-matrix and
$\alpha,\beta$ conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. In Coulomb gauge
$\operatorname{div}\mathbf A=0$, the multiplier equation for any smooth
periodic configuration is
$\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho_q=0$. On the explicitly neutral
branch
$\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q(\mathbf x,t)\,d^3\mathbf x=0$ for every $t\in I$,
the zero-mean scalar potential is the unique smooth periodic solution of
$-\Delta\varphi=\rho_q/\varepsilon_0$. With
$\widehat\rho_q(\mathbf n,t)=L^{-3}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}
\rho_q(\mathbf x,t)e^{-2\pi i\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x/L}\,d^3\mathbf x$ and
$\boldsymbol\kappa_{\mathbf n}=2\pi\mathbf n/L$, the longitudinal energy is

$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}|\nabla\varphi|^2\,d^3\mathbf x =\frac12\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q\varphi\,d^3\mathbf x =\frac{L^3}{2\varepsilon_0} \sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}} \frac{|\widehat\rho_q(\mathbf n,t)|^2}{|\boldsymbol\kappa_{\mathbf n}|^2} \ge0.$$

The corresponding classical Hamiltonian, before imposing the Gauss
constraint, contains

$$H=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\left[ \frac{|\boldsymbol\pi_A|^2}{2\varepsilon_0} +\frac{|\mathbf B|^2}{2\mu_0} +\psi^\dagger\!\left(c\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot (-i\hbar\nabla-q_{\rm SI}\mathbf A)+\beta m_{\rm SI}c^2\right)\!\psi +\varphi(\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A+\rho_q) \right]d^3\mathbf x,$$

with $\pi_\varphi=0$ the primary multiplier momentum. In a separate
truncation to $N\ge1$ orthonormal spatial spinor modes, let $z_j,\bar z_j$
be dimensionless commuting complex-coordinate notation with canonical
brackets $\{z_j,p_k\}=\delta_{jk}$,
$\{\bar z_j,\bar p_k\}=\delta_{jk}$ and all other elementary brackets zero.
For $\hbar>0$, the symmetrized first-order Dirac kinetic term gives the
primary constraints
$C_j=p_j-i\hbar\bar z_j/2$ and
$\bar C_j=\bar p_j+i\hbar z_j/2$ with invertible mixed bracket matrix
$-i\hbar I_N$. This finite-dimensional classical calculation does not
derive fermionic CAR. The neutral torus branch is an explicit hypothesis.
For the selected electron, $q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}\ne0$, so a neutral
single-species commuting-spinor configuration has $\psi=0$; no nontrivial
neutral charged classical Dirac configuration is asserted. The finite-mode
constraint calculation is separate and does not claim to be a solution in
that branch.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For spatial wave vector $\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ put
$\omega(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here
$\omega$ is the temporal wave number, not the SI angular frequency; the
corresponding SI angular frequency is $c\omega$. Energy and momentum are
$E=\hbar c\omega$ in joules and $\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

The natural action is $S/\hbar$. Its canonical density in four dimensions has
unit $\mathrm m^{-4}$; the corresponding physical energy density is
$\hbar c$ times that density and has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
write $\phi_{\rm n}$ for a scalar field with length degree $-1$ and
$\psi_{\rm n}$ for a Dirac field with length degree $-3/2$. These are the

dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous dimensions, when present, are
separate quantities. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized

labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

The Clifford convention is $\gamma^0=\beta$, $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$,

$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$. The phase and Clifford choices are
conventions; this item proves no Dirac representation or field equation.
Time evolution is written $U(t)=\exp(-itH/\hbar)$ when a selected model has
actually constructed a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ and its unitary group; the
corresponding Heisenberg conjugation is $O_H(t)=U(t)^*O\,U(t)$. No such
Hamiltonian or group is constructed here. Where a free-field module uses an
inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the repository's
first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each

$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional

[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction.
Smeared fields are not thereby bounded, symmetric, self-adjoint, or
self-adjointly closable. Locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior are likewise supplied only by the
relevant constructed model modules. Test-function units can be chosen so a
specified smeared observable is dimensionless; there is no universal test
function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

By [A3], $\rho_q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0$ is constant; its
SI density unit is $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$ by [F2] and the stated charge
convention. Thus $Q=q_{\rm SI}\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0L^3<0$ because
$q_{\rm SI}<0$, $\psi_0^\dagger\psi_0>0$, and $L>0$. A smooth periodic
solution of [F1] would satisfy
$\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A=-\rho_q$. Integrate this equality over
the fundamental cube $[0,L]^3$. For each coordinate $i$, the integral of
$\partial_i(\pi_A)_i$ in that coordinate is the value on the face
$x_i=L$ minus the value on $x_i=0$; these are equal by periodicity, so
each face difference is zero. Fubini for the smooth functions on the
compact cube then gives
$\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\operatorname{div}\boldsymbol\pi_A\,d^3\mathbf x=0$.
It follows that $Q=\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\rho_q\,d^3\mathbf x=0$, contradicting
the strict inequality in this step.

Independently, [L1] records the same compatibility requirement for
the Coulomb equation: a smooth periodic potential can exist only for
zero-mean charge density. Thus the contradiction is a consequence of the
specified periodic model and boundary conditions; adding a boundary,
puncture, or compensating source changes the hypotheses and is not
covered.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with the curvature convention and tensors of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Let $\Omega:M\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth and dimensionless, and put $\widetilde g=\Omega^2g$ with the same orientation. Use the metric-selected connection and its tensor derivative of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Define the smooth one-form and its contractions by

$$u:=\Omega^{-1}d\Omega,\qquad H_{ab}:=(\nabla_a u)_b,\qquad \theta:=g^{ab}H_{ab},\qquad s:=g^{ab}u_au_b.$$

Then $H_{ab}=H_{ba}$ and

$$\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-2H_{ab}-g_{ab}\theta+2u_au_b-2g_{ab}s,$$

$$\widetilde S=\Omega^{-2}(S-6\theta-6s),$$

$$\widetilde G_{ab}=G_{ab}-2H_{ab}+2u_au_b+2g_{ab}\theta+g_{ab}s.$$

All curvature conventions are those stated in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. These are mathematical transformation identities, not an assertion that the Einstein equation is conformally invariant.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice. For $\mu\ge0$, define the tempered distribution
$$\Delta_\mu(t,\mathbf x)= \int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3} \frac{\sin(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)t)}{\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)} e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x},$$
with the massless integrand defined off $\mathbf k=0$; its $1/|\mathbf k|$
behavior is locally integrable in three dimensions. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\Delta_\mu \subseteq\{(t,\mathbf x):t^2-|\mathbf x|^2\ge0\},$$
the closed causal cone for the $(-+++)$ metric. For real compactly supported
smooth $f,g$, put
$$\Delta_\mu(f,g)= \int_{\mathbb R^4}\!\int_{\mathbb R^4} f(x)g(y)\Delta_\mu(x-y)\,d^4x\,d^4y.$$
On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the smeared fields of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] satisfy
$$[\Phi_\mu(f),\Phi_\mu(g)]=-i\Delta_\mu(f,g)I.$$
Consequently spacelike-separated supports give commuting fields.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

The test-function topology exists as a Hausdorff locally convex vector topology, induces the prescribed topology on each $\mathcal D_K$, and is the finest locally convex topology making all inclusions $\mathcal D_K\to\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous. A linear map $L:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to E$ to a locally convex space is continuous if and only if each restriction $L|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous. An increasing compact exhaustion whose interiors cover $\Omega$ gives the same topology, independently of the exhaustion. Thus this is an LF topology of the complete metrizable fixed-support spaces. All these claims hold in ZF.

$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.

entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

derivations.claim: Put $u_a=\Omega^{-1}\partial_a\Omega$. Since $\eta_{ab}$ is constant, [F14] gives $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\eta)=0$. Coordinate fields commute, so the curvature definition [F2] gives $R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=0$ for all indices; every curvature component and its Ricci and scalar contractions therefore vanish, in particular $S_\eta=0$. Thus for the base metric $\eta$, $\nabla=\partial$, $\theta=\eta^{ab}\partial_a u_b$, and $s=\eta^{ab}u_au_b$ in [F3]. Applying that conformal formula gives $R_g=-6\Omega^{-2}(\eta^{ab}\partial_a u_b+\eta^{ab}u_au_b)$. Since $\partial_a u_b=\Omega^{-1}\partial_a\partial_b\Omega-\Omega^{-2}(\partial_a\Omega)(\partial_b\Omega)$ and $u_au_b=\Omega^{-2}(\partial_a\Omega)(\partial_b\Omega)$, the gradient-square terms cancel, giving $R_g=-6\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta\Omega$.

Fix compact $K$ and let $f\in\mathcal D_K$. The product rule and boundedness on $K$ of each $x^\alpha\partial^\gamma(\Omega^3)$ give, for each $\alpha,\beta$, $p_{\alpha\beta}(\Omega^3f)\le C_{K,\alpha,\beta}p_{|\beta|}(f)$; multiplication preserves support. Thus $f\mapsto\Omega^3f$ is continuous $\mathcal D_K\to\mathcal S$ by [F11,F12]. For arbitrary $\psi\in\mathcal S$, [F7,F16] identify $K_0\psi$ as the restriction of $\mathcal F_+\psi$ to $p=(|\mathbf k|,\mathbf k)$, where $\mathcal F_+$ is the standard continuous Schwartz Fourier transform followed by a fixed invertible linear change of frequency variables. This pullback is continuous on Schwartz seminorms by the chain rule and fixed linear coordinate bounds. The weight $(1+|p|)^2$ is bounded by a finite sum of coordinate monomials of degree at most two, so $q_2(F):=\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^4}(1+|p|)^2|F(p)|$ is controlled by finitely many Schwartz seminorms from [F11]. Continuity of the Fourier map [F8] therefore gives $q_2(\mathcal F_+\psi)\le C\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in E}p_{\alpha\beta}(\psi)$ for some finite set $E$ and finite $C$. For $r=|\mathbf k|$, the dispersion in [F17] and mass-shell measure in [F20] yield
$$\|K_0\psi\|_{H_0}^2\le\frac{q_2(\mathcal F_+\psi)^2}{2(2\pi)^3}\,4\pi\int_0^\infty r(1+\sqrt2r)^{-4}\,dr<\infty;$$
the radial integrand is $O(r)$ at zero and $O(r^{-3})$ at infinity. This proves continuity $K_0:\mathcal S\to H_0$, so [F13] and the fixed-support multiplier estimates prove continuity $f\mapsto K_0(\Omega^3f)$ from $\mathcal D$ to $H_0$.
For $h\in H_0$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|C_h\|\le\|h\|$. [F9] bounds its tensor extension by the same norm, and by [F19], $P_{s,n+1}$ is the averaging operator $P_+$ of [F10], so it is orthogonal and has norm at most one. The product tensor pairing in [F15] gives $\|h\otimes\Psi_n\|=\|h\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Its sector formulas [F6] therefore imply $\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|\le\sqrt n\|h\|\|\Psi_n\|$ and $\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|\le\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|\|\Psi_n\|$. By [F18], each $\Psi\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has sectors only through some $N$; for either creation or annihilation, different input sectors give orthogonal output sectors. Summing squared sector norms thus bounds each full operator by its largest sector bound, and the triangle inequality between creation and annihilation gives
$$\|\Phi_0(\Omega^3f)\Psi\|\le\bigl(\sqrt N\,\|K_0(\Omega^3\overline f)\|+\sqrt{N+1}\,\|K_0(\Omega^3f)\|\bigr)\|\Psi\|.$$
Both shell-vector terms depend continuously on $f$ (complex conjugation preserves the fixed-support seminorms). For each $\chi,\Psi\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, Cauchy--Schwarz now makes $f\mapsto\langle\chi,\Phi_g(f)\Psi\rangle_2$ continuous; it is complex-linear by [F4] and the second-variable-linear pairing. Hence $\Phi_g$ is the stated weak operator-valued distribution.

For every real compact test $f$, $\Omega^3f$ is real, so [F4] makes $\Phi_g(f)=\Phi_0(\Omega^3f)$ symmetric on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. Each generator preserves $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, so finite products and linear combinations do too; repeated use of symmetry gives $\langle\chi,B\psi\rangle_2=\langle B^*\chi,\psi\rangle_2$ for every polynomial $B$ and $\chi,\psi\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. Define $\omega_g(B):=\langle\varpi_0,B\varpi_0\rangle_2$. Then $\omega_g(B^*B)=\langle B\varpi_0,B\varpi_0\rangle_2=\|B\varpi_0\|^2\ge0$, and $\omega_g(1)=1$.

At every point $g(v,v)=\Omega^2\eta(v,v)$, so the future causal cones for $g$ and $\eta$ coincide and use the direction selected by $\partial_0$. Define causal reachability by piecewise $C^1$ curves whose tangent is future-causal on each smooth piece, allowing constant curves; such a curve is admissible for $g$ exactly when it is admissible for $\eta$. In $(-+++)$ coordinates a future causal tangent satisfies $\dot x^0\ge|\dot{\mathbf x}|$; integrating along each piece and using the triangle inequality gives $|\Delta\mathbf x|\le\Delta x^0$ for a future causal curve. Conversely, if $\Delta x^0\ge|\Delta\mathbf x|$, the straight segment has future causal tangent (including the constant segment when the endpoints agree). Reversing endpoints handles the past direction. Thus two points are causally related exactly when their coordinate difference has nonpositive $\eta$-squared norm, for both $g$ and $\eta$; positive-$\eta$-squared pairs are spacelike for both.

Matrix inversion and $\det(\Omega^2\eta)=-\Omega^8$ give $g^{ab}=\Omega^{-2}\eta^{ab}$ and the density $\Omega^4d^4x$. Thus $\Box_gh=\Omega^{-4}\partial_a(\Omega^2\partial^ah)$, where $\partial^a=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$. For $h=\Omega^{-1}u$, the differentiated numerator is $\partial_a(\Omega\partial^au-u\partial^a\Omega)=\Omega\Box_\eta u-u\Box_\eta\Omega$, because the two cross-gradient terms cancel. Hence $\Box_g(\Omega^{-1}u)=\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta u-\Omega^{-4}u\Box_\eta\Omega$. By step 1.1, $-R_gh/6=+\Omega^{-4}u\Box_\eta\Omega$, so the curvature term cancels the second term and $P_g(\Omega^{-1}u)=\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta u$.

Write $f=f_R+if_I$ and $h=h_R+ih_I$ with real compact tests. Their supports and the supports of $\Omega^3f_R,\Omega^3f_I,\Omega^3h_R,\Omega^3h_I$ lie in the original spacelike-separated support sets by step 1.2; step 1.4 confirms that these pairs are spacelike for $g$ as well as $\eta$. Bilinearity of the commutator and the real-test locality of [F5] on each of the four pairs therefore give $[\Phi_g(f),\Phi_g(h)]=0$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

For $F\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^8;\mathbb C)$ define
$$\mathcal G F(p):=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\!\int_{\mathbb R^4}F(x,y)e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}\,d^4x\,d^4y.$$ 
This is the standard eight-dimensional Fourier transform of $F$ restricted to the fixed injective linear frequency map $p\mapsto((p^0,-\mathbf p),(-p^0,\mathbf p))/(2\pi)$, determined by the phase $p\circ x$; the chain rule and fixed coordinate bounds make this a continuous map $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^8)\to\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$ by [F8]. Let $q_4(G):=\sup_p(1+|p|)^4|G(p)|$. The weight is bounded by finitely many degree-at-most-four coordinate monomials, so [F11] and Fourier continuity give $q_4(\mathcal G F)\le C\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in E}p_{\alpha\beta}(F)$ for some finite set $E$ and constant $C$.
For $p=(|\mathbf k|,\mathbf k)$, $|p|=\sqrt2|\mathbf k|$. Thus [F17,F20] imply
$$\int_{H_0^+}|\mathcal G F(p)|\,d\nu_0(p)\le\frac{q_4(\mathcal G F)}{2(2\pi)^3}\,4\pi\int_0^\infty r(1+\sqrt2r)^{-4}\,dr<\infty;$$
the radial integrand is $O(r)$ at zero and $O(r^{-3})$ at infinity. Define $W_0(F):=\int_{H_0^+}\mathcal G F(p)\,d\nu_0(p)$. On each fixed compact support, every Schwartz seminorm of $F$ in the bound is controlled by a fixed-support derivative seminorm from [F12], since each coordinate weight is bounded there. The bound and the fixed-support criterion [F13] therefore make this a continuous distribution on $\mathbb R^8$. For $F(x,y)=f(x)h(y)$, its pairing is
$$W_0(f,h)=\int_{H_0^+}\overline{K_0\overline f(p)}K_0h(p)\,d\nu_0(p)=\langle K_0\overline f,K_0h\rangle_2,$$
which is the vacuum covariance in [F4].
Since $\Omega$ is smooth and positive, define the curved-volume pairing of $W_g$ on $F$ by $W_g(F):=W_0(\Omega^3(x)\Omega^3(y)F(x,y))$. This is a distribution, and relative to $d\mathrm{vol}_g(x)d\mathrm{vol}_g(y)$ its scalar kernel is $\Omega(x)^{-1}\Omega(y)^{-1}W_0(x,y)$ because $d\mathrm{vol}_g=\Omega^4d^4x$. On product tests it equals $W_0(\Omega^3f,\Omega^3h)$, the covariance of $\Phi_g$ by [F4]; step 1.2 confirms the pulled-back field matrix coefficients are continuous on the same test space.

For compact $f,h$, integrate inside a finite coordinate box containing both supports. Using $\Box_gh=\Omega^{-4}\partial_a(\Omega^2\partial^ah)$ and vanishing boundary terms gives $\int\overline f\,\Box_gh\,d\mathrm{vol}_g=-\int\Omega^2\eta^{ab}(\partial_a\overline f)(\partial_bh)\,d^4x=\int\overline{\Box_gf}\,h\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$. Since $R_g$ is real by step 1.1, the multiplication term $R_g/6$ is symmetric too, so $P_g$ is formally symmetric.

Substituting $u=\Omega f$ in step 2.1 gives $\Omega^3P_gf=\Box_\eta(\Omega f)$, with $\Omega f\in\mathcal D$. For $\psi\in\mathcal D$ and a massless shell point $p=(|\mathbf k|,\mathbf k)$, two integrations by parts in the compact support give
$$K_0(\Box_\eta\psi)(p)=\int\psi(x)(-\partial_0^2+\Delta)e^{i(|\mathbf k|x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x=(\omega_0(\mathbf k)^2-|\mathbf k|^2)K_0\psi(p)=0,$$
and the same holds for $\overline\psi$ because $\Box_\eta$ has real coefficients. The field formula [F4] therefore gives $\Phi_0(\Box_\eta\psi)=a(K_0\Box_\eta\overline\psi)+a^\dagger(K_0\Box_\eta\psi)=0$. Taking $\psi=\Omega f$ proves $\Phi_g(P_gf)=0$. The operator $P_g$ preserves compact smooth tests because its coefficients are smooth.

No convergence of a numerical series is part of this definition. For $d\ge1$, matrices over $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ use the usual finite matrix addition and multiplication.

Use the finite graph phase data of [[def-qft-qed-finite-graph-gauge-data]] and the QED $U(1)$, Clifford, and natural-unit conventions of [[def-qft-qed-gauge-data]]. Let $K_0(\zeta)\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$ be an invertible base matrix and let $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be its finite link-hopping matrix. The admissible covariant families satisfy
$$ K_0(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta K_0(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1},\qquad V(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta V(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}. $$
The scalar base $K_0=mI_d$, $m\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, is an explicit admissible case. Define
$$ K(z;\zeta):=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta),\qquad S(z;\zeta):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-zK_0(\zeta)^{-1}V(\zeta))^nK_0(\zeta)^{-1}. $$

Define the link-hopping matrix $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ by its $x,y$ block indexed by $x,y\in X$

For a smooth scalar component $u:U\to\mathbb R$ or $u:U\to\mathbb C$, define $\partial_a u:=\partial u/\partial x^a$; thus $\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t$ at fixed $\mathbf x$, $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x^j$ for $j=1,2,3$, and each $\partial_a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the transverse space $\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}$ of [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]], with $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$ for $\mathbf k\ne0$ and any assigned value at the null point $\mathbf k=0$. In the QFT length convention, assign $\mathbf k$ units m$^{-1}$ and define the nonnegative measurable multiplier
$$ \omega(\mathbf k):=|\mathbf k|. $$
Its maximal multiplication operator on $\mathcal H_T$ is
$$ (M_\omega f)(\mathbf k):=\omega(\mathbf k)f(\mathbf k),\qquad D(M_\omega):=\{f\in\mathcal H_T:\omega f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3)\}. $$
Because $\omega$ is a scalar multiplier, $\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e. implies $\mathbf k\cdot(M_\omega f)(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e.; thus the displayed multiplication maps its stated domain into $\mathcal H_T$. The value $\omega(0)=0$ is immaterial to the $L^2$ operator. For $\hbar,c>0$, the corresponding one-particle energy convention is $E_1:=\hbar c M_\omega$, in joules.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$

$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$

derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is

for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and

\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\

$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,

[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation

creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the

Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$

of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Since $\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa$ on the support, the radial norm integrals in [F4]–[F6] are finite on these strictly positive finite bounds, so both $f_\epsilon$ and $\omega f_\epsilon$ are square-integrable.

By [F4]–[F6], spherical coordinates give $d^3k=r^2dr\,d\Omega$. Substituting $r=\epsilon u$ in the radial integral and using [F10] gives $\int_\epsilon^\kappa dr/r=\log(\kappa/\epsilon)$, so $\|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\int_\epsilon^\kappa r^{-1}dr=C_b\log(\kappa/\epsilon)$, $\langle f_\epsilon,\omega f_\epsilon\rangle=C_b(\kappa-\epsilon)$, and $\|\omega f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b(\kappa^2-\epsilon^2)/2$.

For any $u,v\in\mathcal H_T$, [F2] gives $\langle u^{\otimes n},v^{\otimes n}\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle^n$ and $\|u^{\otimes n}\|^2=\|u\|^{2n}$. By [F7]–[F8], $\sum_{n\ge0}\|u\|^{2n}/n!=e^{\|u\|^2}<\infty$, so the displayed $\epsilon(u)$ belongs to symmetric Fock space. Its direct-sum pairing with $\epsilon(v)$ is the absolutely convergent series $\sum_{n\ge0}\langle u,v\rangle^n/n!=e^{\langle u,v\rangle}$, by [F7]. The addition and modulus laws [F8]–[F9] therefore give that $C(u)$ has norm one and $|\langle C(u),C(v)\rangle|=e^{-\|u-v\|^2/2}$. This direct tensor calculation requires no separability hypothesis on $\mathcal H_T$. On the full vector space $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, multiplication by $\omega$ commutes with the multiplier $P_T$. Its tensor-power projections therefore commute with the sector multiplier $\sum_j|\mathbf k_j|$; the transverse symmetric Fock space is a reducing subspace for the second-quantized multiplier of [F3]. If $r=\|f_\epsilon\|^2$, $q=\langle f_\epsilon,\omega f_\epsilon\rangle$, and $s=\|\omega f_\epsilon\|^2$, the sector formulas give
$$ \|d\Gamma(\omega)C(f_\epsilon)\|^2 =e^{-r}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n s r^{n-1}+n(n-1)q^2r^{n-2}}{n!} =s+q^2<\infty. $$
The same sector sum with one multiplier gives $\langle C(f_\epsilon),d\Gamma(\omega)C(f_\epsilon)\rangle=q$; [F2] gives $\|C(f_\epsilon)\|=1$. Multiplying by $\hbar c$ and substituting [step 1.2] proves the stated domain and energy claims.

Put $\epsilon_j=\kappa 2^{-j}$ for $j\ge1$. The difference $f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}$ is supported on the shell $(\epsilon_{j+1},\epsilon_j)$, so its squared norm is $C_b\int_{\epsilon_{j+1}}^{\epsilon_j}r^{-1}dr=C_b\log2>0$, using $r=\epsilon_{j+1}u$ and [F10]. $$ |\langle C(f_{\epsilon_j}),C(f_{\epsilon_{j+1}})\rangle| =e^{-\|f_{\epsilon_{j+1}}-f_{\epsilon_j}\|^2/2}=e^{-C_b\log2/2}<1. $$
Thus $\|C(f_{\epsilon_j})-C(f_{\epsilon_{j+1}})\|^2\ge2(1-e^{-C_b\log2/2})>0$, and this sequence is not Cauchy.

Let $\Psi$ have only sectors $0,\ldots,N$. By sectorwise Cauchy–Schwarz [F11],
$$ |\langle\Psi,C(f_\epsilon)\rangle| \le e^{-\|f_\epsilon\|^2/2}\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{\|\Psi_n\|\|f_\epsilon\|^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\longrightarrow0 $$

step 1.2 contains $m$ disjoint dyadic intervals; on each $(a,2a)$,
$\int_a^{2a}dr/r\ge1/2$. Thus $\|f_\epsilon\|^2\ge C_bm/2\to\infty$.

$e^{a^2/2}\ge(a^2/2)^M/M!$. Hence for $0\le n\le N$,
$a^ne^{-a^2/2}\le2^MM!a^{n-2M}\to0$, proving the displayed finite-sum limit. First taking a sufficiently accurate truncation and then the limit just proved gives weak convergence to zero for every Fock vector. A norm limit would have to equal the weak limit zero, contradicting the unit norms.

value $0$.

Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Here
$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.
Coordinates $x$ have length units, momenta have inverse-length units, and the
Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$
Define the measure and one-particle Hilbert space by
$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$
where the omitted massless apex has measure zero. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb
R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$
The Fourier convention is exactly the displayed integral, with no prefactor.
If $\widehat f(\xi^0,\boldsymbol\xi)=
\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]],
then
$$\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p):=\int f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x =\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$
Its inverse is
$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4} \mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)} \,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Let $K(z;\zeta)=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta)$ and $S(z;\zeta)$ be the finite-dimensional formal matrices of [[def-qft-qed-formal-ring]], with $d\ge1$, $K_0(\zeta)$ invertible, and both coefficient matrices covariant under the vertex phase angles of [[def-qft-qed-finite-graph-gauge-data]]. Then $S$ is a two-sided inverse of $K$ in $M_d(\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket)$, and
$$ S(z;\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta S(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1} $$
coefficientwise. For a real vertex tuple $\theta$, put
$\Theta:=\operatorname{diag}_{x\in X}(\theta_xI_r)$,
$\zeta_s:=\zeta^{s\theta}$, and $D_s:=D_{s\theta}=e^{is\Theta}$.
Write $K_s:=K(z;\zeta_s)$ and $S_s:=S(z;\zeta_s)$, and define
$\delta K:=\left.\frac{d}{ds}K_s\right|_{s=0}$ and
$\delta S:=\left.\frac{d}{ds}S_s\right|_{s=0}$ coefficientwise along this
differentiable phase path. The variations satisfy
$$ \delta K=i[\Theta,K],\qquad \delta S=i[\Theta,S]=-S(\delta K)S . $$
For ordinary finite matrices $A,B\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$, the corresponding resolvent identity is $B^{-1}(B-A)A^{-1}=A^{-1}-B^{-1}$. These are formal or finite algebraic statements; they assert no convergence of a perturbation series, continuum limit, or loop Ward identity.

derivations.claim: From the displayed Pauli matrices in [F1], direct multiplication gives $\sigma_j^\dagger=\sigma_j$, $\sigma_j^2=I_2$, and $\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=0$ for $i\ne j$. The block formulas then give $\beta^2=I_4$, $\beta^\dagger=\beta$, $\gamma^{0\dagger}=\gamma^0$, $\gamma^{j\dagger}=-\gamma^j$, and $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=2h^{ab}I_4$. Consequently $\Gamma(p)^2=h(p,p)I_4$ and $\beta\Gamma(p)^\dagger\beta=\Gamma(p)$ for every real $p$.
Multiplying $\Gamma(p)-\mu I_4$ and $\Gamma(p)+\mu I_4$ in either order gives $(h(p,p)-\mu^2)I_4$ by [step 1.1]. Thus $K(p)$ is invertible off shell and its inverse is exactly $S_0(p)$.
Since $\Gamma(p+k)-\Gamma(p)=\Gamma(k)$, the resolvent identity [F3] with $A=K(p)$, $B=K(p+k)$ gives $S_0(p+k)\Gamma(k)S_0(p)=S_0(p)-S_0(p+k)$.

For off-shell $p_0,\ldots,p_N$, put $k_j=p_{j+1}-p_j$. Applying [step 3.1] at each adjacent pair yields $S_0(p_{j+1})\Gamma(k_j)S_0(p_j)=S_0(p_j)-S_0(p_{j+1})$; summing $j=0,\ldots,N-1$ cancels each interior term and leaves $S_0(p_0)-S_0(p_N)$.

If $K(p)u(p)=0$, then taking the adjoint and using $\beta K(p)^\dagger\beta=K(p)$ from [step 1.1] gives $\bar u(p)K(p)=0$. The same calculation applied to $(\Gamma(q)+\mu)v(q)=0$ gives $\bar v(q)(\Gamma(q)+\mu)=0$.

For $k=p-p'$, $\Gamma(k)=\Gamma(p)-\Gamma(p')$; the right equation for $u(p)$ and left equation for $\bar u(p')$ from [step 2.2] therefore give $\bar u(p')\Gamma(k)u(p)=\mu\bar u(p')u(p)-\mu\bar u(p')u(p)=0$. For $k=p+q$, $\Gamma(k)=\Gamma(p)+\Gamma(q)$; the right $u$ equation and left $v$ equation give $\bar v(q)\Gamma(k)u(p)=\mu\bar v(q)u(p)-\mu\bar v(q)u(p)=0$.

$$
M_d:=\bar\psi_1\cdots\bar\psi_d\psi_1\cdots\psi_d
$$
and let $[M_d]P\in R$ denote the coefficient of $M_d$ in $P\in\Lambda_d(R)$. Define the finite Grassmann integral by the $R$-linear functional
$$
\mathcal I_d(P):=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}[M_d]P .
$$
For $K\in M_d(R)$, put $B_K:=\sum_{i,j=1}^d\bar\psi_iK_{ij}\psi_j$. Since every monomial of degree greater than $2d$ vanishes, its exponential is the finite sum
$$
\exp(-B_K):=\sum_{n=0}^{d}\frac{(-B_K)^n}{n!}.
$$
The sign factor in $\mathcal I_d$ is the chosen normalization. Its Gaussian determinant identity, including the value at $K=I_d$, is proved separately.

For a formal indeterminate $z$, let $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ be the commutative ring of sequences $(a_0,a_1,\ldots)$ written $\sum_{n\ge0}a_nz^n$, with coefficientwise addition and Cauchy-product multiplication. No convergence of a numerical series is part of this definition. For $d\ge1$, matrices over $\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket$ use the usual finite matrix addition and multiplication.

Let $K_0(\zeta)\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$ be an invertible base matrix and let $V(\zeta)\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ be its finite link-hopping matrix. The admissible covariant families satisfy
$$ K_0(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta K_0(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1},\qquad V(\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta V(\zeta)D_\theta^{-1}. $$
The scalar base $K_0=mI_d$, $m\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, is an explicit admissible case. Define
$$ K(z;\zeta):=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta),\qquad S(z;\zeta):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-zK_0(\zeta)^{-1}V(\zeta))^nK_0(\zeta)^{-1}. $$

derivations.claim: Put $B_K=\sum_{i,j}\bar\psi_iK_{ij}\psi_j$. Every factor has Grassmann degree two, so a product of more than $d$ such factors has degree greater than $2d$ and vanishes. Hence the exponential is the finite sum $\sum_{n=0}^d(-B_K)^n/n!$, and only its degree-$2d$ term contributes to $[M_d]$.

In $B_K^d/d!$, any term with a repeated row or column index vanishes. The surviving terms are indexed by permutations $\sigma\in S_d$. Reordering $\bar\psi_1\psi_{\sigma(1)}\cdots\bar\psi_d\psi_{\sigma(d)}$ into $M_d$ contributes $(-1)^{d(d-1)/2}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$; the exponential contributes $(-1)^d$. Therefore
$$ [M_d]\exp(-B_K)=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^dK_{i,\sigma(i)} =(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}\det K . $$
Applying the normalization in [F1] proves the Gaussian identity.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the $(-+++)$ coordinate convention, $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, and the Clifford matrices of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]; the shell parameter $\mu>0$ has inverse-length units as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. For $p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in\mathbb R^4$, write
$$
\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j,\qquad
K(p):=\Gamma(p)-\mu I_4.
$$
When $h(p,p)\ne\mu^2$, define the finite rational inverse
$$
S_0(p):=\frac{\Gamma(p)+\mu I_4}{h(p,p)-\mu^2}.
$$
For $p,p+k$ with both denominators nonzero,
$$
S_0(p+k)\Gamma(k)S_0(p)=S_0(p)-S_0(p+k).
$$
For any finite chain of off-shell momenta, the corresponding insertion differences telescope with both endpoint terms retained. If $u(p),u(p')$ satisfy $(\Gamma(p)-\mu)u(p)=0$, $(\Gamma(p')-\mu)u(p')=0$ and $p,p'$ lie on the future shell, then $\bar u(p')\Gamma(p-p')u(p)=0$, where $\bar u=u^\dagger\beta$. If $v(q)$ satisfies $(\Gamma(q)+\mu)v(q)=0$ on the future shell, then $\bar v(q)\Gamma(p+q)u(p)=0$. These are finite rational/tree identities; no Feynman boundary value, singular distribution product, loop theorem, or all-diagram gauge-independence claim is included.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

citations.quote:
Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

derivations.claim: Since [A1] gives $|e|=1$ and $|n|=1$, $|P_T(n)e|^2=e^\top(I_3-nn^\top)e=1-(n\cdot e)^2$. Rotational invariance in [F2] permits taking $e=(0,0,1)$. Use the chart $X(u,\phi)=(\sqrt{1-u^2}\cos\phi,\sqrt{1-u^2}\sin\phi,u)$ for $-1<u<1$ and $0<\phi<2\pi$. Its tangent vectors are orthogonal with squared lengths $(1-u^2)^{-1}$ and $1-u^2$, so [F3] gives area density $1$. The omitted azimuthal seam is a coordinate line in sphere graph charts, and each pole is a singleton in its graph chart; these parameter sets are null by [F4], and their chart integrals vanish. Thus with $u=n_3$ the angular integral is $2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)\,du$.
The integral equals $2\pi[u-u^3/3]_{-1}^{1}=8\pi/3$. Multiplying by $\lambda^2$ yields $C_b=8\pi\lambda^2/3>0$, which is the coefficient required by [F1].

boundaries.evidence: λ=0 is excluded by A1, and step 2.1 proves C_b>0.
The integrand vanishes at n=±e but is positive on a positive-measure belt by step 1.1.
