Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the bounded linear operators on $H$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); for $M\in\mathcal B(H)$, $M^*$ is its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

A **finite bounded Kraus instrument datum** on $H$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, integers $q_a\ge0$ for $a=1,\ldots,m$, and bounded operators $M_{a,r}\in\mathcal B(H)$ for $r=1,\ldots,q_a$. It is **normalized** when

$$\sum_{a=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H.$$

Empty inner sums are zero. For each outcome $a$, define its outcome operator and operation by

$$E_a:=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad \mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*\quad(X\in\mathcal B(H)).$$

These formulas take values in $\mathcal B(H)$: each composition is bounded since $\|M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*x\|\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|X\|\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\,\|x\|$, and the sums are finite. This definition specifies only the displayed finite Kraus form; it is not a representation theorem for arbitrary instruments and does not assert that an apparatus realizes these data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$
be a trace-class operator on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $E$ be a
Hilbert basis of $H$, **supplied as data**
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]];
existence of such a basis is not asserted here). The **trace of $T$ relative to
$E$** is
$$\operatorname{tr}_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle,$$
the sum of the scalar family $(\langle Te,e\rangle)_{e\in E}$ in the
finite-subset-net sense of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

**The family is absolutely summable, uniformly in $E$.** Let
$T=\sum_js_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ be the singular-value series
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]],
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]) with
$(e_j)_{j\in J}$, $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ orthonormal and $\sum_js_j=\|T\|_1<+\infty$
([[def-trace-class-operator]]). For every $e\in H$ the series
$\langle Te,e\rangle=\sum_{j}s_j\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle$
converges absolutely, because the moduli are bounded by
$s_1\sum_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le s_1\|e\|^2$ by
Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[lem-finite-bessel-inequality]]). Consequently, for every finite
$F\subseteq E$, using the interchange of finite sums with the nonnegative
finite-subset supremum over $j$ and then finite Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel twice,
$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

derivations.claim: For each $a,r$, $M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ is self-adjoint because $\langle M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}x,y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}x,M_{a,r}y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}y\rangle$, and its quadratic form is $\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\ge0$. Hence $E_a\ge0$. Normalization gives $I_H-E_a=\sum_{b\ne a}\sum_rM_{b,r}^*M_{b,r}\ge0$, including empty sums, so $E_a$ is an effect.

By [F7], each $M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*$ is trace class, so the finite sum $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is trace class. For all $x,y\in H$, $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,y\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle M_{a,r}^*x,\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle=\langle x,M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*y\rangle$ because $\rho=\rho^*$ and $M_{a,r}^*$ is the Hilbert adjoint. Also $\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,x\rangle=\langle\rho M_{a,r}^*x,M_{a,r}^*x\rangle\ge0$. Finite summation shows $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is self-adjoint and positive.

By [F1], write $\rho=\sum_jw_jT_{u_j,u_j}$ in trace norm. For its partial sums $\rho_N=\sum_{j\le N}w_jT_{u_j,u_j}$, [F7] gives $\|M_{a,r}(\rho-\rho_N)M_{a,r}^*\|_1\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|\rho-\rho_N\|_1\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\to0$. Thus [F4] gives $\mathcal J_a(\rho)=\sum_{r,j}w_jT_{M_{a,r}u_j,M_{a,r}u_j}$ in trace norm; the trace-norm sum is finite since $\sum_jw_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\le\|M_{a,r}\|^2\sum_jw_j=\|M_{a,r}\|^2$ for each $r$. Trace continuity [F5] and [F3] yield $p_a=\sum_{r,j}w_j\|M_{a,r}u_j\|^2\ge0$. Cyclicity [F2] gives $p_a=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$.

Because the outcome and Kraus index sets are finite, [F1] and step 2.1 give $\sum_ap_a=\sum_jw_j\langle(\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jw_j\|u_j\|^2=1$ by normalization. Since every $p_a\ge0$, this also gives $p_a\le1$ for every $a$.

If $p_a>0$, step 1.2 gives a positive trace-class numerator $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ and step 2.1 gives its trace $p_a$, so $\rho_a=\mathcal J_a(\rho)/p_a$ is positive trace class with trace one, hence a density operator by [F1]. The finite sum $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is likewise positive trace class, and its trace is $\sum_ap_a=1$ by step 3.1, so it is a density operator. If $p_a=0$, division by $p_a$ is undefined and no normalized update is asserted.

For a unit vector $\psi$, [F3] gives that $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class with trace $\|\psi\|^2=1$, hence a density operator by [F1]. Also [F4] gives $M_{a,r}T_{\psi,\psi}M_{a,r}^*=T_{M_{a,r}\psi,M_{a,r}\psi}$. Taking traces and summing over the finite Kraus list yields $p_a=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$, as claimed.

derivations.claim: Each $n!$ is a finite complex number, so the sequence $(n!)_{n\ge0}$ defines an element $S(g)=\sum_{n\ge0}n!g^n$ of $\mathbb C\llbracket g\rrbracket$ by [A1], irrespective of numerical convergence.

Fix any $g\ne0$ and put $t_n=n!g^n$. Then $|t_{n+1}|/|t_n|=(n+1)|g|$, which is greater than $2$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $|t_n|$ eventually grows by a factor greater than $2$ at every step, so $t_n$ does not tend to zero.

If the numerical series $\sum_nt_n$ converged, its partial sums $s_N:=\sum_{n=0}^Nt_n$ would converge, so $t_n=s_n-s_{n-1}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$; step 1.2 rules this out for every nonzero $g$. At $g=0$, the convention $g^0=1$ leaves only the constant term, so the series equals $1$. Thus the series converges at no nonzero $g$. For every $r>0$, the point $g=r/2$ lies in $|g|<r$ and gives divergence, so no positive $r$ satisfies the defining property of the radius; $r=0$ satisfies it vacuously. Therefore $R=0$ and the claimed positive radius fails.

citations.quote:
An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: Antisymmetry gives $\eta(U,f_0)=\alpha U^aF_{ab}U^b=0$. On the unit shell, $U_a\Pi_U{}^a{}_b=U_b+(\eta(U,U)/c^2)U_b=0$, so $\eta(U,a_{\rm LL})=0$. The coordinate right-hand side $(U,a_{\rm LL}(x,U))$ is $C^1$ on the open state domain $O\times V$: $F$ is $C^2$, its partials [F3] are $C^1$, and the remaining factors are polynomial in $U$, using [F4]. In a closed coordinate box around any state, its continuous first derivatives are bounded by [F6]; applying [F7] componentwise along line segments proves the field locally Lipschitz. Thus [F5] gives a unique local full-state solution through $(x_0,U_0)$.

For arbitrary $U$, antisymmetry gives $\eta(U,f_0)=0$ and the projector formula gives $\eta(U,\Pi_U B)=(1+\eta(U,U)/c^2)\eta(U,B)$. Along the full solution put $h(\tau)=\eta(U,U)+c^2$; then
$$h'(\tau)=2\eta(U,a_{\rm LL})=\frac{2\tau_e}{c^2}\eta(U,B)h(\tau).$$
The coefficient is continuous. The zero function solves this scalar linear IVP with $h(0)=0$, and the scalar vector field is locally Lipschitz in $h$ because it is linear in that variable, so uniqueness [F5] gives $h=0$ on the full common interval. Thus the proper-time normalization $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ is preserved.

In the inertial frame of [F2], $e_0$ has coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$. For any future timelike $W$, convexity of $C^+$ makes $(1-s)e_0+sW$ timelike for $0\le s\le1$. A timelike vector cannot have zeroth component zero, since then its squared norm would be the nonnegative spatial norm square. If $W^0\le0$, the continuous zeroth component along this segment takes the value zero by [F8], a contradiction. Thus every future timelike vector has $W^0>0$. Along the solution, the preserved shell makes $U$ timelike; if $U^0$ became nonpositive, [F8] on the closed interval between that time and $0$ would force a zero component, again impossible. Since the initial vector is future, $U$ remains in $C^+$ throughout the local interval. No continuation beyond this interval is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The statement quantifies over initial data; if O has no admissible point, the local assertion is vacuous.
Step 1.1 uses no division by alpha or tau_e, so alpha=0 or tau_e=0 is covered.

boundaries.reason: No singleton family or one-index boundary occurs in this local IVP statement.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 handles every shell point because c>0 makes G(u)>0 and the graph remains regular.
Step 1.2 constructs a solution on an open interval about the initial proper-time value; no endpoint extension is claimed.
Steps 1.1–2.1 use a fixed datum and a local ODE; no choice principle is invoked.

citations.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space of dimension four with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and fix an inertial chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=ct$, $c>0$. Let $O\subseteq A$ be open and let $F$ be a $C^2$ alternating covariant two-tensor on $O$. In this chart write $F^a{}_b:=\eta^{ac}F_{cb}$ and let $\partial_b$ denote the coordinate partial derivative. Fix constants $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau_e\geq0$. For every $U\in V$, define

$$\Pi_U{}^a{}_b:=\delta^a_b+\frac{U^aU_b}{c^2},\qquad f_0^a(x,U):=\alpha F^a{}_b(x)U^b,$$

$$B^a(x,U):=\alpha(\partial_bF^a{}_c)(x)U^bU^c +\alpha^2F^a{}_b(x)F^b{}_c(x)U^c, \qquad a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U):=f_0^a(x,U)+\tau_e\Pi_U{}^a{}_bB^b(x,U).$$

For the physical interpretation, $x^a$ are in metres, $\tau$ is in seconds, $c$ is in metres per second, $U$ is in metres per second, $\alpha=q/m$, and $\tau_e$ is a time. Here a **proper-time parameter** means that the parameter is measured in seconds and the four-velocity is normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$; define the future unit shell by $\mathcal S^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. For each initial datum $(x_0,U_0)\in O\times V$ with $U_0\in\mathcal S^+$, the system

$$\frac{dx^a}{d\tau}=U^a,\qquad \frac{dU^a}{d\tau}=a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U),\qquad (x(0),U(0))=(x_0,U_0)$$

has a unique local solution on an open proper-time interval about $0$. Along that interval $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ remains future directed. This is a local ODE statement: it makes no claim of global existence for arbitrary $F$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $|f|$, $f^{2}$ and $fg$ are integrable on $[a,b]$
   ([[def-abs-value]], [[def-integer-power]]);
2. $\max(f,g)$ and $\min(f,g)$, defined pointwise
   ([[def-max-min]]), are integrable on $[a,b]$;
3. the **triangle inequality for the integral**:
   $$\Bigl|\int_a^b f\Bigr| \;\le\; \int_a^b |f| .$$

**Claim 3 is stated with $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** For $u > v$
the right-hand side is $-\int_v^u |f| \le 0$ while the left-hand side is $\ge 0$,
so the inequality as written is false there. The form valid for *every* pair
$u,v$ on which $f$ is integrable ([[def-oriented-integral]]) is

$$\Bigl|\int_u^v f\Bigr| \;\le\; \Bigl|\int_u^v |f|\,\Bigr| ,$$

and that is the form the estimates below on this page use whenever the limits
are not known to be in increasing order.

**The converse of claim 1 fails.** Integrability of $|f|$ does not give
integrability of $f$; the witness is on the companion page.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

derivations.claim: Differentiating $\eta(U_\varepsilon,U_\varepsilon)=-c^2$ gives $\eta(U_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)=0$. Differentiating this identity once more gives $\eta(U_\varepsilon,\dot a_\varepsilon)=-\eta(a_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)$. By [F1], $\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}\dot a_\varepsilon=\dot a_\varepsilon+U_\varepsilon\eta(U_\varepsilon,\dot a_\varepsilon)/c^2=\dot a_\varepsilon-\eta(a_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)U_\varepsilon/c^2$. Therefore [A1] is exactly $a_\varepsilon=f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}\dot a_\varepsilon$.

The product and chain rules [F2], with $\dot x=U$ and $\dot U=a$, give $$\dot f_{0,\varepsilon}^a=\alpha_\varepsilon(\partial_bF^a{}_c)U^bU^c+\alpha_\varepsilon F^a{}_b a_\varepsilon^b, \qquad B_\varepsilon^a=\alpha_\varepsilon(\partial_bF^a{}_c)U^bU^c+\alpha_\varepsilon F^a{}_b f_{0,\varepsilon}^b.$$ Subtracting the equalities and using $\delta_\varepsilon=a_\varepsilon-f_{0,\varepsilon}$ gives $\dot f_{0,\varepsilon}-B_\varepsilon=\alpha_\varepsilon F\delta_\varepsilon$.

Subtract $f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon$ from the reformulated LAD equation in step 1.1. Since $\dot a-B=\dot\delta+(\dot f_0-B)$, step 2.1 yields $$a_\varepsilon-(f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon) =\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}(\dot\delta_\varepsilon+\alpha_\varepsilon F\delta_\varepsilon).$$ Taking Euclidean norms and applying the assumed bounds gives at each $\tau\in I$ $$\left\|a_\varepsilon-(f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon)\right\| \leq\varepsilon P(C_1\varepsilon+A M C_0\varepsilon) =P(C_1+AM C_0)\varepsilon^2.$$ The constants do not depend on $\varepsilon$ or $\tau$, so the estimate is uniform on $I$.

Use the Euclidean phase-space and compact-region conventions of [F8] for the comparison data [A3]. Put $\delta:=C\tau_e^2$ and $r(t):=\|z_1(t)-z_2(t)\|_1$. For each coordinate component $j$, set $h_j(t):=(z_1-z_2)_j(t)-\int_0^t[X_{\tau_e}(z_1(s))-\widetilde X_{\tau_e}(z_2(s))]_j\,ds$. The integrand is continuous because it equals $\dot z_{1,j}-\dot z_{2,j}$ by the pointwise ODEs. By [F3], $h_j$ is continuous on $[0,T]$, differentiable in its interior, and has derivative zero there. Equality of the initial data gives $h_j(0)=0$. The mean value theorem [F6] on $[0,t]$ therefore gives $h_j(t)=0$ for each $0<t\le T$, while this also holds at $t=0$. Consequently $$(z_1-z_2)(t)=\int_0^t\bigl(X_{\tau_e}(z_1(s))-\widetilde X_{\tau_e}(z_2(s))\bigr)\,ds.$$ Apply the scalar integral bound of [F4] to each component and add the finitely many inequalities using linearity; then split the integrand as $X_{\tau_e}(z_1)-X_{\tau_e}(z_2)+X_{\tau_e}(z_2)-\widetilde X_{\tau_e}(z_2)$. The field assumptions and [F9] give $$r(t)\leq\int_0^t\|X_{\tau_e}(z_1(s))-\widetilde X_{\tau_e}(z_2(s))\|_1\,ds\leq L\int_0^t r(s)\,ds+\delta t.$$

citations.quote:
Use the charged/spinning body-model conventions of the now-authored batch-24 carrier [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]: a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-+++)$, coordinates $x^0=ct$ in metres, $c>0$, and a $C^2$ future timelike representative curve $z:I\to M$ parametrized by proper time $\tau$ in seconds, with $U=dz/d\tau$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. The actual supplier defines these quantities and the SI electromagnetic-tensor convention used here. Assume Countable Choice for the GR smooth-structure, convex-normal and parallel-transport suppliers used below.

**(a) Flat isolated-body moments.** In an inertial chart of affine Minkowski space, let $T^{ab}$ be a smooth symmetric stress-energy tensor with components in $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and spatially compact support on every finite time slab. At a fixed time $t$, define
$$p^a(t):=\frac1c\int_{\mathbb R^3}T^{0a}(ct,\mathbf x)\,d^3x,$$
and, for a representative point $z(t)$ on that time slice, define
$$S_z^{ab}(t):=\frac1c\int_{\mathbb R^3}\left((x-z(t))^aT^{0b}(ct,\mathbf x)-(x-z(t))^bT^{0a}(ct,\mathbf x)\right)d^3x.$$
Here $(x-z(t))^0=0$ on the chosen slice, $p$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, and $S_z$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$. These are definitions of moments; no conservation is asserted by clause (a).

**(b) Local curved-body moments.** Let $z\in M$ and let $U_0$ be a convex normal neighborhood containing $z$. Let $\Sigma\subset U_0$ be a spacelike $C^1$ hypersurface through $z$, with future unit normal $n_x$ and induced volume element $d\Sigma$. Let a smooth symmetric stress-energy tensor $T^{ab}$ have support on $\Sigma$ compactly contained in $U_0$, with all displayed integrals finite. For each support point $x\in\Sigma$, let $v(x):=\exp_z^{-1}(x)\in T_zM$ be the unique joining position vector supplied by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]] and [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $H_{x\to z}:T_xM\to T_zM$ be parallel transport along that unique geodesic, with existence, uniqueness and metric preservation as in [[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]]. Define $T^\sharp(n_x)^a:=T^{ab}(x)(n_x)_b$ and
$$p_z:=\frac1c\int_\Sigma H_{x\to z}\!\left(-T^\sharp(n_x)\right)d\Sigma,\qquad S_z:=\frac1c\int_\Sigma v(x)\wedge H_{x\to z}\!\left(-T^\sharp(n_x)\right)d\Sigma,$$
where $(v\wedge w)^{ab}:=v^aw^b-v^bw^a$ and the finite-dimensional vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise in any basis of $T_zM$. The resulting $p_z$ and $S_z$ are a vector and an antisymmetric tensor at $z$; their units are $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$.

Restrict [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]] to its flat affine Minkowski branch, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, proper time $\tau$ in seconds, future four-velocity $U=dx/d\tau$ satisfying $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, constant primitive $m>0$ in kilograms and nonzero charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in coulombs. Let the prescribed external electromagnetic two-form $F$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of the worldline; use the component convention $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. Let $a:=dU/d\tau$ and

$$\alpha:=q/m,\qquad \tau_e:=\frac{q^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0mc^3}>0,\qquad f_0^a:=\alpha F^a{}_bU^b,$$

where $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ follows [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Adopt the flat LAD effective equation

$$a^a=f_0^a+\tau_e\left(\frac{da^a}{d\tau}-\frac{\eta_{bc}a^ba^c}{c^2}U^a\right).$$

The derivative is the ordinary derivative in an inertial affine chart. Its dimensions are consistent: $a$ and $f_0$ are accelerations, the parenthesized term has acceleration per second, and $\tau_e$ is a time. This is an adopted effective model equation for sufficiently regular curves (at least $C^3$); it is not asserted to be an exact law of nature, a point-source Maxwell construction, or a globally well-posed dynamics. In particular, no existence, uniqueness, stability, or empirical claim is part of this postulate.

Use of the equation as a reduced physical approximation carries the source qualification that radiation reaction be small relative to the applied Lorentz force in the particle's instantaneous rest frame (the inertial frame momentarily comoving with $U$). This postulate neither asserts that condition for arbitrary $F$ nor supplies a numerical threshold; the qualification is not used to deduce the local ODE results or the force-free counterexample.

derivations.claim: The flat moments and local curved moments in [F1] are definitions for smooth finite-body stress-energy data; the supplier explicitly says no slice-independence theorem or equation of motion is asserted. Thus these moment definitions alone do not specify a point-particle limit or a value of the self-field on the representative worldline.

The LAD equation in [F2] is adopted for a prescribed external field and makes no source construction. Together with the restricted literature results [L1], this establishes the scope of this remark: those specific shrinking-body results do not convert the adopted postulate into an unrestricted fixed-charge point construction or arbitrary-duration global accuracy theorem. The historical source claims remain reports with their own hypotheses, not proofs supplied by this item.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$

with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums
and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and
for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]])

$$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$

In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$:

$$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$

the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for
every partition $P$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

derivations.claim: Define $I(t):=\int_t^\infty e^{(t-s)/\tau_e}F_{\rm ext}(s)\,ds$, interpreting the integral as a finite Riemann integral after any upper truncation beyond $\max\{t,T\}$; compact support makes the value independent of that truncation. For $t<T$, write $I(t)=e^{t/\tau_e}\int_t^T e^{-s/\tau_e}F_{\rm ext}(s)\,ds$. By [F1] the integrand is integrable on this compact interval, and [F2] together with the fundamental theorem gives $$I'(t)=-F_{\rm ext}(t)+\frac{1}{\tau_e}I(t)\qquad (t<T).$$ For $a=I/(m\tau_e)$ this identity becomes $\tau_e a'= -F_{\rm ext}/m+a$, which rearranges to the displayed Abraham–Lorentz equation. For $t>T$, both $I$ and $F_{\rm ext}$ vanish, so the same equation holds. At $t=T$, smoothness and support imply $F_{\rm ext}(T)=0$, and the one-sided derivatives agree with the displayed identity.

For $t\geq T$, the integration interval contains no point where $F_{\rm ext}$ is nonzero, so $a(t)=0$. For $t<0$, continuity and nonnegativity of the nonzero pulse give a closed subinterval of $(0,T)$ on which $F_{\rm ext}\geq d>0$. The exponential factor is positive and continuous there by [F2, F4]; its minimum is positive by [F5]. The integral over that subinterval is strictly positive by the lower bound [F3], and all remaining contributions are nonnegative. Thus $a(t)>0$. Since $a(t)=0$ for $t\geq T$, it satisfies the future boundary condition.

If $a_1,a_2$ are two solutions, their difference $d=a_1-a_2$ satisfies $d'=d/\tau_e$. The product rule gives $(e^{-t/\tau_e}d(t))'=0$, so [F6] implies this product is a constant $C$. By [F4], $d(t)=Ce^{t/\tau_e}$; if $C\ne0$, then [F7] makes $|d(t)|\to\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$, contradicting $d(t)\to0$. Hence $C=0$ and $d=0$, proving uniqueness. Together with step 2.1, the unique future-decaying solution is strictly positive for all $t<0$: this pre-acceleration is a property of the stated model equation, not an empirical claim.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.
