Restrict [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]] to its flat affine Minkowski branch, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, proper time $\tau$ in seconds, future four-velocity $U=dx/d\tau$ satisfying $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, constant primitive $m>0$ in kilograms and nonzero charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in coulombs. Let the prescribed external electromagnetic two-form $F$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of the worldline; use the component convention $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. Let $a:=dU/d\tau$ and

$$\alpha:=q/m,\qquad \tau_e:=\frac{q^2}{6\pi\epsilon_0mc^3}>0,\qquad f_0^a:=\alpha F^a{}_bU^b,$$

where $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ follows [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Adopt the flat LAD effective equation

$$a^a=f_0^a+\tau_e\left(\frac{da^a}{d\tau}-\frac{\eta_{bc}a^ba^c}{c^2}U^a\right).$$

The derivative is the ordinary derivative in an inertial affine chart. Its dimensions are consistent: $a$ and $f_0$ are accelerations, the parenthesized term has acceleration per second, and $\tau_e$ is a time. This is an adopted effective model equation for sufficiently regular curves (at least $C^3$); it is not asserted to be an exact law of nature, a point-source Maxwell construction, or a globally well-posed dynamics. In particular, no existence, uniqueness, stability, or empirical claim is part of this postulate.

Use of the equation as a reduced physical approximation carries the source qualification that radiation reaction be small relative to the applied Lorentz force in the particle's instantaneous rest frame (the inertial frame momentarily comoving with $U$). This postulate neither asserts that condition for arbitrary $F$ nor supplies a numerical threshold; the qualification is not used to deduce the local ODE results or the force-free counterexample.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space of dimension four with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and fix an inertial chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=ct$, $c>0$. Let $O\subseteq A$ be open and let $F$ be a $C^2$ alternating covariant two-tensor on $O$. In this chart write $F^a{}_b:=\eta^{ac}F_{cb}$ and let $\partial_b$ denote the coordinate partial derivative. Fix constants $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau_e\geq0$. For every $U\in V$, define

$$\Pi_U{}^a{}_b:=\delta^a_b+\frac{U^aU_b}{c^2},\qquad f_0^a(x,U):=\alpha F^a{}_b(x)U^b,$$

$$B^a(x,U):=\alpha(\partial_bF^a{}_c)(x)U^bU^c +\alpha^2F^a{}_b(x)F^b{}_c(x)U^c, \qquad a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U):=f_0^a(x,U)+\tau_e\Pi_U{}^a{}_bB^b(x,U).$$

For the physical interpretation, $x^a$ are in metres, $\tau$ is in seconds, $c$ is in metres per second, $U$ is in metres per second, $\alpha=q/m$, and $\tau_e$ is a time. Here a **proper-time parameter** means that the parameter is measured in seconds and the four-velocity is normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$; define the future unit shell by $\mathcal S^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. For each initial datum $(x_0,U_0)\in O\times V$ with $U_0\in\mathcal S^+$, the system

$$\frac{dx^a}{d\tau}=U^a,\qquad \frac{dU^a}{d\tau}=a_{\rm LL}^a(x,U),\qquad (x(0),U(0))=(x_0,U_0)$$

has a unique local solution on an open proper-time interval about $0$. Along that interval $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ remains future directed. This is a local ODE statement: it makes no claim of global existence for arbitrary $F$.

derivations.claim: The integral defining $x$ is well-defined on every compact $\tau$ interval because $U$ is smooth by [F2]. The fundamental theorem [F2] gives $\dot x=U$. By [F1], $\eta(U,U)=c^2(-\cosh^2\theta+\sinh^2\theta)=-c^2$. Also $U^0=c\cosh\theta>0$, so $U$ is future directed in the chosen inertial chart. Thus $\tau$ is proper time and $x$ is future timelike.

Differentiating with [F1, F2] gives $$a=c\theta'(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0),\qquad \dot a=c\theta''(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)+c(\theta')^2(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0), \qquad \eta(a,a)=c^2(\theta')^2.$$ Consequently $\dot a-\eta(a,a)U/c^2=c\theta''(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$, and the force-free equation [F3] is equivalent to $\theta'=\tau_e\theta''$. The chosen $\theta$ has $\theta'=Ae^{(\tau-\tau_0)/\tau_e}$ and $\theta''=\theta'/\tau_e$, so the equation holds identically. This proves that the curve solves the adopted LAD equation for every real proper time.

The invariant $\eta(a,a)=c^2(\theta')^2$ gives $\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}=c|A|e^{(\tau-\tau_0)/\tau_e}$, which is unbounded toward the future. These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. In the common natural-unit field convention, $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, a scalar field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and a Dirac field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation set $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$, with $A_a$ in tesla-metres and gauge function $\chi$ in webers. With charge $q$ in coulombs define
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical scalar shell conventions of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and the second-variable-linear Hilbert pairing of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. In the fixed inertial coordinates $x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] on the affine Minkowski model [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; these coordinates have length units under [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and momentum coordinate $\mathbf k$ have inverse-length units, and $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same units. The parameter is not identified here with a physical rest mass. Matrix $h_D$ has inverse-length units; the dimensionless spin matrices have no physical unit assignment in this mathematical item.

Use the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. On $\mathbb C^4=\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C^2$, define
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_j=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_j\\\sigma_j&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \gamma^0=\beta,\qquad \gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j.$$
For a spinor column $z\in\mathbb C^4$, its Dirac adjoint is $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$. The Clifford contraction is $\Gamma(p):=\gamma^0p^0-\sum_{j=1}^3\gamma^jp_j$; this contraction uses the effective matrix $-\eta$ in the relation $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$.

Let $\mathcal H_D$ be the space of measurable functions $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^4$, modulo equality almost everywhere, with
$$\|u\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(\mathbf k)^\dagger u(\mathbf k)\,\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}<\infty,$$
and pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u(\mathbf k)^\dagger v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3$. Define the measurable matrix $h_D(\mathbf k)=\sum_j\alpha_j k_j+\beta\mu$ and its maximal multiplication operator with domain $D(h_D)=\{u\in\mathcal H_D:h_Du\in\mathcal H_D\}$. For $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix fields
$$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=\frac12\left(I_4\pm\frac{h_D(\mathbf k)}{\omega(\mathbf k)}\right).$$
When $\mu=0$ at $\mathbf k=0$, set $P_+(0)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,0)$ and $P_-(0)=\operatorname{diag}(0,I_2)$. These are complementary rank-two orthogonal projections; the value at this Lebesgue-null point does not change their multiplication operators. Write $M_{P_\pm}$ for their maximal multiplication operators and $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}M_{P_\pm}$. The companion matrix lemma on this page proves these are bounded orthogonal projections with closed ranges. The conjugate Hilbert space $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ has vectors $\bar u$, scalar multiplication $z\bar u=\overline{\bar z u}$, and pairing $\langle\bar u,\bar v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$.

Use the sine and cosine definitions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. For a length-coordinate increment $t\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega(\mathbf k)>0$, define the matrix multiplier
$$W_D(t,\mathbf k)=\cos(\omega t)I_4+i\frac{\sin(\omega t)}{\omega}h_D(\mathbf k).$$
At the massless apex set $W_D(t,0)=I_4$. Its unitarity, group law and generator identity are proved by the companion matrix lemma on this page.

The symbols $P_+$ and $P_-$ designate the positive- and negative-energy matrix formulas for this fixed free Dirac operator. This is purely mathematical data; no physical spin-statistics postulate or empirical assertion is included.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication of the displayed Pauli matrices gives $\sigma_j^2=I_2$, $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3$, $\sigma_2\sigma_3=i\sigma_1$, $\sigma_3\sigma_1=i\sigma_2$, and the reversed products have the opposite signs. Hence $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I_2+i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$. Block multiplication then gives $\alpha_i^\dagger=\alpha_i$, $\beta^\dagger=\beta$, $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I_4+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$, and $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$. The explicit blocks have trace zero, so $\operatorname{Tr}\gamma^a=0$, and $\operatorname{Tr}I_4=4$. The Clifford relation is $\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=2h^{ab}I_4$. Cyclicity of trace follows by expanding matrix entries; averaging $\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b)$ with its cyclic rearrangement gives $4h^{ab}$. For the four-factor trace, anticommute $\gamma^a$ successively past $\gamma^b,\gamma^c,\gamma^d$; cyclicity makes the final four-factor term the negative of the original, yielding $4(h^{ab}h^{cd}-h^{ac}h^{bd}+h^{ad}h^{bc})$. Finally $\gamma_5^2=I_4$ and $\gamma_5\gamma^a=-\gamma^a\gamma_5$ by the same Clifford relations, so cyclicity gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c)=-\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c)$, hence the three-factor trace is zero.

The relations in 1.1 give $H_\pm^\dagger=H_\pm$ and $H_\pm^2=(|\mathbf p|^2+M^2)I_4=E^2I_4$: the mixed term cancels by $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$. Therefore $P_\pm^\dagger=P_\pm$ and $P_\pm^2=P_\pm$. Since $\operatorname{Tr}\alpha_i=\operatorname{Tr}\beta=0$, $\operatorname{Tr}H_\pm=0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}P_\pm=2$. A Hermitian projection has eigenvalues only $0$ and $1$, so its rank equals its trace and each range has dimension two. A basis can be selected for this fixed finite-dimensional range by Gaussian elimination and orthonormalized by Gram–Schmidt.

The chosen bases give $\sum_s u_su_s^\dagger=2EP_+=EI_4+H_+$ and $\sum_s v_sv_s^\dagger=2EP_-=EI_4+H_-$. Multiplying on the right by $\beta$ yields $EI_4\beta+H_+\beta=E\beta-\beta\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p+MI_4=\not p+M$ and $EI_4\beta+H_-\beta=E\beta-\beta\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p-MI_4=\not p-M$, using $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$ and $\gamma^j=\beta\alpha_j$.

Since $H_+u_s=Eu_s$, multiplication by $\beta$ gives $(\not p-M)u_s=0$; since $H_-v_s=Ev_s$, it gives $(\not p+M)v_s=0$. Also $\gamma^0(\gamma^a)^\dagger\gamma^0=\gamma^a$: for $a=0$ this is $\beta^3=\beta$, and for spatial $a$ it follows from $(\gamma^a)^\dagger=-\gamma^a$ and anticommutation with $\beta$. Thus $(\bar x\gamma^a y)^*=\bar y\gamma^a x$ for all columns $x,y$.

For future energy four-vectors $p_1,p_2$ with nonnegative rest energies $\mathsf M_{1,\mathrm{in}},\mathsf M_{2,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, define the invariant flux when its radicand is nonnegative by

Let $\mathcal S_{\rm in}$ and $\mathcal S_{\rm out}$ be finite nonempty initial and final label sets, respectively, and let $w_i\geq0$ for $i\in\mathcal S_{\rm in}$ satisfy $\sum_iw_i=1$. $$\Gamma_{\mathrm{coeff}}=\frac{1}{2\hbar\mathsf M_0 S_f} \int_{S^2}|\mathcal G(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Phi_2.$$

derivations.claim: Let $a=(a_0,\mathbf a)$ be any future unit vector, so $a_0>0$ and $a_0^2-|\mathbf a|^2=1$. If $\mathbf a=0$, put $B=I$. Otherwise put $r=|\mathbf a|$, $\mathbf n=\mathbf a/r$, and define $B$ to act by $\begin{pmatrix}a_0&r\\r&a_0\end{pmatrix}$ on $\operatorname{span}(e_0,\mathbf n)$ and by the identity on its spatial orthogonal complement. In both cases $B$ preserves $h$, has determinant one, preserves the future cone, and sends $e_0$ to $a$. For any proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda$, apply this construction to $a=\Lambda e_0$; then $B^{-1}\Lambda$ fixes $e_0$ and restricts to a proper spatial rotation on $e_0^\perp$. Thus every such $\Lambda$ is a boost followed by a spatial rotation. The construction also gives, for every future unit vector $a$, an inverse boost taking $a$ to $e_0$.

A spatial rotation has Jacobian one and leaves $E$ fixed. By step 1.1, it remains to check a boost directed along the first spatial axis. For that boost, $p'_1=a_0p_1+rE$ and $E'=a_0E+rp_1$, so $\partial p'_1/\partial p_1=a_0+rp_1/E=E'/E>0$; the other spatial coordinates are unchanged. The inverse boost is obtained by replacing $r$ with $-r$, so this spatial map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. By [F3], $d^3\mathbf p'=(E'/E)d^3\mathbf p$ in every nonnegative Borel integral, and therefore $d^3\mathbf p'/(2E')=d^3\mathbf p/(2E)$. This proves shell-measure invariance under the boost and, using the rotation factorization, under every proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map.

Apply the boost construction in step 1.1 to the future unit vector $P/\sqrt{s}$; its inverse takes $P/\sqrt{s}$ to $e_0$. Step 2.1 preserves each shell measure, and $|\det\Lambda|=1$ preserves the four-dimensional delta under this change of frame. Thus it suffices to evaluate at $P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$. Integrating the spatial delta first sets $\mathbf k_2=-\mathbf k_1$ and gives the remaining radial measure
$$\frac{1}{4(2\pi)^2E_1(r)E_2(r)}r^2\,dr\,d\Omega\,\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r)).$$
Here $d^3\mathbf k_1=r^2dr\,d\Omega$ by [F4].

For $r>0$, $E_1(r)+E_2(r)$ is strictly increasing, with derivative $r(1/E_1+1/E_2)>0$. The threshold assumption gives a unique root $k_*>0$. At this root, $E_1+E_2=\sqrt{s}$ and $E_1-E_2=(\mathsf M_1^2-\mathsf M_2^2)/\sqrt{s}$, so $E_1=(s+\mathsf M_1^2-\mathsf M_2^2)/(2\sqrt{s})$, $E_2=(s-\mathsf M_1^2+\mathsf M_2^2)/(2\sqrt{s})$, and
$$k_*^2=E_1^2-\mathsf M_1^2=\frac{[s-(\mathsf M_1+\mathsf M_2)^2][s-(\mathsf M_1-\mathsf M_2)^2]}{4s}.$$
The derivative at the root is $k_*\sqrt{s}/(E_1E_2)$. Applying [F3] to the one-dimensional increasing change of variable evaluates the energy delta in step 3.1, giving $d\Phi_2=k_*d\Omega/(16\pi^2\sqrt{s})$. By [F4], $\int_{S^2}d\Omega=2\pi\int_{-1}^1du=4\pi$, hence $\int d\Phi_2=k_*/(4\pi\sqrt{s})$. In the incoming center-of-momentum frame from step 3.1, write $p_1=(E_1,\mathbf p_*)$ and $p_2=(E_2,-\mathbf p_*)$, so $E_1+E_2=\sqrt{s}$. The mass-shell equations give $p_1\cdot p_2=E_1E_2+p_*^2$ and $\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}^2=E_i^2-p_*^2$. Direct expansion yields
$$(p_1\cdot p_2)^2-\mathsf M_{1,\mathrm{in}}^2\mathsf M_{2,\mathrm{in}}^2=(E_1E_2+p_*^2)^2-(E_1^2-p_*^2)(E_2^2-p_*^2)=p_*^2(E_1+E_2)^2=sp_*^2,$$
so [F2] gives $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. If the incoming rest energies are equal to $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}$, then $E_1=E_2=\sqrt{s}/2$ and $p_*^2=s/4-\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$; since $p_*>0$, $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. Combining the phase-space density from step 4.1 with [F2]'s coefficient map yields

These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. In the common natural-unit field convention, $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, a scalar field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and a Dirac field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation set $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$, with $A_a$ in tesla-metres and gauge function $\chi$ in webers. With charge $q$ in coulombs define
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Use the finite Dirac matrices and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], and the separate geometric metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and algebraic contraction $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ of [[def-qft-example-data]]. Write $p=(E,\mathbf p)$ for an energy four-vector with components in joules, $M\geq0$ for a rest-energy parameter in joules, and $E=\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2+M^2}>0$. In the natural-length variables of the Dirac definition, $\mathbf k=\mathbf p/(\hbar c)$, $\mu=M/(\hbar c)$, and $\omega=E/(\hbar c)$.

Let $\beta=\gamma^0$, $\alpha_j=\beta\gamma^j$, $\Sigma_j=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_j,\sigma_j)$, and $\gamma_5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$. Define $H_\pm=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf p\pm\beta M$ and $P_\pm=(I_4+H_\pm/E)/2$. Each $P_\pm$ is a Hermitian rank-two projection. Choose orthonormal bases $\xi_{\pm,1},\xi_{\pm,2}$ of their ranges and put $u_s=\sqrt{2E}\xi_{+,s}$ and $v_s=\sqrt{2E}\xi_{-,s}$ for $s=1,2$. With $\bar z=z^\dagger\beta$ and $\not p=\gamma^0E-\sum_j\gamma^jp_j$, the following hold:

$$\operatorname{Tr}I_4=4,\quad \operatorname{Tr}\gamma^a=0,\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b)=4h^{ab},\quad \operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c)=0,$$

$$\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c\gamma^d) =4(h^{ab}h^{cd}-h^{ac}h^{bd}+h^{ad}h^{bc}), \qquad \sum_s u_s\bar u_s=\not p+M,\quad \sum_s v_s\bar v_s=\not p-M.$$

The columns satisfy $(\not p-M)u_s=0$ and $(\not p+M)v_s=0$. For all $x,y\in\mathbb C^4$, complex conjugation of a Dirac current is $\overline{\bar x\gamma^a y}=\bar y\gamma^a x$. The Countable Choice hypothesis written in the current draft [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] is retained as a supplier assumption; this finite-dimensional proof makes no additional choice use.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], and use [[def-qft-example-data]] and [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. Write
$$\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3:E=\sqrt{|\mathbf q|^2+\mathsf M^2}\}$$
for the positive shell in that Definition, and $C_+=\{(E,\mathbf q)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:E\geq|\mathbf q|\}$ for the closed future cone of $h=(+,-,-,-)$. A proper orthochronous linear $h$-Lorentz map is a real linear $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda^Th\Lambda=h$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda(C_+)=C_+$. For energy four-vectors on these positive shells, the shell measure $d^3\mathbf p/((2\pi)^3\,2E)$ is invariant under every such map. Let $\mathsf M_1,\mathsf M_2\geq0$, let $P$ be future timelike, meaning $P^0>0$ and $h(P,P)>0$, set $s=h(P,P)>(\mathsf M_1+\mathsf M_2)^2$, and write $E_i(r)=\sqrt{r^2+\mathsf M_i^2}$. Let $f$ be a nonnegative Borel function on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_1}\times\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_2}$. For a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda_P$ with $\Lambda_P P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$, define the finite Borel measure $\Phi_{2,P}$ as the pushforward of $\frac{k_*}{16\pi^2\sqrt{s}}d\Omega$ under
$$\mathbf n\longmapsto\left(\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_1^*,k_*\mathbf n),\Lambda_P^{-1}(E_2^*,-k_*\mathbf n)\right),$$
where $E_i^*$ and $k_*$ are from [[def-qft-example-two-body-phase-space-data]]. The proof below shows that $\Phi_{2,P}$ is independent of the choice of $\Lambda_P$; for $P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$ it is exactly the center-of-momentum measure $d\Phi_2$ in that Definition. The standard two-body on-shell integral
$$(2\pi)^4\int d\nu_{\mathsf M_1}(k_1)d\nu_{\mathsf M_2}(k_2)\, \delta^{(4)}(P-k_1-k_2)\,f(k_1,k_2)$$
is interpreted by first evaluating the spatial delta in $k_2$, then the one-dimensional energy delta by the increasing radial change of variable $r\mapsto E_1(r)+E_2(r)$. Explicitly, for each fixed angular direction and nonnegative Borel radial function $g:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$, the radial action after spatial evaluation is $\int_0^\infty g(r)\delta(\sqrt{s}-E_1(r)-E_2(r))\,dr=g(k_*)/(d(E_1+E_2)/dr|_{k_*})$; this is the pushforward evaluation under that $C^1$ diffeomorphism, not a product of distributions. It equals $\int f\,d\Phi_{2,P}$. The threshold root is $k_*$ in that Definition, and
$$\int d\Phi_{2,P}=\int d\Phi_2=\frac{k_*}{4\pi\sqrt{s}}.$$
For equal rest energies $\mathsf M_1=\mathsf M_2=\mathsf M$, set $\beta=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/s}$; then $k_*=\sqrt{s}\beta/2$ and $\int d\Phi_{2,P}=\int d\Phi_2=\beta/(8\pi)$. For the scattering flux identities, take incoming $p_i=(E_i,\mathbf p_i)\in\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}}$, where $\mathsf M_{i,\mathrm{in}}\geq0$, and require $p_1+p_2=P$. A center-of-momentum map is a proper orthochronous $h$-Lorentz map $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda P=(\sqrt{s},\mathbf0)$; write $\Lambda p_1=(E_1^*,\mathbf p_1^*)$ and define $p_*=|\mathbf p_1^*|$. The value is independent of the choice of $\Lambda$, since two such maps differ by a spatial rotation. Their invariant flux is $F=4p_*\sqrt{s}$. For equal incoming rest energies $\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}\geq0$ with $s\geq4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2$, define $\beta_{\mathrm{in}}=\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M_{\mathrm{in}}^2/s}$; then $p_*=\sqrt{s}\beta_{\mathrm{in}}/2$ and $F=2s\beta_{\mathrm{in}}$. For finite nonempty incoming and outgoing label sets, normalized initial weights, and the Borel amplitude family of the Definition, whenever $F>0$ the cross-section coefficient map gives
$$\frac{d\sigma_{\mathrm{coeff}}}{d\Omega} =\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{64\pi^2s}\, \frac{k_*}{p_*}\, \frac{\overline{|\mathcal A|^2}}{S_f}.$$
For a parent at rest, represented by $P_0=(\mathsf M_0,\mathbf0)$ with $\mathsf M_0>2\mathsf M$, and two equal-rest-energy daughters on $\mathcal H^+_{\mathsf M}$ with total four-vector $P_0$ and constant amplitude $G_E$ in joules, the rate coefficient is $|G_E|^2\sqrt{1-4\mathsf M^2/\mathsf M_0^2}/(32\pi\hbar\mathsf M_0)$ when the daughters are identical. This is a coefficient calculation, not a claim of exponential survival.

Let $K(z;\zeta)=K_0(\zeta)+zV(\zeta)$ and $S(z;\zeta)$ be the finite-dimensional formal matrices of [[def-qft-qed-formal-ring]], with $d\ge1$, $K_0(\zeta)$ invertible, and both coefficient matrices covariant under the vertex phase angles of [[def-qft-qed-finite-graph-gauge-data]]. Then $S$ is a two-sided inverse of $K$ in $M_d(\mathbb C\llbracket z\rrbracket)$, and
$$ S(z;\zeta^\theta)=D_\theta S(z;\zeta)D_\theta^{-1} $$
coefficientwise. For a real vertex tuple $\theta$, put
$\Theta:=\operatorname{diag}_{x\in X}(\theta_xI_r)$,
$\zeta_s:=\zeta^{s\theta}$, and $D_s:=D_{s\theta}=e^{is\Theta}$.
Write $K_s:=K(z;\zeta_s)$ and $S_s:=S(z;\zeta_s)$, and define
$\delta K:=\left.\frac{d}{ds}K_s\right|_{s=0}$ and
$\delta S:=\left.\frac{d}{ds}S_s\right|_{s=0}$ coefficientwise along this
differentiable phase path. The variations satisfy
$$ \delta K=i[\Theta,K],\qquad \delta S=i[\Theta,S]=-S(\delta K)S . $$
For ordinary finite matrices $A,B\in GL_d(\mathbb C)$, the corresponding resolvent identity is $B^{-1}(B-A)A^{-1}=A^{-1}-B^{-1}$. These are formal or finite algebraic statements; they assert no convergence of a perturbation series, continuum limit, or loop Ward identity.

derivations.claim:
By [F2], the spin sums reduce the squared-current factors to
$$L_e^{ab}=\frac14\operatorname{Tr}[(\not p_2-m)\gamma^a(\not p_1+m)\gamma^b], \qquad L_{\mu,ab}=\operatorname{Tr}[(\not k_1+M)\gamma_a(\not k_2-M)\gamma_b].$$
The odd traces vanish. Expanding the even terms with [F2] and using $p_1\cdot p_2+m^2=s/2$ and $k_1\cdot k_2+M^2=s/2$ gives
$$L_e^{ab}=p_2^ap_1^b+p_2^bp_1^a-\frac{s}{2}h^{ab}, \qquad L_{\mu,ab}=4(k_{1a}k_{2b}+k_{1b}k_{2a}-\frac{s}{2}h_{ab}).$$
These mass-shell dot products follow from $(p_1+p_2)^2=(k_1+k_2)^2=s$.

Contracting the tensors gives
$$L_e^{ab}L_{\mu,ab} =4\{2[(p_2\cdot k_1)(p_1\cdot k_2)+(p_2\cdot k_2)(p_1\cdot k_1)] +s^2-s(p_1\cdot p_2+k_1\cdot k_2)\}.$$
The two cross-metric terms contribute $-s(p_1\cdot p_2+k_1\cdot k_2)$, while the metric-metric term contributes $s^2$; substituting $p_1\cdot p_2=(s-2m^2)/2$ and $k_1\cdot k_2=(s-2M^2)/2$ reduces the last two terms to $s(m^2+M^2)$.

The finite matrix hypothesis [L1] supplies coefficientwise inverse and phase-covariance identities only for its specified finite graph kernel. For the separate amplitude in [A1], the spinor equations from [F2] give $ ar v(p_2)
ot p_2=-m ar v(p_2)$ and $
ot p_1u(p_1)=mu(p_1)$, so their sum contracted with the incoming current is zero. Likewise $ ar u(k_1)
ot k_1=M ar u(k_1)$ and $
ot k_2v(k_2)=-Mv(k_2)$, so the outgoing current is transverse to $P=k_1+k_2$. A longitudinal propagator term is therefore multiplied by two zero contractions. No broader tree-current claim is taken from [L1].

In the center-of-momentum frame take $|\mathbf p_1|=\sqrt{s}\beta_e/2$, $|\mathbf k_1|=\sqrt{s}\beta_\mu/2$, and let $\theta$ be the angle between them. The four cross-dot-products in step 2.1 are $s/4\pm|\mathbf p_1||\mathbf k_1|\cos\theta$, with each sign occurring twice. Substitution into step 2.1 and multiplication by $g^4/s^2$ gives $\overline{|\mathcal M|^2}=g^4[3-\beta_e^2-\beta_\mu^2+\beta_e^2\beta_\mu^2\cos^2\theta]$. The resulting function of $\theta$ is continuous and therefore Borel; the spin-label sums are finite by [F2]. The strict threshold gives positive $\beta_e,\beta_\mu$, and [F3] gives incoming flux $F=2s\beta_e>0$.

For distinguishable final particles, [F3] gives $d\Phi_2/d\Omega=\beta_\mu/(32\pi^2)$ and $F=2s\beta_e$. Substituting the squared amplitude from step 3.1 into [F3] yields the displayed differential coefficient after using $g^4=(4\pi\alpha)^2$. Integrating uses $\int_{S^2}d\Omega=4\pi$ and $\int_{S^2}\cos^2\theta\,d\Omega=4\pi/3$, giving the displayed total coefficient.

For $\delta=4m^2/s\leq1/2$, set $B_0=2-\beta_\mu^2+\beta_\mu^2\cos^2\theta$ and $Q=1-\beta_\mu^2\cos^2\theta$. Then $B_0\geq1$, $0\leq Q\leq1$, and the ratio of the full coefficient to its $m=0$ value is $R=(B_0+\delta Q)/(B_0\sqrt{1-\delta})\geq1$. Also
$$R-1=\frac1{\sqrt{1-\delta}}-1+ \frac{\delta Q}{B_0\sqrt{1-\delta}} \leq2\sqrt2\,\delta\leq4\delta,$$
because $1/\sqrt{1-\delta}-1\leq\sqrt2\,\delta$ and $B_0\sqrt{1-\delta}\geq1/\sqrt2$. This compares only the two formal tree coefficients.

derivations.claim:
For an integer $M\ge2$, integration by parts in $\mathbf x$ gives
$$(1+|\mathbf k|^2)^M\widehat\phi_t(\mathbf k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta_{\mathbf x})^M\phi(t,\cdot)}(\mathbf k).$$
Every boundary term vanishes because $\phi$ is Schwartz. For any fixed $L>3$, Schwartz seminorms bound
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|(1-\Delta_{\mathbf x})^M\phi(t,\mathbf x)|\,d^3\mathbf x\le C_M(\phi)(1+|t|)^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\mathbf x|)^{-L}d^3\mathbf x,$$
so $|\widehat\phi_t(-\mathbf k)|\le C'_M(\phi)(1+|t|)^{-2}(1+|\mathbf k|^2)^{-M}$. The $t$ bound is integrable. In radial $\mathbf k$ coordinates the shell weight is at most a constant times $r\,dr$ because $\omega_\mu(r)\ge r$; hence its product with $(1+r^2)^{-M}$ is integrable at infinity and at $r=0$, including $\mu=0$. Thus the defining integral converges absolutely and is bounded by a finite Schwartz seminorm, proving that $H_\mu$ is tempered.

For each $\omega>0$, let $g_\omega(t)=e^{-i\omega|t|}/(2\omega)$. It is continuous at $0$, with $g_\omega'(0+)=-i/2$ and $g_\omega'(0-)=+i/2$. For a compactly supported smooth test $\eta(t)$, integrating by parts separately on $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$ cancels the boundary terms involving $\eta'(0)$ and leaves the derivative jump times $\eta(0)$; since $g_\omega''=-\omega^2g_\omega$ off $0$, this proves
$$g_\omega''+\omega^2g_\omega=-i\delta_0$$
as a one-dimensional distribution.

By [F4, F5] and Fubini's theorem [F7], the positive-frequency two-point kernel is
$$W_\mu(t,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)}e^{-i\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)t+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}$$
as a distribution. This is the slice of $H_\mu$ for $t>0$. For $t<0$, replacing $\mathbf k$ by $-\mathbf k$ identifies its slice with $W_\mu(-t,-\mathbf x);$ the same substitution proves $H_\mu(t,\mathbf x)=H_\mu(-t,-\mathbf x)$. For real tests, the vacuum expectation of the field commutator is $W_\mu(f,g)-W_\mu(g,f)$; [F6] identifies it with a distribution supported in the causal cone. Thus the two Wightman orderings agree on spacelike-separated supports. For a compactly supported smooth spatial test supported away from $\mathbf x=0$, both slice pairings are continuous in $t$ by [F9] and the integrable bound in 1.1, so no additional term supported at $t=0$ occurs away from the coincidence point. The partial Fourier formula itself specifies the extension at coincidence.

The spatial Fourier multiplier of $\Box-\mu^2$ is $-\partial_t^2-|\mathbf k|^2-\mu^2=-(\partial_t^2+\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)^2)$. Applying it to the kernel in 2.1 and using 1.2 gives $i\delta_0(t)$ times $(2\pi)^{-3}\int e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d^3\mathbf k$. Fourier inversion [F8] identifies the latter as $\delta_0(\mathbf x)$. For $\mu=0$ the excluded apex has measure zero and the shell weight is locally integrable there, as established in 1.1; it contributes no additional distribution. Therefore $(\Box-\mu^2)H_\mu=i\delta_0$ in four dimensions.

below.

Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$
When $\mu=0$, its apex is omitted; thus $\mathbf k\ne0$ in the massless
parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

derivations.claim:
For the scalar action, differentiating its density at $\phi+\varepsilon h$ gives
$$\delta S_\phi=-\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\,\partial_b h+\mu^2\phi h\right)d^4x.$$
For each coordinate, the product $\partial_a\phi\,h$ has compact support; one-dimensional integration by parts on that coordinate has zero boundary term, and Fubini [F4] permits integrating the remaining coordinates. Hence
$$\delta S_\phi=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\phi-\mu^2\phi\right)d^4x=\int_{\mathbb R^4}h(\Box-\mu^2)\phi\,d^4x.$$

Put $R_D=(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi$. From [F1], $\beta^\dagger=\beta$ and $\beta^2=I_4$. Each $\sigma_j$ is Hermitian, so $\alpha_j^\dagger=\alpha_j$; the off-diagonal blocks give $\alpha_j\beta=-\beta\alpha_j$. Hence $\gamma^0=\beta$ is Hermitian and $(\gamma^j)^\dagger=(\beta\alpha_j)^\dagger=\alpha_j\beta=-\beta\alpha_j=-\gamma^j$, so $(\gamma^a)^\dagger\beta=\beta\gamma^a$ for every $a$. Varying $\psi$ and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger\beta$ together along a real parameter gives
$$\delta S_D=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\chi R_D+\bar\psi(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\chi\,d^4x.$$
Integrating the second term by parts coordinatewise, with zero boundary terms since $\chi$ is compactly supported, yields
$$\delta S_D=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\chi R_D+\left(-i\partial_a\bar\psi\,\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi\right)\chi\,d^4x=2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R^4}\chi^\dagger\beta R_D\,d^4x,$$
because $R_D^\dagger\beta=-i\partial_a\bar\psi\,\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi$.

If $(\Box-\mu^2)\phi=0$, step 1.1 makes every variation vanish. Conversely, if the smooth residual $R_\phi=(\Box-\mu^2)\phi$ is nonzero at a point, continuity gives a ball on which it has one strict sign; choosing the nonnegative bump from [F3] inside that ball gives $\int hR_\phi\ne0$. Thus scalar stationarity for all compactly supported real $h$ is equivalent to the Klein–Gordon equation.

If $R_D=0$, step 1.2 gives stationarity. Conversely, if $R_D(x_0)\ne0$, continuity gives a ball on which $|R_D|>0$. Choose a nonnegative bump $\rho$ supported there and positive on a smaller ball [F3], and take the admissible variation $\chi=\rho\,\beta R_D$. Then
$$\delta S_D=2\int_{\mathbb R^4}\rho\,|R_D|^2\,d^4x>0,$$
contradicting stationarity. Thus $R_D=0$ pointwise. Its adjoint is $-i\partial_a\bar\psi\,\gamma^a-\mu\bar\psi=0$, and conversely that adjoint equation implies $R_D=0$ since $\beta$ is invertible.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 construct a compactly supported variation contradicting stationarity whenever the residual is nonzero.

Applying [F5] with one-particle multiplier vector $(1,\omega_\mu,-k_1,-k_2,-k_3)$ gives the self-adjoint scalar operators $N_s,H_s,P_{s,j}$. On sector $n$, their multipliers are $n$, $\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)$, and $-\sum_{r=1}^n k_{r,j}$. Squaring these multipliers and integrating against the completed product measure yields exactly the stated domains.

The Dirac data in [F6] satisfy the measurable, finite-multiplier hypotheses of [F7], and [F16] supplies the complementary orthogonal projections and closed ranges required by that carrier. The one-particle measure is sigma-finite: each of the two species copies of R^3 is the countable union of bounded balls with finite Lebesgue measure. Let Y_m be the two species copies restricted to the ball of radius m; each Y_m has finite measure. For fixed n, the product sets Y_m^n have finite product measure and cover X^n as m grows. Their countable union over n and m is a sigma-finite cover of the Fock direct-sum measure. The particle and antiparticle sector multipliers are therefore self-adjoint on the maximal domains in [F7], which are the displayed square-integrability conditions for $H_D$ and each $P_{D,j}$. The field boundedness and equal-time CAR are exactly the inspected interfaces in [F8].

For real $f$, [F3] identifies the scalar field on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ with $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)$. The Hilbert space $H_\mu$ is separable by [F13], so the hypothesis of the Segal-domain result [F4] holds. Multiplication by the nonzero scalar $\sqrt2$ does not change an operator domain; hence the closure is self-adjoint on the domain in [F4] with $h=K_\mu f$. If $K_\mu f=0$, both operators are zero on all Fock space.

For a normalized $\Psi\in D(A)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $|\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle|\le\|A\Psi\|<\infty$. Since $A$ is self-adjoint, this expectation is real. The vector $A\Psi-\langle A\rangle_\Psi\Psi$ belongs to the Hilbert space because both terms do, so its norm and the stated variance are finite without requiring $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. By [F14], a product $AB$ acts only on vectors $\Psi\in D(B)$ for which $B\Psi\in D(A)$; it is not defined merely because both $A$ and $B$ separately exist on a common dense core.

Choose $b_d$ from [F18] for $d=3,4$. Put
$Z_d=\int b_d(x)\,d^dx$ and $\rho_d=Z_d^{-1}b_d$.
The integral is finite because $0\le b_d\le1$ and its support lies in a
bounded ball, and it is positive because $b_d=1$ on a ball of positive
volume. Every derivative of $b_d$ is continuous with compact support, so
all its coordinate-weighted derivatives are bounded. Thus $\rho_d$ is
Schwartz, nonnegative, nonzero, and has integral one. In particular
$0<\|\rho_d\|_2<\infty$. Define
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)=\int e^{-i\xi\cdot x}\rho_d(x)\,d^dx$.
The integral triangle inequality gives $|\widehat\rho_d(\xi)|\le\int\rho_d=1$;
dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\rho_d$, gives
$\widehat\rho_d(\xi)\to1$ as $\xi\to0$.
Set $\rho=\rho_4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)=\varepsilon^{-4}\rho_4((x-x_0)/\varepsilon)$. For every Schwartz test $\phi$, change of variables and dominated convergence [F10], with majorant $\|\phi\|_\infty\rho_4(y)$, give $\int\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(x)\phi(x)\,d^4x\to\phi(x_0)$, so this is a point-mass approximation. For $p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in H_\mu^+$ the same change of variables gives
$$K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)=e^{ip\circ x_0}\widehat\rho_4\bigl(\varepsilon(-p^0,\mathbf p)\bigr).$$
Thus $K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)\to e^{ip\circ x_0}$ for every fixed shell momentum and $|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon,x_0}(p)|\le1$. The shell measure has infinite total mass: in radial coordinates, for $r\ge\max(1,\mu)$, $\omega_\mu(r)\le\sqrt2\,r$, so its radial density is bounded below by a positive constant times $r\,dr$, whose integral diverges. Fatou's lemma [F11] therefore gives $\liminf_{\varepsilon_m\downarrow0}\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|^2\ge\int_{H_\mu^+}1\,d\nu_\mu=\infty$. By [F1, F3] and the creation formula on the vacuum, $\|\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0})\Omega\|=\|K_\mu\rho_{\varepsilon_m,x_0}\|$, so these vacuum vectors have no finite-norm point-field limit.

The scalar one-particle space contains a unit vector $e$, for example a normalized indicator of an annulus $1<|\mathbf k|<2$, whose shell measure is finite and positive by [F2]. The symmetric vectors $e^{\otimes n}$ are unit vectors in mutually orthogonal sectors. Put $C=(\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-4})^{-1/2}$ and $\Psi_n=Cn^{-2}e^{\otimes n}$. By [F15], $\sum n^{-4}$ converges and is positive, so $C$ is well-defined and $\Psi$ is normalized. Its image under one more application of $N_s$ would have squared norm $C^2\sum_{n\ge1}1=\infty$, so $N_s\Psi\notin D(N_s)$. By the composition-domain rule [F14] with $A=B=N_s$, $\Psi\notin D(N_s^2)$. Fix a unit spinor $z\in\mathbb C^4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $u_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\rho_3((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/\varepsilon)z$. For $A_\varepsilon=\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)$, [F8] gives $A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon=\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2I$. By [F17], the creation and annihilation terms are bounded, hence so is their sum. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $\sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle A_\varepsilon x,y\rangle|\le\|A_\varepsilon\|$, while choosing $y=A_\varepsilon x/\|A_\varepsilon x\|$ for each unit $x$ with $A_\varepsilon x\ne0$ gives equality after taking the supremum over $x$. On $t<0$, $g_\omega(t)=e^{i\omega t}/(2\omega)$ and $g_\omega'(t)=+\tfrac i2e^{i\omega t}$, so $g_\omega'(0-)=+i/2$. citations.quote:
Fix a working system $s$ of constitution $c$ and a closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints as in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. A cycle of the working system is such a record with $x_P^-=x_P^+$; the reservoirs and work store need not return to their initial energy states.

An ideal thermal reservoir $b$ has an energy interval $J_b\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in joules and a finite entropy function $S_b:J_b\to\mathbb R$ measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. On the energy interval admitted for a cycle, assume the exact affine law
$
S_b(E_b)=s_{b,0}+\frac{E_b}{T_b}
$
for a constant $s_{b,0}$ and fixed $T_b>0$ kelvins. Thus $S_b'(E_b)=1/T_b$ in the interior and every admitted endpoint change is exactly $\Delta S_b=\Delta E_b/T_b$. This constant is the absolute thermodynamic temperature under [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. The affine entropy law on the admitted interval is the ideal-bath model; a finite reservoir whose temperature changes is outside this definition.

An ideal work store is a named auxiliary with an energy coordinate $E_w$ measured in joules and an assigned entropy $S_w(E_w)=s_w$ constant on the energy interval used by the cycle. It exchanges only mechanical work and no matter or heat. Its energy may change, while its entropy change is zero by this model definition.

A two-reservoir cycle contains one working-system cycle, one hot bath at $T_h$, one cold bath at $T_c$, and the ideal work store. They lie inside one isolated outer boundary in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]], so the full compound has no external matter or energy transfer. There are no unlisted heat, work, matter, kinetic-energy, or external-potential-energy changes. The admitted process and transfer signs are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The model declares the endpoint entropy split
$
S_{\mathrm{tot}}=S_{\mathrm{ws}}(x_{\mathrm{ws}})+S_h(E_h)+S_{\mathrm{cold}}(E_c)+S_w(E_w),
$
where $S_{\mathrm{ws}}$ is the working-system entropy and the bath and work-store functions are those defined here. This additive constituent split is assumed to be one admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] and is the entropy supplied to [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]; $S_w$ contributes zero change. Reversibility of the full record is as in [[def-td-reversible-process]].

When the second law is applied to the cycle, the model also supplies an admitted closed process record for the full compound. At both endpoints its constituent preparations, with the declared contact controls locked or insulated, are an equilibrium macrostate for that record; its separately tracked center-of-mass kinetic and external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change. This total-compound record is the input to the second law; the working-system record $P$ is the input to its first-law balance.

In the heat-engine mode, the positive magnitudes $Q_h,Q_c$ in joules mean respectively heat taken from the hot bath into the working system and heat rejected by the working system to the cold bath; accordingly $\Delta E_h=-Q_h$, $\Delta E_c=Q_c$, $Q[P]=Q_h-Q_c$, and work output is $W_{\mathrm{out}}=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$. The work store gains exactly this transferred work, so $\Delta E_w=W_{\mathrm{out}}$. In the refrigerator mode, $Q_c>0$ is heat taken from the cold bath into the working system, $Q_h>0$ is heat rejected to the hot bath, so $\Delta E_c=-Q_c$, $\Delta E_h=Q_h$, $Q[P]=Q_c-Q_h$, and work input is $W_{\mathrm{in}}=W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$. The store supplies that work, so $\Delta E_w=-W_{\mathrm{in}}$. These are idealized model conventions, not claims that a particular apparatus realizes the cycle.

For every admitted $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-,x_P^+\in D_c$, fixed material constitution, zero change in center-of-mass kinetic energy, and zero change in separately tracked external-field potential energy in the fixed chart selected by the process model, the adopted model balance is
$$U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P],$$
where $U_c$ is the dimensioned energy-coordinate map of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]].

Here the internal-energy coordinate is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame as in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], while $Q[P]$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ are the protocol transfers defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], in joules as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The sign convention is positive $Q$ into the system and positive $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ for work done on it. If $P$ is adiabatic, its defining condition is $Q[P]=0$, so the same adopted balance gives $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=U_c(x_P^+)-U_c(x_P^-)$.

This equation is an adopted physical postulate of the stated framework. It is not deduced here from a mechanical model or from experimental observations. Records with matter exchange or nonzero changes in omitted kinetic or external-field energy require a separately specified balance and are outside this item.

For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound. Fix the finite constituent split $s_1,\ldots,s_m$ used for the endpoint bookkeeping, with $m\in\mathbb N$, $m\ge1$, and constitutions $c_1,\ldots,c_m$. The split accounts for every constituent whose entropy can change; any included auxiliary not represented in it must have an explicitly model-declared zero entropy change between these endpoints. Its endpoint product is

$$\mathcal D:=D_{c_1}\times\cdots\times D_{c_m},\qquad \mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal D,$$

where $\mathcal F$ is the model-declared feasible endpoint set for the fixed totals, retained barriers, and permitted exchanges, as in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The process model supplies an endpoint association on the two formal endpoint labels $-$ and $+$:

$$\rho_P:\{-,+\}\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad \rho_P(-)=\mathbf x_P^-=(x_{1,P}^-,\ldots,x_{m,P}^-),\qquad \rho_P(+)=\mathbf x_P^+=(x_{1,P}^+,\ldots,x_{m,P}^+),$$

where $\mathbf x_P^-$ and $\mathbf x_P^+$ are respectively the declared constituent-state tuples representing the aggregate equilibrium endpoints $x_P^-$ and $x_P^+$ of $P$. Both tuples must belong to the same $\mathcal F$. Restrict to endpoint splits admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] as a collection of independent separated macroscopic systems, so that its additive entropy rule applies. On this admitted $\mathcal F$, define

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i)\qquad\left(\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal F\right).$$

This uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]].

The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))\ge0.$$

The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(+))-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\rho_P(-))=0$. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

Fix a working system of constitution $c$ and a closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(c)$ with equilibrium endpoints as in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. A cycle of the working system is such a record with $x_P^-=x_P^+$; the reservoirs and work store need not return to their initial energy states.

An ideal thermal reservoir $b$ has an energy interval $J_b\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in joules and a finite entropy function $S_b:J_b\to\mathbb R$ measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. On the energy interval admitted for a cycle, assume the exact affine law
$
S_b(E_b)=s_{b,0}+\frac{E_b}{T_b}
$
for a constant $s_{b,0}$ and fixed $T_b>0$ kelvins. Thus $S_b'(E_b)=1/T_b$ in the interior and every admitted endpoint change is exactly $\Delta S_b=\Delta E_b/T_b$. This constant is the absolute thermodynamic temperature under [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. The affine entropy law on the admitted interval is the ideal-bath model; a finite reservoir whose temperature changes is outside this definition.

An ideal work store is a named auxiliary with an energy coordinate $E_w$ measured in joules and an assigned entropy $S_w(E_w)=s_w$ constant on the energy interval used by the cycle. It exchanges only mechanical work and no matter or heat. Its energy may change, while its entropy change is zero by this model definition.

A two-reservoir cycle contains one working-system cycle, one hot bath at $T_h$, one cold bath at $T_c$, and the ideal work store. They lie inside one isolated outer boundary in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]], so the full compound has no external matter or energy transfer. There are no unlisted heat, work, matter, kinetic-energy, or external-potential-energy changes. The admitted process and transfer signs are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The model declares the endpoint entropy split
$
S_{\mathrm{tot}}=S_{\mathrm{ws}}(x_{\mathrm{ws}})+S_h(E_h)+S_{\mathrm{cold}}(E_c)+S_w(E_w),
$
where $S_{\mathrm{ws}}$ is the working-system entropy and the bath and work-store functions are those defined here. This additive constituent split is assumed to be one admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] and is the entropy supplied to [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]; $S_w$ contributes zero change. Reversibility of the full record is as in [[def-td-reversible-process]].

When the second law is applied to the cycle, the model also supplies an admitted closed process record for the full compound. At both endpoints its constituent preparations, with the declared contact controls locked or insulated, are an equilibrium macrostate for that record; its separately tracked center-of-mass kinetic and external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change. This total-compound record is the input to the second law; the working-system record $P$ is the input to its first-law balance.

In the heat-engine mode, the positive magnitudes $Q_h,Q_c$ in joules mean respectively heat taken from the hot bath into the working system and heat rejected by the working system to the cold bath; accordingly $\Delta E_h=-Q_h$, $\Delta E_c=Q_c$, $Q[P]=Q_h-Q_c$, and work output is $W_{\mathrm{out}}=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$. In the refrigerator mode, $Q_c>0$ is heat taken from the cold bath into the working system, $Q_h>0$ is heat rejected to the hot bath, so $\Delta E_c=-Q_c$, $\Delta E_h=Q_h$, $Q[P]=Q_c-Q_h$, and work input is $W_{\mathrm{in}}=W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$. These are idealized model conventions, not claims that a particular apparatus realizes the cycle.

Let an admitted heat-engine cycle in the sense of [[def-td-reservoir-cycle]] operate between fixed ideal-bath temperatures $0<T_c<T_h$, absorb $Q_h>0$, reject $Q_c>0$, and deliver $W_{\mathrm{out}}>0$. Define its efficiency by $\eta=W_{\mathrm{out}}/Q_h$. Then
$
\eta\le 1-\frac{T_c}{T_h}.
$
Equality holds exactly when the total entropy change of the isolated compound is zero. In particular, a reversible cycle in the stated boundary model saturates the bound; zero entropy change is not here asserted to imply full reversibility.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

Fix a constitution $c$ and an open dimensionless subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the single-phase region of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Its physical chart is $\Omega=\Phi_c(O)$, where $\Phi_c$ is the SI coordinate map defined in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. For fixed physical amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ with nonempty slice $\Omega_n:=\{(U,V):(U,V,n)\in\Omega\}$, this slice is open in $\mathbb R^2$. Use $T,p$ from [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] as functions of the physical coordinates on $\Omega_n$. For a response derivative, restrict to an open neighborhood in $\Omega_n$ where the required natural-coordinate map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto an open image, so its inverse expresses the physical $(U,V)$ as $C^1$ functions of those natural coordinates ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Specifically, $C_V$ uses $(U,V)\mapsto(T,V)$ at fixed $n$, while $C_p$, $\kappa_T$, and $\alpha_p$ use $(U,V)\mapsto(T,p)$ at fixed $n$. The existence of each such local chart is a hypothesis for its response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. Each derivative uses the indicated natural variables and holds all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

Fix a material constitution $c$, with $r$ named species and dimensionless equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in D_c$, define the diagonal SI coordinate map

$$\Phi_c(x):=(U_c(x),V_c(x),n_{c,1}(x),\ldots,n_{c,r}(x))=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\ldots,\hat n_r\,\mathrm{mol}).$$

In SI numerical coordinates this is a diagonal linear bijection with a diagonal linear inverse, so it maps ambient open sets to open sets and its inverse is defined on its image.

Choose an open subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the ambient dimensionless Euclidean coordinates that is designated as a single-phase chart, and set $\Omega:=\Phi_c(O)$, an open chart of physical SI coordinate values. Here $U$ is the internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. If $S_c:D_c\to\mathbb R$ is the entropy adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], define its physical-coordinate representative on $\Omega$ by

$$S_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R.$$

When its arguments are the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, write this representative as $S_c(U,V,n)$ for brevity. On $\Omega$, assume the finite representative is $C^2$ and has $S_{c,U}>0$, as adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in the physical $U$ coordinate while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; in particular the conversion factor from $\hat U$ is included.

Explicitly, with the partial derivatives on the right taken in the dimensionless coordinates on $O$ while holding every other hatted coordinate fixed, the physical partials are

$$S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial_{\hat U}S_c,\qquad S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{m^3})^{-1}\partial_{\hat V}S_c,\qquad S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{mol})^{-1}\partial_{\hat n_j}S_c,$$

using the coordinate-conversion convention of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]].

Define the physical-coordinate representatives of the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}},\qquad p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}},\qquad \mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}:=-T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}.$$

For a state-domain point $x\in O$, define the corresponding state functions by pullback, $T_c(x):=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, $p_c(x):=p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, and $\mu_{c,j}(x):=\mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$. When the argument is a physical tuple $(U,V,n)$, write $T_c(U,V,n)$, $p_c(U,V,n)$, and $\mu_{c,j}(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representatives. Thus both notations refer to the same state functions through $\Phi_c$.

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c, d \in F$.

1. **Translation invariance.** If $a < b$ then $a + c < b + c$.
2. **Adding inequalities.** If $a < b$ and $c < d$ then $a + c < b + d$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$. For $x,y\in I$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, the point $\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y$ belongs to $I$. The function $f$ is **convex** when the convex-combination inequality holds for every weight in $[0,1]$:

$$f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).$$

It is **strictly convex** when this inequality is strict whenever $x\ne y$ and $0<\lambda<1$. It is **concave** (respectively **strictly concave**) when $-f$ is convex (respectively strictly convex). It is **midpoint convex** when the displayed inequality is required only at $\lambda=1/2$.
If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim:
Repeated use of the power derivative [L1] and scalar chain, sum, and product rules [L2] shows that $S_c$ is $C^2$ on the positive open chart. Differentiating $\theta(U)$ gives $\theta_U=(C_*T_*)^{-1}\theta^{-1/2}$, so $S_U=C_*\theta^{-1/2}\theta_U=1/(T_*\theta)$ and $S_{UU}=-(C_*T_*^2)^{-1}\theta^{-5/2}<0$. At fixed $V,n$, [L6] applied to $-S_c$ shows that $S_c$ is concave as a function of $U$; because $S_c$ is independent of $V,n$, the same convex-combination inequality holds on the full product chart. Thus the entropy is concave there and $S_U$ is finite and positive, as required by [F4]. By [F2], the absolute temperature is $T=1/S_U=T_*\theta$. Differentiating the explicit branch functions $U(T),S(T)$ in [A1] by [L1,L2] gives
$$U_T=C_*\theta^{1/2},\qquad S_T=\frac{C_*}{T_*}\theta^{-1/2}.$$
The response definition [F1] now gives $C_V=U_T=C_*\theta^{1/2}=T S_T$. The displayed inverse branch and these continuous derivatives give a valid local response chart.

For $0<\epsilon<T$, the integrand $C_V(t)/t$ is continuous on $[\epsilon,T]$ and is Riemann integrable there by [L7]; it agrees on its interior with the derivative of $2C_*\sqrt{t/T_*}$. By [L8],
$$\int_\epsilon^T\frac{C_V(t)}{t}\,dt=2C_*\left(\sqrt{T/T_*}-\sqrt{\epsilon/T_*}\right).$$
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, this tends to $2C_*\sqrt{\theta}=S(T)-S_0$, so the improper entropy integral converges and the entropy has the finite limit $S_0$.

Fix any dimensionless real exponent $q\ge1$, any proposed $M>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, and any dimensionless $\delta\in(0,1]$. Since $0<\theta<1$ implies $\log\theta<0$ by [L3], ordered-field arithmetic [L4] gives $(q-1)\log\theta\le0$ and hence $q\log\theta\le\log\theta$. Thus $\theta^q=\exp(q\log\theta)\le\exp(\log\theta)=\theta$ by [L1,L3]. Choose $0<\theta<\min\{\delta,(C_*/M)^2,1\}$. Then $M\theta^q\le M\theta<C_*\sqrt{\theta}=C_V(T)$, so the proposed bound fails at this temperature. As $M$ and $\delta$ were arbitrary, no constants in the stated big-$O$ definition work for this $q$; since $q\ge1$ was arbitrary, the assertion fails for every real exponent $q\ge1$.

Fix a constitution $c$ and a smooth physical-coordinate chart in $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], with fixed amounts $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ and $T,p$ as in [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. A **valid response chart** is an open neighborhood on which the relevant independent coordinates used below have a $C^1$ inverse to the physical $(U,V)$ coordinates; a $C^1$ diffeomorphism has a $C^1$ inverse on open neighborhoods by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The existence of such a chart is a hypothesis for a response derivative, not a consequence of this definition. The derivatives use the indicated natural variables and hold all other listed coordinates fixed.

The **constant-volume heat capacity** and **constant-pressure heat capacity** of the whole system are, where the derivatives exist and are finite,

$$C_V:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,n},\qquad H:=U+pV,\qquad C_p:=\left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Here $H$ is the enthalpy in joules; both heat capacities are in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, not per mole. The **isothermal compressibility** and **isobaric thermal expansion coefficient** are

$$\kappa_T:=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_{T,n},\qquad \alpha_p:=\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{p,n}.$$

Since $V>0$ and the coordinates use SI units ([[def-td-si-quantities]]), $\kappa_T$ has units $\mathrm{Pa^{-1}}$ and $\alpha_p$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. This definition asserts no sign for any response, no identity among them, and no finite value at a critical or otherwise singular chart.

Fix a material constitution $c$ and its equilibrium state domain $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Let $\Omega\subseteq D_c$ be a specified open, single-phase chart in physical SI coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, with $U$ evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. On $\Omega$, use the finite $C^2$ entropy function $S_c$ and the strict positivity $S_{c,U}>0$ adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in that coordinate direction while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Define the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}},\qquad p_c:=T_cS_{c,V},\qquad \mu_{c,j}:=-T_cS_{c,n_j}.$$

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

supplier_excerpts.excerpt:
For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.
