citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

derivations.claim: By openness choose $R>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,2R)\subset U$. Continuity of $X$ and $DX$ at $q_0$ gives finite $M,L\ge0$ bounding $\|X\|$ on $\overline B(q_0,R)$ and $\|DX\|$ on $B(q_0,2R)$. By [F1] $X$ is totally differentiable there, and [F2] applied to the convex ball $B(q_0,2R)$ gives $\|X(u)-X(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|$ for $u,v\in\overline B(q_0,R)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ with $M\delta\le R/2$ and $L\delta<1$, and let $\mathcal C:=\{\gamma\in C([-\delta,\delta],\mathbb R^m):\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)\text{ for every }t\}$ with the supremum norm. It is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(\gamma_k)$, [F5] gives the pointwise limit $\gamma(t)\in\mathbb R^m$; the supremum-Cauchy estimate, passed to that pointwise limit, gives uniform convergence to $\gamma$. The limit is continuous: given $\varepsilon>0$ and $t_0$, choose $k$ with $\|\gamma_k-\gamma\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then continuity gives $\rho>0$ such that $\|\gamma_k(t)-\gamma_k(t_0)\|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $|t-t_0|<\rho$; the triangle inequality yields $\|\gamma(t)-\gamma(t_0)\|<\varepsilon$. Also $\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)$ for every $t$, since this Euclidean ball is closed and each $\gamma_k(t)$ lies in it. Thus $\gamma\in\mathcal C$. For $p\in\overline B(q_0,R/2)$ define $T_p\gamma(t):=p+\int_0^t X(\gamma(s))\,ds$. The integrand is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. Then $T_p$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, since $\|T_p\gamma(t)-q_0\|\le\|p-q_0\|+M|t|\le R$, and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$.

Starting at the constant curve $\gamma_0(t)=p$, iterate $\gamma_{k+1}=T_p\gamma_k$. If $\kappa=L\delta<1$, then $\|\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_k\|_\infty\le\kappa^k\|\gamma_1-\gamma_0\|_\infty$; the geometric tail bound makes $(\gamma_k)$ uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $\phi(\cdot,p)\in\mathcal C$ is a fixed point by the contraction bound. Any two fixed points have distance at most $\kappa$ times that distance, so they coincide.

For $g(s)=X(\phi(s,p))$, continuity and [F3] make every component Riemann integrable. At an interior $t$, the difference quotient of $\phi(t,p)=p+\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ differs from $g(t)$ by at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|$, which tends to zero by continuity; thus $\partial_t\phi=X(\phi)$. Conversely any $C^1$ solution staying in the ball satisfies the fixed-point equation by [F4], so uniqueness of the fixed point is uniqueness of the IVP.

If $p,p'$ lie in $\overline B(q_0,R/2)$, subtract their fixed-point equations from step 3.1 and take suprema to obtain $\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty\le\|p-p'\|+L\delta\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty$. Since $L\delta<1$, division gives the local Lipschitz estimate $(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|p-p'\|$.

Whenever the compositions remain in the chosen ball, both $t\mapsto\phi(t+s,p)$ and $t\mapsto\phi(t,\phi(s,p))$ solve the same IVP at $t=0$, with initial value $\phi(s,p)$. Uniqueness from step 4.1 gives the local flow law; setting $t=-s$ gives the local inverse relation.

citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

derivations.claim: For $p$ near $q$ put $\Delta_h(t):=\phi_X^t(p+h)-\phi_X^t(p)$. The integral equations from [F1] and the one-variable fundamental theorem applied to $\theta\mapsto X(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))$ give $$\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_0^t A_h(s)\Delta_h(s)\,ds,\quad A_h(s):=\int_0^1DX(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))\,d\theta.$$ The segments lie in $K$ after shrinking the initial ball and time interval. The local Lipschitz estimate in [F1] gives $\sup_t\|\Delta_h(t)\|=O(\|h\|)$. Uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$ from [F4] makes $A_h(s)$ converge uniformly to $DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ as $h\to0$.

Let $\mathcal I=[-\delta,\delta]$ and let $\mathcal C_1=C(\mathcal I,M_m(\mathbb R))$ with the supremum operator norm. This space is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(J_k)$, each matrix entry at each $s$ is Cauchy because $|A_{ij}|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$; [F5] applied to the $m^2$ entries gives a pointwise matrix limit $J(s)$, and the uniform Cauchy estimate passed to each entry gives uniform convergence of all entries. Each limit entry is continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ argument for uniform limits of continuous functions. The finite-coordinate bound $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$ then gives uniform operator-norm convergence, so $J\in\mathcal C_1$. The space is nonempty because it contains the constant zero matrix curve. Put $A_0(s):=DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ and define $T(J)(t):=I_m+\int_0^t A_0(s)J(s)\,ds$. It maps $\mathcal C_1$ into itself and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta<1$. By [F6], it has a unique fixed point $J$. Define $R_h(t):=\Delta_h(t)-J(t)h$. Subtracting the integral equations and writing the integrand difference as $(A_h-A_0)\Delta_h+A_0R_h$ gives $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+\delta\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\|\Delta_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|)$, by step 1.1 and uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$. Thus $D_q\phi_X^t(p)=J(t,p)$. The continuous integrand in the equation for $J$ has average over $[t,t+h]$ tending to its value at $t$: the quotient error is at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|DX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s,p)-DX(\phi_X^t(p))J(t,p)\|$, which tends to zero. Thus $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(p))J$ and $J(0,p)=I_m$.

Write $J_h(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $J_0(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p)$. Subtracting their integral equations gives $J_h-J_0=\int_0^t A_0(J_h-J_0)\,ds+\int_0^t(A_h-A_0)J_h\,ds$, where $A_h=DX(\phi_h)$, $A_0=DX(\phi_0)$, $\phi_h=\phi_X^s(p+h)$, and $\phi_0=\phi_X^s(p)$. The line-segment chain rule and Newton–Leibniz supplier claims in [F2]–[F3], applied entrywise to $DX$ along the segment from $\phi_0$ to $\phi_h$, give the exact formula $A_h-A_0=\int_0^1D^2X(\phi_0+\theta(\phi_h-\phi_0))[\phi_h-\phi_0,\cdot]\,d\theta$ and therefore $\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\le M_2\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty$. By [F1], $\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty=O(\|h\|)$; the integral equation gives $\|J_h\|_\infty\le(1-L\delta)^{-1}$. Absorbing the first integral using $L\delta<1$ yields $J_h-J_0=O(\|h\|)$ uniformly in time. Uniform continuity of $D^2X$ on $K$, the same line-segment formula, and $\phi_h-\phi_0=J_0h+o(\|h\|)$ from step 2.1 now give $A_h-A_0=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|)$ uniformly, and hence $(A_h-A_0)J_h=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,J_0(\cdot)]+o(\|h\|)$. For each base point $p$, define $\mathcal C_2=C(\mathcal I,\operatorname{Bil}(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^m))$ with the supremum bilinear-operator norm. The coordinatewise completeness proof of step 2.1 applies with $m^3$ coefficients, so $\mathcal C_2$ is complete; it is nonempty because it contains the zero bilinear-map curve. The map $(\mathcal T K)(t)[u,v]:=\int_0^t\big(A_0(s)K(s)[u,v]+D^2X(\phi_0(s))[J_0(s)u,J_0(s)v]\big)\,ds$ is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$ on $\mathcal C_2$. By [F6] it has a unique fixed point $K_p$. Subtracting its equation evaluated at $(h,v)$ from the equation for $J_h-J_0$ gives $R_h:=J_h-J_0-K_p[h,\cdot]$ with $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+o(\|h\|)$, so $R_h=o(\|h\|)$. Therefore $D_pJ[h](v)=K_p[h,v]$, and $K_p$ is the second derivative $D_q^2\phi_X$. Its equation makes it bilinear. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. For $k\in\{1,2\}$, a $C^k$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is $k$ times continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For a $C^1$ scalar function $S:W\to\mathbb R$ on an open $W\subseteq U$, its differential is the one-form defined by

$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

$$\Delta=\int_0^h\!\int_0^k S_{ij}(q+se_i+te_j)\,dt\,ds=\int_0^k\!\int_0^h S_{ji}(q+se_i+te_j)\,ds\,dt.$$
Each equality follows by taking the two endpoint differences in the outer coordinate and then applying Newton–Leibniz to the inner difference; both integrands are continuous by $S\in C^2$.

Divide both expressions in step 1.1 by $hk$ and let $h,k\downarrow0$. Continuity of $S_{ij}$ and $S_{ji}$ makes each average tend to its value at $q$, so $S_{ij}(q)=S_{ji}(q)$. Since $q,i,j$ were arbitrary, the coordinate formula in [F1] gives $d(dS)=0$.

Put $\lambda:=1/\mu\in C^1(U)$. Then $\omega=\lambda dS$. Expanding the coordinate derivative by the product rule and using step 2.1 yields $d\omega=d\lambda\wedge dS$. Put $c_i:=-a_i/b$ and $X_i:=\partial_{x_i}+c_i\partial_z$. Then $X_i\in C^2$, $\omega(X_i)=a_i+bc_i=0$, and the $X_i$ are a basis of $\ker\omega$ because their first $n$ components form the standard basis.

Define $[X,Y]:=DY\,X-DX\,Y$. Coordinate expansion of the displayed formula for $d\omega$ gives $d\omega(X,Y)=X[\omega(Y)]-Y[\omega(X)]-\omega([X,Y])$. Thus for horizontal fields $d\omega(X_i,X_j)=-\omega([X_i,X_j])$. Also $[X_i,X_j]$ has zero $x$-components, hence is vertical. Evaluating the three-form on $(\partial_z,X_i,X_j)$ gives $(\omega\wedge d\omega)(\partial_z,X_i,X_j)=b\,d\omega(X_i,X_j)$. Under (i), $d\omega(X_i,X_j)=0$; then $\omega([X_i,X_j])=0$, and a vertical vector $v\partial_z$ has $\omega(v\partial_z)=vb$, so $[X_i,X_j]=0$.

Each $X_i$ changes only $x_i$, at rate one, so the first $n$ coordinates of $\Phi(x,\eta)$ are exactly $x$. Commutation and the transported-field identity in [F3] give $\partial_{x_i}\Phi=X_i(\Phi)$. At $(0,z_0)$ the columns of $D\Phi$ are $X_1,\ldots,X_n,\partial_z$; their first $n$ components form $I_n$ and the last column is $\partial_z$, so $D\Phi$ is invertible.

Let $N=n+1$. On an open product neighborhood of $(u_0,y_0)=((0,z_0),(0,z_0))$ where $\Phi$ is defined, set $H(u,y):=\Phi(u)-y$. Then $H(u_0,y_0)=0$ and its $u$-derivative $D_uH=D\Phi(u_0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2N$ and target dimension $N$, permuting the input coordinates to $(y,u)$ so the $y$ block is free and the solved $u$ block has the invertible minor: conditionally, the zero set is the graph of a unique local $C^1$ map $G(y)$, so $\Phi(G(y))=y$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open and let $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i dx_i+b dz$ be a $C^2$ one-form with $\omega_{q_0}\ne0$ at $q_0\in U$. Relabel coordinates so one coefficient $b$ is nonzero at $q_0$ and shrink to a neighborhood where it stays nonzero. The following conditions, both local at $q_0$, are equivalent: (i) there is a neighborhood $U_0$ of $q_0$ on which $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$; (ii) there is a neighborhood $W$ of $q_0$ and $\mu\in C^1(W)$ nowhere zero and $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ on $W$. The theorem gives no global exactness or thermodynamic calibration.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open, and let $\omega$ be a nowhere-zero $C^2$ one-form, with the horizontal paths of [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]. Assume that every point has a neighborhood $W$ with $S\in C^2(W)$ and nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ satisfying $dS=\mu\omega$. For every $q\in U$, its horizontal reachability class in $U$ is contained in a countable union of compact subsets of $U$ with empty interior. Consequently every nonempty open $V\subseteq U$ contains a point not horizontally reachable from $q$ by any horizontal path in $U$. In particular, if $q\in V$, that point is not reachable by a path contained in $V$. No global first integral or choice axiom is assumed.

Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then $E$ is connected ([[def-connected-r]]) if and
only if $E$ is **order-convex** ([[def-interval]]), that is, if and only if

$$x, z \in E \text{ and } x \le w \le z \;\Longrightarrow\; w \in E .$$

**On the word "interval".** Order-convexity is exactly the defining property
that [[def-interval]] proves for each of its nine forms, and in that sense the
theorem says that the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the intervals. The
converse classification, that every order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is empty
or one of the nine forms, is true and is explicitly **not proved anywhere in
this library**; [[def-interval]] records that omission in its own remarks. So
the statement proved below is the equivalence with order-convexity, and the
phrase "is an interval" is to be read as "is order-convex" throughout this page.

Then $\Psi_r(0)=r$ and its derivative has the independent columns $X_1(r),\ldots,X_n(r),Y_t(r)$. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. For $k\in\{1,2\}$, a $C^k$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is $k$ times continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For a $C^1$ scalar function $S:W\to\mathbb R$ on an open $W\subseteq U$, its differential is the one-form defined by

$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For any piecewise-$C^1$ horizontal path $\gamma$, the identity in step 1.1 and [F1]–[F2] give $(S\circ\gamma)'=dS(\dot\gamma)=\mu\omega(\dot\gamma)=0$ on each smooth piece; therefore $S$ is constant along every finite concatenation of horizontal pieces.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: Let $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with $P(x,y)=-y/(x^2+y^2)$ and $Q(x,y)=x/(x^2+y^2)$. The domain $D$ is open since each nonzero point has a ball avoiding the origin, and the coefficients are smooth with $(P,Q)\ne(0,0)$ at every point. It is path-connected: if the segment joining $p,q\in D$ avoids $0$, use that segment; if it contains $0$, then $p,q,0$ are collinear, and a nonzero vector $r$ perpendicular to $p$ makes both segments $[p,r]$ and $[r,q]$ avoid $0$.
Writing $r^2=x^2+y^2$, direct differentiation gives $\partial_xQ=(y^2-x^2)/r^4=\partial_yP$, so $d\omega=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)dx\wedge dy=0$ on $D$.

The unit circle $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, lies in the domain and uses the form defined in step 1.1. Along it $(P,Q)=(-\sin t,\cos t)=\gamma'(t)$, hence [F2] gives $\int_\gamma\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi$ by [F4].

The closedness is proved in step 2.1. If $\omega=dS$ globally on $D$, then $F=\nabla S$ for the corresponding vector field, and [F3] would give $\int_\gamma\omega=S(\gamma(2\pi))-S(\gamma(0))=0$, contradicting step 2.2. Thus $\omega$ is closed but not globally exact. This does not assert that every possible global integrating factor is absent.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. For $k\in\{1,2\}$, a $C^k$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is $k$ times continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For a $C^1$ scalar function $S:W\to\mathbb R$ on an open $W\subseteq U$, its differential is the one-form defined by

$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then $E$ is connected ([[def-connected-r]]) if and
only if $E$ is **order-convex** ([[def-interval]]), that is, if and only if

$$x, z \in E \text{ and } x \le w \le z \;\Longrightarrow\; w \in E .$$

**On the word "interval".** Order-convexity is exactly the defining property
that [[def-interval]] proves for each of its nine forms, and in that sense the
theorem says that the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the intervals. The
converse classification, that every order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is empty
or one of the nine forms, is true and is explicitly **not proved anywhere in
this library**; [[def-interval]] records that omission in its own remarks. So
the statement proved below is the equivalence with order-convexity, and the
phrase "is an interval" is to be read as "is order-convex" throughout this page.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

derivations.claim: Use the local first integrals in the Statement. Write $\omega=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\omega_j dx_j$ in the fixed Euclidean coordinates and set $w=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{n+1})$ and $Z_j=e_j-(\omega_j/|w|^2)w$. These globally defined $C^2$ vector fields are horizontal and span $\ker\omega$ at each point, since their matrix is the orthogonal projection onto that kernel. On every neighborhood supplied by the hypothesis, $dS=\mu\omega$ has nonzero derivative, and each $Z_j$-flow preserves $S$ as long as its trajectory remains there, by [F3]. Its derivative therefore preserves horizontal tangent vectors there: differentiating $S(\phi_j^t(x))=S(x)$ gives $dS_{\phi_j^t(x)}D\phi_j^t(x)v=dS_xv=0$ for horizontal $v$. The compact image of any finite flow trajectory has a finite subcover by such neighborhoods; a sufficiently fine finite subdivision of its compact time interval puts each subtrajectory in one of them. This follows directly from compactness: otherwise shrinking subintervals failing the subdivision would have a limiting time whose neighborhood contains them. Composing the local derivative identities obtains preservation over the full duration. Local flow uniqueness makes these continuations consistent, and [F2] gives $C^2$ dependence on durations and initial points wherever the finite composition is defined.

Fix $q\in U$ and a neighborhood $W$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ as in the hypothesis. Since $dS_q=\mu(q)\omega_q\ne0$, apply [L1] to $x\mapsto S(x)-S(q)$ with ambient dimension $n+1$ and target dimension $1$; after choosing the solved coordinate, its zero set is a local $C^1$ graph plaque $P$ through $q$, parameterized by its $n$ free coordinates. Let $\pi$ be projection to those free coordinates. Choose $n$ of the fields $Z_j$ that form a basis of $\ker\omega_q=\ker dS_q$, and for $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)$ near $0$ let $E(s)$ be the endpoint at $q$ of the successive local flows of these fields for durations $s_1,\ldots,s_n$. Shrink the open duration domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ so all flow segments stay in $W$. Step 1.1 shows that each flow preserves $S$, so $E(D)\subseteq P$; moreover $DE(0)$ has the chosen basis as its columns. The differential $D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is therefore an invertible $n\times n$ matrix, because $D\pi_q$ is an isomorphism from the tangent space of the graph plaque to its free-coordinate space. Choose an open neighborhood $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $y_0=\pi(q)$ and shrink $D$ so that the target-augmented map $H:D\times Y\to\mathbb R^n$, $H(s,y):=\pi(E(s))-y$, is defined. It satisfies $H(0,y_0)=0$ and its solved block $D_sH(0,y_0)=D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2n$ and target dimension $n<2n$, permuting inputs to $(y,s)$ so $y$ is free and $s$ is solved. For every $y$ near $y_0$ this gives $s(y)$ with $\pi(E(s(y)))=y$; uniqueness of the graph plaque then says the endpoints $E(s(y))$ fill a relative neighborhood of $q$ in $P$. Each is reachable by a finite word of horizontal flows inside $W$. Conversely, a horizontal path preserves the local $S$ on each short subarc in a first-integral neighborhood by [F3]. Thus near each parameter value its image lies in the relative plaque neighborhood just shown to be reachable by such a finite word. The finite-word orbits are equivalence classes by flow reversal and concatenation, so their preimages along the path are relatively open in its interval domain. By [F4], connectedness of that interval forces one class. Hence every point horizontally reachable from $q$ lies in its finite-word orbit; the reverse inclusion follows because every word is a horizontal concatenation.

For a fixed finite word $\alpha$ of length $m\ge1$, write $F_\alpha:O_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to U$ for its endpoint map from $q$, on the open set of admissible duration tuples. Each duration derivative is a field vector transported by the later flows and is horizontal by step 1.1. Near any $s\in O_\alpha$, continuity puts the endpoint image in a neighborhood with the first integral $S$ from the hypothesis; hence $D(S\circ F_\alpha)=0$. On a small convex parameter ball, [F3] makes $S\circ F_\alpha$ constant. Choose a closed box with rational endpoints, containing $s$ in its interior and contained in that ball. Its image under $F_\alpha$ is compact by [F6], lies in one level of $S$, and has empty interior in $U$: a nonempty open subset of that image would make $S$ constant on an open set, contradicting $dS=\mu\omega\ne0$. Thus the image is a closed nowhere-dense subset of $U$. By [F5], enumerate the countable collection of all finite words and rational closed parameter boxes; for an admissible box whose compact image has empty interior record that image, and otherwise record the empty set. Include the singleton $\{q\}$ for the empty word. This explicitly defined sequence $(K_j)$ of closed nowhere-dense sets covers $\mathcal O(q)$, since every duration tuple admits the small box just constructed. No countable atlas or choice of first integrals is needed for the enumeration.

Let $V$ be any nonempty open subset of $U$. Choose a rational open Euclidean ball with closure contained in $V$. Recursively choose the first ball in a fixed enumeration of rational balls whose closure is inside the preceding open ball, disjoint from $K_j$, and whose radius is below $2^{-j}$. Such a ball exists because $K_j$ is closed with empty interior. If the $j$th ball has center $c_j$ and radius $r_j<2^{-j}$, then all later centers lie in its closed ball, so $|c_k-c_j|\le r_j$ for $k>j$. Thus the centers form a Cauchy sequence; [F7] gives a limit $p$ in all the nested closed balls, hence in $V$ and outside every $K_j$. Each selection is the least natural-number index satisfying explicit nonempty conditions, so it uses no choice axiom. Since the $K_j$ cover $\mathcal O(q)$, step 2.1 shows $p$ is not horizontally reachable from $q$ even by a path in $U$, and therefore not by one in $V$. This proves the asserted conclusion for every nonempty open $V$, using no global first integral or choice axiom.

derivations.claim: On $GL(4,\mathbb R)$ define $\Phi(L)=L^T\eta L$ with values in the ten-dimensional space of symmetric matrices. At $\Phi(L)=\eta$, its derivative is $D\Phi_L(\Delta)=\Delta^T\eta L+L^T\eta\Delta$. For any symmetric $S$, set $\Delta=L\eta^{-1}S/2$; using $L^T\eta L=\eta$ and $S^T=S$, each summand equals $S/2$. Thus $D\Phi_L$ is onto.

Every point of $\Phi^{-1}(\eta)$ is regular by step 1.1, and the level is nonempty because it contains $I$. Thus [F3] makes $O(1,3)=\Phi^{-1}(\eta)$ an embedded six-dimensional submanifold of $GL(4,\mathbb R)$. For $L\in O(1,3)$, $Le_0$ is timelike and $L$ is a homeomorphism of the timelike set; [F4] implies that $L$ preserves the selected future component exactly when $Le_0$ lies in that component. Since $e_0$ is the positive time-axis vector, this is exactly $L^0{}_0>0$. Also $|L^0{}_0|\ge1$, and taking determinants in $L^T\eta L=\eta$ gives $(\det L)^2=1$. Therefore $\det L=1$ and $L^0{}_0>0$ select an open subset of $O(1,3)$. By [F1] this subset is $SO^+(1,3)$. Matrix multiplication and inversion restrict smoothly from $GL(4)$, so this subgroup is a six-dimensional Lie group.

Give $G=\mathbb R^4\times SO^+(1,3)$ the product manifold structure from step 2.1 and multiplication $(a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L)$. Both parenthesizations of a triple product equal $(a+\Lambda b+\Lambda Lc,\Lambda LM)$; the identity is $(0,I)$; and direct substitution shows $(-\Lambda^{-1}a,\Lambda^{-1})$ is a left and right inverse. Multiplication and inversion are smooth because matrix multiplication and inversion on $SO^+(1,3)$ are smooth and the translation operations are smooth. The affine matrix map $\rho(a,\Lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is injective, has smooth inverse onto its image by block projection, and is a group homomorphism because matrix multiplication gives $\rho(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L)$. The product manifold tangent at identity is $\mathbb R^4\times T_I SO^+(1,3)$. By [F5], the latter tangent space is contained in the six-dimensional space of matrices satisfying $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$; both have dimension six by step 2.1 and [F5], so they are equal. Hence $d\rho_I(a,A)=\begin{pmatrix}A&a\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. A group homomorphism carries left-invariant vector fields to related left-invariant fields: differentiating $\rho\circ L_g=L_{\rho(g)}\circ\rho$ gives this relation. Related fields' brackets are related, since applying each bracket to a smooth test function and expanding $X(Yf)-Y(Xf)$ gives the same identity after composition with $\rho$. For matrices $M,N$, the left-invariant fields on $GL(5)$ are $g\mapsto gM$ and $g\mapsto gN$; differentiating these fields gives their commutator at the identity as $MN-NM$. Thus the bracket of two pair matrices is $\begin{pmatrix}[A,B]&Ab-Ba\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, yielding $[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B])$.

The cotangent lift preserves the covector-tangent pairing: $p'(dx')=(\Lambda^{-T}p)(\Lambda dx)=p(dx)$. For the one-parameter element $\exp(-s(a,A))$, differentiation of $x'=\Lambda_s x+a_s$ gives the fundamental field $(-(a+Ax),A^Tp)$ on $(x,p)$; its negative is the positive cotangent-lifted field $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pairing the covector with the positive base generator gives $\ell=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c)$.

Antisymmetry of $A^{bc}$ gives $J_{bc}A^{bc}=-2p_bA^b{}_cx^c$: expand $J_{bc}=x_bp_c-x_cp_b$ and interchange $b,c$ in the first term. Substitution yields $\ell=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$. The definitions of $P,J$ then give $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$ from $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[p]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, and $[c]=\mathrm{m/s}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the referenced cotangent and symplectic-action conventions. Work on affine Minkowski spacetime with inertial coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres, metric matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and cotangent coordinates $(x^a,p_a)$, where each $p_a$ has SI momentum units. Fix the future cone as the timelike component containing the positive $x^0$ axis, equivalently $v^0>\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. Let $SO^+(1,3)$ denote the determinant-one, future-cone-preserving Lorentz subgroup. Define the proper orthochronous Poincaré group and its multiplication by

$$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3),\qquad (a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L).$$

Its action on spacetime and the cotangent lift are $x'=\Lambda x+a$ and $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$. The Lie algebra consists of pairs $(a,A)$ with $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, bracket

$$[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B]).$$

Use the library convention $\xi_M=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp_G(-s\xi)\cdot z$. Thus the positive affine generator on spacetime is $Y_{(a,A)}(x)=a+Ax$, the fundamental field is its negative, and the cotangent-lifted positive field is $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pair the cotangent point with a Lie-algebra element by

$$\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c).$$

Define $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$. The equivalent dual pairing is $\ell_{(a,A)}=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$, where $A^{bc}=A^b{}_d\eta^{dc}$ and $J_{bc}=\eta_{bd}\eta_{ce}J^{de}$. Here $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are charge-space definitions on the full cotangent bundle; shell reduction and the moment-map identities are stated separately. No spin or particle model is included.

Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold as in [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]], and write its cotangent phase space in induced coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$. With $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$, define $X_H$ by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ and define the Poisson bracket by $\{F,G\}:=X_G(F)$. Then

$$X_H=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q^i}-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i},\qquad \{F,G\}=F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i}.$$

The bracket is coordinate independent and makes smooth functions a Poisson algebra. If $H_t$ is smooth on an open time-dependent domain $D\subset\mathbb R\times T^*Q$, each solution of $\dot z=X_{H_t}(z)$ has local uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial data and parameters; on its actual interval,

$$\frac{d}{dt}F(t,z(t))=\partial_tF+\{F,H_t\}.$$

No completeness or global flow is asserted. If $H$ is smooth, each local time-$t$ flow map preserves ω.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let a smooth left action of $G$ on a smooth
manifold $Q$ be given and let $\mu_0:G\times Q\to Q$ denote it. Define the
**cotangent-lifted action** on $T^*Q$ by

$$\widehat g(q,p):=\bigl(g\cdot q,(d(a_g)_q^{-1})^*p\bigr),$$

where $a_g(q)=g\cdot q$. Then the lifted action is a smooth left action
preserving the canonical symplectic form $\omega_{\mathrm{can}}=-d\lambda$, and
the **tautological moment map**

$$\bigl\langle\mu(q,p),\xi\bigr\rangle:=-p\bigl(\xi_Q(q)\bigr), \qquad \xi\in\mathfrak g,$$

satisfies the component moment equations
$d\mu^\xi=-\iota_{\xi_{T^*Q}}\omega_{\mathrm{can}}$ for the lifted fundamental
fields. Its coadjoint equivariance, which makes $\mu$ an equivariant moment
map, is verified in the companion lemma.

In affine Minkowski space with inertial coordinates $x^0,x^i$ measured in metres and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, let $m\ge0$ and let

$$\Sigma_m^+=\{(x,p): -p_0=P^0=\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2},\ p_0<0\},$$

where $\mathbf p\ne0$ when $m=0$, and write $P^i=p_i$ for the spatial raised momentum components. The characteristic flow of the restricted canonical form is $(x,p)\mapsto(x+\alpha P,p)$, and its orbit space is globally diffeomorphic to $B_m=\mathbb R^3_a\times\mathbb R^3_p$ for $m>0$, or $\mathbb R^3_a\times(\mathbb R^3_p\setminus\{0\})$ for $m=0$, by

$$a^i=x^i-\frac{P^i}{P^0}x^0,\qquad p_i=p_i.$$

The reduced symplectic form is $da^i\wedge dp_i$. The quotient is Hausdorff and second countable and each full characteristic line meets each slice $x^0=ct$ exactly once. This is an explicit free flat quotient, not a conclusion about arbitrary first-class systems.

In affine Minkowski space with $x^0=ct$, let $m\ge0$, $p_i$ be spatial momentum components and $p_i\ne0$ for $m=0$. On the future shell, $p_0=-E/c$, where

$$E(\mathbf p)=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}.$$

On any compact interval $J=[t_1,t_2]$ of inertial time with $t_1<t_2$, the gauge $x^0=ct$ reduces the first-order shell action to

$$I_J=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(p_i\dot q^i-E(\mathbf p)\right)dt,\qquad q^i=x^i.$$

For this variational statement, take $q^i$ and $p_i$ smooth on a neighborhood of $J$ and restrict to variations that are smooth one-parameter families, fix $q$ at both endpoints, and vary $p$ freely; in the massless case the paths and sufficiently small variations stay in $\mathbf p\ne0$. The resulting Hamilton equations hold on the interior of $J$.

The gauge pair $C_m=0$, $\psi=x^0-ct=0$ is second class because $\{C_m,\psi\}=-P^0\ne0$ on the future shell; its Dirac reduction gives the canonical spatial bracket. The reduced Hamilton equations are $\dot q^i=c^2p_i/E$, $\dot p_i=0$, agreeing with the unreduced characteristic trajectories. On this full flat future shell every characteristic line meets each inertial-time slice once; this global assertion does not extend by this proof to a curved temporal chart.

derivations.claim: For $\xi=(a,A)$ the cotangent lift has positive infinitesimal field $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)=-\xi_{T^*Q}$ because the library fundamental vector is generated by $\exp(-s\xi)$. With $\omega=dx^a\wedge dp_a$, $\iota_{X_{\ell_\xi}}\omega=d\ell_\xi$ by [L1], as $\partial_p\ell=a+Ax$ and $-\partial_x\ell=-A^Tp$. Therefore $d\ell_\xi=-\iota_{\xi_{T^*Q}}\omega$. The cotangent lift is symplectic and equivariant by [F2], so $\mu$ is the claimed equivariant moment map.

Substituting $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$ into [L1]'s canonical bracket, Leibniz gives $\{P^a,P^b\}=0$ and $\{J^{ab},P^c\}=\eta^{ac}P^b-\eta^{bc}P^a$. Applying Leibniz to the four products in $\{J^{ab},J^{cd}\}$ gives the four displayed metric terms, with signs fixed by $\{x^a,p_b\}=\delta^a_b$.

The full dual action follows directly from the semidirect group law, without restricting to the cotangent moment-map image. For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, multiplication and inversion give $\operatorname{Ad}_g(b,B)=(\Lambda b-\Lambda B\Lambda^{-1}a,\Lambda B\Lambda^{-1})$, hence $\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}(b,B)=(\Lambda^{-1}(b+Ba),\Lambda^{-1}B\Lambda)$. For an arbitrary dual charge $(P,J)$ use the pairing in [F1], $\langle(P,J),(b,B)\rangle=P_b b^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}B^{bc}$, and define $g\cdot(P,J)$ by pairing with $\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}(b,B)$. Lorentz invariance of $\eta$ transforms the first term to $P'_b b^b+P'_bB^b{}_ca^c$, where $P'=\Lambda P$, and the second term to $-\tfrac12(\Lambda J\Lambda^T)_{bc}B^{bc}$. Antisymmetry gives $P'_bB^b{}_ca^c=-\tfrac12(a\wedge P')_{bc}B^{bc}$. Thus for every $(b,B)$ the pairing equals that of $(\Lambda P,\Lambda J\Lambda^T+a\wedge\Lambda P)$; uniqueness of the dual coordinates proves the formula on all of $\mathfrak g^*$. For cotangent-image charges it also agrees with $x'=\Lambda x+a$, $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$, and $J'=x'\wedge P'$, as required by equivariance.

For $\eta=(b,B)$, the canonical bracket gives $\{\ell_\xi,\ell_\eta\}=p\cdot A(b+Bx)-p\cdot B(a+Ax)=p\cdot(Ab-Ba+[A,B]x)=\ell_{[(a,A),(b,B)]},$ using the semidirect Lie bracket from [F1]. This proves the full dual generator identity.

At $x^0=ct$, $P^0=E/c$, hence $B_i=J^{0i}=ct p_i-q^iE/c$. With the reduced canonical bracket from [L2]–[L3], $\{B_i,E\}=-cp_i$ and $\partial_tB_i=cp_i$. Their sum is zero, so $B_i$ is conserved along the free reduced motion, with the partial-time term essential.

On either future shell, the characteristic shift changes $J$ by $\alpha P\wedge P=0$ and leaves $P$ fixed, so each charge is constant on quotient fibres. In H8 coordinates $(a,p)$ the descended $P$ and $J$ are explicit smooth functions, so they descend smoothly through the quotient of [L2]. Lorentz invariance of $p^2$ gives $\{\ell_\xi,C_m\}=0$ for Lorentz generators; translations are constants in flat spacetime, so their brackets with $C_m$ also vanish.

$$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. $$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the referenced cotangent and symplectic-action conventions. Work on affine Minkowski spacetime with inertial coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres, metric matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and cotangent coordinates $(x^a,p_a)$, where each $p_a$ has SI momentum units. Fix the future cone as the timelike component containing the positive $x^0$ axis, equivalently $v^0>\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. Let $SO^+(1,3)$ denote the determinant-one, future-cone-preserving Lorentz subgroup. Define the proper orthochronous Poincaré group and its multiplication by

$$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3),\qquad (a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L).$$

Its action on spacetime and the cotangent lift are $x'=\Lambda x+a$ and $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$. The Lie algebra consists of pairs $(a,A)$ with $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, bracket

$$[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B]).$$

Use the library convention $\xi_M=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp_G(-s\xi)\cdot z$. Thus the positive affine generator on spacetime is $Y_{(a,A)}(x)=a+Ax$, the fundamental field is its negative, and the cotangent-lifted positive field is $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pair the cotangent point with a Lie-algebra element by

$$\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c).$$

Define $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$. The equivalent dual pairing is $\ell_{(a,A)}=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$, where $A^{bc}=A^b{}_d\eta^{dc}$ and $J_{bc}=\eta_{bd}\eta_{ce}J^{de}$. Here $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are charge-space definitions on the full cotangent bundle; shell reduction and the moment-map identities are stated separately. No spin or particle model is included.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For the group and cotangent conventions of [[def-rpm-h-poincare-charge-space]], the map $\mu:T^*\mathbb R^4\to\mathfrak g^*$ defined by $\langle\mu(x,p),(a,A)\rangle=\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)$ is a smooth equivariant moment map and obeys

$$\{\ell_\xi,\ell_\eta\}=\ell_{[\xi,\eta]},\quad \{P^a,P^b\}=0,\quad \{J^{ab},P^c\}=\eta^{ac}P^b-\eta^{bc}P^a,$$

$$\{J^{ab},J^{cd}\}=\eta^{ac}J^{bd}-\eta^{ad}J^{bc}-\eta^{bc}J^{ad}+\eta^{bd}J^{ac}.$$

For shell coordinates write $\mathbf p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ and $|\mathbf p|^2:=p_1^2+p_2^2+p_3^2$. For each future massive shell with $m>0$ in kg, $c>0$ in m/s, $p_0=-E/c$, and $E=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}$, or nonzero future null shell with $m=0$ and $|\mathbf p|>0$, its Poincare charges descend to the global ray quotient. For vectors $u,v\in\mathbb R^4$, define $(u\wedge v)^{ab}:=u^av^b-u^bv^a$. The induced dual action is $(P,J)\mapsto(\Lambda P,\Lambda J\Lambda^T+a\wedge\Lambda P)$. On the fixed-time slice $x^0=ct$, with physical position $q^i=x^i$, the boost component $B_i=J^{0i}=ct p_i-q^iE/c$ is explicitly time dependent and satisfies $\partial_tB_i+\{B_i,E\}=0$. These are mathematical identities; conservation is conditional on the stated free-shell evolution.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathfrak g^*$ be a
coadjoint orbit with its canonical immersed homogeneous-space structure and let
$\omega$ be the KKS form of
[[def-kirillov-kostant-souriau-form-on-a-coadjoint-orbit]]. Then $\omega$ is a
smooth, closed, nondegenerate two-form on $\mathcal O$, so $(\mathcal O,\omega)$
is a symplectic manifold. It is $G$-invariant, and the inclusion
$\Phi:\mathcal O\hookrightarrow\mathfrak g^*$ satisfies the component moment
equations $d\langle\Phi,\xi\rangle=-\iota_{\xi_{\mathcal O}}\omega$ for the
coadjoint action. It is the unique two-form on $\mathcal O$ for which the
inclusion is an infinitesimal moment map, hence in particular the unique
$G$-invariant symplectic form with that property.

derivations.claim: In the rest frame $P=(mc,0)$, the spatial components of $W$ are the three independent duals of $J^{ij}$, multiplied by the nonzero factor $mc$. Thus $|\mathbf W|=mcs$ and $W^0=0$, so $W\cdot P=0$ and $W^2=m^2c^2s^2$. Under translations, $J$ changes by $a\wedge P$; inserting this into $W$ adds an epsilon contraction with two copies of $P$, which vanishes by antisymmetry. Lorentz covariance of $\varepsilon$ under $SO^+$ and the charge action [L1] preserve these scalar identities over the orbit.

Any future timelike $P$ with $P^2=-m^2c^2$ can be sent to rest by a proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation. In that frame, choose the translation part $a$ to remove the three $J^{0i}$ components; the remaining spatial spin vector has norm $s$ by step 1.1, and a spatial rotation sends it to the specified $J^{12}=s$ axis. Therefore every pair with the stated invariants lies in the rest representative's orbit; the converse follows from step 1.1.

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. $$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. $$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.
