Assume $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ and let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold. A finite family of smooth functions $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ defined on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ is a **regular primary constraint family** on

$$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

On a prescribed background $(M,g,T)$, adopt a distinct massless classical particle model with fields $x:I\to M$, $p(\lambda)\in T^*_{x(\lambda)}M$, and a positive smooth multiplier $e(\lambda)>0$:

$$S_0[x,p,e]=\int_I\left[p_a x'^a-eC_0(x,p)\right]d\lambda,\qquad C_0=\tfrac12g^{ab}p_ap_b.$$

Variations of $p,e$ are independent; the physical branch is $p\ne0$, $p^\sharp$ future null. With all spacetime coordinates measured in metres and dimensionless λ, $p_a$ has units kg m/s, $C_0$ has units kg²m²/s² and $e$ has units s/kg, making the action J s. Other parameter units scale $e$ accordingly. This is a separate adopted model: null curves have no proper-time parameter, the model does not arise by setting $m=0$ in $P=mU$, and its positive momentum scale is additional initial data. On the nonzero branch, the vertical differential is $d_pC_0=p^\sharp\ne0$: nondegeneracy of $g^{-1}$ and $p\ne0$ give $p^\sharp\ne0$. Hence the shell is a regular primary constraint in the sense of [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. This postulate is not an empirical observation or a deduction from the massive model.

The cotangent phase-space carrier convention assumes countable choice ACω only; full choice is not assumed.

No completeness or global flow is asserted. If $H$ is smooth, each local time-$t$ flow map preserves ω.

Let $(M,g,T)$ be a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-+++)$. Work in a spacetime chart on a compact parameter interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$; take $x,p,e$ smooth on a neighbourhood of that interval, $e>0$, and $m\ge0$. Restrict to the future shell branch: when $m>0$, $p^\sharp$ is future timelike; when $m=0$, require $p\ne0$ and $p^\sharp$ future null. Set $C_m=\tfrac12(g^{ab}p_ap_b+m^2c^2)$ and define the first-order functional

$$I_m[x,p,e]=\int_a^b\left(p_ax'^a-eC_m(x,p)\right)d\lambda.$$

Take independent smooth variations of $p,e$ and fixed-endpoint variations of $x$. Stationarity on the chart segment is equivalent to

$$x'^a=e g^{ab}p_b,\quad p'_a=-\tfrac e2\partial_a g^{bc}p_bp_c,\quad C_m=0.$$

On the massive future branch $m>0$, these equations are equivalent to stationary paths of the square-root action in [[post-rpm-h-free-test-particle-action]]; the mechanical covector is $p=mc\,x'^\flat/\sqrt{-g(x',x')}$, and proper-time gauge has $e=1/m$. For the separate nonzero future-null branch $m=0$, the equations describe a null geodesic with an arbitrary positive parameter multiplier; no proper-time parameter exists. In both cases the unparameterized path is a geodesic, and no existence or completeness claim is made.

$$\Sigma_m^+=\{(x,p): -p_0=P^0=\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2},\ p_0<0\},$$

where $\mathbf p\ne0$ when $m=0$, and write $P^i=p_i$ for the spatial raised momentum components. The characteristic flow of the restricted canonical form is $(x,p)\mapsto(x+\alpha P,p)$, and its orbit space is globally diffeomorphic to $B_m=\mathbb R^3_a\times\mathbb R^3_p$ for $m>0$, or $\mathbb R^3_a\times(\mathbb R^3_p\setminus\{0\})$ for $m=0$, by

$$a^i=x^i-\frac{P^i}{P^0}x^0,\qquad p_i=p_i.$$

The reduced symplectic form is $da^i\wedge dp_i$. The quotient is Hausdorff and second countable and each full characteristic line meets each slice $x^0=ct$ exactly once. This is an explicit free flat quotient, not a conclusion about arbitrary first-class systems.

In affine Minkowski space with $x^0=ct$, let $m\ge0$, $p_i$ be spatial momentum components and $p_i\ne0$ for $m=0$. On the future shell, $p_0=-E/c$, where

$$E(\mathbf p)=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}.$$

On any compact interval $J=[t_1,t_2]$ of inertial time, the gauge $x^0=ct$ reduces the first-order shell action to

$$I_J=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(p_i\dot q^i-E(\mathbf p)\right)dt,\qquad q^i=x^i.$$

The gauge pair $C_m=0$, $\psi=x^0-ct=0$ is second class because $\{C_m,\psi\}=-P^0\ne0$ on the future shell; its Dirac reduction gives the canonical spatial bracket. The reduced Hamilton equations are $\dot q^i=c^2p_i/E$, $\dot p_i=0$, agreeing with the unreduced characteristic trajectories. On this full flat future shell every characteristic line meets each inertial-time slice once; this global assertion does not extend by this proof to a curved temporal chart.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(P,\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold with its induced Poisson bracket, and let $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ be a regular constraint family on a common zero surface $N=\{z:\chi_a(z)=0\}$ as defined by [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. The family is **first-class on $N$** when

$$\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}(z)=0\qquad\text{for every }z\in N\text{ and all }a,b.$$

Equivalently, each pairwise bracket is weakly zero in the notation $F\approx0$ of [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. The Poisson bracket convention is that of [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]. This definition is a pointwise closure condition on the stated regular surface; it does not assert multiplier-algorithm termination or global quotient regularity.

Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold as in [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]], and write its cotangent phase space in induced coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$. With $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$, define $X_H$ by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ and define the Poisson bracket by $\{F,G\}:=X_G(F)$. Then

$$X_H=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q^i}-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i},\qquad \{F,G\}=F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i}.$$

The bracket is coordinate independent and makes smooth functions a Poisson algebra. If $H_t$ is smooth on an open time-dependent domain $D\subset\mathbb R\times T^*Q$, each solution of $\dot z=X_{H_t}(z)$ has local uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial data and parameters; on its actual interval,

$$\frac{d}{dt}F(t,z(t))=\partial_tF+\{F,H_t\}.$$

No completeness or global flow is asserted. If $H$ is smooth, each local time-$t$ flow map preserves ω.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open interval and $(P,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold. Let $\chi_a:I\times P\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and suppose the covectors $d_z\chi_a(\lambda,z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in N_\lambda:=\{z:\chi_1(\lambda,z)=\cdots=\chi_r(\lambda,z)=0\}$; this is the regular constraint condition of [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]] on each slice. Let $H_c:I\times P\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth ambient extension of a specified descended Hamiltonian. Work in a Darboux chart with coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$ and local potential $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$, so $d\theta=-\omega$ under the convention $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$; paths stay in this chart.
For any compact interval $[a,b]\subset I$ with $a<b$, take paths $z:[a,b]\to P$ that extend smoothly to a neighborhood of $[a,b]$ and stay in the chart, and multipliers $u^a$ that extend smoothly to a neighborhood of $[a,b]$. Their action is

$$I[z,u]=\int_a^b\left[\theta(\dot z)-H_c(\lambda,z)-u^a(\lambda)\chi_a(\lambda,z)\right]d\lambda.$$

Use smooth one-parameter families of such $z$ with fixed endpoints, whose paths remain in the chart, and unrestricted smooth one-parameter variations of $u$. These classes satisfy the $C^2$ path and fixed-endpoint hypotheses of [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]]. They imply $z(\lambda)\in N_\lambda$ and $\dot z=X_{H_c(\lambda,\cdot)}+u^a(\lambda)X_{\chi_a(\lambda,\cdot)}$. A trajectory remains in the moving level set only when

$$\partial_\lambda\chi_a+\{\chi_a,H_c(\lambda,\cdot)\}+u^b(\lambda)\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}=0\quad\text{on }N_\lambda.$$

For constraints independent of $\lambda$, the first term is zero.

derivations.claim: The potential derivatives are $\partial_{x_1^a}V=2V'(r^2)r_a$ and $\partial_{x_2^a}V=-2V'(r^2)r_a$. The kinetic terms have $\partial_{p_i^a}C_i=P_i^a$. In $\{C_1,C_2\}$, the first particle contributes $-P_1^a(2V'r_a)$ and the second contributes $(-2V'r_a)P_2^a$; all other cross terms vanish. Their sum is the displayed bracket.

Choose $r=(0,R,0,0)$ with $R>0$, $V(z)=\lambda z$, and $\lambda>0$. Let $P_i^1=u_i>0$, other spatial components zero, and $P_i^0=\sqrt{m_i^2c^2+2\lambda R^2+u_i^2}$. Then $p_i^2=-(P_i^0)^2+u_i^2=-m_i^2c^2-2\lambda R^2$, so both $C_i=0$, while $r\cdot(P_1+P_2)=R(u_1+u_2)>0$. Each constraint differential has nonzero momentum component $P_i$ in its own cotangent factor, so $dC_1,dC_2$ are independent at this witness. Independence persists on a sufficiently small neighborhood, making the local joint level regular. The bracket is $\{C_1,C_2\}=-2\lambda R(u_1+u_2)\ne0$ there, so [F1] says the pair is not first-class on that local regular surface. With autonomous constraints and $H_c=0$, [L1] gives $\dot C_1=u^2\{C_1,C_2\}$ and $\dot C_2=u^1\{C_2,C_1\}$; hence preserving both constraints at this point forces $u^1=u^2=0$. Thus arbitrary independent nonzero multipliers need not preserve the joint surface.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary, of dimension $n$. Its cotangent bundle is

$$T^*Q=\coprod_{q\in Q}T_q^*Q,\qquad \pi:T^*Q\to Q,\quad \pi(q,p)=q,$$

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. The use of $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ is exactly the use in the smooth cotangent-bundle suppliers; no full Axiom of Choice is used.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ and let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold. A finite family of smooth functions $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ defined on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ is a **regular primary constraint family** on

$$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open interval and $(P,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold. Let $\chi_a:I\times P\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and suppose the covectors $d_z\chi_a(\lambda,z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in N_\lambda:=\{z:\chi_1(\lambda,z)=\cdots=\chi_r(\lambda,z)=0\}$; this is the regular constraint condition of [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]] on each slice. Let $H_c:I\times P\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth ambient extension of a specified descended Hamiltonian. Work in a Darboux chart with coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$ and local potential $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$, so $d\theta=-\omega$ under the convention $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$; paths stay in this chart.
For any compact interval $[a,b]\subset I$ with $a<b$, paths $z:[a,b]\to P$ that stay in the chart and smooth multipliers $u^a:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ have action

$$I[z,u]=\int_a^b\left[\theta(\dot z)-H_c(\lambda,z)-u^a(\lambda)\chi_a(\lambda,z)\right]d\lambda.$$

Fixed-endpoint variations of $z$ and unrestricted variations of $u$ imply $z(\lambda)\in N_\lambda$ and $\dot z=X_{H_c(\lambda,\cdot)}+u^a(\lambda)X_{\chi_a(\lambda,\cdot)}$. A trajectory remains in the moving level set only when

$$\partial_\lambda\chi_a+\{\chi_a,H_c(\lambda,\cdot)\}+u^b(\lambda)\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}=0\quad\text{on }N_\lambda.$$

For constraints independent of $\lambda$, the first term is zero.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $H\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb R)$ on an open set $U\subset\mathbb R\times T^*\mathbb R^n$, with coordinates $(t,q,p)$, and let $S_0\in C^\infty(Q_0,\mathbb R)$ on an open $Q_0\subset\mathbb R^n$. The Hamilton characteristic ODE is $\dot q^i=\partial H/\partial p_i$ and $\dot p_i=-\partial H/\partial q^i$. For a covector $p$ and vector $v$ in the canonical coordinates, write $p\cdot v:=\sum_i p_i v^i$. For each $a_0\in Q_0$ such that $(0,a_0,dS_0(a_0))\in U$, there are neighbourhoods of $(0,a_0)$ and a time interval on which this ODE with $q(0,a)=a$, $p(0,a)=dS_0(a)$ has a smooth solution and $(t,a)\mapsto(t,q(t,a))$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image after restriction. On that image the function

$$S(t,q(t,a))=S_0(a)+\int_0^t[p(u,a)\cdot\dot q(u,a)-H(u,q(u,a),p(u,a))],du$$

is smooth, has initial value $S_0$, and satisfies $S_t+H(t,q,S_q)=0$. The claim is local to the invertible projection domain; it asserts no continuation after a caustic. $S$ has action units, so $[S]=\mathrm{J\,s}$, $[S_q]=[p]$, and $[S_t]=\mathrm J$ when $t,q,p,H$ use SI time, length, momentum, and energy units.

In affine Minkowski space with $x^0=ct$, let $m\ge0$, $p_i$ be spatial momentum components and $p_i\ne0$ for $m=0$. On the future shell, $p_0=-E/c$, where

$$E(\mathbf p)=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}.$$

On any compact interval $J=[t_1,t_2]$ of inertial time with $t_1<t_2$, the gauge $x^0=ct$ reduces the first-order shell action to

$$I_J=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(p_i\dot q^i-E(\mathbf p)\right)dt,\qquad q^i=x^i.$$

For this variational statement, take $q^i$ and $p_i$ smooth on a neighborhood of $J$ and restrict to variations that are smooth one-parameter families, fix $q$ at both endpoints, and vary $p$ freely; in the massless case the paths and sufficiently small variations stay in $\mathbf p\ne0$. The resulting Hamilton equations hold on the interior of $J$.

The gauge pair $C_m=0$, $\psi=x^0-ct=0$ is second class because $\{C_m,\psi\}=-P^0\ne0$ on the future shell; its Dirac reduction gives the canonical spatial bracket. The reduced Hamilton equations are $\dot q^i=c^2p_i/E$, $\dot p_i=0$, agreeing with the unreduced characteristic trajectories. On this full flat future shell every characteristic line meets each inertial-time slice once; this global assertion does not extend by this proof to a curved temporal chart.

derivations.claim: Hamilton's equations from [L2] give $\dot p=0$, so $p(t,a)=S_0'(a)=-\kappa a$. Also $\dot q=E_p=c^2p/E$, hence integration with $q(0,a)=a$ gives the displayed formula.

Differentiate: $\partial_aq=1-t\kappa c^2\frac d{dp}(p/E)$. Since $E^2=m^2c^4+c^2p^2$, $\frac d{dp}(p/E)=m^2c^4/E^3$. Thus $\partial_aq=1-t\kappa m^2c^6/E^3$. Because $E\ge mc^2$, this is at least $1-t\kappa/m$, positive for $t<m/\kappa$. At $a=0$, $p=0$ and $E=mc^2$, so it equals zero at $t=m/\kappa$; this is the first singular point.

At that point $\partial_ap=-\kappa$. If a smooth graph $p=S_q(t,q(t,a))$ extended through it, the chain rule would give $\partial_ap=S_{qq}\partial_aq=0$, contradicting $-\kappa\ne0$. Hence no such smooth single-valued graph extension exists through that projection singularity.

Assume countable choice ACω, as in [[def-countable-choice]], for the smooth cotangent-bundle carrier convention used by this page; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $\mathcal D$ be an open subset of the time-dependent tangent bundle $\mathbb R\times TQ$ of a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $Q$, and let $L:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. For fixed $t$, the **fibre derivative** is the map

$$\mathbb F L(t,q,v)=(t,q,p),\qquad p(w)=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=0}L(t,q,v+sw),$$

as in [[def-fibre-derivative-and-legendre-transform-of-a-lagrangian]]. In induced coordinates $p_i=\partial L/\partial v^i$.

The Lagrangian is **regular** at $(t,q,v)$ when the velocity Hessian $(\partial^2L/\partial v^i\partial v^j)$ is invertible there; regularity gives only a local inverse branch. It is **hyperregular on a declared domain** when $\mathbb F L$ is a diffeomorphism from that entire domain onto an open subset of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$.

It is **almost regular on a declared domain $\mathcal D_0\subseteq\mathcal D$** when the following are all assumed: $\mathbb F L|_{\mathcal D_0}$ has constant rank; its image $N$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$; its corestriction $\mathcal D_0\to N$ is a surjective submersion (its differential is surjective at every point); and every fibre of that corestriction is connected. These hypotheses are not consequences of singularity alone.

Assume countable choice ACω, as in [[def-countable-choice]], for the smooth cotangent-bundle carrier convention used by this page; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Fix a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,T)$ with signature $(-+++)$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Here $T$ denotes the supplied smooth timelike field selecting the future cone, called $N$ in that geometric definition. Use the distinction among a spacetime, a worldline, a pointwise observer, an observer congruence, a tetrad and a chart given in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. This definition does not make $g$ dynamical.

In this relativistic-particle model, $m>0$ is a fixed **primitive mass parameter** measured in kilograms, and $c>0$ is a fixed **primitive conversion parameter** measured in metres per second. They are parameters of the adopted physical formulation, not quantities derived by this definition. Coordinates $x^a$ in an SI chart have length units; a cotangent vector $p=p_a\,dx^a$ has units of momentum, $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, when all four coordinates are in metres. The canonical one-form $p_a\,dx^a$ therefore has action units $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Along a future-directed timelike curve with tangent $V=dx/d\lambda$, set $s:=\sqrt{-g(V,V)}$; then $d\tau=s\,d\lambda/c$, independently of the increasing regular parameter. The length action $-mc\int s\,d\lambda$ has action units. For a future unit observer $n$ and future causal covector $p$, define the model normal-observer energy and spatial momentum covector by

$$E_n(p):=-c\,p(n),\qquad q_n(p):=p+p(n)n^\flat,$$

where $n^\flat=g(n,\cdot)$. The restriction of $g^{-1}$ to covectors annihilating $n$ is positive definite, so it supplies the norm of $q_n(p)$. These are quantity definitions and unit conventions; they do not identify canonical momentum with mechanical momentum, assert that an apparatus measured these values, or establish a dynamical law.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary, of dimension $n$. Its cotangent bundle is

$$T^*Q=\coprod_{q\in Q}T_q^*Q,\qquad \pi:T^*Q\to Q,\quad \pi(q,p)=q,$$

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. The use of $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ is exactly the use in the smooth cotangent-bundle suppliers; no full Axiom of Choice is used.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ and let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold. A finite family of smooth functions $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ defined on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ is a **regular primary constraint family** on

$$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

$$S_0[x,p,e]=\int_I\left[p_a x'^a-eC_0(x,p)\right]d\lambda,\qquad C_0=\tfrac12g^{ab}p_ap_b.$$

On the nonzero branch, the vertical differential is $d_pC_0=p^\sharp\ne0$: nondegeneracy of $g^{-1}$ and $p\ne0$ give $p^\sharp\ne0$. Hence the shell is a regular primary constraint in the sense of [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. This postulate is not an empirical observation or a deduction from the massive model.

Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold as in [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]], and write its cotangent phase space in induced coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$. With $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$, define $X_H$ by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ and define the Poisson bracket by $\{F,G\}:=X_G(F)$. Then

$$X_H=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q^i}-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i},\qquad \{F,G\}=F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i}.$$

The bracket is coordinate independent and makes smooth functions a Poisson algebra. If $H_t$ is smooth on an open time-dependent domain $D\subset\mathbb R\times T^*Q$, each solution of $\dot z=X_{H_t}(z)$ has local uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial data and parameters; on its actual interval,

$$\frac{d}{dt}F(t,z(t))=\partial_tF+\{F,H_t\}.$$

No completeness or global flow is asserted. If $H$ is smooth, each local time-$t$ flow map preserves ω.

Let $(M,g,T)$ be a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-+++)$. Work in a spacetime chart on a compact parameter interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$; take $x,p,e$ smooth on a neighbourhood of that interval, $e>0$, and $m\ge0$. Restrict to the future shell branch: when $m>0$, $p^\sharp$ is future timelike; when $m=0$, require $p\ne0$ and $p^\sharp$ future null. Set $C_m=\tfrac12(g^{ab}p_ap_b+m^2c^2)$ and define the first-order functional

$$I_m[x,p,e]=\int_a^b\left(p_ax'^a-eC_m(x,p)\right)d\lambda.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the cotangent/HJ supplier chain and let $n\ge1$. Let $U_H\subset\mathbb R\times T^*\mathbb R^n$ be open and $H\in C^\infty(U_H,\mathbb R)$. Let $D_S\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n_q\times\mathbb R^n_\alpha$ be open and $S\in C^3(D_S,\mathbb R)$, with $S_t+H(t,q,S_q)=0$ wherever $(t,q,\alpha)\in D_S$ and $(t,q,S_q(t,q,\alpha))\in U_H$. If the mixed matrix $S_{q\alpha}$ is invertible at $(t,q,\alpha)$, then after restricting neighborhoods the equations $p_i=S_{q^i}$, $\beta^i=S_{\alpha_i}$ define a local $C^2$ diffeomorphism $F_t:(q,p)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$ at each fixed $t$. Equip the old chart $(q,p)$ with $\omega_{\rm old}=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ and the target chart, whose position coordinates are $\beta^i$ and momentum coordinates are $\alpha_i$, with $\omega_{\rm new}=\sum_i d\beta^i\wedge d\alpha_i$. Then $F_t^*\omega_{\rm new}=\omega_{\rm old}$, so this is a local canonical transformation in the stated convention, and $\beta$ is constant along the Hamilton characteristics $\dot q=H_p$, $\dot p=-H_q$. Such a family is a complete integral only on that nonsingular local domain. In the physical interpretation, $q^i,\beta^i$ have units m, $p_i,\alpha_i$ have units kg m/s, $t$ has units s, and $S$ has units J s. In a temporal spacetime chart satisfying H9, the covariant future-shell equation $g^{ab}S_aS_b+m^2c^2=0$ reduces to the time Hamilton–Jacobi equation with $p_0=S_t/c=-H/c$; for $m=0$ require a nonzero future null covector. $S$ is an action, not a dimensionless phase.

For the relativistic shell equation, $m$ is measured in kilograms and $c$ in metres per second.

In affine Minkowski space with $x^0=ct$, let $m\ge0$, $p_i$ be spatial momentum components and $p_i\ne0$ for $m=0$. On the future shell, $p_0=-E/c$, where

$$E(\mathbf p)=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}.$$

On any compact interval $J=[t_1,t_2]$ of inertial time with $t_1<t_2$, the gauge $x^0=ct$ reduces the first-order shell action to

$$I_J=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(p_i\dot q^i-E(\mathbf p)\right)dt,\qquad q^i=x^i.$$

For this variational statement, take $q^i$ and $p_i$ smooth on a neighborhood of $J$ and restrict to variations that are smooth one-parameter families, fix $q$ at both endpoints, and vary $p$ freely; in the massless case the paths and sufficiently small variations stay in $\mathbf p\ne0$. The resulting Hamilton equations hold on the interior of $J$.

The gauge pair $C_m=0$, $\psi=x^0-ct=0$ is second class because $\{C_m,\psi\}=-P^0\ne0$ on the future shell; its Dirac reduction gives the canonical spatial bracket. The reduced Hamilton equations are $\dot q^i=c^2p_i/E$, $\dot p_i=0$, agreeing with the unreduced characteristic trajectories. On this full flat future shell every characteristic line meets each inertial-time slice once; this global assertion does not extend by this proof to a curved temporal chart.

derivations.claim: Differentiation gives $S_q=\alpha$, $S_t=-E(\alpha)$, and hence $S_t+E(S_q)=0$. Also $S_{q_i\alpha_j}=\delta_{ij}$, so its determinant is one. By [L1] this nonsingular family supplies local canonical integration coordinates on the stated domain.

Differentiating $E$ gives $\partial_{\alpha_i}E=c^2\alpha_i/E$ wherever $E>0$. Thus $\beta=S_\alpha=q-tc^2\alpha/E$ and rearranging yields the stated trajectory formula. For $m=0$, $E=c|\alpha|>0$ and differentiability requires $\alpha\ne0$, which is exactly the given domain.

The products $q\cdot\alpha$ and $tE$ have action units, while $\alpha$ is momentum and $\partial_\alpha S$ is length. Hence the generating function and canonical coordinates have the claimed physical dimensions.

Let $\mathcal D$ be an open subset of the time-dependent tangent bundle $\mathbb R\times TQ$ of a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $Q$, and let $L:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. For fixed $t$, the **fibre derivative** is the map

$$\mathbb F L(t,q,v)=(t,q,p),\qquad p(w)=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=0}L(t,q,v+sw),$$

as in [[def-fibre-derivative-and-legendre-transform-of-a-lagrangian]]. In induced coordinates $p_i=\partial L/\partial v^i$.

The Lagrangian is **regular** at $(t,q,v)$ when the velocity Hessian $(\partial^2L/\partial v^i\partial v^j)$ is invertible there; regularity gives only a local inverse branch. It is **hyperregular on a declared domain** when $\mathbb F L$ is a diffeomorphism from that entire domain onto an open subset of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$.

It is **almost regular on a declared domain $\mathcal D_0\subseteq\mathcal D$** when the following are all assumed: $\mathbb F L|_{\mathcal D_0}$ has constant rank; its image $N$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$; its corestriction $\mathcal D_0\to N$ is a surjective submersion (its differential is surjective at every point); and every fibre of that corestriction is connected. These hypotheses are not consequences of singularity alone.

$$E_n(p):=-c\,p(n),\qquad q_n(p):=p+p(n)n^\flat,$$

where $n^\flat=g(n,\cdot)$. The restriction of $g^{-1}$ to covectors annihilating $n$ is positive definite, so it supplies the norm of $q_n(p)$. $$T^*Q=\coprod_{q\in Q}T_q^*Q,\qquad \pi:T^*Q\to Q,\quad \pi(q,p)=q,$$

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. $$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

An **observer at an event** $p\in M$ is a future unit timelike vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. Its instantaneous rest space is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$. This is a pointwise vector-space construction; the definition does not assign a clock reading or a moving frame to a lone observer.

An **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth field of future unit timelike vectors on $U$, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]; its observer curves are its integral curves. A **tetrad** is a chosen orthonormal frame field, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **chart** is a coordinate map; an adapted chart is a chart whose spatial coordinates are constant along the congruence's integral curves. These objects are distinct: a chart need not be inertial, a tetrad need not be coordinate induced, and a congruence is a field of observers rather than a chart or a frame. This distinction agrees with [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]].

The coordinates and units used later are SI: in an inertial chart $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ are metres, $t$ is seconds, $c>0$ is metres per second, and proper time is measured in seconds. In a general chart, coordinate components inherit their coordinate units; invariant equations are tensorial. No global inertial chart, global tetrad, or global observer congruence is asserted to exist.

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Gamma=(V,E,s,t,\mathcal P)$ be a finite oriented graph with nonempty finite vertex set $V$, nonempty finite link set $E$, endpoint maps $s,t:E\to V$, and a finite list $\mathcal P$ of oriented simple cycles. Parallel links and self-loops are allowed. An oriented simple cycle $p\in\mathcal P$ is a finite closed path using each link at most once; write $\sigma_{p,e}\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for its signed use of link $e$, so its signed incidence at every vertex is zero. Fix enumerations $E=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_N)$ and $V=(v_1,\ldots,v_M)$, where $N=|E|$ and $M=|V|$. Write $\mathbb T_1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb T_{2\pi}=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$, and set $\mathbb T=\mathbb T_{2\pi}$ with normalized Haar measure $d\theta/(2\pi)$ and product measure $m_E$ on $\mathbb T^E$.

The coordinatewise map
$$\Phi_E:\mathbb T_{2\pi}^E\to\mathbb T_1^E,\qquad ([\theta_e])_{e\in E}\mapsto([\theta_e/(2\pi)])_{e\in E},$$
is a well-defined measure-preserving group isomorphism for the normalized product Haar measures. The fixed enumeration of $E$ identifies $\mathbb T_1^E$ with $\mathbb T_1^N$; pulling back the Fourier characters $x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\sum_{e\in E}n_ex_e)$ along $\Phi_E$ gives $e_{\mathbf n}(\theta)=\exp(i\sum_{e\in E}n_e\theta_e)$. Thus the Fourier basis theorem [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], whose torus is $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and whose characters are $\exp(2\pi i kx)$, gives an orthonormal basis $\{e_{\mathbf n}:\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^E\}$ of $L^2(\mathbb T^E)$. The second-variable-linear $L^2$ pairing used below is the conjugate of the first-variable-linear pairing in that theorem, so orthonormality and completeness are unchanged.

Fix an integer $s\ge1$ and let $\mathcal K=\bigoplus_{x\in V}\mathbb C^s$ with orthonormal modes $e_{x\alpha}$, $1\le\alpha\le s$. This is finite-dimensional and hence separable. Fix the lexicographic order on $J=V\times\{1,\ldots,s\}$ induced by the chosen order on $V$ and the usual order on $\{1,\ldots,s\}$. Use the antisymmetric Fock space and second-variable-linear inner product convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The current draft supplier [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] states that, assuming Countable Choice, $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$ is a Hilbert space and its creation and annihilation operators are bounded and satisfy the CAR; that supplier is still a draft carrier, not an accepted result in this run. For $\mathbf m=(m_{x\alpha})\in\{0,1\}^J$, put $S(\mathbf m)=\{(x,\alpha):m_{x\alpha}=1\}$ and write $\xi_{\mathbf m}=\xi_{S(\mathbf m)}$ for the ordered wedge basis vector of [[lem-qft-finite-mode-occupation-basis]]. This is a complete orthonormal basis of $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$; changing the chosen order changes individual wedge vectors only by signs. Write $c_{x\alpha}=c(e_{x\alpha})$, $c^\dagger_{x\alpha}=c^\dagger(e_{x\alpha})$, and $n_x=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s c^\dagger_{x\alpha}c_{x\alpha}$. On $\xi_{\mathbf m}$, $n_x$ acts by $N_x(\mathbf m)=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}$; it is bounded self-adjoint with spectrum contained in $\{0,\ldots,s\}$.

Use the second-variable-linear $L^2$ pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb T^E}\overline{f(\theta)}g(\theta)\,dm_E(\theta)$. The kinematical Hilbert space is
$$\mathcal H_{\rm kin}=L^2(\mathbb T^E)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K),$$
where $\widehat\otimes$ has the same completion norm as [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] and the second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating its first-variable-linear tensor pairing, as in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Concretely, the tensor supplier is applied to the conjugate first-variable-linear pairings $(f,g)_1=\langle g,f\rangle_2$ and $(\Phi,\Psi)_1=\langle\Psi,\Phi\rangle_2$, and the resulting tensor pairing is conjugated; this preserves the norm and the product-basis assertion. Consequently
$$\{e_{\mathbf n}\otimes\xi_{\mathbf m}:\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^E,\ \mathbf m\in\{0,1\}^J\}$$

derivations.claim: The finite-support linear combinations of the joint basis vectors are dense in $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$. On each joint basis vector, $G_x$ multiplies by the real number $\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)$. The maximal diagonal operator is self-adjoint: if $\phi\in D(G_x^*)$ and $G_x^*\phi=\eta$, testing the adjoint identity against each basis vector gives $\eta_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}=\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)\phi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}$. Every $G_x$ is diagonal in the same basis. Thus the spectral projections of any two $G_x$ are diagonal coordinate projections and commute, which proves strong commutation. On a basis vector, $U(\alpha)$ multiplies by $e^{i\sum_x\alpha_x\gamma_x}$; integer $\gamma_x$ makes it $2\pi$-periodic in each coordinate, and the diagonal phases give $U(\alpha+\beta)=U(\alpha)U(\beta)$ and $U(0)=I$.

For finite linear combinations of basis vectors, $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$ is a finite sum of continuous characters. Such vectors are dense and all $U(\alpha)$ have norm one, so for arbitrary $\psi$ approximation by a finite combination proves norm continuity of $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$. derivations.claim: In the joint basis, $H_0$ multiplies coefficients by the real nonnegative number $h(\mathbf n)=\lambda_E\sum_e n_e^2$. If $\phi\in D(H_0^*)$ with $H_0^*\phi=\eta$, testing against each basis vector gives $\eta_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}=h(\mathbf n)\phi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}$, so $\eta\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$ forces $\sum h(\mathbf n)^2|\phi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty$ and $\phi\in D(H_0)$. Conversely that weighted square summability and Cauchy–Schwarz give the adjoint identity. Hence $H_0^*=H_0$. Truncating a vector to finite subsets of the joint basis converges both in norm and in the $H_0$ graph norm, so finite sums are a graph core.

Every $W_p$ is unitary, so $\|W_p+W_p^\dagger\|\le2$ and $W_p+W_p^\dagger$ is self-adjoint. Each CAR operator has norm at most one by the conditional supplier in [F1]; every displayed fermion/link term is a finite sum of products of bounded operators, and pairing each term with its adjoint makes $V_F$ self-adjoint. Since the graph, plaquette list, site modes, and matrices are all finite-dimensional or finite in number, $V$ is bounded and self-adjoint.

Let $\beta>\|V\|$ and $z=\pm i\beta$. The diagonal resolvent $R_0(z)=(H_0-z)^{-1}$ satisfies $\|R_0(z)\|\le1/\beta$, and $$H-z=(I+VR_0(z))(H_0-z).$$ The Neumann series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-VR_0(z))^k$ converges in operator norm because $\|VR_0(z)\|<1$, so $I+VR_0(z)$ is onto and invertible. Thus both $H-i\beta$ and $H+i\beta$ are onto $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$.

On $D(H_0)$, $H$ is densely defined and symmetric because $H_0$ and $V$ are. To prove self-adjointness directly, take $y\in D(H^*)$ and choose $x\in D(H)$ with $(H+i\beta)x=(H^*+i\beta)y$, using the surjectivity from step 3.1. Then $y-x\in\ker(H^*+i\beta)=\operatorname{Ran}(H-i\beta)^\perp=\{0\}$, again by step 3.1. Therefore $D(H^*)\subseteq D(H)$; symmetry gives the reverse inclusion and $H=H^*$. Its domain is exactly the original $D(H_0)$ because the sum with bounded $V$ was defined there.

Each $U(\alpha)$ is diagonal in the same Fourier/occupation basis as $H_0$, so it preserves $D(H_0)$ and commutes with $H_0$. The link relation $[E_e,U_e]=U_e$ and the CAR relation $[n_x,c_{y\beta}]=-\delta_{xy}c_{y\beta}$ give $U(\alpha)U_eU(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{i(\alpha_{s(e)}-\alpha_{t(e)})}U_e$ and $U(\alpha)c_{x\beta}U(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{i\alpha_x}c_{x\beta}$. A cycle's link phases telescope to $1$; in a hopping term the phases multiply to $e^{-i\alpha_{s(e)}}e^{i(\alpha_{s(e)}-\alpha_{t(e)})}e^{i\alpha_{t(e)}}=1$, and each onsite bilinear has phase $e^{-i\alpha_x}e^{i\alpha_x}=1$. Therefore $U(\alpha)VU(\alpha)^\dagger=V$ and $U(\alpha)HU(\alpha)^\dagger=H$ on $D(H_0)$.

derivations.claim: Since $H$ is self-adjoint, $T=-H/\hbar$ is self-adjoint. Stone's theorem [F3] gives $\mathcal U(t)=e^{itT}=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ as a strongly continuous unitary group with the stated derivative at $t=0$ and exact generator domain $D(H)$.

For $x\in D(H)$ and fixed $t$, the difference quotient at zero for $\mathcal U(h)\mathcal U(t)x=\mathcal U(t)\mathcal U(h)x$ equals $\mathcal U(t)(\mathcal U(h)x-x)/h$ and converges to $-i\mathcal U(t)Hx/\hbar$. The exact domain characterization in [F3] therefore gives $\mathcal U(t)x\in D(H)$ and $H\mathcal U(t)x=\mathcal U(t)Hx$.

For each $\alpha$, the conjugated family $V_\alpha(t)=U(\alpha)\mathcal U(t)U(\alpha)^\dagger$ is a strongly continuous unitary group. By [F2], its generator is $-iH/\hbar$ on exactly $D(H)$, the same generator as $\mathcal U(t)$. Uniqueness in Stone's theorem gives $V_\alpha(t)=\mathcal U(t)$ for every $t$.

Averaging the commutation $U(\alpha)\mathcal U(t)=\mathcal U(t)U(\alpha)$ over normalized Haar measure gives $P\mathcal U(t)=\mathcal U(t)P$. Thus $\mathcal U(t)$ and its inverse preserve $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, and the restricted group is unitary and strongly continuous on that closed Hilbert subspace.

For $x\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, the restricted difference quotient is the same norm limit as in $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$. It exists exactly when $x\in D(H)$ by [F3]; therefore the restricted group generator has domain $D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ and is $-iH/\hbar$ there. Stone's theorem on $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ identifies its self-adjoint Stone operator as $-H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}/\hbar$. Since multiplication by the nonzero real scalar $-\hbar$ preserves self-adjointness, the restricted physical Hamiltonian is self-adjoint.

Adopt the postulates [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]],
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]],
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]] and
[[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] of the classical gravitational
framework, with the field law in its direct-equation presentation and the unit
conventions of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let
$(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*>0$ with
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and static congruence
$n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), and let the model's stress-energy
tensor be the vacuum prescription

$$T:=0\qquad\text{on }M,\qquad \Lambda:=0 .$$

Then all statements below are conditional deductions inside the model so
specified; they assert nothing about nature.

**(a) The Schwarzschild vacuum model.** $(M,g,N)$ satisfies the spacetime
postulate, $T=0$ is a smooth symmetric stress-energy tensor field on the
matter domain $M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]], the
prescription is admissible, and the adopted field law
$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds identically on $M$. A **vacuum solution with zero cosmological parameter** here means
precisely a datum satisfying that equation with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$;
this datum is such a solution, read as a model of the framework. The model is not locally flat: its curvature tensor is nowhere
zero, while its Ricci tensor and Einstein tensor vanish identically
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]] clause (d)).

**(b) Static clock readings.** The integral curves of $n$ are the static
observer worldlines at constant radius $r_0$
([[lem-gr-schwarzschild-static-congruence-and-clock-rates]] clause (b));
adopting the clock rule of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]] clause (i),
the reading difference of an ideal clock carried along such a worldline
between two events whose coordinate times differ by $\Delta t$ is

$$\Delta\tau=\sqrt{f(r_0)}\,\Delta t=\sqrt{1-\frac{s}{r_0}}\;\Delta t,$$

so two static clocks at radii $r_1,r_2$ compared over the same coordinate
interval with $\Delta t\ne0$ satisfy $\Delta\tau_1/\Delta\tau_2=\sqrt{f(r_1)/f(r_2)}$. The static
worldlines are not geodesics: their acceleration is
$a=\frac{s}{2r^2}\partial_r\ne0$, so the model assigns them to accelerated
(constrained) bodies and not to freely falling ones.

**(c) The mass parameter.** The parameter $m_*$ enters the model only through
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and through the quantities below; the framework reads $m_*$ as
the mass parameter of the model in kilograms
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]] clause (a),
[[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]] clause (a)):

1. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth future timelike geodesic, parametrized
   by proper time $\tau$ on an interval with nonempty interior, with
   $r\circ\gamma\equiv r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. Put $\sigma:=\iota\circ\gamma:I\to S^2$
   and $t:=(x^0\circ\gamma)/c$. Its **angular speed with respect to $t$** is
   $\Omega:=\sqrt{\gamma_{S^2}(d\sigma/dt,d\sigma/dt)}$, where
   $d\sigma/dt:=\sigma'(\tau)/t'(\tau)$ and $t'(\tau)>0$ by future
   timelikeness. It has units $\mathrm s^{-1}$ and satisfies
   $\Omega^2=G_Nm_*/r_0^3$ in every angular orientation. For an equatorial
   curve, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and $\Omega^2=(d\varphi/dt)^2$ in local polar

   clause (a) and proof step 2.2). This is the Kepler-like law in which
   $m_*$ plays the role of the central mass;
2. in the isotropic chart of
   [[lem-gr-schwarzschild-isotropic-coordinate-form]], with
   $a=s/(4\rho)$, the exact identity
   $g_{00}+1=1-\bigl((1-a)/(1+a)\bigr)^2=4a/(1+a)^2$ gives
   $$g_{00}+1=+\frac{s}{\rho}+O(\rho^{-2})=+\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2\rho}+O(\rho^{-2}).$$
   Under the weak-field convention $g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)$ to leading order

The reading is a statement about the model's own identities and the adopted
unit and weak-field conventions; no numerical value of $G_N$ or $m_*$, no
Newtonian source model realized by matter and no comparison with any reported

**(d) Scope.** The model is an idealized vacuum model of the framework, not a
claim about the actual universe: no observation, apparatus, calibration or

interpretation of coordinates, clocks and bodies remains the adopted one of

Adopt as physical assumptions of the classical gravitational framework, in
addition to [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and the matter-content
assumptions of the framework, the following rules by which ideal clocks, test
bodies and light couple to the metric $g$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** An **ideal clock** is an idealized physical device
carried along a future timelike worldline ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]])
whose readings are assumed to reproduce the proper time of that worldline:
the difference of two readings taken at two events of the worldline is the
proper-time increment between those events as defined by the metric, and it is
independent of the construction of the clock. Two ideal clocks moving along
the same worldline differ only by an additive constant (their choice of zero);
different worldlines generally accrue different proper times between the same
pair of events. The physical constant $c$ and the unit of duration are those
of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(ii) Free fall of massive test bodies.** A **test body** is an uncharged
idealized body whose internal structure is small compared with the scale over
which the geometry of the model varies and whose gravitational self-field is
negligible within the model. An **ideal freely falling massive test body** is
assumed to have a worldline that is a future timelike geodesic of the
metric-selected connection ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]), traversed with physical
four-velocity $U=d\gamma/d\tau$ satisfying

worldline ([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]). The
worldline is determined by the event at which the body is released together
with its four-velocity there, by the uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value
problem ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]); no force, charge, or
rest mass of the body enters this rule.

**(iii) Light rays.** In the geometric-optics approximation an **ideal light
ray** propagating in the model is assumed to be a future null geodesic of the
metric-selected connection
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]). A null worldline carries no proper
time and no four-velocity in the sense of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]; within the approximation the
propagation of an ideal ray is independent of its frequency, and only the
ray's direction in the tangent space is fixed, not a scale along it.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** The three rules are adopted in the test-field
regime of the smooth classical model: the clocks, bodies and rays do not
back-react on the geometry, and the geometry varies smoothly on the scales
relevant to them. Configurations requiring the body's own gravitational field,
radiation reaction, an electromagnetic or other self-force, finite-size or
tidal couplings beyond the test-body idealization, non-geometric-optics
propagation, dispersion or dissipation of light, or quantum effects are
outside these assumptions and require additional model content. The
assumptions do not assert that any real clock, body or light ray is exactly
ideal, nor do they attach measured readings to any model.

[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-timelike-geodesic-reduction]]; it is a **circular
orbit** at radius $r_0$. Its angular velocity in the coordinate $x^0$ is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\Bigl(\frac{s}{2r_0^3}\Bigr)^{1/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\Bigr)^2=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r_0^3},$$

$t=x^0/c$.

**(b) The circular-orbit condition is necessary.** Conversely, if
$\gamma:I\to M$ is any future timelike geodesic parametrized by proper time with
$r(\tau)\equiv r_0>s$ constant on an interval of positive length, then
$r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. If $\gamma$ is equatorial, its conserved angular
momentum additionally satisfies $\ell^2=\dfrac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}$.
Consequently no timelike circular geodesic, in any angular orientation, exists
with $s<r_0\le\frac{3s}{2}$.

**(c) Stability threshold of the radial potential.** For each radius
$r>\frac{3s}{2}$ set $\ell_r^2:=c^2sr^2/(2r-3s)$ and regard $\ell_r$ as a
constant in the function $V_{\ell_r}(x):=\tfrac12 f(x)(c^2+\ell_r^2/x^2)$.
Differentiate with respect to $x$ at fixed $\ell_r$, then evaluate at $x=r$.
The result, evaluated at the circular value $\ell_r$, is

$$V_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)},\qquad r>\frac{3s}{2},$$

so $V_\ell$ has a strict local minimum at the circular-orbit radius exactly
for $r>3s$, a strict local maximum exactly for $\frac{3s}{2}<r<3s$, and
$V_\ell''(3s)=0$; the radius $r=3s$ is the **innermost stable circular orbit
radius** of the restricted model in this potential sense.

**(d) The photon sphere at $r=3s/2$.** Let $\ell\neq0$ and put
$r_0=\frac{3s}{2}$ and $e_0:=\dfrac{\lvert\ell\rvert\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0}=\dfrac{2\lvert\ell\rvert}{3\sqrt3\,s}>0$.
Then the globally defined curve
$$\eta(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e_0}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr),\qquad \tau\in\mathbb R,$$
whose local polar expressions have $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and longitude
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to chart shifts, is a future null geodesic (a
**null circular orbit** or **photon sphere**
orbit) with conserved quantities $e_0=-g(\eta',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\eta',\Phi)$, and its angular velocity is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e_0}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\,\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0},\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}\Bigr)^2=\frac{f(r_0)}{r_0^2}=\frac{4}{27s^2}.$$

The **null effective potential** $W^{\mathrm n}_\ell(r):=f(r)\ell^2/r^2$
satisfies $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)'(3s/2)=0$ and
$(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)''(3s/2)=-\dfrac{32\ell^2}{81s^4}<0$, so the photon-sphere
radius is a strict local maximum of the null potential.

**(e) Scope.** All statements are exact data of the restricted model: the
orbits are ideal geodesics of the metric on the exterior domain, the
stability claim is the sign of the second derivative of the stated potential,
and no claim is made about nonlinear stability, about orbital decay, about
observations or about the interior region. The case $r_0=s$ is excluded, and
the reduction is stated only where $r>s$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. Consider the autonomous first-order system

$$z'(t)=F(z(t)),$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with $D=\mathbb R\times U$ and right-hand side $(t,z)\mapsto F(z)$. A **solution** below means a solution of this system on an interval containing $0$; a solution whose interval is $[0,\infty)$ or contains it is said to be **defined for all $t\ge0$**.

A solution $\tilde z:J\to U$ **extends** $z:I\to U$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $\tilde z|_I=z$; the extension is proper if $I\subsetneq J$. A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]). All stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions whose intervals contain $0$; their local restrictions remain solutions. This convention asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of maximal solutions for an arbitrary map $F$.

A point $z_*\in U$ is an **equilibrium** (also **fixed point** or **zero**) of $F$ when $F(z_*)=0$; then the constant function $z(t)=z_*$ is a solution on every interval containing $0$.

Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium.

1. $z_*$ is **Lyapunov stable** (or simply **stable**) when for every Euclidean ball $B_\varepsilon(z_*)$ with $\overline{B_\varepsilon(z_*)}\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t)-z_*\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

2. $z_*$ is **asymptotically stable** when it is Lyapunov stable and in addition there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|z(t)-z_*\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

An equilibrium which is not Lyapunov stable is **unstable**. An equilibrium is **globally asymptotically stable** when it is asymptotically stable and every maximal solution of the system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to it as $t\to\infty$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the reduced vector field is $F_\ell(r,w)=(w,-W_\ell'(r)/2)$ on the open set $(s,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. It is smooth there and [F4] gives a unique local solution through every state. Differentiating $W_\ell=f(c^2+\ell^2/r^2)$ gives $W_\ell'=c^2s/r^2-2\ell^2/r^3+3s\ell^2/r^4$; substituting the circular value of $\ell^2$ from [F2] yields $W_\ell'(r_c)=0$, so $F_\ell(r_c,0)=0$. Along every solution, $H_\ell(r,w):=\tfrac12(w^2+W_\ell(r))$ satisfies $dH_\ell/d\tau=w(-W_\ell'/2)+(W_\ell'/2)w=0$. Thus $H_\ell$ is constant on each solution interval.

Suppose $r_c>3s$. By [F2], $W_\ell''(r_c)>0$, so continuity gives an interval about $r_c$ on which $W_\ell''>0$. Since $W_\ell'(r_c)=0$, the derivative is negative to the left and positive to the right there; hence $W_\ell$ has a strict local minimum. Fix any phase-space radius $\varepsilon>0$ whose closed ball about $z_c$ lies in $(s,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Choose $0<\eta<\varepsilon/2$ so $[r_c-\eta, r_c+\eta]\subset(s,\infty)$ and both boundary values of $W_\ell$ exceed $W_\ell(r_c)$. By continuity of $H_\ell$, choose $0<\delta\le\varepsilon$ so every state within $\delta$ of $z_c$ has $|r-r_c|<\eta/2$, energy below both boundary potential halves, and $H_\ell-W_\ell(r_c)/2<\varepsilon^2/8$. Conservation in 1.1 prevents such a solution from reaching either radial boundary, since there $H_\ell\ge W_\ell(r_c\pm\eta)/2$. Inside the resulting radial interval $W_\ell(r)\ge W_\ell(r_c)$, so $w^2/2=H_\ell-W_\ell(r)/2<\varepsilon^2/8$ and $|w|<\varepsilon/2$. The state stays in a compact subset of the open domain; [F5] rules out a finite forward maximal endpoint. With $|r-r_c|<\eta<\varepsilon/2$ and $|w|<\varepsilon/2$, it remains inside the prescribed phase-space ball for every $\tau\ge0$. This is Lyapunov stability by [F3].

Suppose $3s/2<r_c<3s$. By [F2], $W_\ell''(r_c)<0$; shrink $\eta>0$ so $W_\ell'(r)<0$ on $(r_c,r_c+\eta]$. For any proposed initial-state radius $\delta>0$, choose $r_0\in(r_c,r_c+\min\{\eta/2,\delta/2\})$ and initial data $(r_0,0)$. [F4] supplies a local solution. Its acceleration is $-W_\ell'(r_0)/2>0$, and conservation of $H_\ell$ gives, on the outgoing branch, $w=\sqrt{W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)}$. The solution reaches $r_c+\eta$ in finite time: the travel-time integral is $\int_{r_0}^{r_c+\eta}[W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)]^{-1/2}dr$, whose only endpoint singularity is bounded by a constant times $(r-r_0)^{-1/2}$ because $W_\ell'(r_0)<0$. Hence initial data arbitrarily close to $z_c$ leave the fixed neighborhood of radius $\eta$, contradicting [F3].

At $r_c=3s$, the circular relation gives $\ell^2=3c^2s^2$. Differentiating $W_\ell(r)=c^2(1-s/r)+\ell^2(r^{-2}-sr^{-3})$ at this fixed $\ell$ gives $W_\ell'(r)=c^2s(r-3s)^2/r^4$ and $W_\ell''(r)=-2c^2s(r-3s)(r-6s)/r^5$. Thus $W_\ell'$ is positive except at $3s$ and $W_\ell''$ changes sign there, so the equilibrium is a stationary inflection. Fix $0<\eta<s$ and, for any $\delta>0$, choose $r_0\in(3s-\min\{\eta/2,\delta/2\},3s)$ with initial data $(r_0,0)$. [F4] supplies a local solution. The acceleration is negative. On the inward branch energy conservation yields $w=-\sqrt{W_\ell(r_0)-W_\ell(r)}$ for $3s-\eta\le r<r_0$, since $W_\ell$ is strictly increasing on that interval. The travel-time integral to $3s-\eta$ is finite; near $r_0$ its integrand is bounded by a constant times $(r_0-r)^{-1/2}$ because $W_\ell'(r_0)>0$. Thus arbitrarily close initial data leave the fixed neighborhood of radius $\eta$, so [F3] says the equilibrium is not Lyapunov stable.

The two subcritical cases in 2.2–2.3 are not Lyapunov stable, while the supercritical case in 2.1 is Lyapunov stable. These are deductions under the adopted Schwarzschild free-fall model [A1] and concern only its fixed-angular-momentum radial subsystem.
