Let $m,c,\kappa>0$, let $x,p\in\mathbb R^3$, and set

$$D:=(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R^3,\qquad r:=|x|,\qquad \mathcal E(p):=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|p|^2}.$$

The **repulsive relativistic Coulomb Hamiltonian** is

$$H(x,p):=\mathcal E(p)+\frac{\kappa}{r},$$

and its **phase system** is the autonomous ODE on the open set $D$

$$\dot x=\nabla_pH=\frac{c^2p}{\mathcal E(p)},\qquad \dot p=-\nabla_xH=\frac{\kappa x}{r^3}.$$

Here the system parameter $t$ is time in seconds and dot denotes $d/dt$; $m$ is a positive mass parameter (kilograms in the SI interpretation), $c$ a positive speed parameter (metres per second), and $\kappa$ a positive energy-times-length parameter (joule-metres). Define the radial momentum $p_r:=x\cdot p/r$ and angular-momentum vector $J:=x\times p$. A trajectory is a $C^1$ solution of this ODE on an interval; maximality is in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]].

This is only a mathematical phase system. Its physical interpretation as a charged particle in an externally prescribed Coulomb field requires separate model assumptions.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)\cap[t_0,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

The restriction

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

is continuous, strictly increasing, and bijective.

Sine is differentiable, hence continuous, and strictly increasing on
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; its endpoint values are $-1$ and $1$
([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],
[[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]), let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and injective
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and let $g : f[I] \to I$ be the
inverse of $f : I \to f[I]$ supplied by [[thm-continuous-inverse]]. Let
$c \in I$ and put $b := f(c)$.

Then $c$ is a limit point of $I$ and $b$ is a limit point of $f[I]$, so that
$f'(c)$ and $g'(b)$ are meaningful symbols ([[def-derivative]]), and, assuming
$f$ is differentiable at $c$:

1. if $f'(c) \ne 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $b$ and
   $$g'(b) \;=\; \frac{1}{f'(c)} ;$$
2. if $f'(c) = 0$, then $g$ is **not** differentiable at $b$.

**The two claims together say that the inverse inherits differentiability
exactly where the derivative does not vanish.** Nothing is asserted at a point
of $f[I]$ that is not of the form $f(c)$ with $f$ differentiable at $c$, and
nothing is asserted about $g$ being differentiable *on* a set.

**No compactness and no boundedness is assumed.** $I$ may be open, half-open or
unbounded; all that is used of it is order-convexity and the presence of two
distinct points, the latter being exactly what makes every point of $I$ a limit
point of $I$ ([[def-derivative]]).

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words
*nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of
[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.
4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on
   $I$.

Conversely, with no continuity hypothesis and no hypothesis at any other point:

5. If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing on $I$ and differentiable at a
   point $c \in I$ that is a limit point of $I$, then $f'(c) \ge 0$; if $f$ is
   nonincreasing and differentiable at such a $c$, then $f'(c) \le 0$.

**No strict converse is claimed here, and none is true.** Claim 5 gives the
weak inequality only, and it cannot be improved: an increasing function may have
a vanishing derivative at a point. That failure is recorded separately, as a
false statement later on this page, with its witness worked out on the companion
page. Reading claim 2 backwards is the single most common misuse of this
theorem, and this statement does not license it.

**Claims 1 to 4 need the interval; claim 5 does not.** The forward direction
runs through the mean value theorem on a segment joining two points of $I$, so
order-convexity is essential. Claim 5 is a statement about one point and uses
only that the difference quotients have a constant sign.

The limit over nonzero real $x$ is

$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1.$$

derivations.claim:
Along any solution of [F1], $\dot H=
abla_xH\cdot\dot x+
abla_pH\cdot\dot p=
abla_xH\cdot
abla_pH-
abla_pH\cdot
abla_xH=0,$ and $\dot J=\dot x	imes p+x	imes\dot p=0$ because $\dot x$ is parallel to $p$ and $\dot p$ is parallel to $x$. Thus $W$ and $J$ are constant. With $u=1/r$, the energy relation gives $\mathcal E=W-\kappa u$, so $c^2|p|^2=(W-\kappa u)^2-m^2c^4,$ and $|p|^2=p_r^2+J^2/r^2$. Rearranging yields $p_r^2=A-2du-Cu^2=Q(u)$.

Since $Q(0)=A>0$ and $Q((W-mc^2)/\kappa)=-J^2((W-mc^2)/\kappa)^2<0$, continuity gives a positive root below $(W-mc^2)/\kappa$. The other root is negative because the product of the roots is $-A/C<0$, so the positive root is unique. The quadratic formula gives the displayed $u_*$; $Q'(u_*)=-2(d+Cu_*)<0$, hence the root is simple. At this root $\mathcal E=W-\kappa u_*>mc^2$, so the momentum is real and the point lies in $D$.

Choose $x=r_*e_1$ and $p=(J/r_*)e_2$ at the turning point. The root equation in 2.1 gives $H(x,p)=W$, and [F2] gives a local solution. At the turn, direct differentiation gives $\dot p_r=c^2J^2/(\mathcal E r^3)+\kappa/r^2>0$, so $p_r$ changes from negative to positive. Since $p_r^2=Q(1/r)$ and 2.1 gives the unique positive root, $p_r$ cannot vanish again; consequently $r$ decreases on the incoming tail and increases on the outgoing tail. On every allowed state $0<u\le u_*<(W-mc^2)/\kappa$, hence $r\ge r_*$ and $mc^2<\mathcal E=W-\kappa u<W$, which gives $|p|<\sqrt A$. The force and velocity are bounded; on every finite time interval $x$ remains bounded and $|x|\ge r_*$, so the state stays in a compact subset of $D$ and [F2] extends it past every finite endpoint. Each monotone radial tail must be unbounded: if it had a finite limit greater than $r_*$, then $Q(1/r)$ and $\mathcal E$ would give $|\dot r|$ a positive lower bound, contradicting that finite limit. Thus $r\to\infty$ on both tails and $\dot r=c^2p_r/\mathcal E\to\pm c^2\sqrt A/W$, so $r$ grows linearly there. Then $|\dot p|=\kappa/r^2$ is integrable, and $p$ converges to incoming and outgoing limits of magnitude $\sqrt A$. Since the tangential momentum has magnitude $J/r\to0$, the limiting momenta point along the limiting radial directions, establishing the two asymptotes.

Orient the orbital plane so its polar angle increases with $J=|x\times p|$. Then $\dot\varphi=c^2J/(\mathcal E r^2)$ and $\dot r=c^2p_r/\mathcal E$, so $|d\varphi/du|=J/\sqrt{Q(u)}$ and the half-angle is $\Delta=\int_0^{u_*}J\,du/\sqrt{A-2du-Cu^2}$. Completing the square gives $Q=(d^2+CA)/C-C(u+d/C)^2$. With $y=(Cu+d)/\sqrt{d^2+CA}$, the root relation in 2.1 makes the endpoints $d/\sqrt{d^2+CA}$ and $1$, and the integral becomes $(J/\sqrt C)\int dy/\sqrt{1-y^2}=(J/\sqrt C)[\arcsin y]_{d/\sqrt{d^2+CA}}^1$. Put $\alpha=\arctan(\sqrt{CA}/d)\in(0,\pi/2)$. Since $\tan\alpha=\sqrt{CA}/d$, the Pythagorean identity and positivity of sine and cosine in [F3] give $\cos\alpha=d/\sqrt{d^2+CA}$; the quarter-turn identity then gives $\arcsin(d/\sqrt{d^2+CA})=\pi/2-\alpha$ because both angles lie in $[0,\pi/2]$. The evaluated integral is therefore $\Delta=(J/\sqrt C)\arctan(\sqrt{CA}/d)$.

Put $\alpha=\kappa/(cJ)\in(0,1)$, $q=\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\in(0,1)$, and $\beta=\sqrt{1-m^2c^4/W^2}\in(0,1)$. If $a=\arcsin q$, then [F3] gives $a\in(0,\pi/2)$, $\sin a=q$, and $\cos a=\sqrt{1-q^2}>0$; hence $\tan a=q/\sqrt{1-q^2}$ and the principal inverse identity gives $a=\arctan(q/\sqrt{1-q^2})$. The formula from 3.2 becomes $\Delta=q^{-1}\arctan(\beta q/\sqrt{1-q^2})$; since $0<\beta<1$ and $\arctan$ is strictly increasing, $0<\Delta<\arcsin(q)/q$.

Define $g(x)=\sin x-2x/\pi$ on $[0,\pi/2]$. By [F3], $g(0)=g(\pi/2)=0$ and $g''(x)=-\sin x\le0$. Since $g'$ is differentiable and $g''\le0$, [F5] makes $g'$ nonincreasing. For any $0<x<\pi/2$, [F5] applied to $g$ on $[0,x]$ and $[x,\pi/2]$ gives $g(x)/x=g'(\xi_1)$ and $-g(x)/(\pi/2-x)=g'(\xi_2)$ for some $0<\xi_1<x<\xi_2<\pi/2$. Thus $g(x)/x\ge-g(x)/(\pi/2-x)$; multiplying by the positive $x(\pi/2-x)$ yields $g(x)\ge0$. Taking $x=\arcsin q$ gives $\arcsin q\le\pi q/2$, hence step 4.1 gives $\Delta<\pi/2$.

On either asymptotic tail, $|d\varphi/dr|=J/(r^2\sqrt{Q(1/r)})\sim J/(\sqrt A r^2)$. For every $0<\epsilon<1$, the definition of this limit bounds the integrand between $(1-\epsilon)J/(\sqrt A r^2)$ and $(1+\epsilon)J/(\sqrt A r^2)$ for all sufficiently large radii; integration from $r$ to infinity gives the angular gap $\delta(r)\sim J/(\sqrt A r)$. Step 3.1's asymptotic momentum and [F6] now give $r\sin\delta(r)\to J/\sqrt A$, the limiting perpendicular distance of each asymptotic line from the force center; this is $b$. The incoming momentum points opposite its limiting radial direction and the outgoing momentum along its own, so their angular separation is $\theta=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ by step 5.1.

The unique noncollision turning branch, impact parameter and exact deflection angle follow from steps 1.1–6.1. The hypotheses $W>mc^2$ and $J>\kappa/c$ are essential to the positive scattering root and are not relaxed.

citations.quote:
Use the smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian background $(M,g,N)$, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and the distinct chart, observer, congruence, tetrad and worldline meanings of [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. The metric and time orientation are prescribed data, not dynamical variables. A **charged spinning test body** in this definition consists of the following model quantities along a massive worldline $z:I\to M$:

- $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval whose parameter is proper time $\tau$ in seconds; $z$ is $C^2$, future-directed and timelike, and $U:=dz/d\tau$ obeys $g(U,U)=-c^2$. The SI conversion constant is $c>0$ metres per second; in a flat specialization use the affine Minkowski model and the proper-time decomposition of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].
- The constant rest-mass parameter $m>0$ has unit kilogram, and the constant charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ has unit coulomb. They are primitive model parameters; this definition does not derive them from the background field or from another framework.
- The **kinetic four-momentum** is the derived vector $P:=mU$ along $z$, with unit kilogram metre per second. It is distinct from the potential-dependent covector defined in [[lem-rpm-charge-gauge-boundary]].
- The **spin or polarization vector** is a $C^1$ tangent vector field $s(\tau)\in T_{z(\tau)}M$ constrained by $g(s,U)=0$, so it lies in the positive-definite instantaneous rest space $U^\perp$. Its unit is angular momentum, kilogram metre squared per second. This is a classical model vector; no quantization or quantum spin state is defined here.
- The gyromagnetic ratio $g_s\in\mathbb R$ is a dimensionless primitive species parameter. In the instantaneous rest space the model defines the magnetic-moment vector by $\mu=(g_s q/2m)s$, with unit ampere metre squared. No value $g_s=2$ is assumed, and this constitutive relation is not deduced from Lorentz covariance or classical electromagnetism.
- The prescribed external electromagnetic field is a $C^1$ alternating covariant two-tensor $F$ on an open region of $M$, independent of the unknown curve. Define $F^\sharp:T M\to T M$ by $g(F^\sharp(v),w)=F(w,v)$. In the flat specialization, a named inertial chart with $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres uses $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, matching [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]. On the curved background, $F$ is only a two-form; at an event its components in a chosen orthonormal tetrad use the same algebraic convention. Such a tetrad is a basis field, not a coordinate chart or an observer congruence, as distinguished in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. The components in an orthonormal tetrad have tesla units. This is an explicit curved-background model input. The cited EM supplier is a flat Minkowski definition and does not derive a curved field or curved Maxwell system.
- On any open potential domain where a $C^2$ covector field $A$ exists, $F=dA$ with components $F_{ab}=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a$ and $A$ has tesla metre components in the stated coordinates. No global potential is assumed, and no Maxwell equation or constitutive law is imposed here.

This is a test-body model on a fixed background: self-gravity, gravitational backreaction, self-field evaluation, radiation reaction, collisions, electric dipole moments, field-gradient translational forces and higher multipoles are outside this definition. Units follow the framework-local SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and do not identify quantities across frameworks.

For dependent deductions, the adopted premise is that on a finite fixed-endpoint timelike segment in a local potential domain, the model trajectory is stationary for the displayed action. The potential and metric are fixed inputs, $m>0$ and $q$ are constant, and this premise asserts neither a global potential nor global trajectory existence.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the
flat spacetime model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and the SI unit
conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], together with
the framework's idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and ideal light
signals:

**(i) Mass and momentum.** Every massive classical particle of the model
carries a positive constant invariant mass parameter $m>0$ and has
four-momentum $P=mU$, where $U$ is the four-velocity of its future timelike
worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]],
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]); $P$ is a vector of $V$
whose SI unit is kilogram metre per second. The formula is adopted only for
$m>0$; the case $m=0$ is not defined by it and is the separate premise
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. In particular $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$
is a consequence of the four-velocity normalisation, not a separate
assumption.

**(ii) Observer measurement identification.** Relative to a future unit
observer $n$, the model identifies the measured energy of the particle with
$E_n(P)$, its measured spatial momentum with $q_n(P)$, its kinetic energy with
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ and its rest energy with $mc^2$, where $E_n,q_n,T_n$ are
the quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; the
units are the joule, kilogram metre per second and kilogram of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. This clause is a formulation
convention identifying mathematical quantities with the quantities the model
calls measured; it is not a measurement report and no experiment is claimed.

**(iii) Isolated collision balance.** An isolated collision is represented by
a mass-specified on-shell collision datum at an event, with finite nonempty
incoming and outgoing lists of the massive particles of (i) and/or the ideal
massless particles of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]], and with
no external four-momentum transfer or omitted leg. The interaction is
idealized as confined to that event. The sum of the incoming four-momenta equals the sum of the
outgoing four-momenta, in the sense of the collision data of
[[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: the model adopts
$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$ for such an isolated datum. No particular
collision is asserted to occur, and no mechanism, probability, cross section
or amplitude is supplied by this clause.

**(iv) Equation of motion for a stipulated force.** Put
$H_c^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. A stipulated force law is a given
map $F:D\to V$ on a given subset $D\subseteq A\times H_c^+$,
with force components in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$. No regularity
away from the specified worldline is assumed. Along a given $C^2$ massive worldline
$x:I\to A$ with $(x(s),U(s))\in D$ for all $s\in I$, the model's particle
equation is $m\,dU/d\tau=F(x,U)$, with
$dU/d\tau$ the proper-time derivative of
[[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], so that the stipulated $F$
is the four-force of the motion. A particular force law, and the existence,
uniqueness and domain of solutions of the resulting equation, are not adopted
here and belong to a separate model.

Empirical support for these assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the
framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks,
ideal light signals and flat spacetime are inherited and travel to every
consumer of this premise.

Assume the charged test-body quantities of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]], the field convention of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and the stationary-action equivalence [[pthm-rpm-external-charge-action-equivalence]], and assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure. For every future-timelike initial datum $(x_0,U_0)$ with $g(U_0,U_0)=-c^2$, the equation of motion has a unique local solution by [[lem-rpm-external-charge-local-ivp]]. Along it the kinetic four-momentum $P=mU$ remains future timelike and satisfies

$$g(P,P)=-m^2c^2.$$

In the flat Minkowski specialization, use the massive-particle momentum result [[pthm-sr-momentum-and-four-force]] under its stated model assumptions, and choose a named inertial chart with $x^0=ct$, $E,B$ defined by [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and $\mathbf v$ the Euclidean spatial chart velocity. Set $\gamma:=(1-|\mathbf v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. Then, with $\mathbf p=m\gamma\mathbf v$ and $E_{\rm part}=\gamma mc^2$ supplied by [[pthm-sr-momentum-and-four-force]], the same equation gives

$$\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B),\qquad \frac{dE_{\rm part}}{dt}=q\,\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v.$$

The mass-shell and force statements are conditional deductions within the specified model; they do not establish empirical applicability.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $m,c,\kappa>0$, let $x,p\in\mathbb R^3$, and set

$$D:=(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R^3,\qquad r:=|x|,\qquad \mathcal E(p):=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|p|^2}.$$

The **repulsive relativistic Coulomb Hamiltonian** is

$$H(x,p):=\mathcal E(p)+\frac{\kappa}{r},$$

and its **phase system** is the autonomous ODE on the open set $D$

$$\dot x=\nabla_pH=\frac{c^2p}{\mathcal E(p)},\qquad \dot p=-\nabla_xH=\frac{\kappa x}{r^3}.$$

Here the system parameter $t$ is time in seconds and dot denotes $d/dt$; $m$ is a positive mass parameter (kilograms in the SI interpretation), $c$ a positive speed parameter (metres per second), and $\kappa$ a positive energy-times-length parameter (joule-metres). Define the radial momentum $p_r:=x\cdot p/r$ and angular-momentum vector $J:=x\times p$. A trajectory is a $C^1$ solution of this ODE on an interval; maximality is in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]].

This is only a mathematical phase system. Its physical interpretation as a charged particle in an externally prescribed Coulomb field requires separate model assumptions.

Consider the phase system of [[def-rpm-relativistic-coulomb-phase-system]] with $m,c,\kappa>0$. Let a trajectory have conserved energy $W>mc^2$ and angular-momentum magnitude $J:=|x\times p|>\kappa/c$. Define

$$A:=\frac{W^2-m^2c^4}{c^2}>0,\qquad d:=\frac{W\kappa}{c^2}>0,\qquad C:=J^2-\frac{\kappa^2}{c^2}>0.$$

Then its squared radial momentum is

$$p_r^2=Q(u):=A-2du-Cu^2,\qquad u:=1/r.$$

There is a unique positive simple root

$$u_*:=\frac{\sqrt{d^2+CA}-d}{C},\qquad 0<u_*<\frac{W-mc^2}{\kappa}.$$

The trajectory through the turning data $r_*=1/u_*$, $p_r=0$, and $|x\times p|=J$ is global for all system times, has one noncollision periapsis, and is asymptotically incoming and outgoing. Its impact parameter, defined as the limiting perpendicular distance of either asymptote from the force center, is

$$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt A}>0.$$

If $\Delta$ is the positive azimuthal change from either asymptote to periapsis, then

$$\Delta=\frac{J}{\sqrt C}\arctan\left(\frac{\sqrt{CA}}{d}\right),\qquad \theta:=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi),$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the incoming and outgoing asymptotic velocity vectors. This formula is for the repulsive branch $J>\kappa/c$; it does not cover $J\le\kappa/c$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Assume the charged test-body quantities and local potential domain of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]], the flat-space sign convention of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and the adopted fixed-endpoint action postulate [[post-rpm-external-charge-action]], and assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure. For a finite $C^2$ future-timelike curve segment $z:[a,b]\to O$ in that domain, where $a<b$ are proper-time endpoints, and the local $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variations of the postulate, choose the orientation-preserving parameter $\lambda=\tau$; the segment is stationary for the adopted action if and only if

$$m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U),\qquad (\nabla_UU)_a=\frac qm F_{ab}U^b.$$

This is a model deduction: it establishes the equation equivalent to stationarity of the postulated functional, not the physical truth of the postulate.

derivations.claim: On any finite proper-time segment $z:[a,b]\to O$ of the adopted $C^2$ future-timelike worldline, set $T(\tau)=x^0(z(\tau))/c$. Then $T$ is $C^2$ and $T'=U^0/c>0$ in the future-oriented inertial chart. By [F4], $T$ is strictly increasing and has local $C^1$ inverses; injectivity makes them agree to give its inverse $\phi:[T(a),T(b)]\to[a,b]$. Its derivative is $\phi'=1/(T'\circ\phi)>0$, and the chain and reciprocal rules give $\phi''=-(T''\circ\phi)/(T'\circ\phi)^3$, which is continuous. The same local argument extends to the endpoints using the worldline on a neighborhood of the segment (or the one-sided $C^2$ restrictions). Thus $\phi$ is an admissible $C^2$ orientation-preserving diffeomorphism in [A1]. The action-equivalence supplier proves invariance of the action and stationarity under this fixed parameter change applied to the entire variation family. Coordinate-time spatial variations with fixed endpoint positions, represented by $(ct,\mathbf x_\epsilon(t))$, are among its admissible variations: on a compact segment $|\mathbf v|<c$ has a positive margin, so sufficiently small $C^2$ variations remain future timelike, and composing with the fixed $T$ transports them to the original parameter interval with endpoints fixed.
derivations.rule: scalar positive-derivative inverse, second derivative formula, fixed reparameterization of variation family
derivations.hypotheses: C2 future-timelike worldline on finite compact proper-time segment; future-oriented inertial x0=ct chart; fixed endpoints; positive derivative Tprime=U0/c; exact external action stationary-family invariance

derivations.claim: In the inertial chart, $dx^0/dt=c$ and $|d\mathbf x/dt|=|\mathbf v|$. The action density from [A1] is therefore $L(\mathbf x,\mathbf v)=-mc^2\sqrt{1-|\mathbf v|^2/c^2}+qA_0c=-mc^2\sqrt{1-|\mathbf v|^2/c^2}-q\phi(r).$ Its spatial canonical momentum is $\partial L/\partial\mathbf v=m\gamma\mathbf v$; because $A_i=0$, it is also the kinetic momentum in [F1]. The Legendre expression $\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf v-L$ equals $\gamma mc^2+q\phi=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}+qQ/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r)$. With $\kappa=qQ/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)>0$, this is precisely the Hamiltonian in [F3].

From [F2], $\mathbf E=-\nabla\phi=Q\mathbf x/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3)$. Since $\mathbf B=0$, [F1] gives $\dot{\mathbf p}=q\mathbf E=\kappa\mathbf x/r^3$. The Hamiltonian derivative gives $\dot{\mathbf x}=c^2\mathbf p/\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}$. These are exactly the two phase equations of [F3], so each local physical solution in the prescribed model is a trajectory of that mathematical system.

For $W>mc^2$ and $J>\kappa/c$, all hypotheses of the exact repulsive scattering proposition [F3] hold. It supplies the unique outer turning branch and the stated impact parameter and deflection formula, with $A,d,C$ as defined in the statement. The conclusion is conditional on [A1], [A2], and [A3] and the fixed-source idealization.
The exact angle is therefore a model prediction for the stated branch. The derivation makes no claim for $J\le\kappa/c$, for source recoil or radiation, or for any experimental result.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
$f'=s/r^2$. Then:

For arbitrary $x^0_0,\varphi_0\in\mathbb R$, put
$\omega_0=(\cos\varphi_0,\sin\varphi_0,0)\in S^2$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$
define the rotation
$$R_\alpha(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(y_1\cos\alpha-y_2\sin\alpha,\ y_1\sin\alpha+y_2\cos\alpha,\ y_3),$$
and the global axial vector field $\Phi(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(-y_2,y_1,0)$ on $S^2$;
it is tangent because $y\cdot\Phi(y)=0$ for $y\in S^2$.
In every spherical-polar chart near the equator, $\Phi=\partial_\varphi$;
longitude expressions below are local chart expressions for the global sphere
curve $R_\alpha\omega_0$.

In this item, a **timelike circular geodesic** means a future timelike
geodesic whose areal radius $r$ is constant on an interval of positive length;
its angular orientation is unrestricted.

**(a) Existence of circular timelike geodesics.** Let $r_0>3s/2$ and choose
$\ell\in\mathbb R$ with

$$\ell^2=\frac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}>0,\qquad e:=\Bigl(f(r_0)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\Bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2} =\frac{c(r_0-s)\sqrt 2}{\sqrt{r_0(2r_0-3s)}}>0 .$$

Then the globally defined curve $\gamma:\mathbb R\to M$ is

$$\gamma(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr).$$
In each local polar chart along it, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and the longitude is
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to a constant multiple of $2\pi$.

It is a future timelike geodesic of the datum, with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-c^2$
and with the conserved quantities $e=-g(\gamma',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\gamma',\Phi)$ of
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-timelike-geodesic-reduction]]; it is a **circular
orbit** at radius $r_0$. Its angular velocity in the coordinate $x^0$ is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\Bigl(\frac{s}{2r_0^3}\Bigr)^{1/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\Bigr)^2=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r_0^3},$$

$t=x^0/c$.

**(b) The circular-orbit condition is necessary.** Conversely, if
$\gamma:I\to M$ is any future timelike geodesic parametrized by proper time with
$r(\tau)\equiv r_0>s$ constant on an interval of positive length, then
$r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. If $\gamma$ is equatorial, its conserved angular
momentum additionally satisfies $\ell^2=\dfrac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}$.
Consequently no timelike circular geodesic, in any angular orientation, exists
with $s<r_0\le\frac{3s}{2}$.

**(c) Stability threshold of the radial potential.** For each radius
$r>\frac{3s}{2}$ set $\ell_r^2:=c^2sr^2/(2r-3s)$ and regard $\ell_r$ as a
constant in the function $V_{\ell_r}(x):=\tfrac12 f(x)(c^2+\ell_r^2/x^2)$.
Differentiate with respect to $x$ at fixed $\ell_r$, then evaluate at $x=r$.
The result, evaluated at the circular value $\ell_r$, is

$$V_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)},\qquad r>\frac{3s}{2},$$

so $V_\ell$ has a strict local minimum at the circular-orbit radius exactly
for $r>3s$, a strict local maximum exactly for $\frac{3s}{2}<r<3s$, and
$V_\ell''(3s)=0$; the radius $r=3s$ is the **innermost stable circular orbit
radius** of the restricted model in this potential sense.

**(d) The photon sphere at $r=3s/2$.** Let $\ell\neq0$ and put
$r_0=\frac{3s}{2}$ and $e_0:=\dfrac{\lvert\ell\rvert\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0}=\dfrac{2\lvert\ell\rvert}{3\sqrt3\,s}>0$.
Then the globally defined curve
$$\eta(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e_0}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr),\qquad \tau\in\mathbb R,$$
whose local polar expressions have $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and longitude
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to chart shifts, is a future null geodesic (a
**null circular orbit** or **photon sphere**
orbit) with conserved quantities $e_0=-g(\eta',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\eta',\Phi)$, and its angular velocity is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e_0}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\,\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0},\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}\Bigr)^2=\frac{f(r_0)}{r_0^2}=\frac{4}{27s^2}.$$

The **null effective potential** $W^{\mathrm n}_\ell(r):=f(r)\ell^2/r^2$
satisfies $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)'(3s/2)=0$ and
$(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)''(3s/2)=-\dfrac{32\ell^2}{81s^4}<0$, so the photon-sphere
radius is a strict local maximum of the null potential.

**(e) Scope.** All statements are exact data of the restricted model: the
orbits are ideal geodesics of the metric on the exterior domain, the
stability claim is the sign of the second derivative of the stated potential,
and no claim is made about nonlinear stability, about orbital decay, about
observations or about the interior region. The case $r_0=s$ is excluded, and
the reduction is stated only where $r>s$.

Adopt the Schwarzschild vacuum exterior model with $m_*>0$, $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$, together with its ideal-free-fall rule that a massive test body follows a future timelike geodesic. For a fixed angular-momentum magnitude $\ell>0$, set

$$W_\ell(r)=f(r)\left(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2}\right),\qquad r>s.$$

The equatorial reduced radial system is

$$\dot r=w,\qquad \dot w=-\frac12 W_\ell'(r),$$

where dot denotes proper-time derivative and $\ell$ is held fixed. For every circular timelike radius $r_c>3s/2$, the corresponding equilibrium is

$$z_c=(r_c,0),\qquad \ell^2=\frac{c^2s r_c^2}{2r_c-3s}.$$

Then this equilibrium is Lyapunov stable in the Euclidean phase space $(r,w)$ when $r_c>3s$, and is not Lyapunov stable when $3s/2<r_c\le3s$. At $r_c=3s$ the equilibrium is a stationary inflection of $W_\ell$, not a strict extremum, and is still not Lyapunov stable. These are conclusions about the reduced radial system at fixed $\ell$ only.

derivations.claim: At $r_0=4s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=c^2s(16s^2)/(8s-3s)=16c^2s^2/5$ and [F1] gives $W_\ell''=2V_\ell''=c^2/(160s^2)>0$. Since $4s>3s$, [F2] classifies the equilibrium as Lyapunov stable in the fixed-$\ell$ radial state.
At $r_0=2s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=4c^2s^2$ and $W_\ell''=2V_\ell''=-c^2/(4s^2)<0$. Since $3s/2<2s<3s$, [F2] classifies this equilibrium as unstable.

At $r_0=3s$, substitution gives $\ell^2=3c^2s^2$. The formula for $W_\ell'$ in [F1] at this angular momentum is $c^2s(r-3s)^2/r^4$, positive away from $3s$ and zero at $3s$. The equilibrium is a stationary inflection; [F2] classifies it as not Lyapunov stable. All three results are restricted radial-model classifications.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$ on $r>s$. Let $\gamma(\lambda)$ be an affinely parametrized null geodesic of its metric-selected connection whose image lies in the equatorial plane $\vartheta=\pi/2$, and choose the orientation so that

$$E:=f(r)\frac{dx^0}{d\lambda}>0,\qquad L:=r^2\frac{d\varphi}{d\lambda}\ge0.$$

Both quantities are constant along $\gamma$. With impact parameter $b:=L/E\ge0$ and $H(r):=f(r)/r^2$, its radial equation is

$$\left(\frac{dr}{d\lambda}\right)^2=E^2\bigl(1-b^2H(r)\bigr).$$

Moreover, $H'(r)=(3s-2r)/r^4$, so $H$ has its unique exterior maximum at $r_{\rm ph}=3s/2$, with $H(r_{\rm ph})=4/(27s^2)$. Thus the critical impact parameter for a radial turning point is $b_{\rm c}=3\sqrt3\,s/2$.

Adopt the Schwarzschild exterior vacuum model with $s>0$ and the ideal-light rule that rays are future null geodesics. For an equatorial incoming ray with constants $E>0$, $L\ge0$, impact parameter $b=L/E$, and

$$H(r)=\frac{1-s/r}{r^2},\qquad b_{\rm c}=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}s,\qquad r_{\rm ph}=\frac32s,$$

the radial first integral is $\dot r^2=E^2[1-b^2H(r)]$ as in [[lem-rpm-schwarzschild-null-geodesic-reduction]], where dot denotes affine-parameter derivative. Then:

1. If $b>b_{\rm c}$, there is a unique outer turning point $r_*(b)>r_{\rm ph}$, which is reached in finite affine parameter; the ray from infinity turns and returns to infinity. Its total azimuthal advance is

   $$\Delta\varphi=2\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{b\,dr}{r^2\sqrt{1-b^2H(r)}}.$$

   This integral converges at both endpoints.
2. If $b=b_{\rm c}$, the incoming branch from infinity approaches $r_{\rm ph}$ only as affine parameter tends to $+\infty$; its azimuthal advance diverges logarithmically.
3. If $0\le b<b_{\rm c}$, the inward branch has no exterior turning point and reaches the boundary $r=s$ of the Schwarzschild exterior in finite affine parameter. Only if the ray is continued in the specified Kruskal model, once it lies in the region $U\ge0$, does the causal escape result imply that it cannot return to the right exterior.

These are geodesic-model deductions. The impact threshold is not by itself an observable shadow radius.

derivations.claim: Since $(2\sqrt2s)^2=8s^2$ and $H(2s)=1/(8s^2)$, the radial factor vanishes at $2s$. Also $2\sqrt2s>3\sqrt3s/2$ because $32>27$, and $H$ is strictly decreasing above $3s/2$, so this is the unique outer root. The turning and return classification follows from [F2].

Substituting $b_c^2=27s^2/4$ and $H=(r-s)/r^3$ and expanding the numerator verifies the displayed factorization. The double zero at $r=3s/2$ and the theorem's affine and angular quadratures then give the critical asymptote and logarithmic divergence.
These are exact ideal-geodesic conclusions in the Schwarzschild model; no wave-optics or observational statement is added.

Let $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2>0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$, and let $r_E,r_R>s$ be the emitter and receiver radii of static observers in the adopted Schwarzschild exterior model. With $n=f^{-1/2}\partial_0$ the unit static congruence and $U=cn$ the corresponding four-velocity, the ideal-clock and geometric-optics predictions are

$$\frac{\Delta\tau_R}{\Delta\tau_E}=\frac{\omega_E}{\omega_R}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_R)}{f(r_E)}},\qquad \frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\sqrt{\frac{f(r_E)}{f(r_R)}}.$$

The proper four-acceleration magnitude required to remain static at radius $r>s$ is

$$a(r)=\sqrt{g(\nabla_UU,\nabla_UU)}=\frac{c^2s}{2r^2\sqrt{f(r)}}=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r^2\sqrt{1-s/r}}.$$

For any $0\le\rho<1$ and radii satisfying $0<s/r_E,s/r_R\le\rho$, define $x_i=s/r_i$ and write $\log:=L$ for the natural integral logarithm of [[def-integral-logarithm]]. The exact logarithmic ratio has the uniform expansion

$$\log\frac{\omega_R}{\omega_E}=\frac{s}{2}\left(\frac1{r_R}-\frac1{r_E}\right)+R,\qquad |R|\le\frac{x_E^2+x_R^2}{4(1-\rho)}.$$

These are conditional deductions of the idealized model; no measured redshift or acceleration is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum of mass parameter $m_*$,
Schwarzschild radius $s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with curvature data as in
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-ricci-and-einstein-tensors]]. On each spherical-polar
product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ define the local frame field

$$e_{\hat0}:=f^{-1/2}\partial_0,\qquad e_{\hat1}:=f^{1/2}\partial_1,\qquad e_{\hat2}:=r^{-1}\partial_2,\qquad e_{\hat3}:=(r\sin\vartheta)^{-1}\partial_3,$$

and for the curvature tensor define the **frame components**

$$\hat R_{\hat a\hat b\hat c\hat d}:=g\bigl(R(e_{\hat c},e_{\hat d})e_{\hat b},e_{\hat a}\bigr).$$

Then:

**(a) The frame field.** $(e_{\hat0},e_{\hat1},e_{\hat2},e_{\hat3})$ is a
smooth $g$-orthonormal frame (tetrad field) on the chart domain, with
$g(e_{\hat a},e_{\hat b})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{\hat a\hat b}$, and
$e_{\hat0}$ is future-directed timelike; it is a tetrad field in the sense of
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. It is not a coordinate frame.

**(b) Frame components.** The nonzero frame components, up to the
symmetries $R_{abcd}=-R_{bacd}=-R_{abdc}=R_{cdab}$ of
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]], are

$$\hat R_{\hat0\hat1\hat0\hat1}=\frac{f''}{2},\qquad \hat R_{\hat0\hat2\hat0\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat0\hat3\hat0\hat3}=\frac{f'}{2r},$$

$$\hat R_{\hat1\hat2\hat1\hat2}=\hat R_{\hat1\hat3\hat1\hat3}=-\frac{f'}{2r},\qquad \hat R_{\hat2\hat3\hat2\hat3}=\frac{1-f}{r^2},$$

with $f'=s/r^2$ and $f''=-2s/r^3$; all other frame components vanish.

**(c) Kretschmann scalar.** Define the global smooth scalar field
$K:=R_{abcd}R^{abcd}$, with indices raised by the inverse metric. On the
spherical-polar chart locus its component expression is

$$K=f''^2+\frac{4(f')^2}{r^2}+\frac{4(1-f)^2}{r^4},$$

and for the model function $f=1-s/r$ this is

$$K=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}=\frac{48\,G_N^2m_*^2}{c^4\,r^6}.$$

The scalar identity is first computed on the regular angular locus and holds
on all of $M$ by smoothness and density. Since $r>s$ on $M$, one has
$0<K=12s^2/r^6<12/s^4$ at every point; as $r\downarrow s$ the expression has
the finite boundary value $12/s^4$, and the expression $12s^2/r^6$, read as a
function of $r>0$, grows without bound as $r\downarrow0$.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma computes curvature data of the exterior datum on
$r>s$. The limit $r\downarrow s$ is the boundary value on $M$ of the smooth
expression $12s^2/r^6$; no value of the metric at $r=s$ or at $r=0$ is used
or asserted here, those regions being outside the datum (the regular
continuation across $r=s$ is the separate extension lemma of this page).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with Schwarzschild radius
$s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Let
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times S^2$ carry the product
smooth structure and let $\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}:M_{\mathrm{ext}}\to S^2$ be the
third projection. Its product atlas includes ordinary sphere charts at the
poles ([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]).
Define the **tortoise function**

$$r_*(r):=r+s\log\left|\frac{r}{s}-1\right|,\qquad r>0,\ r\ne s,$$

on each of the two intervals $(0,s)$ and $(s,\infty)$, and define the
**advanced-chart metric** globally on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$ by

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv\otimes dv+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+r^2\,\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In spherical-polar product charts its components are

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\,d\Omega^2,$$

namely $g_{vv}=-f$, $g_{vr}=g_{rv}=1$,
$g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=r^2$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$ and all
other components zero. In another sphere chart the angular block is
$r^2(\gamma_{ij})$. Then:

**(a) Smooth Lorentzian metric.** $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and at every point it is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; hence $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$
is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on all of
$r>0$, including $r=s$.

**(b) Time orientation.** The smooth vector field

$$N_{\mathrm{ext}}:=A(r)\,\partial_v-\partial_r,\qquad A(r):=\frac{f(r)+\sqrt{f(r)^2+4}}{2}>0,$$

satisfies $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},N_{\mathrm{ext}})<0$ everywhere
and $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},\partial_v)<0$ everywhere; hence
$N_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a time orientation of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and on the
region $r>s$ it determines the same future cone as the datum's time
orientation $\partial_v=\partial_0$.

**(c) Isometric embedding of the exterior.** The map
$\Phi:M\to M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, $(x^0,r,\omega)\mapsto(x^0+r_*(r),r,\omega)$
restricts to a diffeomorphism of $M$ onto the open subset $\{r>s\}$ of
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and $\Phi^*g_{\mathrm{ext}}=g$; the exterior datum is
therefore isometric to the region $r>s$ of the extension.

**(d) Vacuum and Kretschmann scalar of the extension.** The
metric-selected connection of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ exists and is unique, its
Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and Einstein tensor vanish identically on
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and its Kretschmann scalar equals

$$R_{abcd}R^{abcd}=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}$$

on all of $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$. In particular the scalar is smooth and finite on
the horizon $r=s$, where it takes the value $12/s^4$.

**(e) The horizon is a null hypersurface.** The level set $\{r=s\}$ is a
smooth null hypersurface of $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$ whose null
generator direction is $\partial_v$; every smooth product-chart frame remains
a basis across $r=s$. In spherical-polar charts
$\det(g_{\mathrm{ext}})=-r^4\sin^2\vartheta$; in an arbitrary sphere chart
the determinant is $-r^4\det(\gamma_{ij})$, which is nonzero.

**(f) Scope.** The extension constructed here is a smooth Lorentzian
manifold containing the exterior isometrically and regular across $r=s$; it
is not claimed to be maximal, and no uniqueness or global structure theorem
is asserted. The region $r\le0$ and the surfaces relevant to the Kruskal
model of this page are outside this statement.

derivations.claim: Substitution gives $f_E=1/2$ and $f_R=3/4$. Applying [F1] yields the frequency and clock ratios. The acceleration at $2s$ is $c^2s/[2(2s)^2\sqrt{1/2}]=c^2/(4\sqrt2s)$.

At $r=s(1+\epsilon)$, $f=\epsilon/(1+\epsilon)$, so [F1] gives $a=c^2/[2s\sqrt\epsilon(1+\epsilon)^{3/2}]$, which diverges as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. By [F2], $K=12s^2/[s^6(1+\epsilon)^6]$ tends to $12/s^4$, a finite value.

[F3] supplies a smooth extension through the same $r=s$ boundary. Hence the divergence in 1.2 is the static-observer acceleration requirement in the exterior chart, while this curvature scalar remains finite and the metric has the stated smooth extension. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the
flat spacetime model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and the SI unit
conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], together with
the framework's idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and ideal light
signals:

**(i) Mass and momentum.** Every massive classical particle of the model
carries a positive constant invariant mass parameter $m>0$ and has
four-momentum $P=mU$, where $U$ is the four-velocity of its future timelike
worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]],
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]); $P$ is a vector of $V$
whose SI unit is kilogram metre per second. The formula is adopted only for
$m>0$; the case $m=0$ is not defined by it and is the separate premise
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. In particular $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$
is a consequence of the four-velocity normalisation, not a separate
assumption.

**(ii) Observer measurement identification.** Relative to a future unit
observer $n$, the model identifies the measured energy of the particle with
$E_n(P)$, its measured spatial momentum with $q_n(P)$, its kinetic energy with
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ and its rest energy with $mc^2$, where $E_n,q_n,T_n$ are
the quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; the
units are the joule, kilogram metre per second and kilogram of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. This clause is a formulation
convention identifying mathematical quantities with the quantities the model
calls measured; it is not a measurement report and no experiment is claimed.

**(iii) Isolated collision balance.** An isolated collision is represented by
a mass-specified on-shell collision datum at an event, with finite nonempty
incoming and outgoing lists of the massive particles of (i) and/or the ideal
massless particles of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]], and with
no external four-momentum transfer or omitted leg. The interaction is
idealized as confined to that event. The sum of the incoming four-momenta equals the sum of the
outgoing four-momenta, in the sense of the collision data of
[[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: the model adopts
$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$ for such an isolated datum. No particular
collision is asserted to occur, and no mechanism, probability, cross section
or amplitude is supplied by this clause.

**(iv) Equation of motion for a stipulated force.** Put
$H_c^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. A stipulated force law is a given
map $F:D\to V$ on a given subset $D\subseteq A\times H_c^+$,
with force components in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$. No regularity
away from the specified worldline is assumed. Along a given $C^2$ massive worldline
$x:I\to A$ with $(x(s),U(s))\in D$ for all $s\in I$, the model's particle
equation is $m\,dU/d\tau=F(x,U)$, with
$dU/d\tau$ the proper-time derivative of
[[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], so that the stipulated $F$
is the four-force of the motion. A particular force law, and the existence,
uniqueness and domain of solutions of the resulting equation, are not adopted
here and belong to a separate model.

Empirical support for these assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the
framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks,
ideal light signals and flat spacetime are inherited and travel to every
consumer of this premise.

Consider the phase system of [[def-rpm-relativistic-coulomb-phase-system]] with $m,c,\kappa>0$. Let a trajectory have conserved energy $W>mc^2$ and angular-momentum magnitude $J:=|x\times p|>\kappa/c$. Define

$$A:=\frac{W^2-m^2c^4}{c^2}>0,\qquad d:=\frac{W\kappa}{c^2}>0,\qquad C:=J^2-\frac{\kappa^2}{c^2}>0.$$

Then its squared radial momentum is

$$p_r^2=Q(u):=A-2du-Cu^2,\qquad u:=1/r.$$

There is a unique positive simple root

$$u_*:=\frac{\sqrt{d^2+CA}-d}{C},\qquad 0<u_*<\frac{W-mc^2}{\kappa}.$$

The trajectory through the turning data $r_*=1/u_*$, $p_r=0$, and $|x\times p|=J$ is global for all system times, has one noncollision periapsis, and is asymptotically incoming and outgoing. Its impact parameter, defined as the limiting perpendicular distance of either asymptote from the force center, is

$$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt A}>0.$$

If $\Delta$ is the positive azimuthal change from either asymptote to periapsis, then

$$\Delta=\frac{J}{\sqrt C}\arctan\left(\frac{\sqrt{CA}}{d}\right),\qquad \theta:=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi),$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the incoming and outgoing asymptotic velocity vectors. This formula is for the repulsive branch $J>\kappa/c$; it does not cover $J\le\kappa/c$.

Let a massive charged test body of mass $m>0$ and charge $q$ move in flat Minkowski spacetime in the prescribed field of a fixed point source with charge $Q$, where $qQ>0$. Use SI units, $x^0=ct$, $A_0=-\phi/c$, $A_i=0$, and

$$\phi(r)=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r},\qquad \mathbf E(r)=\frac{Q\mathbf x}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3},\qquad \mathbf B=0,\qquad \kappa:=\frac{qQ}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}>0.$$

Under the adopted fixed-endpoint charged-particle action and its proved Lorentz-force consequence, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure as required by those suppliers. In the flat specialization also adopt the massive-particle momentum model of [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]. Then the canonical spatial momentum equals the kinetic momentum $\mathbf p=m\gamma\mathbf v$, and the coordinate-time Hamiltonian is

$$H(\mathbf x,\mathbf p)=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|\mathbf p|^2}+\frac{\kappa}{r}.$$

Thus the trajectories are those of [[def-rpm-relativistic-coulomb-phase-system]]. On a scattering branch of energy $W>mc^2$ and angular-momentum magnitude $J>\kappa/c$, define

$$A=\frac{W^2-m^2c^4}{c^2},\qquad d=\frac{W\kappa}{c^2},\qquad C=J^2-\frac{\kappa^2}{c^2}.$$

Its exact angle between incoming and outgoing momenta is

$$\theta=\pi-\frac{2J}{\sqrt C}\arctan\left(\frac{\sqrt{CA}}{d}\right)\in(0,\pi).$$

This is a model deduction, not a measured scattering law. The inequality $J>\kappa/c$ is part of the result's domain; no conclusion is made for $J\le\kappa/c$.

Let $\mu>0$, let $\kappa>0$ and $U(r)=\kappa/r$ on $(0,\infty)$ (the repulsive
Coulomb potential, of class $C^2$), let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put
$$V(r):=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2},\qquad b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{Eb}>0.$$
Then:

1. $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $V(r)\to\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$
   and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; hence there is exactly one $r_*>0$ with
   $V(r_*)=E$, it is simple ($V'(r_*)<0$), and $V(r)<E$ for all $r>r_*$.
2. Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with
   constant angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$
   for all $t\in I$ and with $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$
   extends uniquely to all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho=|r|\ge r_*>0$
   (no collision), $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and
   strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the asymptotic velocities
   $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$.
   Moreover the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its
   limiting direction exists and equals
   $$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_\pm|}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b|v_\pm| .$$
The distance in clause 2 means the limit of $|r(t)\times v_\pm|/|v_\pm|$ as $t\to\pm\infty$, the distance to the line through the origin in the limiting velocity direction; it does not assert a free tail or a finite longitudinal intercept.

3. For the polar angle, with $u_*:=1/r_*$,
   $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}} =\int_0^{u_*}\frac{b\,\mathrm du}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\kappa}{E}u-b^2u^2}} =\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$

4. Write $n_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r(t)/|r(t)|$. Then
   $n_+=v_+/|v_+|$, $n_-=-v_-/|v_-|$, and in an oriented polar plane
   the outgoing velocity direction is the incoming direction rotated by
   $2\Delta-\pi\in(-\pi,0)$. In particular
   $$\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-||v_+|}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta),\qquad \theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$
   For fixed $\mu,\kappa,E$ this gives an actual family for every $b>0$,
   with angular momentum $J(b)=\sqrt{2\mu E}\,b$: choose its unique turning
   radius and initial data $r(0)=r_*e_1$, $r'(0)=J(b)e_2/(\mu r_*)$.
   Local existence and the extension in clause 2 give a member of the family
   for every $b$, unique up to apsis time and oriented plane placement.

For every $y>0$,

$$\arctan y+\arctan(1/y)=\frac{\pi}{2},$$

where $\arctan$ takes values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a
continuous strictly increasing bijection

$$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$

Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent**

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$

Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while
$\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval.
The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

derivations.claim: With $W_c=mc^2+K$, $A_c=2mK+\frac{K^2}{c^2},\quad d_c=\frac{W_c\kappa}{c^2}=m\kappa+\frac{K\kappa}{c^2},\quad C_c=J_c^2-\frac{\kappa^2}{c^2}=2mKb^2+\frac{K^2b^2-\kappa^2}{c^2}.$ Thus $J_c/\sqrt{C_c}\to1$ and $\sqrt{C_cA_c}/d_c\to2Kb/\kappa$. By [F3] and continuity, [F1] gives $\theta_c\to\pi-2\arctan(2Kb/\kappa)$. Apply [F3] with $y=2Kb/\kappa>0$ to rewrite this limit as $2\arctan(\kappa/(2Kb))$. This limit retains [A1] and [A2] only when it is read through the physical model theorem.
The final expression is exactly [F2]. The agreement is a formal limit with fixed model parameters, not a measured result or validation of the model assumptions.
