Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: For each configuration, the product $\prod_{i=1}^N T_{s_i,s_{i+1}}$ has bond contribution $e^{\beta J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}}$ and field contribution $e^{\beta h\sum_i(s_i+s_{i+1})/2}=e^{\beta h\sum_i s_i}$. These factors equal $e^{-\beta H_N(s)}$. Summing over the finite spin sequences gives $Z_N=\sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_N}T_{s_1s_2}\cdots T_{s_Ns_1}=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)$.

In the ordered basis $+1,-1$, $T=\begin{pmatrix}e^{\beta J+\beta h}&e^{-\beta J}\\e^{-\beta J}&e^{\beta J-\beta h}\end{pmatrix}$. Put $A=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)$ and $B=\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}$. The diagonal entries give $\operatorname{tr}T=2A$; direct multiplication gives $\det T=e^{2\beta J}-e^{-2\beta J}$. Using $\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1$, which follows by expanding their definitions, $A^2-\det T=e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}=B^2$. Thus the characteristic polynomial has roots $A\pm B=\lambda_\pm$. Since $A,B>0$, $A+B>|A-B|$, hence $\lambda_+>|\lambda_-|$.

For a $2\times2$ matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, direct multiplication gives $M^2-(a+d)M+(ad-bc)I=0$. Apply this identity to $T$ and multiply by $T^n$; taking traces gives $z_{n+2}=(\operatorname{tr}T)z_{n+1}-(\det T)z_n$, where $z_n=\operatorname{tr}(T^n)$, $z_0=2$, and $z_1=\lambda_++\lambda_-$. The sequence $\lambda_+^n+\lambda_-^n$ has the same recurrence and initial values, so induction gives $Z_N=z_N=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N$.

Set $r=\lambda_-/\lambda_+$. Then $Z_N=\lambda_+^N(1+r^N)$ and $|r|<1$, so $1+r^N>0$. Therefore $N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log\lambda_++N^{-1}\log(1+r^N)$, whose second term tends to zero. For a compact parameter set, continuity and $|r|<1$ give $0<\rho<1$ with $|r|\le\rho$. The positive radicand in $B$ is a smooth positive combination of exponentials; the real-power derivative in [F4] with exponent $1/2$, followed inductively by chain and product rules, makes $B$ and $\lambda_\pm$ smooth. Since $\lambda_+>0$, its reciprocal and logarithm are smooth as well, by the real-power derivative with exponent $-1$ and the logarithm derivative in [F4]. Every fixed finite collection of derivatives of $r$ is therefore bounded on the compact set. For a multi-index $\alpha$ of order at most $k$ and $N\ge k$, repeated product differentiation of the $N$ factors gives at most $C_kN^k$ terms; each has at least $N-k$ undifferentiated factors $r$, so $|\partial^\alpha(r^N)|\le C_kN^k\rho^{N-k}$. Put $u=r^N$. Since $1+u\ge1-\rho$, repeated differentiation of $\log(1+u)$ gives finite sums of products of derivatives of $u$ divided by powers of $1+u$. Each term has at least one derivative factor and the product bounds yield $|\partial^\alpha\log(1+u)|\le C'_kN^k\rho^{N-k}$ after enlarging the constant. Divide by $N$; [F5] implies $N^{k-1}\rho^{N-k}\to0$. The zero-order logarithm term also tends uniformly to zero. Hence the correction and every fixed-order derivative vanish uniformly on the compact set.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Fix $\beta>0$ and $J,h\in\mathbb R$. For $N\ge2$, let $s_i\in\{-1,1\}$, $s_{N+1}=s_1$, $H_N(s)=-J\sum_{i=1}^Ns_is_{i+1}-h\sum_{i=1}^Ns_i$, and $Z_N=\sum_se^{-\beta H_N(s)}$. Define $\cosh x:=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$, $\sinh x:=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, and $T_{s,t}:=e^{\beta Jst+\beta h(s+t)/2}$. Then $Z_N=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N$, where $\lambda_\pm=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)\pm\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}$ and $\lambda_+>|\lambda_-|$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For each shape let $\Phi_a:\mathcal A^{S_a}\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded interaction function. Set $J_0:=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. On $\Lambda_L:=\{1,\ldots,L\}^d$, define the free-boundary energy $H_L(s):=\sum_a\sum_{x:x+S_a\subseteq\Lambda_L}\Phi_a((s_{x+u})_{u\in S_a})$, for configurations $s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}$. For $\beta>0$, define the finite partition sum $Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_L(s)}$ and normalized log-partition density $p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\beta)$.

Fix integers $d\ge1$, $L\ge1$, a finite alphabet $\mathcal A$ of cardinality $q\ge1$, and a finite, possibly empty, list of interaction shapes $S_a\subset\mathbb Z^d$, each nonempty and contained in $[-R,R]^d$ for some integer $R\ge0$. $\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$ is finite because its domain is finite. For each shape let $\Phi_a:\mathcal A^{S_a}\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded interaction function. Set $J_0:=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. On $\Lambda_L:=\{1,\ldots,L\}^d$, define the free-boundary energy $H_L(s):=\sum_a\sum_{x:x+S_a\subseteq\Lambda_L}\Phi_a((s_{x+u})_{u\in S_a})$, for configurations $s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}$. For $\beta>0$, define the finite partition sum $Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_L(s)}$ and normalized log-partition density $p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\beta)$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-integers]]) with $b > 0$. Then there exist
integers $q$ and $r$ with

$$a \;=\; qb + r, \qquad 0 \le r < b,$$

and the pair $(q,r)$ with these two properties is unique.

We say $b$ **divides** $a$, written $b \mid a$, when $a = qb$ for some
$q \in \mathbb{Z}$; by the above, for $b > 0$ this holds exactly when the
remainder $r$ is $0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Write $V=L^d$ and $J_0=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. Each configuration satisfies $|H_L(s)|\le J_0V$, so $q^Ve^{-\beta J_0V}\le Z_L\le q^Ve^{\beta J_0V}$. Hence $p_L$ is bounded above and below uniformly in $L$.

Fix an integer block length $\ell>2R$ and write $L=k\ell+r$ with $0\le r<\ell$ using [F3]. Partition $\Lambda_L$ into $k^d$ disjoint $\ell$-cubes and an outer remainder. Form $H_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}$ by retaining only interactions whose entire support lies in one full cube and assigning zero energy to remainder sites. For a fixed shape, every eligible anchor lies in $[1-R,L+R]^d$. If its support crosses an internal block seam, its coordinate normal to that seam lies in at most $2R+1$ integer positions; the other coordinates have at most $(L+2R)^{d-1}$ choices. If it is not in such a seam strip but the interaction is omitted, its support meets the outer remainder, so its anchor lies within $\ell+2R+1$ layers of one of the $d$ outer faces. Counting at most $d(k-1)$ internal seams and $d$ outer faces bounds the omitted anchors per shape by $d(2R+1)(L/\ell)(L+2R)^{d-1}+d(\ell+2R+1)(L+2R)^{d-1}$. Therefore $\sup_s|H_L(s)-H_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}(s)|\le J_0d[(2R+1)(L/\ell)+\ell+2R+1](L+2R)^{d-1}$.

If two energies on a finite state set differ pointwise by at most $D$, their partition sums satisfy $e^{-\beta D}Z'\le Z\le e^{\beta D}Z'$, so their log partition sums differ by at most $\beta D$ using [F2]. The cut energy factorizes over the cubes and has zero-energy remainder, hence $Z_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}=Z_\ell^{k^d}q^{L^d-k^d\ell^d}$. Divide the comparison by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell$ fixed; the remainder fraction tends to zero, $k^d/L^d\to\ell^{-d}$, and the energy error has limsup at most $2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$.

It follows for every $\ell>2R$ that $\limsup_L p_L\le p_\ell+2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$ and $\liminf_L p_L\ge p_\ell-2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$. Thus $0\le\limsup_Lp_L-\liminf_Lp_L\le2^d\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$ for every such $\ell$. Letting $\ell\to\infty$ makes the difference zero; boundedness from step 1.1 then gives a finite limit.
For $\widetilde H_L$, the finite-state comparison of step 2.1 gives $|L^{-d}\log\widetilde Z_L-p_L|\le\beta C_b/L$, which tends to zero. Its limit is therefore the same.

The result covers finite-alphabet, bounded, translation-invariant finite-range interactions on cubic boxes; it asserts no continuum-particle or long-range limit.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Differentiating the finite sum gives $p_L'=-L^{-d}\mathbb E_{\beta,L}H_L$ and $p_L''=L^{-d}\operatorname{Var}_{\beta,L}(H_L)\ge0$. Thus $p_L$ is convex. Passing the two-point convexity inequality to the pointwise limit shows that $p$ is convex too.

For any small $h>0$ with $\beta\pm h\in J$, convexity and differentiability of $p_L$ give $[p_L(\beta)-p_L(\beta-h)]/h\le p_L'(\beta)\le[p_L(\beta+h)-p_L(\beta)]/h$. Take lower and upper limits in $L$, use [F1], then let $h\downarrow0$; differentiability of $p$ forces $p_L'(\beta)\to p'(\beta)$. The identity in step 1.1 yields the claimed mean limit.

Fix $t>0$ small enough that $\beta\pm t\in J$. For the upper tail, the pointwise inequality $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\ge L^d(e+\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{t(H_L-L^d(e+\varepsilon))}$ and finite summation give $\mathbb P(H_L/L^d\ge e+\varepsilon)\le\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta-t)-p_L(\beta)-t(e+\varepsilon)]\}$. Differentiability of $p$ and $e=-p'(\beta)$ imply $p(\beta-t)=p(\beta)+te+o(t)$; choose $t$ so the bracket's limit is at most $-3t\varepsilon/4$. Pointwise convergence at $\beta-t$ and $\beta$ then makes the bracket at most $-t\varepsilon/2$ for all sufficiently large $L$.

For the lower tail use $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\le L^d(e-\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{-t(H_L-L^d(e-\varepsilon))}$; its expectation is $\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta+t)-p_L(\beta)+t(e-\varepsilon)]\}$. Since $p(\beta+t)=p(\beta)-te+o(t)$, possibly reducing $t$ and increasing $L_0$ makes this at most $e^{-L^dt\varepsilon/2}$. Adding both tail bounds yields the result with $c=t\varepsilon/2$.

Steps 1.2–2.2 bound the two tails whose union is $\{|H_L/L^d-e|\ge\varepsilon\}$; the theorem is conditional on differentiability of $p$ and does not assert convergence of second derivatives or equivalence for arbitrary observables.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: Factor $e^{-\beta E_0}$ from the partition sum to obtain $Z=e^{-\beta E_0}(g+\sum_{i:E_i>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_i-E_0)})$. Every gap is positive, and there are finitely many, so the parenthesized sum tends to $g$. Thus each ground probability tends to $1/g$ and every excited probability tends to zero.

Ground-state entropy terms tend to $-g(1/g)\log(1/g)=\log g$. For an excited state with gap $\Delta_i>0$, step 1.1 gives $p_i=O(e^{-\beta\Delta_i})$ and $\log p_i=-\beta\Delta_i-\log D(\beta)$, where $D(\beta):=g+\sum_{j:E_j>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_j-E_0)}\to g>0$ by step 1.1, so $\log D(\beta)$ is bounded by continuity of $\log$; hence $|p_i\log p_i|=O((1+\beta)e^{-\beta\Delta_i})\to0$ by [F3]. The excited sum is finite, so its limit is zero and the total entropy tends to $\log g$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: For every $r$ with $a_r>0$, the numbers $q(m|r)$ are nonnegative and sum to one. The joint identity $p(m,r)=a_rq(m|r)$ on positive entries gives $\log p(m,r)=\log a_r+\log q(m|r)$; summing $-p\log p$ over each fixed $r$ yields $-a_r\log a_r+a_r[-\sum_mq(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Terms with $a_r=0$ have all $p(m,r)=0$ and contribute nothing. Summing over finite $r$ proves the chain rule.
For each positive conditional probability $q(m|r)\le1$, [F2] gives $-q(m|r)\log q(m|r)\ge0$. Multiplying by $a_r\ge0$ and summing proves $H(M|R)\ge0$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement a joint probability table has total mass one, hence at least one positive cell. Conditional terms are taken only for a_r>0; an empty register support cannot carry that law.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

boundaries.evidence: Zero joint entries and zero register marginals are omitted explicitly in the statement and handled in step 1.1.
A deterministic conditional law has entropy zero, as the positive-probability terms in step 2.1 show.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Define $\phi(t):=t-1-\log t$ for $t>0$. Its derivative is $1-1/t$, nonpositive on $(0,1]$ and nonnegative on $[1,\infty)$; the mean-value theorem [F4] gives $\phi(t)\ge\phi(1)=0$, with equality only at $t=1$. Thus $-\log t\ge1-t$, strictly unless $t=1$.
Expanding the finite logarithmic sum gives $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)$; applying [F2] rewrites it as $H(M)-H(M|R)$.

Put $q(m,r):=p_M(m)p_R(r)$. For $p(m,r)>0$, $q(m,r)>0$ by [F1], and step 1.1 with $t=q/p$ gives $p\log(p/q)\ge p-q$. Summing over the support of $p$ yields $I(M;R)\ge1-\sum_{p>0}q\ge0$. Equality forces $q=p$ on the support and no $q$-mass outside it, hence equality at every pair; conversely independence makes each positive logarithm zero.

boundaries.evidence: Statement a normalized finite joint law has nonempty positive support. On a positive joint cell both marginals are positive, and zero-probability cells are omitted rather than evaluated inside a logarithm.
